Commentary on Surah Al ʿImran

It is a Madinan surah. Al-Qurtubi said: by consensus (ijma'). What indicates this is that its opening, up to the eighty-third verse, was revealed concerning the delegation of Najran, and their arrival was in the ninth year after the Hijrah.

Al-Bayhaqi related in al-Dala'il, through several chains, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Surat Al ʿImran was revealed in Madinah." Already mentioned at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah is what is shared between it and this surah of the hadiths indicating their virtue, and likewise what has been transmitted concerning the Sab' al-Tiwal (the seven long surahs).

Al-Tabarani related with a weak chain (sanad), from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites the surah in which Al ʿImran is mentioned on Friday, Allah will send blessings upon him and His angels until the sun sets." Sa'id ibn Mansur and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman related from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, who said: "Whoever recites al-Baqarah, Al ʿImran and al-Nisa', he is written among the wise (al-hukama') with Allah."

Al-Daylami, Muhammad ibn Nasr and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman related from Ibn Masʿud: "Whoever recites Al ʿImran is rich (ghani)." Al-Darimi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd and al-Bayhaqi related from him, who said: "How excellent is the treasure of the poor man (kanz al-su'luk) is Al ʿImran, a man stands in prayer with it in the last part of the night."

Sa'id ibn Mansur related from Abu ʿAtif, who said: "The name of Al ʿImran in the Torah is Tayyibah." Ibn Abi Shaybah related from ʿAbd al-Malik ibn ʿUmayr, who said: A man recited al-Baqarah and Al ʿImran, and Ka'b said: "He has recited the two surahs, in which is the Name which, when called upon by it, He answers."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Al-Hasan, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, 'Asim ibn Abi al-Najud and Abu Ja'far al-Rawwasi recited ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim. Allah﴾ with the connecting alif (alif al-wasl) elided, treating the letters as if pausing on "Alif-Lam-Mim" (waqf, pause), just as they pause on number names such as "wahid, ithnan, thalatha, arba'a" even when they are joined to what follows. Al-Akhfash said: It is also permissible to read "Alif-Lam-Mim Allah" with a kasra on the hamza, because two unvowelled letters meet.

Al-Zajjaj said: This is an error, and the Arabs do not say it, because it is heavy. Sibawayh mentioned in his Kitab that the opening letters of the surahs, which are not in the form of a single word, are pronounced only as a citation (hikayah), and their final letters are unvowelled as a pause. This holds whether they are treated as names or recited as a sequence in the pattern of enumeration. Even if two unvowelled letters meet, this is excused in the context of pausing. So the proper course for this opening is to pause on it and then begin with what follows, as al-Hasan and those with him did in the citation-style recitation mentioned earlier.

As for the opening of the mim with a fatha in the well-known recitation, its justification is what is reported from Sibawayh: the mim was given a fatha because two unvowelled letters met. Al-Kisa'i said: when the letters of spelling (huruf al-tahajji) are followed by an alif of connection, the alif is dropped and the mim is vowelled with the vowel of the alif. Al-Farra' said likewise.

If these opening letters are taken as a sequence in the pattern of enumeration, they have no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis). If they are taken as names of the surah, their place is either nominative, as predicates of suppressed subjects before them, or accusative, by supposing verbs that the context requires, such as "remember" (udhkur) or "recite" (iqra'), or similar. What has been said at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah suffices and needs no repetition.

His words ﴿Allah, there is no god but He﴾ form a subject and predicate, and the sentence is a fresh statement; that is, He is the one deserving of worship.

﴿The Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾ are two further predicates of the noble name, or two predicates of a suppressed subject; that is, He is the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting. It has been said that they are two attributes of the first subject, or two appositives of it or of the predicate. The meanings of "the Ever-Living" and "the Self-Subsisting" were explained earlier. Some of the Companions read "al-Qayyam" instead: 'Umar, Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn Mas'ud.

His words ﴿He has sent down to you the Book﴾, that is, the Qur'an. He placed the adverbial phrase before the direct object to give attention to the one to whom it was sent down, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family. This sentence is either a fresh statement or another predicate of the first subject.

His words ﴿with truth﴾ mean with sincerity. It has also been said: with a decisive proof. It is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state (hal).

His words ﴿confirming﴾ are another circumstantial state of the Book, emphatic (mu'akkadah), because it could only be confirming, so the state does not change at all. This is the view of the majority. Some allowed that it be a changing state, in the sense that it confirms itself and others. His words ﴿what is before it﴾ mean the earlier revealed Books, and this depends on "confirming," with the lam serving for emphasis.

His words ﴿and He sent down the Torah and the Gospel﴾: this sentence has the force of an explanation of "what is before it." He said "sent down" here and "sent down" earlier, because the Qur'an was sent down in portions, while the two Books were sent down all at once. He did not mention the person to whom the two Books were sent down, whereas earlier he mentioned that the Book was sent down upon the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family, because the purpose here is only to mention the two Books, not those upon whom they were sent down.

His words ﴿from before﴾ mean that He sent down the Torah and the Gospel before the sending down of the Book. His words ﴿as guidance for mankind﴾ are either a circumstantial state of the two Books or the reason for their sending down.

By "mankind" is meant the People of the Two Books, or something more general, because this Ummah is bound by those laws that have not been abrogated. Ibn Fawrak said: guidance for mankind who are pious, as He said in al-Baqarah, "guidance for the pious."

His words ﴿and He sent down the Criterion﴾ mean the one that distinguishes between truth and falsehood, which is the Qur'an. He repeated its mention to honour it, along with what this second mention includes in describing it as separating truth from falsehood. He mentioned "sending down" (tanzil) first and "sending down" (inzal) second, because it combines both descriptions: it was sent down to the lowest heaven all at once, and then it came down from there to the Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family, in portions, according to events, as has been mentioned.

It has been said that by "the Criterion" He meant all the Books sent down by Allah to His messengers. It has also been said that He meant the Psalms (Zabur), because of their contents of fine admonitions.

His words ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah﴾ mean in whatever truly qualifies as a sign, from the revealed Books and other things, or in what is in the mentioned revealed Books, placing "the signs of Allah" in the position of a pronoun referring back to them. Herein is an explanation of the matter for which they deserved disbelief: because of this disbelief, ﴿there is a severe punishment for them﴾, that is, a great one. ﴿And Allah is All-Mighty, none can overpower Him, Owner of Retribution﴾, a great retribution. Nigmah means punishment. One says "intaqama minhu" when he punishes him for a sin that he had committed earlier.

His words ﴿Indeed, nothing is hidden from Allah, on the earth or in the heaven﴾: this sentence is a fresh statement, to show the breadth of His knowledge and His encompassing of all that is known. He expressed His knowledge of things by "on the earth and in the heaven," although they are broader than that, because His servants are incapable of knowing what lies beyond those two places, the places of His creatures and all their other known things. Among what is not hidden from Him is the faith of whoever believes among His creation and the disbelief of whoever disbelieves.

His words ﴿He is the One who forms you in the wombs as He wills﴾: the root of the word "sura" (form) is from "sara-hu ila kadha," meaning he inclined it toward something. So the form is inclined, to show the comprehensiveness of His knowledge, and that among His knowledge is what does not enter into existence, namely the shaping of His servants in their mothers' wombs from their fathers' drops, as He wills, whether beautiful or ugly, black or white, tall or short. "As He wills" is the object of "wills," and the clause is a circumstantial clause.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn al-Zubayr who said: The delegation of Najran, sixty riders, came to the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family, among them fourteen men of their nobles. Among those who spoke with the Messenger of Allah were Abu Harithah ibn 'Alqamah, al-'Aqib, 'Abd al-Masih and al-Sayyid, who was al-Ayham. Then they related the story of the discussion that took place between them and the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family, and that Allah sent down in that regard the beginning of Surat Al 'Imran, up to some eighty verses of it. (p-201)

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Rabi', who mentioned the delegation of Najran and their dispute with the Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family, concerning 'Isa, peace be upon him, and that Allah sent down: "Alif-Lam-Mim. Allah, there is no god but He, the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿confirming what is before it﴾, that he said: "What is before it" of a Book or a Messenger. Ibn Abi Hatim reported a similar statement from al-Hasan.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported a similar statement from Qatadah, and he said regarding His words ﴿and He sent down the Criterion﴾: it is the Qur'an, which separates truth from falsehood. In it He made lawful what is lawful and made unlawful what is unlawful, legislated its laws, set its limits, prescribed its obligations, explained its explanations, commanded obedience to it, and forbade disobedience to it. Ibn Jarir reported from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr regarding His words ﴿and He sent down the Criterion﴾, that it means the decisive distinction between truth and falsehood in what the factions differed about concerning the matter of 'Isa and others. Regarding His words ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah, for them is a severe punishment, and Allah is All-Mighty, Owner of Retribution﴾, that means: Allah takes retribution against whoever disbelieves in His signs after knowing them and recognising what has come from Him concerning them.

Regarding His words ﴿Indeed, nothing is hidden from Allah on the earth or in the heaven﴾, that means: He knows what they intend, what they plot, and what they imitate by their saying about 'Isa when they made him a lord and a god, while they had other knowledge of Him, out of heedlessness of Allah and disbelief in Him. ﴿He is the One who forms you in the wombs as He wills﴾: 'Isa was among those who were formed in the wombs, and they did not deny this or reject it, just as other children of Adam were formed. So how could he be a god when he was in that state? Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Mas'ud regarding His words ﴿He forms you in the wombs as He wills﴾, that he said: males and females.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and some of the Companions regarding His words ﴿He forms you in the wombs as He wills﴾, that he said: When the drop enters the womb, it moves in the body for forty days; then it becomes a clot ('alaqah) for forty days; then it becomes a lump of flesh (mudghah) for forty days. When it reaches the point of being created, Allah sends an angel to form it. The angel brings dust between his two fingers and mixes some of it into the lump, kneads it with it, and then shapes it as he is commanded, and says: Male or female? Wretched or happy? What is its provision? What is its lifespan? What are its deeds? What are its calamities? Allah decrees, and the angel writes. When that body dies, it is buried where that dust was taken from.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Qatadah regarding His words ﴿He forms you in the wombs as He wills﴾, that he said: male or female, red or black, complete in form or incomplete in form.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Al-Zajjaj said: This is an error, and the Arabs do not say it, because it is heavy. Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verses 7–9 (part 1 of 3):

Al-kitab (the Book) is the Qur'an, so the definite article (al-lam) is for prior reference (al-'ahd). He placed the adverbial phrase ʿalayka (upon you) first because of the restriction (ikhtisas) it conveys.

As for His saying ﴿Among it are verses that are decisive﴾, the construction that conforms to the rules of Arabic grammar (qawa'id al-'arabiyya) is for the adverbial phrase to be a fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam). Semantically, however, it is preferable for it to be the subject (mubtada'), with the implied sense "From the Book are verses that are clear," in the manner of what preceded in His saying ﴿And among the people is one who says﴾. It is preferable because the intended meaning is the division of the Book into the two categories mentioned, not merely the statement that they are from the Book. The clause is either in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) or is a resumptive new sentence (mustaʾnafa) with no grammatical position.

The scholars differed in their interpretation of the muhkamat (decisive verses) and the mutashabihat (ambiguous verses), with several opinions:

1. It was said that the muhkam is that whose interpretation is known and whose meaning and explanation are understood, while the mutashabih is that for which no one has any path to knowledge. Among those who held this view were Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, al-Shaʿbi and Sufyan al-Thawri. They said: this is like the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'a) at the beginnings of surahs.

2. It was said: the muhkam is that which admits only one meaning, while the mutashabih is that which admits several meanings. When the latter is referred back to one meaning and the rest are invalidated, the mutashabih becomes muhkam.

3. It was said: the muhkam is its abrogating verse (nasikh), its lawful and unlawful matters (halal and haram), its obligations (fara'id), and what we believe in and act upon. The mutashabih is its abrogated verse (mansukh), its parables (amthal), its oaths (aqsam), and what we believe in but do not act upon.

This was reported from Ibn ʿAbbas. It was also said: the muhkam is the nasikh, and the mutashabih is the mansukh; this was reported from Ibn Masʿud, Qatada and al-Rabiʿ. It was also said: the mutashabih is that which contains alteration (tasrif), prohibition (tahrim) and interpretation (ta'wil); this was said by Mujahid and Ibn Ishaq. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: this is the best of the opinions.

It was also said: the muhkam is that which is self-standing and does not need to be referred to anything else, while the mutashabih is that which needs to be referred to something else.

Al-Nahhas said: this is the best of what has been said about the muhkamat and mutashabihat. Al-Qurtubi said: what al-Nahhas said clarifies what Ibn ʿAtiyya preferred, and it is what conforms to the usage of the language. The muhkam is a passive participle (ism maf'ul) from ahkama, and ihkam means perfection (itqan). There is no doubt that what has a clear meaning, with no ambiguity or hesitation, is so only because its individual words are clear and their composition is perfect. When either of these two matters is lacking, ambiguity and difficulty arise.

Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: the mutashabih has several aspects. One is when the scholars differ over which of two verses abrogated the other, as in the case of a pregnant woman whose husband has died. Some of the Companions said that the verse on delivering the pregnancy (ayat wad' al-haml) abrogated the verse of four months and ten days, and others said the opposite. Another is their disagreement over bequests to an heir, and another is the conflict between analogies (ta'arud al-aqyisa). This is the sense of his statement.

The most appropriate formulation is to say: the muhkam is that whose meaning is clear and whose indication is evident, either by virtue of itself or by virtue of something else; and the mutashabih is that whose meaning is not clear, or whose indication is not apparent, neither by virtue of itself nor by virtue of something else. Once you understand this, you will know that the difference we have mentioned is not as it should be, because the proponents of each view defined the muhkam by some of its attributes and defined the mutashabih by what is opposite to them.

The explanation of this is that the proponents of the first view made the muhkam that for which a path to knowledge exists, and the mutashabih that for which no path to knowledge exists. There is no doubt that the concept of the muhkam and mutashabih is broader in scope than what they mentioned, for mere obscurity, lack of clarity, possibility of several meanings, or hesitation, necessitates ambiguity. The proponents of the second view restricted the muhkam to that which admits no possibility of multiple meanings, and the mutashabih to that which admits them. There is no doubt that this is one of the attributes of the muhkam and mutashabih, not all of them. The same applies to the proponents of the third view, who restricted each of the two categories to those specific attributes to the exclusion of others. The proponents of the fourth view restricted each of them to some of the attributes mentioned by the proponents of the third view, whereas the matter is broader than all they have said. The proponents of the fifth view restricted the muhkam to the attribute of not being subject to alteration (tasrif) or distortion (tahrif), and made the mutashabih its opposite, neglecting what is more important than that, namely what cannot be acted upon without alteration and distortion, such as the disjointed letters at the beginnings of surahs. The proponents of the sixth view restricted the muhkam to that which stands by itself, and the mutashabih to that which does not; this is indeed one of their attributes. The proponent of the seventh view, Ibn Khuwayz Mandad, made the instances of agreement into the muhkam and the instances of disagreement and conflict into the mutashabih, neglecting what is the most specific attribute of each of them, namely whether, in itself, its meaning is understood or not.

As for His saying ﴿They are the mother of the Book﴾: that is, they are its foundation upon which one relies, and to which whatever contradicts them is referred back. This clause is a description (sifa) of what precedes it.

As for His saying ﴿and others that are ambiguous﴾: it is a description of an implied, understood noun; that is, "and other verses that are ambiguous." Ukhar (others) is the plural of ukhra, and it is not declined (lam yanşarif) because it was made to deviate from al-akhar (the other), since its original form was like that. Abu ʿUbayd said it is not declined because its singular does not take nunation (tanwin) either as a definite or indefinite noun, but al-Mubarrid rejected this. Al-Kisa'i said it is not declined because it is a descriptive adjective, and al-Mubarrid also rejected this. Sibawayh said: it is not permissible for ukhar to be a word deviated from al-alif wa-l-lam (the definite article), because if it were deviated from that it would be definite. Do you not see that sahar (dawn) is definite in all the sayings, since it is deviated?

As for His saying ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation﴾: zaygh means inclination. From it come the expressions "the sun declined" and "the eyes swerved." One says zagha yazighu zaygh when he abandons the right course. From it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [al-Saff: 5]. This verse encompasses every group among the groups that stray from the truth. The occasion of revelation was the Christians of Najran, as mentioned earlier, and it will come again.

As for His saying ﴿so they follow that which is ambiguous of it﴾: that is, they cling to the ambiguous parts of the Book and cast doubt upon the believers by means of it, and they make it an evidence for the innovation (bid'a) they are in, which deviates from the truth, as you find in every innovating group. They toy with the Book of Allah with great trickery, and they present from it, to make their ignorance appear sound, what has nothing to do with proof.

As for His saying ﴿seeking discord﴾: that is, seeking its interpretation according to the way they want it, and in accordance with their corrupt doctrines. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of their seeking its interpretation is that they sought the interpretation of their resurrection and revival; so Allah, mighty and majestic, informed them that the interpretation and timing of that is known only to Allah. He said: the evidence for this is His saying ﴿Do they await anything but its interpretation? On the day its interpretation comes﴾ [al-A'raf: 53]; that is, on the day they see what they were promised of resurrection, rising and punishment. ﴿Those who had forgotten it will say﴾ [al-A'raf: 53]; that is, those who abandoned it. ﴿The messengers of our Lord had come with the truth﴾ [al-A'raf: 53]; that is, we have now seen the interpretation of what the messengers informed us of.

As for His saying ﴿and none knows its interpretation except Allah﴾: ta'wil has the meaning of tafsir (explanation), as in the saying "the interpretation of this word is such-and-such," that is, its explanation. It also has the meaning of what a matter ends up being (ma ya'ulu ilayhi al-amr). Its derivation is from āla al-amr ila kadha, ya'ulu ilayhi, meaning "the matter came to be such"; and awwaltuhu ta'wilan means "I made it so." This clause is circumstantial (haliyya); that is, they follow the ambiguous parts seeking its interpretation, while the case is that none knows its interpretation except Allah.

The scholars have differed over His saying ﴿and those firmly grounded in knowledge﴾: is it a separate statement (kalam maqta') unconnected to what precedes, or is it conjoined (ma'tuf) to what precedes, so that the conjunction (waw) would be for all of them? The view held by most is that it is separate from what precedes, and that the statement is complete at His saying "except Allah." This is the view of Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿAʾisha, ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, Abu al-Shaʿthaʾ, Abu Nuhayk and others. It is the position of al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', al-Akhfash and Abu ʿUbayd, and al-Tabari transmitted it from Malik and chose it.

Al-Khattabi transmitted it from Ibn Masʿud and Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, and said: what was reported from Mujahid is that he conjoined the firmly grounded to what precedes, and claimed that they know it. He said: some philologists argued for him, saying: the meaning is "and those firmly grounded in knowledge know it, saying: we believe in it," and he claimed that the position of ﴿saying﴾ is accusative as a circumstantial clause. But the majority of philologists deny this and consider it unlikely, because the Arabs do not omit both the verb and the object together, and do not mention a circumstantial clause except when the verb is apparent. If no verb appears, there is no circumstantial clause. Had that been permissible, it would be permissible to say "Abd Allah riding," meaning "Abd Allah came riding." It is permissible only when the verb is mentioned, as in His saying: "Abd Allah speaks, reconciling between people," so that "reconciling" is a circumstantial clause, as in the verse of the poet: "I sent into it a man, short and stocky, who shortens and walks, and lengthens, blessing." So the view of the majority of scholars, with the support of the grammarians' positions, is preferable to the view of Mujahid alone.

Furthermore, it is not permissible for Allah, glorified is He, to negate something from creation and then attribute it to Himself, so that He would have a partner in that. Do you not see His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿Say: none in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah﴾ [al-Naml: 65], and His saying: ﴿None will reveal it at its time except Him﴾ [al-A'raf: 187], and His saying: ﴿Everything will perish except His Face﴾ [al-Qasas: 88]. Likewise His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and none knows its interpretation except Allah.﴾ All of this is what Allah, glorified is He, has kept exclusively to Himself, with no one sharing it with Him. Had the waw in His saying "and those firmly grounded" been for conjunction, His saying ﴿Each is from our Lord﴾ would have had no purpose. End of quotation.

Al-Qurtubi said: what al-Khattabi transmitted, that no one other than him held the view of Mujahid, is correct.

It has been reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that the firmly grounded are conjoined to the name of Allah, mighty and majestic, and that they are included in the knowledge of the ambiguous, and that they, with their knowledge of it, say: "We believe in it."

Al-Rabiʿ, Muhammad ibn Jaʿfar ibn al-Zubayr, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad and others said: according to this interpretation, ﴿saying﴾ is accusative as a circumstantial clause from ﴿those firmly grounded﴾, as the poet said: "The wind weeps with its grief, and the lightning gleams in the cloud."

[p. 203]

This verse admits both meanings. It is possible that "and the lightning" is the subject (mubtada'), with the predicate "gleams," according to the first interpretation, in which case it is separate from what precedes. It is also possible that it is conjoined to "the wind," and "gleams" is in the position of a circumstantial clause according to the second interpretation, meaning "gleaming." End of quotation.

You are not unaware that what al-Khattabi said about the reason why "saying: we believe in it" cannot be a circumstantial clause, namely that the Arabs do not mention a circumstantial clause except when the verb is apparent, and so on to the end of his statement, holds only on the assumption that there is no verb here. That is not the case, for the verb is mentioned, namely His saying "and none knows its interpretation," but the circumstantial clause comes from the conjoined element, namely "and those firmly grounded," rather than from the element it is conjoined to, namely "except Allah." This is permissible in the Arabic language.

Similar constructions have also occurred in the Noble Book.

And among its examples is His saying, ﴿For the poor emigrants who were expelled from their homes﴾ [al-Hashr: 8], up to His saying, ﴿And those who came after them say: "Our Lord, forgive us"﴾ [al-Hashr: 10], and the verse. Also like His saying, ﴿And your Lord comes, and the angels, rank upon rank﴾ [al-Fajr: 22], meaning: "and the angels came, rank upon rank." But there is another obstacle to making it a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), namely that restricting their knowledge of its interpretation to the state in which they are saying "We believe in it" is not sound. The firmly grounded in knowledge (al-rāsikhūn fī al-ʿilm), according to those who hold the conjunction (ʿaṭf) on the noble Name, know it in every state, not only in this particular state. For this reason, it was required to make His saying, ﴿and those firmly grounded in knowledge﴾, a subject (mubtadaʾ) whose predicate (khabar) is ﴿say﴾. Among the things the proponents of the conjunction used as evidence is that God, glory be to Him, praised them for being firmly grounded in knowledge, so how could He praise them if they do not know it? This is answered by saying that their leaving off the pursuit of the knowledge of what God has not permitted, and their not making any path for His creation to know it, is itself part of their being firmly grounded, because they knew that this is among the things God has kept exclusively for His own knowledge, and that those who follow it are the ones in whose hearts is deviation. And this is sufficient as a measure of firmness.

The origin of rusūkh (firmness) in the language of the Arabs is steadfastness in a thing, and everything steadfast is rāsikh. Its original use concerning physical bodies is for horses or trees to take root in the ground. From this is the saying of the poet:

*Indeed, a love for Layla has taken firm root in my breast,*
*Its signs refused to change.*

These, then, are steadfast in carrying out what came to them from God, namely leaving off following the ambiguous (mutashābih) and returning its knowledge to God, glory be to Him.

Among the scholars there are those who took a middle position between the two positions, and said: "Ta'wīl (interpretation) is used, and in the Qur'an it is meant in two senses. One of them is ta'wīl in the sense of the reality of a thing and what its matter ultimately comes to. From this is His saying, ﴿This is the interpretation of my dream﴾ [Yūsuf: 100], and His saying, ﴿Do they await anything but its ta'wīl? On the day its ta'wīl comes﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 53], meaning: the reality of what they were told about the matter of the Return. If ta'wīl is meant in this sense, then the pause (waqf) is on the Name (Allāh), because the realities of matters and their essence none knows except God, mighty and majestic, and His saying, ﴿and those firmly grounded in knowledge﴾ is a subject, and ﴿say: "We believe in it"﴾ is its predicate.

But if the other meaning of ta'wīl is intended, which is tafsīr (exegesis), clarification, and expressing the meaning of a thing, as in His saying, ﴿Inform us of its ta'wīl﴾ [Yūsuf: 36], meaning: its tafsīr, then the pause is on ﴿and those firmly grounded in knowledge﴾, because they know and understand what they have been addressed with in this sense, even if they do not comprehend the realities of things as they are in their essence. In this case, ﴿say: "We believe in it"﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from them." Ibn Fawrak preferred that those firmly grounded in knowledge know its ta'wīl, and he elaborated on this at length. Likewise a group of the verifying exegetes preferred this view.

Al-Qurṭubī said: "Our shaykh Abū al-ʿAbbās Aḥmad ibn ʿUmar said: 'This is the correct view, for calling them firmly grounded implies that they know more than the decisive verses (al-muḥkam), whose knowledge all who understand the speech of the Arabs share. What would be their firmness if they only knew what everyone knows? But the ambiguous verses vary. Among them is what cannot be known at all, such as the matter of the Spirit (al-rūḥ) and the Hour, which God has kept for His own knowledge. No one attempts to know this. So whoever among the skilled scholars says that the firmly grounded do not know the knowledge of the ambiguous verses, he means only this type. As for what can be carried to several meanings in the language, it is interpreted, its correct ta'wīl is known, and what in it is of incorrect interpretation is removed.'" End of quotation.

Know that the great cause of this disturbance in the statements of the scholars is their disagreement over determining the meaning of the decisive and the ambiguous. We have already set out for you what is correct in determining these two, and we add here further clarification and explanation. We say: among the things that fit the definition of the ambiguous which we previously mentioned are the opening letters of the surahs (fawātiḥ al-suwar), for their meaning is neither clear nor apparent in its indication, neither in relation to themselves, since no one knows, by the language of the Arabs or by the customary usage of the Sharīʿa, what ﴿Alif Lām Mīm﴾, ﴿Alif Lām Mīm Rā﴾, ﴿Ḥā Mīm﴾, ﴿Ṭā Sīn﴾, ﴿Ṭā Sīn Mīm﴾ and the like mean, because one does not find their explanation in any speech of the Arabs or in the speech of the Sharīʿa. So they are not clear in meaning, either by themselves or by reference to another matter that explains and clarifies them. Similar to this are words borrowed from the languages of non-Arabs (ʿajam), and strange words that are not found in the language of the Arabs nor in the customary usage of the Sharīʿa to clarify them. Likewise is what God has kept for His own knowledge, such as the Spirit, and what is in His saying, ﴿Indeed, God has with Him the knowledge of the Hour﴾ [Luqmān: 34], up to the end of the verse, and similar matters. Likewise is what has an indication that is not apparent, neither by itself nor by reference to something else, such as a word occurring that is ambiguous between two meanings, with neither meaning preferred over the other by reference to the thing itself. This is like homonymous words (al-alfāẓ al-mushtarakah) when there comes nothing outside the wording that specifies which of the shared meanings is intended. Similarly, two evidences that conflict in a complete conflict, such that it is not possible to prefer one over the other, neither by reference to itself nor by reference to some other matter that prefers it.

As for what is clear in meaning by itself, either because it is known in the language of the Arabs or in the customary usage of the Sharīʿa, or by reference to something else, such as the general matters (al-umūr al-mujmalah) whose explanation has come in another place in the Noble Book or in the purified Sunnah, or matters whose indications conflicted and then something came that shows which of them is stronger than the weaker, in another place of the Book or the Sunnah, or in the other known preferential considerations recognized among the scholars of legal theory (uṣūl al-fiqh) and accepted among the fair-minded, then there is no doubt whatsoever that these belong to the decisive, not the ambiguous. Whoever claims that they are of the ambiguous has been confused about the correct view. So hold firmly to this, for by it you will be saved from narrow passes and slippery places into which people have fallen in this matter, to the point that every sect calls whatever supports its position "decisive," and whatever supports the position of those who oppose it "ambiguous." This is especially true of the people of dialectical theology (ʿilm al-kalām). Whoever denies this, let him look at their books.

Know that the Noble Book contains what indicates that all of it is decisive, but not in the sense mentioned in this verse, rather in another sense. Among this is His saying, ﴿A Book whose verses have been made firm﴾ [Hūd: 1], and His saying, ﴿These are the verses of the Wise Book﴾ [Yūnus: 1]. What is meant by "decisive" in this sense is that its wording is sound, its meanings upright, and it surpasses every speech in eloquence and fluency. It also contains what indicates that all of it is ambiguous, but not in the sense mentioned in this verse that we are explaining, rather in another sense. Among this is His saying, ﴿a Book, ambiguous, [its parts] resembling one another﴾ [al-Zumar: 23]. What is meant by "ambiguous" in this sense is that some of it resembles the rest in soundness, eloquence, goodness, and rhetorical excellence.

The scholars have mentioned several benefits to the presence of the ambiguous in the Qur'an. Among them is that reaching the truth, while it is present, involves greater difficulty and hardship, and this entails greater reward for those who extract the truth, namely the mujtahids (qualified jurists) who are imams. Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, and others mentioned several explanations; this one is the best of them, and the rest do not merit mention here.

His saying, ﴿Each is from our Lord﴾: there is an implied pronoun referring to the two categories, the decisive and the ambiguous, meaning "all of it," or the omitted element is not a pronoun, meaning "each one of them." This is part of the statement quoted before it.

His saying, ﴿But none reflects except those of understanding﴾, meaning the pure intellects. They are those firmly grounded in knowledge, who stop at its ambiguous parts, who know its decisive parts, and who act upon what God has guided them to in this verse.

His saying, "﴿Our Lord, let not our hearts deviate﴾" and what follows is part of what the firmly grounded say. That is, they say, "We believe in it, all of it is from our Lord," and they say, "Our Lord, let not our hearts deviate." Ibn Kaysān said: "They asked not to deviate, lest their hearts deviate, like His saying, ﴿So when they deviated, God caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [al-Ṣaff: 5]. It is as if, when they heard His saying, ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow what is ambiguous of it﴾, they said, ﴿Our Lord, let not our hearts deviate by following the ambiguous after You have guided us to the truth, by what You have permitted us of acting upon the decisive verses.'" The time phrase, which is ﴿after﴾ (baʿda), is governed by ﴿let not … deviate﴾.

His saying, ﴿And grant us from Yourself mercy﴾, meaning mercy coming from You. The particle min indicates the starting point. ﴿Ladun﴾ is pronounced with a fatḥah on the lām, a ḍammah on the dāl, and a sukūn on the nūn, and there are other dialectal forms, but this is the most eloquent. It is a locative adverb, and it may be used with reference to time. The indefinite ﴿mercy﴾ indicates magnitude, meaning great and vast mercy. His saying, ﴿Indeed You are the Bestower﴾, is a reason for the request or for the granting of what is requested.

His saying, ﴿Our Lord, indeed You are the gatherer of mankind﴾, meaning the one who raises them and brings them back to life after their dispersal, ﴿for a Day﴾, which is the Day of Resurrection, meaning for the reckoning of a Day, or for the recompense of a Day, on the assumption that an attached noun has been omitted and the noun it was attached to has taken its place.

His saying, ﴿there is no doubt about it﴾, meaning about its occurrence and the occurrence of the reckoning and recompense within it. The meaning of doubt has already been explained. The clause ﴿indeed God does not fail in His promise﴾ is a justification for the content of what precedes it, meaning: fulfilling a promise is the attribute of God, glory be to Him, and failing to keep it contradicts divinity, just as divinity itself negates and is incompatible with it.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: "The decisive (al-muḥkamāt) are its abrogating (nāsikh) verses, its lawful and unlawful matters, its limits, its obligations, and what we believe in and act upon. The ambiguous (al-mutashābihāt) are its abrogated (mansūkh) verses, its preceding and succeeding verses, its parables and its oaths, and what we believe in but do not act upon."

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim, who declared it sound, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said, concerning His saying, ﴿Among it are decisive verses﴾: "The three verses at the end of Sūrat al-Anʿām, ﴿Say: "Come, I will recite"﴾ [al-Anʿām: 151], and the two verses after them are decisive."

In another narration from him, related by ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim, concerning His saying, ﴿decisive verses﴾, he said: "From here, ﴿Say: "Come"﴾, up to three verses, and from here, ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 23], up to three verses after it."

I say: May God have mercy on Ibn ʿAbbās, how little benefit there is in this statement transmitted from him! For specifying three verses, or ten, or a hundred out of all the verses of the Qur'an and describing them as decisive has no benefit beneath it at all. The decisive verses are, according to all the opinions, most of the Qur'an, even according to his statement quoted shortly before, that the decisive verses are its abrogating verses, its lawful and unlawful matters, and so on. So what is the point of specifying those verses from the end of Sūrat al-Anʿām?

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd related from him that he said: "The decisive: the lawful and the unlawful." The early generations (al-salaf) have many other statements, all of which return to what we set out at the beginning of this discussion.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: "﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation﴾" means the people of doubt, who interpret the decisive by the ambiguous and the ambiguous by the decisive, and who confuse matters, so God confuses them, and ﴿none knows its ta'wīl except God﴾." He said: "Its ta'wīl is on the Day of Resurrection; none knows it except God."

Ibn Jarīr related from Ibn Masʿūd that he explained ﴿zaigh﴾ (deviation) as doubt. In the two Ṣaḥīḥs and others, from ʿĀʾishah, she said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited ﴿He it is who sent down to you the Book﴾ up to His saying, ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation﴾, up to His saying, ﴿men of understanding﴾." She said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'When you see those who dispute concerning it, those are the ones whom God has named, so beware of them.'"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verses 7–9 (part 3 of 3):

In another wording: "When you see those who follow what is ambiguous of it, those are the ones whom Allah has named, so beware of them." This is the wording of al-Bukhari. The wording of Ibn Jarir and others is: "When you see those who follow what is ambiguous of it, and those who dispute concerning it, they are the ones Allah means, so do not sit with them."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ahmad, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from Abu Umamah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning his saying: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow that of it which is ambiguous﴾ (p. 205), that he said: "They are the Kharijites."

Ibn Jarir and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from Ibn Masʿud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The first Book used to descend from one gate, in one harf (mode). The Qur'an descended in seven ahruf (modes): commanding, forbidding, lawful, unlawful, clear (muhkam), ambiguous (mutashabih), and parables. So make lawful what is lawful in it, make unlawful what is unlawful in it, do what you are commanded, refrain from what you are forbidden, take heed from its parables, act upon its clear verses, believe in its ambiguous verses, and say: 'We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord.'" Ibn Abi Hatim also related it from Ibn Masʿud as a mawquf (a statement of a Companion only).

al-Tabarani related from ʿUmar ibn Abi Salamah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, and he mentioned something similar. al-Bukhari in al-Tarikh related from ʿAli, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) with a weak chain, something similar. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Dawud in al-Masahif related from Ibn Masʿud something similar.

Ibn Jarir and Abu Yaʿla related from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Qur'an descended in seven ahruf, and disputing about the Qur'an is kufr (disbelief). What you know, act upon; what you do not know of it, refer it to its knowledgeable one." Its chain is sahih.

al-Bayhaqi in al-Shuʿab related from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), and in it: "Follow the clear (muhkam) and believe in the ambiguous (mutashabih)."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from Tawus who said: Ibn ʿAbbas used to recite it (and none knows its interpretation except Allah, and those firm in knowledge say: "We believe in it").

Ibn Abi Dawud in al-Masahif related from al-Aʿmash who said, regarding the reading of ʿAbd Allah: "Indeed, the true interpretation of it is only with Allah, and those firm in knowledge say, 'We believe in it.'"

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-Shaʿthaʾ and Abu Nahik who said: "You join this verse while it is cut off: 'None knows its interpretation except Allah,' and 'those firm in knowledge say: We believe in it, all of it is from our Lord.' Their knowledge ends at their saying what they said."

Ibn Jarir related from ʿUrwah who said: "Those firm in knowledge do not know its interpretation, but they say: 'We believe in it, all of it is from our Lord.'"

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz something similar.

Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf related from Ubayy who said: "The Book of Allah is what is clear, so act upon it; and what is ambiguous to you, believe in it and entrust it to its knowledgeable one."

He also related from Ibn Masʿud who said: "Indeed the Qur'an has a minaret like the minaret of the road. What you recognize, hold fast to it; and what is ambiguous to you, leave it."

He also related from Muʿadh something similar.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "The tafsir (exegesis) of the Qur'an is in four aspects: a tafsir that the scholars know; a tafsir that people are excused for not knowing, concerning lawful or unlawful; a tafsir that the Arabs know by their language; and a tafsir whose interpretation none knows except Allah. Whoever claims to know it is a liar."

Ibn Jarir related from him who said: "The Qur'an was revealed in seven ahruf: lawful and unlawful, about which no one is excused for ignorance; tafsir which the Arabs explain; tafsir which the scholars explain; and the ambiguous, which none knows except Allah. Whoever claims to know it apart from Allah is a liar."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from him who said: "I am among those who know its interpretation."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related through ʿAtiyyah al-ʿAwfi from him, concerning his saying: "They say: We believe in it." "We believe in the clear and we act upon it; and we believe in the ambiguous and we do not act upon it; and all of it is from Allah."

al-Darimi in his Musnad and Nasr al-Maqdisi in al-Hujjah related from Sulayman ibn Yasar that a man called Dubayʿ came to Madinah and began asking about the ambiguous verses of the Qur'an. ʿUmar sent for him, having prepared palm-fronds for him, and said: "Who are you?" He said: "I am ʿAbd Allah Dubayʿ." ʿUmar said: "And I am ʿAbd Allah ʿUmar." Then ʿUmar took a stalk from those palm-fronds and struck him until his head bled. He said: "O Commander of the Believers, enough! What I used to find in my head has gone."

al-Darimi also related it through another route, in which: he struck him three times, leaving him each time until he healed, then he struck him again. Ibn ʿAsakir in his History related the origin of the story from Anas.

al-Darimi and Ibn ʿAsakir related that ʿUmar wrote to the people of Basrah that they should not sit with Dubayʿ. A group has related this story.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani related from Anas, Abu Umamah, Wathilah ibn al-Asqaʿ and Abu al-Darda', that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about "those firm in knowledge," and he said: "Whoever is righteous in his oath, truthful in his tongue, upright in his heart, and chaste in his belly and private parts, those are among those firm in knowledge."

Ibn ʿAsakir related through ʿAbd Allah ibn Yazid al-Azdi from Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

Abu Dawud and al-Hakim related from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Disputing about the Qur'an is kufr."

Nasr al-Maqdisi in al-Hujjah related from Ibn ʿUmar who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out, and behind his chamber was a people disputing about the Qur'an. He came out with his cheeks reddened, as though blood were dripping from them, and said: 'O people, do not dispute about the Qur'an, for those before you went astray only through their disputing. The Qur'an was not revealed so that some of it would deny other parts; rather it was revealed so that some of it confirms other parts. So what is clear of it, act upon it, and what is ambiguous of it, believe in it.'"

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Umm Salamah that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say: "O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion," then he recited: ﴿Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us﴾, the verse.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh related from her, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar but longer. Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad and Ibn Mardawayh related from ʿAisha, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar. Something similar has been transmitted through other routes.

Ibn al-Najjar in his History related, concerning the saying: ﴿Our Lord, You are the gatherer of mankind for a Day﴾, the verse, from Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad al-Khaldi who said: It was narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites this verse over something that he has lost, Allah will return it to him, and after reciting it he should say: 'O gatherer of mankind for a Day about which there is no doubt, gather between me and my wealth, for You are capable of all things.'"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verses 7–9 (part 1 of 3):

Al-kitab (the Book) is the Qur'an, so the definite article (al-lam) is for prior reference (al-'ahd). He placed the adverbial phrase ʿalayka (upon you) first because of the restriction (ikhtisas) it conveys.

As for His saying ﴿Among it are verses that are decisive﴾, the construction that conforms to the rules of Arabic grammar (qawa'id al-'arabiyya) is for the adverbial phrase to be a fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam). Semantically, however, it is preferable for it to be the subject (mubtada'), with the implied sense "From the Book are verses that are clear," in the manner of what preceded in His saying ﴿And among the people is one who says﴾. It is preferable because the intended meaning is the division of the Book into the two categories mentioned, not merely the statement that they are from the Book. The clause is either in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) or is a resumptive new sentence (mustaʾnafa) with no grammatical position.

The scholars differed in their interpretation of the muhkamat (decisive verses) and the mutashabihat (ambiguous verses), with several opinions:

1. It was said that the muhkam is that whose interpretation is known and whose meaning and explanation are understood, while the mutashabih is that for which no one has any path to knowledge. Among those who held this view were Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, al-Shaʿbi and Sufyan al-Thawri. They said: this is like the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'a) at the beginnings of surahs.

2. It was said: the muhkam is that which admits only one meaning, while the mutashabih is that which admits several meanings. When the latter is referred back to one meaning and the rest are invalidated, the mutashabih becomes muhkam.

3. It was said: the muhkam is its abrogating verse (nasikh), its lawful and unlawful matters (halal and haram), its obligations (fara'id), and what we believe in and act upon. The mutashabih is its abrogated verse (mansukh), its parables (amthal), its oaths (aqsam), and what we believe in but do not act upon.

This was reported from Ibn ʿAbbas. It was also said: the muhkam is the nasikh, and the mutashabih is the mansukh; this was reported from Ibn Masʿud, Qatada and al-Rabiʿ. It was also said: the mutashabih is that which contains alteration (tasrif), prohibition (tahrim) and interpretation (ta'wil); this was said by Mujahid and Ibn Ishaq. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: this is the best of the opinions.

It was also said: the muhkam is that which is self-standing and does not need to be referred to anything else, while the mutashabih is that which needs to be referred to something else.

Al-Nahhas said: this is the best of what has been said about the muhkamat and mutashabihat. Al-Qurtubi said: what al-Nahhas said clarifies what Ibn ʿAtiyya preferred, and it is what conforms to the usage of the language. The muhkam is a passive participle (ism maf'ul) from ahkama, and ihkam means perfection (itqan). There is no doubt that what has a clear meaning, with no ambiguity or hesitation, is so only because its individual words are clear and their composition is perfect. When either of these two matters is lacking, ambiguity and difficulty arise.

Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: the mutashabih has several aspects. One is when the scholars differ over which of two verses abrogated the other, as in the case of a pregnant woman whose husband has died. Some of the Companions said that the verse on delivering the pregnancy (ayat wad' al-haml) abrogated the verse of four months and ten days, and others said the opposite. Another is their disagreement over bequests to an heir, and another is the conflict between analogies (ta'arud al-aqyisa). This is the sense of his statement.

The most appropriate formulation is to say: the muhkam is that whose meaning is clear and whose indication is evident, either by virtue of itself or by virtue of something else; and the mutashabih is that whose meaning is not clear, or whose indication is not apparent, neither by virtue of itself nor by virtue of something else. Once you understand this, you will know that the difference we have mentioned is not as it should be, because the proponents of each view defined the muhkam by some of its attributes and defined the mutashabih by what is opposite to them.

The explanation of this is that the proponents of the first view made the muhkam that for which a path to knowledge exists, and the mutashabih that for which no path to knowledge exists. There is no doubt that the concept of the muhkam and mutashabih is broader in scope than what they mentioned, for mere obscurity, lack of clarity, possibility of several meanings, or hesitation, necessitates ambiguity. The proponents of the second view restricted the muhkam to that which admits no possibility of multiple meanings, and the mutashabih to that which admits them. There is no doubt that this is one of the attributes of the muhkam and mutashabih, not all of them. The same applies to the proponents of the third view, who restricted each of the two categories to those specific attributes to the exclusion of others. The proponents of the fourth view restricted each of them to some of the attributes mentioned by the proponents of the third view, whereas the matter is broader than all they have said. The proponents of the fifth view restricted the muhkam to the attribute of not being subject to alteration (tasrif) or distortion (tahrif), and made the mutashabih its opposite, neglecting what is more important than that, namely what cannot be acted upon without alteration and distortion, such as the disjointed letters at the beginnings of surahs. The proponents of the sixth view restricted the muhkam to that which stands by itself, and the mutashabih to that which does not; this is indeed one of their attributes. The proponent of the seventh view, Ibn Khuwayz Mandad, made the instances of agreement into the muhkam and the instances of disagreement and conflict into the mutashabih, neglecting what is the most specific attribute of each of them, namely whether, in itself, its meaning is understood or not.

As for His saying ﴿They are the mother of the Book﴾: that is, they are its foundation upon which one relies, and to which whatever contradicts them is referred back. This clause is a description (sifa) of what precedes it.

As for His saying ﴿and others that are ambiguous﴾: it is a description of an implied, understood noun; that is, "and other verses that are ambiguous." Ukhar (others) is the plural of ukhra, and it is not declined (lam yanşarif) because it was made to deviate from al-akhar (the other), since its original form was like that. Abu ʿUbayd said it is not declined because its singular does not take nunation (tanwin) either as a definite or indefinite noun, but al-Mubarrid rejected this. Al-Kisa'i said it is not declined because it is a descriptive adjective, and al-Mubarrid also rejected this. Sibawayh said: it is not permissible for ukhar to be a word deviated from al-alif wa-l-lam (the definite article), because if it were deviated from that it would be definite. Do you not see that sahar (dawn) is definite in all the sayings, since it is deviated?

As for His saying ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation﴾: zaygh means inclination. From it come the expressions "the sun declined" and "the eyes swerved." One says zagha yazighu zaygh when he abandons the right course. From it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [al-Saff: 5]. This verse encompasses every group among the groups that stray from the truth. The occasion of revelation was the Christians of Najran, as mentioned earlier, and it will come again.

As for His saying ﴿so they follow that which is ambiguous of it﴾: that is, they cling to the ambiguous parts of the Book and cast doubt upon the believers by means of it, and they make it an evidence for the innovation (bid'a) they are in, which deviates from the truth, as you find in every innovating group. They toy with the Book of Allah with great trickery, and they present from it, to make their ignorance appear sound, what has nothing to do with proof.

As for His saying ﴿seeking discord﴾: that is, seeking its interpretation according to the way they want it, and in accordance with their corrupt doctrines. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of their seeking its interpretation is that they sought the interpretation of their resurrection and revival; so Allah, mighty and majestic, informed them that the interpretation and timing of that is known only to Allah. He said: the evidence for this is His saying ﴿Do they await anything but its interpretation? On the day its interpretation comes﴾ [al-A'raf: 53]; that is, on the day they see what they were promised of resurrection, rising and punishment. ﴿Those who had forgotten it will say﴾ [al-A'raf: 53]; that is, those who abandoned it. ﴿The messengers of our Lord had come with the truth﴾ [al-A'raf: 53]; that is, we have now seen the interpretation of what the messengers informed us of.

As for His saying ﴿and none knows its interpretation except Allah﴾: ta'wil has the meaning of tafsir (explanation), as in the saying "the interpretation of this word is such-and-such," that is, its explanation. It also has the meaning of what a matter ends up being (ma ya'ulu ilayhi al-amr). Its derivation is from āla al-amr ila kadha, ya'ulu ilayhi, meaning "the matter came to be such"; and awwaltuhu ta'wilan means "I made it so." This clause is circumstantial (haliyya); that is, they follow the ambiguous parts seeking its interpretation, while the case is that none knows its interpretation except Allah.

The scholars have differed over His saying ﴿and those firmly grounded in knowledge﴾: is it a separate statement (kalam maqta') unconnected to what precedes, or is it conjoined (ma'tuf) to what precedes, so that the conjunction (waw) would be for all of them? The view held by most is that it is separate from what precedes, and that the statement is complete at His saying "except Allah." This is the view of Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿAʾisha, ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, Abu al-Shaʿthaʾ, Abu Nuhayk and others. It is the position of al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', al-Akhfash and Abu ʿUbayd, and al-Tabari transmitted it from Malik and chose it.

Al-Khattabi transmitted it from Ibn Masʿud and Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, and said: what was reported from Mujahid is that he conjoined the firmly grounded to what precedes, and claimed that they know it. He said: some philologists argued for him, saying: the meaning is "and those firmly grounded in knowledge know it, saying: we believe in it," and he claimed that the position of ﴿saying﴾ is accusative as a circumstantial clause. But the majority of philologists deny this and consider it unlikely, because the Arabs do not omit both the verb and the object together, and do not mention a circumstantial clause except when the verb is apparent. If no verb appears, there is no circumstantial clause. Had that been permissible, it would be permissible to say "Abd Allah riding," meaning "Abd Allah came riding." It is permissible only when the verb is mentioned, as in His saying: "Abd Allah speaks, reconciling between people," so that "reconciling" is a circumstantial clause, as in the verse of the poet: "I sent into it a man, short and stocky, who shortens and walks, and lengthens, blessing." So the view of the majority of scholars, with the support of the grammarians' positions, is preferable to the view of Mujahid alone.

Furthermore, it is not permissible for Allah, glorified is He, to negate something from creation and then attribute it to Himself, so that He would have a partner in that. Do you not see His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿Say: none in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah﴾ [al-Naml: 65], and His saying: ﴿None will reveal it at its time except Him﴾ [al-A'raf: 187], and His saying: ﴿Everything will perish except His Face﴾ [al-Qasas: 88]. Likewise His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and none knows its interpretation except Allah.﴾ All of this is what Allah, glorified is He, has kept exclusively to Himself, with no one sharing it with Him. Had the waw in His saying "and those firmly grounded" been for conjunction, His saying ﴿Each is from our Lord﴾ would have had no purpose. End of quotation.

Al-Qurtubi said: what al-Khattabi transmitted, that no one other than him held the view of Mujahid, is correct.

It has been reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that the firmly grounded are conjoined to the name of Allah, mighty and majestic, and that they are included in the knowledge of the ambiguous, and that they, with their knowledge of it, say: "We believe in it."

Al-Rabiʿ, Muhammad ibn Jaʿfar ibn al-Zubayr, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad and others said: according to this interpretation, ﴿saying﴾ is accusative as a circumstantial clause from ﴿those firmly grounded﴾, as the poet said: "The wind weeps with its grief, and the lightning gleams in the cloud."

[p. 203]

This verse admits both meanings. It is possible that "and the lightning" is the subject (mubtada'), with the predicate "gleams," according to the first interpretation, in which case it is separate from what precedes. It is also possible that it is conjoined to "the wind," and "gleams" is in the position of a circumstantial clause according to the second interpretation, meaning "gleaming." End of quotation.

You are not unaware that what al-Khattabi said about the reason why "saying: we believe in it" cannot be a circumstantial clause, namely that the Arabs do not mention a circumstantial clause except when the verb is apparent, and so on to the end of his statement, holds only on the assumption that there is no verb here. That is not the case, for the verb is mentioned, namely His saying "and none knows its interpretation," but the circumstantial clause comes from the conjoined element, namely "and those firmly grounded," rather than from the element it is conjoined to, namely "except Allah." This is permissible in the Arabic language.

Similar constructions have also occurred in the Noble Book.

And among its examples is His saying, ﴿For the poor emigrants who were expelled from their homes﴾ [al-Hashr: 8], up to His saying, ﴿And those who came after them say: "Our Lord, forgive us"﴾ [al-Hashr: 10], and the verse. Also like His saying, ﴿And your Lord comes, and the angels, rank upon rank﴾ [al-Fajr: 22], meaning: "and the angels came, rank upon rank." But there is another obstacle to making it a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), namely that restricting their knowledge of its interpretation to the state in which they are saying "We believe in it" is not sound. The firmly grounded in knowledge (al-rāsikhūn fī al-ʿilm), according to those who hold the conjunction (ʿaṭf) on the noble Name, know it in every state, not only in this particular state. For this reason, it was required to make His saying, ﴿and those firmly grounded in knowledge﴾, a subject (mubtadaʾ) whose predicate (khabar) is ﴿say﴾. Among the things the proponents of the conjunction used as evidence is that God, glory be to Him, praised them for being firmly grounded in knowledge, so how could He praise them if they do not know it? This is answered by saying that their leaving off the pursuit of the knowledge of what God has not permitted, and their not making any path for His creation to know it, is itself part of their being firmly grounded, because they knew that this is among the things God has kept exclusively for His own knowledge, and that those who follow it are the ones in whose hearts is deviation. And this is sufficient as a measure of firmness.

The origin of rusūkh (firmness) in the language of the Arabs is steadfastness in a thing, and everything steadfast is rāsikh. Its original use concerning physical bodies is for horses or trees to take root in the ground. From this is the saying of the poet:

*Indeed, a love for Layla has taken firm root in my breast,*
*Its signs refused to change.*

These, then, are steadfast in carrying out what came to them from God, namely leaving off following the ambiguous (mutashābih) and returning its knowledge to God, glory be to Him.

Among the scholars there are those who took a middle position between the two positions, and said: "Ta'wīl (interpretation) is used, and in the Qur'an it is meant in two senses. One of them is ta'wīl in the sense of the reality of a thing and what its matter ultimately comes to. From this is His saying, ﴿This is the interpretation of my dream﴾ [Yūsuf: 100], and His saying, ﴿Do they await anything but its ta'wīl? On the day its ta'wīl comes﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 53], meaning: the reality of what they were told about the matter of the Return. If ta'wīl is meant in this sense, then the pause (waqf) is on the Name (Allāh), because the realities of matters and their essence none knows except God, mighty and majestic, and His saying, ﴿and those firmly grounded in knowledge﴾ is a subject, and ﴿say: "We believe in it"﴾ is its predicate.

But if the other meaning of ta'wīl is intended, which is tafsīr (exegesis), clarification, and expressing the meaning of a thing, as in His saying, ﴿Inform us of its ta'wīl﴾ [Yūsuf: 36], meaning: its tafsīr, then the pause is on ﴿and those firmly grounded in knowledge﴾, because they know and understand what they have been addressed with in this sense, even if they do not comprehend the realities of things as they are in their essence. In this case, ﴿say: "We believe in it"﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from them." Ibn Fawrak preferred that those firmly grounded in knowledge know its ta'wīl, and he elaborated on this at length. Likewise a group of the verifying exegetes preferred this view.

Al-Qurṭubī said: "Our shaykh Abū al-ʿAbbās Aḥmad ibn ʿUmar said: 'This is the correct view, for calling them firmly grounded implies that they know more than the decisive verses (al-muḥkam), whose knowledge all who understand the speech of the Arabs share. What would be their firmness if they only knew what everyone knows? But the ambiguous verses vary. Among them is what cannot be known at all, such as the matter of the Spirit (al-rūḥ) and the Hour, which God has kept for His own knowledge. No one attempts to know this. So whoever among the skilled scholars says that the firmly grounded do not know the knowledge of the ambiguous verses, he means only this type. As for what can be carried to several meanings in the language, it is interpreted, its correct ta'wīl is known, and what in it is of incorrect interpretation is removed.'" End of quotation.

Know that the great cause of this disturbance in the statements of the scholars is their disagreement over determining the meaning of the decisive and the ambiguous. We have already set out for you what is correct in determining these two, and we add here further clarification and explanation. We say: among the things that fit the definition of the ambiguous which we previously mentioned are the opening letters of the surahs (fawātiḥ al-suwar), for their meaning is neither clear nor apparent in its indication, neither in relation to themselves, since no one knows, by the language of the Arabs or by the customary usage of the Sharīʿa, what ﴿Alif Lām Mīm﴾, ﴿Alif Lām Mīm Rā﴾, ﴿Ḥā Mīm﴾, ﴿Ṭā Sīn﴾, ﴿Ṭā Sīn Mīm﴾ and the like mean, because one does not find their explanation in any speech of the Arabs or in the speech of the Sharīʿa. So they are not clear in meaning, either by themselves or by reference to another matter that explains and clarifies them. Similar to this are words borrowed from the languages of non-Arabs (ʿajam), and strange words that are not found in the language of the Arabs nor in the customary usage of the Sharīʿa to clarify them. Likewise is what God has kept for His own knowledge, such as the Spirit, and what is in His saying, ﴿Indeed, God has with Him the knowledge of the Hour﴾ [Luqmān: 34], up to the end of the verse, and similar matters. Likewise is what has an indication that is not apparent, neither by itself nor by reference to something else, such as a word occurring that is ambiguous between two meanings, with neither meaning preferred over the other by reference to the thing itself. This is like homonymous words (al-alfāẓ al-mushtarakah) when there comes nothing outside the wording that specifies which of the shared meanings is intended. Similarly, two evidences that conflict in a complete conflict, such that it is not possible to prefer one over the other, neither by reference to itself nor by reference to some other matter that prefers it.

As for what is clear in meaning by itself, either because it is known in the language of the Arabs or in the customary usage of the Sharīʿa, or by reference to something else, such as the general matters (al-umūr al-mujmalah) whose explanation has come in another place in the Noble Book or in the purified Sunnah, or matters whose indications conflicted and then something came that shows which of them is stronger than the weaker, in another place of the Book or the Sunnah, or in the other known preferential considerations recognized among the scholars of legal theory (uṣūl al-fiqh) and accepted among the fair-minded, then there is no doubt whatsoever that these belong to the decisive, not the ambiguous. Whoever claims that they are of the ambiguous has been confused about the correct view. So hold firmly to this, for by it you will be saved from narrow passes and slippery places into which people have fallen in this matter, to the point that every sect calls whatever supports its position "decisive," and whatever supports the position of those who oppose it "ambiguous." This is especially true of the people of dialectical theology (ʿilm al-kalām). Whoever denies this, let him look at their books.

Know that the Noble Book contains what indicates that all of it is decisive, but not in the sense mentioned in this verse, rather in another sense. Among this is His saying, ﴿A Book whose verses have been made firm﴾ [Hūd: 1], and His saying, ﴿These are the verses of the Wise Book﴾ [Yūnus: 1]. What is meant by "decisive" in this sense is that its wording is sound, its meanings upright, and it surpasses every speech in eloquence and fluency. It also contains what indicates that all of it is ambiguous, but not in the sense mentioned in this verse that we are explaining, rather in another sense. Among this is His saying, ﴿a Book, ambiguous, [its parts] resembling one another﴾ [al-Zumar: 23]. What is meant by "ambiguous" in this sense is that some of it resembles the rest in soundness, eloquence, goodness, and rhetorical excellence.

The scholars have mentioned several benefits to the presence of the ambiguous in the Qur'an. Among them is that reaching the truth, while it is present, involves greater difficulty and hardship, and this entails greater reward for those who extract the truth, namely the mujtahids (qualified jurists) who are imams. Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, and others mentioned several explanations; this one is the best of them, and the rest do not merit mention here.

His saying, ﴿Each is from our Lord﴾: there is an implied pronoun referring to the two categories, the decisive and the ambiguous, meaning "all of it," or the omitted element is not a pronoun, meaning "each one of them." This is part of the statement quoted before it.

His saying, ﴿But none reflects except those of understanding﴾, meaning the pure intellects. They are those firmly grounded in knowledge, who stop at its ambiguous parts, who know its decisive parts, and who act upon what God has guided them to in this verse.

His saying, "﴿Our Lord, let not our hearts deviate﴾" and what follows is part of what the firmly grounded say. That is, they say, "We believe in it, all of it is from our Lord," and they say, "Our Lord, let not our hearts deviate." Ibn Kaysān said: "They asked not to deviate, lest their hearts deviate, like His saying, ﴿So when they deviated, God caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [al-Ṣaff: 5]. It is as if, when they heard His saying, ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow what is ambiguous of it﴾, they said, ﴿Our Lord, let not our hearts deviate by following the ambiguous after You have guided us to the truth, by what You have permitted us of acting upon the decisive verses.'" The time phrase, which is ﴿after﴾ (baʿda), is governed by ﴿let not … deviate﴾.

His saying, ﴿And grant us from Yourself mercy﴾, meaning mercy coming from You. The particle min indicates the starting point. ﴿Ladun﴾ is pronounced with a fatḥah on the lām, a ḍammah on the dāl, and a sukūn on the nūn, and there are other dialectal forms, but this is the most eloquent. It is a locative adverb, and it may be used with reference to time. The indefinite ﴿mercy﴾ indicates magnitude, meaning great and vast mercy. His saying, ﴿Indeed You are the Bestower﴾, is a reason for the request or for the granting of what is requested.

His saying, ﴿Our Lord, indeed You are the gatherer of mankind﴾, meaning the one who raises them and brings them back to life after their dispersal, ﴿for a Day﴾, which is the Day of Resurrection, meaning for the reckoning of a Day, or for the recompense of a Day, on the assumption that an attached noun has been omitted and the noun it was attached to has taken its place.

His saying, ﴿there is no doubt about it﴾, meaning about its occurrence and the occurrence of the reckoning and recompense within it. The meaning of doubt has already been explained. The clause ﴿indeed God does not fail in His promise﴾ is a justification for the content of what precedes it, meaning: fulfilling a promise is the attribute of God, glory be to Him, and failing to keep it contradicts divinity, just as divinity itself negates and is incompatible with it.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: "The decisive (al-muḥkamāt) are its abrogating (nāsikh) verses, its lawful and unlawful matters, its limits, its obligations, and what we believe in and act upon. The ambiguous (al-mutashābihāt) are its abrogated (mansūkh) verses, its preceding and succeeding verses, its parables and its oaths, and what we believe in but do not act upon."

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim, who declared it sound, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said, concerning His saying, ﴿Among it are decisive verses﴾: "The three verses at the end of Sūrat al-Anʿām, ﴿Say: "Come, I will recite"﴾ [al-Anʿām: 151], and the two verses after them are decisive."

In another narration from him, related by ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim, concerning His saying, ﴿decisive verses﴾, he said: "From here, ﴿Say: "Come"﴾, up to three verses, and from here, ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 23], up to three verses after it."

I say: May God have mercy on Ibn ʿAbbās, how little benefit there is in this statement transmitted from him! For specifying three verses, or ten, or a hundred out of all the verses of the Qur'an and describing them as decisive has no benefit beneath it at all. The decisive verses are, according to all the opinions, most of the Qur'an, even according to his statement quoted shortly before, that the decisive verses are its abrogating verses, its lawful and unlawful matters, and so on. So what is the point of specifying those verses from the end of Sūrat al-Anʿām?

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd related from him that he said: "The decisive: the lawful and the unlawful." The early generations (al-salaf) have many other statements, all of which return to what we set out at the beginning of this discussion.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: "﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation﴾" means the people of doubt, who interpret the decisive by the ambiguous and the ambiguous by the decisive, and who confuse matters, so God confuses them, and ﴿none knows its ta'wīl except God﴾." He said: "Its ta'wīl is on the Day of Resurrection; none knows it except God."

Ibn Jarīr related from Ibn Masʿūd that he explained ﴿zaigh﴾ (deviation) as doubt. In the two Ṣaḥīḥs and others, from ʿĀʾishah, she said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited ﴿He it is who sent down to you the Book﴾ up to His saying, ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation﴾, up to His saying, ﴿men of understanding﴾." She said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'When you see those who dispute concerning it, those are the ones whom God has named, so beware of them.'"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verses 7–9 (part 3 of 3):

In another wording: "When you see those who follow what is ambiguous of it, those are the ones whom Allah has named, so beware of them." This is the wording of al-Bukhari. The wording of Ibn Jarir and others is: "When you see those who follow what is ambiguous of it, and those who dispute concerning it, they are the ones Allah means, so do not sit with them."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ahmad, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from Abu Umamah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning his saying: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow that of it which is ambiguous﴾ (p. 205), that he said: "They are the Kharijites."

Ibn Jarir and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from Ibn Masʿud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The first Book used to descend from one gate, in one harf (mode). The Qur'an descended in seven ahruf (modes): commanding, forbidding, lawful, unlawful, clear (muhkam), ambiguous (mutashabih), and parables. So make lawful what is lawful in it, make unlawful what is unlawful in it, do what you are commanded, refrain from what you are forbidden, take heed from its parables, act upon its clear verses, believe in its ambiguous verses, and say: 'We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord.'" Ibn Abi Hatim also related it from Ibn Masʿud as a mawquf (a statement of a Companion only).

al-Tabarani related from ʿUmar ibn Abi Salamah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, and he mentioned something similar. al-Bukhari in al-Tarikh related from ʿAli, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) with a weak chain, something similar.
