Al-Kisa'i said: I read both in the accusative, meaning His saying "Allah bore witness that He" and His saying "indeed the religion with Allah is Islam," in the sense of "Allah bore witness that He is such-and-such, and that the religion with Allah is Islam." Ibn Kaysan said: the second is an appositive of the first.

Most scholars hold that Islam here means faith (iman), even though the two are originally distinct, as in the hadith of Jibril in which the Prophet (ﷺ) explained the meaning of Islam and the meaning of faith, and Jibril confirmed it. It is in the two Sahihs and elsewhere. But each of them may be called by the name of the other, and this has occurred in the Book and the Sunna.

His saying: ﴿And those who were given the Scripture did not differ except after knowledge had come to them, out of rivalry among themselves﴾. In it is the report that the difference between the Jews and the Christians was merely out of rivalry, after they had known that it is obligatory for them to enter the religion of Islam by what their revealed books contain.

Al-Akhfash said: there is inversion in the speech, and the meaning is: "Those who were given the Scripture did not differ out of rivalry among themselves except after knowledge had come to them."

What is meant by this disagreement that occurred among them is their disagreement over whether our Prophet (ﷺ) is a prophet or not. It has been said: their disagreement over the prophethood of 'Isa. It has been said: their disagreement among themselves, to the point that the Jews said: "The Christians are not upon anything," and the Christians said: "The Jews are not upon anything."

His saying: ﴿And whoever disbelieves in the signs of Allah﴾, that is, in the signs indicating that the religion with Allah is Islam, then indeed Allah is swift in reckoning, so He will requite him and punish him for his disbelief in His signs. The explicit mention of "Allah" in His saying "then indeed Allah" instead of a pronoun is for the purpose of terrifying them and threatening them.

His saying: ﴿So if they argue with you﴾, that is, dispute with you using false doubts and distorted claims, then say: ﴿I have submitted my face to Allah﴾, that is, I have devoted my self to Allah. He expressed it by "face" for the rest of the self, because it is the most noble of human limbs and the one that gathers the senses. It has been said: "face" here means intention.

His saying: ﴿and whoever follows me﴾ is conjoined to the subject of "aslamtu" and is permissible because of the separation. Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub retained the yā' in "ittaba'anī" as in the original form, while others omitted it following the orthography of the Mushaf. It is also permissible that the waw means "with." The "Ummiyyin" here means the polytheists of the Arabs.

His saying: ﴿Have you submitted?﴾ is an interrogative of confirmation which implies a command, that is: "Submit!" This is what Ibn Jarir and others said.

Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿Have you submitted?﴾ is a threat. The meaning: there has come to you of proofs what necessitates Islam, so have you known what necessitates that or not? It is a rebuke for them and a belittling of their standing in fairness and acceptance of the truth.

His saying: ﴿Then they have been guided﴾, that is, they have attained guidance, which is the greatest share, and they have won the good of this world and the Hereafter. ﴿But if they turn away﴾, that is, they turn away from accepting the proof and do not act by its requirement, ﴿then upon you is only the delivering (of the message)﴾, that is, your duty is only to convey to them what has been revealed to you. ﴿And you are not over them a controller﴾, so do not let yourself go to waste over them in regret. "Al-balagh" is a verbal noun.

His saying: ﴿And Allah is Seeing of the servants﴾ contains both promise and warning, since it implies that He knows all their conditions.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Hasan regarding His saying "standing in justice" that he said: "with equity." He also reported the same from Ibn 'Abbas. 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Qatada regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ that he said: Islam is the testimony that there is no god but Allah, and affirmation of what came from Allah. It is the religion of Allah which He legislated for Himself, sent His messengers with, and indicated to His friends, and He accepts nothing other than it. Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Dahhak that he said: Allah did not send any messenger except with Islam. 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said: Around the House there were three hundred and sixty idols, for each tribe of the Arab tribes an idol or two. So Allah sent down ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no god but He﴾ and the rest of the verse, and all the idols fell down prostrating toward the Ka'ba.

Ibn al-Sunni in 'Amal al-yawm wal-layla and Abu Mansur al-Shahhami in al-Arba'in reported from 'Ali that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed the Opening of the Book, the Verse of the Throne, and the two verses of Al 'Imran: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no god but He, and the angels and those possessed of knowledge, standing in justice; there is no god but He, the Mighty, the Wise﴾ ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ ... ﴿Say: O Allah, Owner of sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will, and You take sovereignty from whom You will, and You honour whom You will, and You humble whom You will﴾ up to His saying ﴿without account﴾ [Al 'Imran: 26-27]. They are suspended from the Throne, and between them and Allah there is a veil. They say: 'O Lord, shall we descend to Your earth and to one who disobeys You?' Allah says: 'I have sworn that no servant of Mine will recite you after every prescribed prayer except that I will make Paradise his abode for what he has done, and unless I settle him in the enclosure of holiness, and unless I look at him with My hidden eye seventy looks every day, and unless I fulfil for him seventy needs every day, the least of which is forgiveness, and unless I protect him from every enemy and help him against it.'"

Al-Daylami in Musnad al-Firdaws reported from Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar, and in it: "No servant recites them after every obligatory prayer except that I will forgive him what he has done, settle him in the Paradise of Firdaws, look at him every day seventy times, and fulfil for him seventy needs, the least of which is forgiveness."

Ahmad, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn al-Sunni reported from al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam that he said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while at 'Arafa reciting this verse: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no god but He, and the angels and those possessed of knowledge, standing in justice; there is no god but He, the Mighty, the Wise﴾, and he said: 'And I am among the witnesses to that.'" The wording of al-Tabarani is: "And I testify that there is no god but You, the Mighty, the Wise."

Ibn 'Adi, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman (and he declared it weak), al-Khatib in his History, and Ibn al-Najjar reported from Ghalib al-Qattan that he said: I came to Kufa on business, and I passed by this verse: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no god but...﴾ up to His saying ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾, and he said: "And I testify to what Allah testified, and I entrust this testimony to Allah; it is a deposit for me with Allah," and he said it several times. I said: "He must have heard something about it," so I asked him, and he said: Abu Wa'il narrated to me from 'Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Its possessor will be brought on the Day of Resurrection, and Allah will say: 'My servant made a covenant with Me, and I am most worthy to fulfil the covenant. Admit My servant to Paradise.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding His saying: "﴿Those who were given the Scripture﴾" that he said: the Children of Israel.

Ibn Jarir reported from Abu al-'Aliyya regarding His saying "out of rivalry among themselves" that he says: out of rivalry over this world and the seeking of its kingdom and authority, so some of them killed others over the world, after they had been the scholars of the people.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Hasan regarding His saying: "﴿So if they argue with you﴾" that he said: if the Jews and the Christians argue with you.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jarir something similar. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding "﴿And say to those who were given the Scripture﴾" that he said: the Jews and the Christians, and "the Ummiyyin," and he said: they are those who do not write.

Al-Shawkani's commentary (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 3, verses 21–25:

His saying "in the signs of Allah": its apparent meaning is that there is no distinction between one sign and another. "And they kill the prophets without right" means that the Jews killed the prophets. "And they kill those who enjoin justice among the people," meaning justice (al-qist), and these are the ones who enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong.

Al-Mubarrad said: Some people of the Children of Israel were visited by prophets who called them to Allah, and they killed them. Then, after them, some believers stood up and commanded them to embrace Islam, and they killed them. It was concerning these that the verse was revealed.

His saying ﴿So give them the good news of a painful punishment﴾: this is the predicate of "Indeed, those who disbelieve..." and so on. The fa' (fa, "so") has entered it because the relative clause contains the meaning of a conditional. Some grammarians (ahl al-nahw) held that the predicate is his saying "those whose deeds have become void," and they said that the fa' does not enter the predicate of inna even if its subject contains the meaning of a conditional, because it has been abrogated (nusikha, "superseded") by the entry of inna upon it. Among them were Sibawayh and al-Akhfash. Others held that what the subject contains of the meaning of a conditional is not abrogated by the entry of inna upon it, and the same applies to the open alif of anna (ana) as to the kasra of inna. Among this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And know that whatever you obtain of spoils, then indeed for Allah is one-fifth of it﴾ [al-Anfal: 41].

His saying "their deeds have become void": the meaning of ihbat (voiding) has already been explained. The meaning of their deeds being void in this world and the Hereafter is that no effect of their good deeds remains in this world, so that they are not treated in it as the people of good deeds are treated. Rather, they are treated as the people of evil deeds: they are cursed, and disgrace and humiliation descend upon them. And in the Hereafter they have the punishment of the Fire.

His saying ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture?﴾: in it is an expression of wonder directed at the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and at everyone who is capable of seeing, regarding the condition of these people, who are the rabbis of the Jews.

"The Scripture" is the Torah. The indefiniteness of "a portion" (nasibun) is for magnification, meaning a great portion, as the context of emphasis indicates. Whoever says that the indefiniteness is for belittlement has not hit the mark. They were called to the Book of Allah, the ones who were given a portion of it, which is the Torah, so that it might judge between them; then a party of them turned away, while they were averse to answering the call to what they were summoned to, despite their knowledge of it and their acknowledgment of the obligation to answer it.

"That" refers to the turning away and aversion mentioned earlier, because of their saying ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days﴾, which is the duration of their worship of the calf. The explanation of this has already been given.

"What they used to fabricate deluded them in their religion": that is, the lies they invented, of which this saying is one.

His saying ﴿So how will it be when We gather them for a Day about which there is no doubt﴾: in it is a rebuttal of them and a refutation of what deluded them of lies. That is, how will their condition be when We gather them for a Day about which there is no doubt, which is the Day of Recompense, whose occurrence no doubter doubts? They will certainly face it, and they will be unable to repel it through tricks and lies. ﴿And every soul will be paid in full what it earned﴾: that is, the recompense of what it earned, with the omission of a modifier. ﴿And they will not be wronged﴾ by any addition or reduction.

The intended meaning is all people, indicated by "every soul."

Al-Kisa'i said: the lam in His saying "for a Day" (li-yawmin) means fi ("in"). The Basrans said: the meaning is "for the reckoning of a Day." Ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: the meaning is "for what happens on a Day."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, which of the people will have the most severe punishment on the Day of Resurrection? He said: A man who killed a prophet, or a man who enjoined what is right and forbade what is wrong." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right and kill those who enjoin justice among the people﴾ up to His saying ﴿and they will have no helpers﴾. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Abu Ubaydah, the Children of Israel killed forty-three prophets at the beginning of the day in a single hour. Then a hundred men and seventy men of the worshippers of the Children of Israel stood up and commanded those who were killing them to do what is right and forbade them from what is wrong, and they were all killed by the end of that day. They are the ones whom Allah mentioned."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: Isa (Jesus) sent Yahya ibn Zakariyya (John son of Zechariah) with twelve men of the disciples to teach the people. He used to forbid marriage to the daughter of a brother. A king had a niece who pleased him, and he desired her and began to grant her a request every day. Her mother said to her: "When he asks you what you want, say: 'My request is that you kill Yahya ibn Zakariyya.'" So he said: "Ask for something other than this." She said: "I will ask you for nothing other than this." When she refused, he ordered him to be brought, and he was slaughtered over a basin. A drop of his blood splashed out and kept boiling until Allah sent Bukhtanassar (Nebuchadnezzar). An old woman pointed to him, and it was inspired in his heart that he should not stop killing until this blood became still. He killed seventy thousand in one day, with one strike and one age, and then it became still.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ma'qil ibn Abi Miskin concerning the verse: "Revelation used to come to the Children of Israel, and they would remind their people, but no book came to them. Then men who followed them and believed them would stand up and remind their people, and they would be killed. These are the ones who enjoin justice among the people." Ibn Jarir transmitted a similar report from Qatadah.

Ibn Asakir transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Those who enjoin justice among the people" are the rulers of justice.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered the house of study (bayt al-midras) where a group of Jews were, and he called them to Allah. Al-Nu'man ibn Amr and al-Harith ibn Zayd said to him: 'On what religion have you come, O Muhammad?' He said: 'On the religion and creed of Ibrahim.' They said: 'Ibrahim was a Jew.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said to them both: 'Come then to the Torah; it is between us and you.' They refused, so Allah revealed: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture, who are called to the Book of Allah...﴾, the verse."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Abu Malik concerning His saying "a portion" (nasiban): "a share of the Scripture," he said: the Torah.

Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from Mujahid concerning His saying ﴿They said: The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days﴾: he said: "They mean the days in which Allah created Adam."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Qatadah concerning His saying "What they used to fabricate deluded them in their religion": "when they said: 'We are the sons of Allah and His beloved ones.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning His saying ﴿And every soul will be paid in full﴾: "that is, every soul, pious or wicked, will be paid in full what it earned, whether of good or evil, and they will not be wronged" means in their deeds.

Al-Mubarrad said: Some people of the Children of Israel were visited by prophets who called them to Allah, and they killed them. Then, after them, some believers stood up and commanded them to embrace Islam, and they killed them. It was concerning these that the verse was revealed.

**His statement: "Say, O Allah (al-Lahumma)."**

Al-Khalil (ibn Ahmad) and Sibawayh, and all the Basran grammarians (al-Basriyyun), said: the original form of *Allahumma* is *ya Allah* (O Allah). When the word was used without the vocative particle *ya*, which is the particle of address, they replaced it with this doubled *mim*. So they brought two letters, the two *mim*s, in place of two letters, the *ya* and the *alif*. The *damma* on the *ha'* is the *damma* of the singular addressed noun (al-ism al-munada al-mufrad).

Al-Farra' and the Kufan grammarians (al-Kufiyyun) held that the original form of *Allahumma* is *ya Allah ummana bi-khayr* (O Allah, aim us toward good). It was shortened and the two phrases were blended. The *damma* on the *ha'* is the *damma* that was in *ummana*. When the *hamza* was dropped, the vowel (al-harakah) moved to the *ha'*.

Al-Nahhas said: this is, according to the Basrans, a grave error. The correct view is what al-Khalil and Sibawayh said.

The Kufans said: the vocative particle may indeed be prefixed to *Allahumma*, and they cited in support the words of a rajaz poet:

> *"You forgave, or You punished, O Allahumma!"* (ghafarta aw adhabta ya Allahumma)

and the words of another:

> *"And there is nothing wrong for you in saying, whenever you glorify (Him) or proclaim His oneness, O Allahumma!"* (wa ma 'alayka an taqula kullama ∗∗∗ sabbahta aw hallalta ya lillahumma)

and the words of another:

> *"Indeed, when a calamity befalls me, I say: O Allahumma, O Allahumma!"* (inni idha ma hadathun almma ∗∗∗ aqulu ya lillahumma ya lillahumma)

They argued: if the *mim* were a substitute for the vocative particle, the two could not be combined. Al-Zajjaj said: this is anomalous (shadh), and its speaker is not known. Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: whoever says *Allahumma* has called upon Allah by all His names.

**His statement: ﴿Owner of sovereignty﴾ (Malik al-mulk)**

That is, the Owner of the kind of sovereignty in absolute terms. *Malik* is in the accusative according to Sibawayh, as a second vocative: "O Owner of sovereignty." According to him, it cannot be an adjective (wasf) of *Allahumma*, because the *mim* prevents adjectival description.

Muhammad ibn Yazid al-Mubarrad and Ibrahim ibn al-Sari al-Zajjaj said: it is an adjective of the name of Allah, the Exalted. Likewise is His saying, ﴿Say, O Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Zumar: 46].

Abu Ali al-Farisi said: this is the view of al-Mubarrad, but what Sibawayh said is more correct and clearer, because it is a single noun to which a sound (sawt) has been added, and sounds are not described by adjectives, like *ghaq* and similar words.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "Owner of the servants and what they possess." It was also said: the meaning is "Owner of this world and the Hereafter." It was also said: *al-mulk* here means prophethood, or dominion (al-ghalabah), or wealth and slaves.

The apparent meaning is that it encompasses everything that the term *mulk* applies to, without restriction. ﴿You give sovereignty to whom You will﴾, that is, to whom You will giving it to him, ﴿and You take sovereignty away from whom You will﴾, taking it from him.

What is meant by the sovereignty He gives and takes away is a type of that general sovereignty.

**His statement: ﴿You exalt whom You will﴾**

That is, in this world or in the Hereafter, or in both. *'Azza* is said when one prevails, as in ﴿and he overpowered me in speech﴾ [Sad: 23].

**His statement: ﴿and You humble whom You will﴾**

That is, in this world or in the Hereafter, or in both. It is said: *dhalla yadhillu dhullan* when one prevails and subdues.

**His statement: ﴿In Your hand is the good﴾**

The fronting of the predicate (taqdim al-khabar) is for restriction (takhsis). That is: in Your hand is the good, not in the hand of anyone else. He mentioned the good and not the evil, because the good comes from pure bounty, unlike evil, which is a recompense for an action that reaches the one who does it. It was also said: because every evil, insofar as it is from His decree, glorified be He, contains good, so all His acts are good. It was also said: it was elided, as in His saying, ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81], and the original is "In Your hand is the good and the evil." It was also said: He specified the good because the context is one of supplication.

**His statement: ﴿Indeed, You are over all things competent﴾**

This is a justification (ta'lil) for what preceded, and a confirmation of it.

**His statement: ﴿You cause the night to enter the day and You cause the day to enter the night﴾**

That is, You make what is lost from one of them enter into the other. It was also said: the meaning is that they alternate, and the disappearance of one of them is its entering into the other.

**His statement: ﴿You bring the living out of the dead and You bring the dead out of the living﴾**

It was said: what is meant is the bringing forth of a living animal from a sperm-drop, which is dead, and the bringing forth of a sperm-drop, which is dead, from a living animal. It was also said: what is meant is the bringing forth of a living bird from an egg, which is dead, and the bringing forth of an egg, which is dead, from a living hen. It was also said: what is meant is the bringing forth of the believer from the disbeliever and the disbeliever from the believer.

**His statement: ﴿without account﴾**

That is, without restriction or stinginess, as you say, "So-and-so gives without account." The *ba'* is connected to an elided word that functions as a circumstantial state (hal).

**Narrations (al-athar)**

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah, who said: "It was mentioned to us that the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) asked his Lord that the kingdom of Persia and Rome be given to his community (ummah), and then this verse was revealed."

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Greatest Name of Allah is ﴿Say, O Allah, Owner of sovereignty﴾ up to His saying ﴿without account﴾."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and al-Tabarani transmitted from Mu'adh that he complained to the Prophet (ﷺ) about a debt upon him, so he taught him to recite this verse and then say: "O Lord of this world and the Hereafter and their Merciful One, You give from both to whom You will and withhold from whom You will. Have mercy upon me with a mercy that makes me independent of the mercy of anyone other than You. O Allah, make me free from poverty and settle my debt for me."

Al-Tabarani related it in al-Saghir from the hadith of Anas, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Mu'adh: "Shall I not teach you a supplication with which, if you had a debt like Mount Uhud, Allah would pay it for you?" and then he mentioned it. Its chain is good (isnaduhu jayyid). Some of this verse's virtues were mentioned earlier in the commentary on His saying, ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 18].

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿You give sovereignty to whom You will﴾, that he said: "Prophethood."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, concerning His saying ﴿You cause the night to enter the day﴾ up to the verse, that he said: "He takes summer from winter and takes winter from summer." ﴿And You bring the living out of the dead﴾: "You bring the living man out of the dead sperm-drop." ﴿And You bring the dead out of the living﴾: "You bring the dead sperm-drop out of the living man."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, concerning ﴿You cause the night to enter the day﴾, that he said: "What is lost from the day You make into the night, and what is lost from the night You make into the day." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted similarly from al-Suddi. Abd ibn Humayd transmitted similarly from Mujahid. Abd ibn Humayd also transmitted similarly from al-Dahhak.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, concerning ﴿You bring the living out of the dead﴾, that he said: "You bring the dead sperm-drop out of the living, then from the sperm-drop You bring forth a living human being." Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted similarly from Mujahid.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ikrimah, concerning ﴿You bring the living out of the dead﴾, that he said: "It is the egg that comes out of the living hen while it is dead, then from it comes the living one."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him, who said: "The date palm comes from the date stone and the date stone from the date palm; the grain comes from the ear and the ear from the grain."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted similarly from Abu Malik.

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from al-Hasan, who said: "The believer from the disbeliever, and the disbeliever from the believer. The believer is a servant whose heart is alive, and the disbeliever is a servant whose heart is dead."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi transmitted similarly from Salman al-Farisi. Ibn Mardawayh transmitted similarly from him as a marfu' report (traced to the Prophet), and he also transmitted it from him, or from Ibn Mas'ud, as a marfu' report.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ubayd Allah ibn Abd Allah that "Khalidah bint al-Aswad ibn Abd Yaghuth entered upon the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'Who is this?' It was said: 'Khalidah bint al-Aswad.' He said: 'Glory be to Him who brings the living out of the dead.' She was a righteous woman, and her father was a disbeliever." Ibn Sa'd transmitted similarly from Aisha.

**His statement: "Say, O Allah (al-Lahumma)."**

Al-Khalil (ibn Ahmad) and Sibawayh, and all the Basran grammarians (al-Basriyyun), said: the original form of *Allahumma* is *ya Allah* (O Allah). When the word was used without the vocative particle *ya*, which is the particle of address, they replaced it with this doubled *mim*. So they brought two letters, the two *mim*s, in place of two letters, the *ya* and the *alif*. The *damma* on the *ha'* is the *damma* of the singular addressed noun (al-ism al-munada al-mufrad).

Al-Farra' and the Kufan grammarians (al-Kufiyyun) held that the original form of *Allahumma* is *ya Allah ummana bi-khayr* (O Allah, aim us toward good). It was shortened and the two phrases were blended. The *damma* on the *ha'* is the *damma* that was in *ummana*. When the *hamza* was dropped, the vowel (al-harakah) moved to the *ha'*.

Al-Nahhas said: this is, according to the Basrans, a grave error. The correct view is what al-Khalil and Sibawayh said.

The Kufans said: the vocative particle may indeed be prefixed to *Allahumma*, and they cited in support the words of a rajaz poet:

> *"You forgave, or You punished, O Allahumma!"* (ghafarta aw adhabta ya Allahumma)

and the words of another:

> *"And there is nothing wrong for you in saying, whenever you glorify (Him) or proclaim His oneness, O Allahumma!"* (wa ma 'alayka an taqula kullama ∗∗∗ sabbahta aw hallalta ya lillahumma)

and the words of another:

> *"Indeed, when a calamity befalls me, I say: O Allahumma, O Allahumma!"* (inni idha ma hadathun almma ∗∗∗ aqulu ya lillahumma ya lillahumma)

They argued: if the *mim* were a substitute for the vocative particle, the two could not be combined. Al-Zajjaj said: this is anomalous (shadh), and its speaker is not known. Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: whoever says *Allahumma* has called upon Allah by all His names.

**His statement: ﴿Owner of sovereignty﴾ (Malik al-mulk)**

That is, the Owner of the kind of sovereignty in absolute terms. *Malik* is in the accusative according to Sibawayh, as a second vocative: "O Owner of sovereignty." According to him, it cannot be an adjective (wasf) of *Allahumma*, because the *mim* prevents adjectival description.

Muhammad ibn Yazid al-Mubarrad and Ibrahim ibn al-Sari al-Zajjaj said: it is an adjective of the name of Allah, the Exalted. Likewise is His saying, ﴿Say, O Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Zumar: 46].

Abu Ali al-Farisi said: this is the view of al-Mubarrad, but what Sibawayh said is more correct and clearer, because it is a single noun to which a sound (sawt) has been added, and sounds are not described by adjectives, like *ghaq* and similar words.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "Owner of the servants and what they possess." It was also said: the meaning is "Owner of this world and the Hereafter." It was also said: *al-mulk* here means prophethood, or dominion (al-ghalabah), or wealth and slaves.

The apparent meaning is that it encompasses everything that the term *mulk* applies to, without restriction. ﴿You give sovereignty to whom You will﴾, that is, to whom You will giving it to him, ﴿and You take sovereignty away from whom You will﴾, taking it from him.

What is meant by the sovereignty He gives and takes away is a type of that general sovereignty.

**His statement: ﴿You exalt whom You will﴾**

That is, in this world or in the Hereafter, or in both. *'Azza* is said when one prevails, as in ﴿and he overpowered me in speech﴾ [Sad: 23].

**His statement: ﴿and You humble whom You will﴾**

That is, in this world or in the Hereafter, or in both. It is said: *dhalla yadhillu dhullan* when one prevails and subdues.

**His statement: ﴿In Your hand is the good﴾**

The fronting of the predicate (taqdim al-khabar) is for restriction (takhsis). That is: in Your hand is the good, not in the hand of anyone else. He mentioned the good and not the evil, because the good comes from pure bounty, unlike evil, which is a recompense for an action that reaches the one who does it. It was also said: because every evil, insofar as it is from His decree, glorified be He, contains good, so all His acts are good. It was also said: it was elided, as in His saying, ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81], and the original is "In Your hand is the good and the evil." It was also said: He specified the good because the context is one of supplication.

**His statement: ﴿Indeed, You are over all things competent﴾**

This is a justification (ta'lil) for what preceded, and a confirmation of it.

**His statement: ﴿You cause the night to enter the day and You cause the day to enter the night﴾**

That is, You make what is lost from one of them enter into the other. It was also said: the meaning is that they alternate, and the disappearance of one of them is its entering into the other.

**His statement: ﴿You bring the living out of the dead and You bring the dead out of the living﴾**

It was said: what is meant is the bringing forth of a living animal from a sperm-drop, which is dead, and the bringing forth of a sperm-drop, which is dead, from a living animal. It was also said: what is meant is the bringing forth of a living bird from an egg, which is dead, and the bringing forth of an egg, which is dead, from a living hen. It was also said: what is meant is the bringing forth of the believer from the disbeliever and the disbeliever from the believer.

**His statement: ﴿without account﴾**

That is, without restriction or stinginess, as you say, "So-and-so gives without account." The *ba'* is connected to an elided word that functions as a circumstantial state (hal).

**Narrations (al-athar)**

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah, who said: "It was mentioned to us that the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) asked his Lord that the kingdom of Persia and Rome be given to his community (ummah), and then this verse was revealed."

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Greatest Name of Allah is ﴿Say, O Allah, Owner of sovereignty﴾ up to His saying ﴿without account﴾."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and al-Tabarani transmitted from Mu'adh that he complained to the Prophet (ﷺ) about a debt upon him, so he taught him to recite this verse and then say: "O Lord of this world and the Hereafter and their Merciful One, You give from both to whom You will and withhold from whom You will. Have mercy upon me with a mercy that makes me independent of the mercy of anyone other than You. O Allah, make me free from poverty and settle my debt for me."

Al-Tabarani related it in al-Saghir from the hadith of Anas, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Mu'adh: "Shall I not teach you a supplication with which, if you had a debt like Mount Uhud, Allah would pay it for you?" and then he mentioned it. Its chain is good (isnaduhu jayyid). Some of this verse's virtues were mentioned earlier in the commentary on His saying, ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 18].

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿You give sovereignty to whom You will﴾, that he said: "Prophethood."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, concerning His saying ﴿You cause the night to enter the day﴾ up to the verse, that he said: "He takes summer from winter and takes winter from summer." ﴿And You bring the living out of the dead﴾: "You bring the living man out of the dead sperm-drop." ﴿And You bring the dead out of the living﴾: "You bring the dead sperm-drop out of the living man."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, concerning ﴿You cause the night to enter the day﴾, that he said: "What is lost from the day You make into the night, and what is lost from the night You make into the day." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted similarly from al-Suddi. Abd ibn Humayd transmitted similarly from Mujahid. Abd ibn Humayd also transmitted similarly from al-Dahhak.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, concerning ﴿You bring the living out of the dead﴾, that he said: "You bring the dead sperm-drop out of the living, then from the sperm-drop You bring forth a living human being." Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted similarly from Mujahid.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ikrimah, concerning ﴿You bring the living out of the dead﴾, that he said: "It is the egg that comes out of the living hen while it is dead, then from it comes the living one."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him, who said: "The date palm comes from the date stone and the date stone from the date palm; the grain comes from the ear and the ear from the grain."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted similarly from Abu Malik.

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from al-Hasan, who said: "The believer from the disbeliever, and the disbeliever from the believer. The believer is a servant whose heart is alive, and the disbeliever is a servant whose heart is dead."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi transmitted similarly from Salman al-Farisi. Ibn Mardawayh transmitted similarly from him as a marfu' report (traced to the Prophet), and he also transmitted it from him, or from Ibn Mas'ud, as a marfu' report.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ubayd Allah ibn Abd Allah that "Khalidah bint al-Aswad ibn Abd Yaghuth entered upon the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'Who is this?' It was said: 'Khalidah bint al-Aswad.' He said: 'Glory be to Him who brings the living out of the dead.' She was a righteous woman, and her father was a disbeliever." Ibn Sa'd transmitted similarly from Aisha.

**Al-Shawkani, *Fath al-Qadir*, on Surah Al 'Imran, verses 28–30**

His saying, ﴿Let not take﴾: In it is a prohibition to the believers against taking the disbelievers as allies (muwalah) for any reason. Similar to it is His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Do not take as intimates (bitanah) others than yourselves﴾ [Al 'Imran: 118], and the verse; and His saying, ﴿Whoever among you takes them as allies, then he is one of them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 51]; and His saying, ﴿You will not find a people who believe in Allah﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 22], and the verse; and His saying, ﴿Do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 51]; and His saying, ﴿O you who believe, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 1].

His saying, ﴿other than the believers﴾, is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: going beyond the believers to the disbelievers, either independently or jointly. The reference of His saying, ﴿And whoever does that﴾, is to the act of taking (ittihad) indicated by His saying "let not take." The meaning of His saying, ﴿then he has nothing to do with Allah﴾, is: he has no part of His guardianship (wilayah) in anything at all; rather, he is completely cut off from Him in every state.

His saying, ﴿except that you fear them with a fear﴾ is in the form of address by way of iltifat (a shift of grammatical person); meaning: except that you fear from them a matter that must be guarded against. It is an exceptive clause (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general of circumstances.

Tuqah is a verbal noun standing in the place of the object (maf'ul). Its origin is wiqyah, on the pattern of fi'lah; the waw was changed into a ta' and the ya' into an alif. Raja' and Qatadah read taqiyyah.

In this is evidence for the permissibility of (p-213) allegiance toward them when one fears them, but it must be outward and not inward.

Some of the early generations (salaf) disagreed with this, saying: there is no taqiyyah after Allah has honored Islam.

His saying, ﴿And Allah warns you of Himself﴾: meaning His holy essence. Applying this to Him, glorified is He, is permissible by way of musha'alah (a figure of speech in which a word is used because of its association with another word) as in His saying, ﴿You know what is in my self, and I do not know what is in Your self﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116], and in other places. Some later scholars held that this is not permitted except as musha'alah. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is, "And Allah warns you of Himself," meaning, "Allah warns you of Himself (i.e., of His punishment)." Then they dispensed with that through this, and it became the usual usage.

He said: As for His saying, ﴿You know what is in my self and I do not know what is in Your self﴾, its meaning is: You know what is with me and what is in my reality, and I do not know what is with You nor what is in Your reality. Some of the people of knowledge said: its meaning is, "And Allah warns you of His punishment," like ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82], so the word "self" was placed where the implied term would be. In this verse is a severe threat and a great warning to His servants that they should not expose themselves to His punishment by allying with His enemies.

His saying, ﴿Say: If you conceal what is in your breasts﴾, the verse: in it is that everything that the servant conceals or hides, or shows or manifests, is known to Allah, glorified is He. Nothing of it is hidden from Him, and not even the weight of an atom escapes Him. ﴿And He knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth﴾, which is more general than the matters that they conceal or disclose, so nothing that is more specific than that is hidden from Him.

His saying, ﴿The day when every soul will find﴾, is in the accusative by His saying, ﴿And Allah warns you of Himself﴾; and it was said that it is governed by an omitted verb, meaning: remember. "Muhdaran" is a circumstantial clause (hal). His saying, ﴿and what it has done of evil﴾, is conjoined to the first "ma" (what); meaning: and it will find what it has done of evil present, wishing that between it and that there were a great distance.

"Muhdaran" is omitted because the first occurrence indicates it. This is when "tajidu" means "to find" in the sense of finding a lost thing. But when it is from "wajada" meaning "to know," then "muhdaran" is the second object. It is also possible that His saying, ﴿and what it has done of evil, it wishes that between it and that there were a great distance﴾ is an independent sentence, and the "ma" in "ma 'amilat" is the subject (mubtada'), and "yawaddu" is its predicate.

Al-amad means the limit (ghayah), and its plural is amad; meaning: it wishes that between it and what it has done of evil there were a great distance. It was also said that His saying, "the day," is governed by His saying, "yawaddu," and the pronoun in His saying, "wa baynahu," refers to the day; but this is far-fetched. He repeated His saying, ﴿And Allah warns you of Himself﴾, for emphasis and to bring it to mind, so that this great threat would be remembered by them. In His saying, ﴿And Allah is Compassionate to the servants﴾, is evidence that this severe warning is accompanied by His compassion toward His servants, glorified is He, showing them kindness. How excellent is what is related of one of the Arabs: it was said to him, "You will die, and be resurrected, and return to Allah," and he said: "Do you threaten me with One from whom I have never seen good except from Him?"

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: al-Hajjaj ibn 'Amr was an ally of Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, and Ibn Abi al-Haqiq and Qays ibn Zayd. They had made intimate ties (battanu) with a group of the Ansar in order to seduce them from their religion. Rifa'ah ibn al-Mundhir, 'Abd Allah ibn Jubayr and Sa'd ibn Khaythamah said to those men: ... Then Allah revealed concerning them: ﴿The believers should not take the disbelievers﴾ up to His saying, ﴿and Allah is over all things competent﴾.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related through various chains from him, who said: Allah forbade the believers to show kindness to the disbelievers and to take them as confidants (wilijah) other than the believers, except that the disbelievers should be dominant over them; then they show them kindness and oppose them in religion. That is His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿except that you fear them with a fear﴾.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi concerning ﴿And whoever does that, then he has nothing to do with Allah﴾, that Allah has disowned him. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related through the chain of al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying, ﴿except that you fear them with a fear﴾, that he said: taqiyyah is with the tongue, for one who is compelled to say something that is disobedience to Allah, so he says it out of fear of people while his heart is at peace with faith; this does not harm him. Taqiyyah is only with the tongue.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan*, related from him concerning the verse: he said: taqiyyah is speaking with the tongue while the heart is at peace with faith; one does not extend his hand and kill, nor commit sin, for he has no excuse then.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-'Aliyah concerning the verse, he said: taqiyyah is with the tongue, not with action. 'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah, ﴿except that you fear them with a fear﴾, he said: except that there be between you and him a kinship, so you maintain ties with him for that reason. 'Abd ibn Humayd and al-Bukhari related from al-Hasan, he said: taqiyyah is permissible until the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Bukhari related from Abu al-Darda' that he said: "We smile in the faces of people while our hearts curse them." Evidence for the permissibility of taqiyyah is His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿except one who is compelled while his heart is at peace with faith; but whoever opens his breast to disbelief, upon them is wrath from Allah, and for them is a great punishment﴾ [al-Nahl: 106]. Among those who held the permissibility of taqiyyah with the tongue are Abu al-Sha'tha', al-Dahhak and al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi concerning His saying, ﴿Say: If you conceal﴾, the verse, that he said: He informed them that He knows what they keep secret and what they make public. 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah concerning His saying, "muhdaran," he says: "muwaffaran" (in full).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan concerning the verse, he said: One of you would be glad never to meet that deed of his, and that would be his wish. As for in this world, his sin was something he enjoyed.

Both of them (Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim) also related from al-Suddi, ﴿a great distance﴾, he said: a far place. Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Jurayj, "amad," he said: a term (ajal). Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan concerning His saying, ﴿And Allah warns you of Himself, and Allah is Compassionate to the servants﴾, he said: out of His compassion toward them, He warned them of Himself.

'Abd ibn Humayd and al-Bukhari related from al-Hasan, he said: taqiyyah is permissible until the Day of Resurrection.

**Al-Shawkani, *Fath al-Qadir*, on Surah Al 'Imran, verses 28–30**

His saying, ﴿Let not take﴾: In it is a prohibition to the believers against taking the disbelievers as allies (muwalah) for any reason. Similar to it is His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Do not take as intimates (bitanah) others than yourselves﴾ [Al 'Imran: 118], and the verse; and His saying, ﴿Whoever among you takes them as allies, then he is one of them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 51]; and His saying, ﴿You will not find a people who believe in Allah﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 22], and the verse; and His saying, ﴿Do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 51]; and His saying, ﴿O you who believe, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 1].

His saying, ﴿other than the believers﴾, is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: going beyond the believers to the disbelievers, either independently or jointly. The reference of His saying, ﴿And whoever does that﴾, is to the act of taking (ittihad) indicated by His saying "let not take." The meaning of His saying, ﴿then he has nothing to do with Allah﴾, is: he has no part of His guardianship (wilayah) in anything at all; rather, he is completely cut off from Him in every state.

His saying, ﴿except that you fear them with a fear﴾ is in the form of address by way of iltifat (a shift of grammatical person); meaning: except that you fear from them a matter that must be guarded against. It is an exceptive clause (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general of circumstances.

Tuqah is a verbal noun standing in the place of the object (maf'ul). Its origin is wiqyah, on the pattern of fi'lah; the waw was changed into a ta' and the ya' into an alif. Raja' and Qatadah read taqiyyah.

In this is evidence for the permissibility of (p-213) allegiance toward them when one fears them, but it must be outward and not inward.

Some of the early generations (salaf) disagreed with this, saying: there is no taqiyyah after Allah has honored Islam.

His saying, ﴿And Allah warns you of Himself﴾: meaning His holy essence. Applying this to Him, glorified is He, is permissible by way of musha'alah (a figure of speech in which a word is used because of its association with another word) as in His saying, ﴿You know what is in my self, and I do not know what is in Your self﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116], and in other places. Some later scholars held that this is not permitted except as musha'alah. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is, "And Allah warns you of Himself," meaning, "Allah warns you of Himself (i.e., of His punishment)." Then they dispensed with that through this, and it became the usual usage.

He said: As for His saying, ﴿You know what is in my self and I do not know what is in Your self﴾, its meaning is: You know what is with me and what is in my reality, and I do not know what is with You nor what is in Your reality. Some of the people of knowledge said: its meaning is, "And Allah warns you of His punishment," like ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82], so the word "self" was placed where the implied term would be. In this verse is a severe threat and a great warning to His servants that they should not expose themselves to His punishment by allying with His enemies.

His saying, ﴿Say: If you conceal what is in your breasts﴾, the verse: in it is that everything that the servant conceals or hides, or shows or manifests, is known to Allah, glorified is He. Nothing of it is hidden from Him, and not even the weight of an atom escapes Him. ﴿And He knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth﴾, which is more general than the matters that they conceal or disclose, so nothing that is more specific than that is hidden from Him.

His saying, ﴿The day when every soul will find﴾, is in the accusative by His saying, ﴿And Allah warns you of Himself﴾; and it was said that it is governed by an omitted verb, meaning: remember. "Muhdaran" is a circumstantial clause (hal). His saying, ﴿and what it has done of evil﴾, is conjoined to the first "ma" (what); meaning: and it will find what it has done of evil present, wishing that between it and that there were a great distance.

"Muhdaran" is omitted because the first occurrence indicates it. This is when "tajidu" means "to find" in the sense of finding a lost thing. But when it is from "wajada" meaning "to know," then "muhdaran" is the second object. It is also possible that His saying, ﴿and what it has done of evil, it wishes that between it and that there were a great distance﴾ is an independent sentence, and the "ma" in "ma 'amilat" is the subject (mubtada'), and "yawaddu" is its predicate.

Al-amad means the limit (ghayah), and its plural is amad; meaning: it wishes that between it and what it has done of evil there were a great distance. It was also said that His saying, "the day," is governed by His saying, "yawaddu," and the pronoun in His saying, "wa baynahu," refers to the day; but this is far-fetched. He repeated His saying, ﴿And Allah warns you of Himself﴾, for emphasis and to bring it to mind, so that this great threat would be remembered by them. In His saying, ﴿And Allah is Compassionate to the servants﴾, is evidence that this severe warning is accompanied by His compassion toward His servants, glorified is He, showing them kindness. How excellent is what is related of one of the Arabs: it was said to him, "You will die, and be resurrected, and return to Allah," and he said: "Do you threaten me with One from whom I have never seen good except from Him?"

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on Surah 3, verses 31–34**

Al-ḥubb and al-maḥabba (love) mean the soul's inclination toward a thing. One says *aḥabbahu*, so he is *muḥibb* (one who loves), and *ḥabbahu yaḥibbuhu* with a kasra in the present tense, so he is *maḥbūb* (one who is loved). Al-Jawhari said: "This is anomalous (*shādhdh*), because the pattern *yafʿilu* with a kasra does not occur in the doubled (*muḍaʿʿaf*) verbs."

Ibn al-Dahhan said: For *ḥabba* there are two dialects, *ḥabba* and *aḥabba*. The root of *ḥabba* in this sense is *ḥababa*, like *ṭaraqa*. The love of God, glorified is He, has been interpreted as the will to obey Him. Al-Azhari said: The love of the servant for God and His Messenger is his obedience to them both and his following of their command, and the love of God for the servants is His bestowing favor upon them through forgiveness. Abu Raja al-ʿUtaridi read *fa-ittabaʿūnī* with a fatḥa on the *bāʾ* (i.e., *fa-ittabaʿūnī* as a verb form with a different vocalization, as recorded).

It is related from Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ that he assimilated (*adgham*) the *rāʾ* of *yaghfir* into the *lām*. Al-Nahhas said: Al-Khalil and Sibawayh do not permit the assimilation of *rāʾ* into *lām*, and Abu ʿAmr is too exalted to err in this. Perhaps he was concealing the vowel (*ikhfāʾ al-ḥaraka*), as he did in many other matters.

His saying: ﴿Say: Obey God and the Messenger﴾. The omission of the object (*ḥadhf al-mutaʿallaq*) indicates generality, i.e., in all commands and prohibitions.

His saying "*fa-in tawallaw*" (but if they turn away) may be part of the speech of God, in which case it is in the past tense.

His saying ﴿Indeed God does not love the disbelievers﴾: the negation of love is a metonymy (*kināya*) for hatred and wrath.

As for the explicit noun in His saying "*fa-inna Allāh*" (indeed God), although the context calls for a pronoun, it is for the purpose of magnifying (*taʿẓīm*) or generalizing (*taʿmīm*).

His saying ﴿Indeed God chose Adam﴾, etc. When He, glorified is He, finished explaining that the religion that is approved is Islam, and that Muhammad, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, is the Messenger whom no one can truly love God without following, and that the disagreement of the People of the Two Books concerning him was merely out of rebellion against him and envy of him, He began to establish the message of the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, and clarified that he is from the people of the household of prophethood and the source of the message. *Al-iṣṭifāʾ* means choosing.

Al-Zajjaj said: He chose them with prophethood over the worlds of their times. It was also said that the speech is according to an elided genitive construction (*taqdīr muḍāf*), i.e., "He chose the religion of Adam," etc. The meaning of "the worlds" has already been discussed. Adam is singled out for mention because he is the father of mankind, and likewise Noah, for he is the second Adam. As for the family of Abraham, it is because the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, is from them, along with the abundance of prophets among them.

As for the family of ʿImrān, although they are from the family of Abraham, since ʿIsā, peace be upon him, was from them, there is a reason for singling them out for mention. It was also said: the intended meaning of "the family of Abraham" is Abraham himself, and "the family of ʿImrān" is ʿImrān himself.

His saying ﴿offspring, some of them from others﴾: *dhurriyyatan* is in the accusative as a substitute (*badal*) for what precedes it, as said by al-Zajjaj, or in the accusative as a circumstantial (*ḥāl*), as said by al-Akhfash. The explanation of *dhurriyya* has already been given. *Baʿḍuhā min baʿḍ* (some of them from others) is in an accusative position as a qualifier of *dhurriyya*. Its meaning is: descended from one another, branching out, or supporting one another and strengthening each other in religion.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan through several chains, saying: Some people during the time of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, said: "By God, O Muhammad, we love our Lord!" So God revealed ﴿Say: If you love God...﴾, the verse. Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi related a similar report from Yahya ibn Kathir, and Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related a similar report from Ibn Jurayj. Ibn Jarir related from Muhammad ibn Jaʿfar ibn al-Zubayr, regarding His saying ﴿Say: If you love God﴾: that is, if this is your saying about ʿIsā out of love for God and magnifying Him, ﴿then follow me, and God will love you and forgive you your sins﴾, that is, what has passed of your disbelief, ﴿and God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-Darda', regarding His saying: ﴿Say: If you love God, then follow me; God will love you﴾, he said: "upon righteousness, piety, humility, and the lowering of the self." It was also related by al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Abu Nuʿaym, al-Daylami, and Ibn ʿAsakir from him. Ibn ʿAsakir related the like from ʿĀʾisha. Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu Nuʿaym in *al-Ḥilya*, and al-Hakim related from ʿĀʾisha, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, said: "Polytheism is more hidden than the crawling of an ant on a rock on a dark night, and the least of it is that one loves in respect of some injustice and hates in respect of some justice. Is religion anything but love and hatred for the sake of God?" God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say: If you love God...﴾, the verse.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying ﴿the family of Abraham and the family of ʿImrān﴾, he said: They are the believers from the family of Abraham, the family of ʿImrān, the family of Yasin, and the family of Muhammad. ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatada, regarding His saying ﴿offspring, some of them from others﴾, he said: in intention, action, sincerity, and monotheism.

Al-Zajjaj said: He chose them with prophethood over the worlds of their times. It was also said that the speech is according to an elided genitive construction (*taqdīr muḍāf*), i.e., "He chose the religion of Adam," etc. The meaning of "the worlds" has already been discussed. Adam is singled out for mention because he is the father of mankind, and likewise Noah, for he is the second Adam. As for the family of Abraham, it is because the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, is from them, along with the abundance of prophets among them.

As for the family of ʿImrān, although they are from the family of Abraham, since ʿIsā, peace be upon him, was from them, there is a reason for singling them out for mention. It was also said: the intended meaning of "the family of Abraham" is Abraham himself, and "the family of ʿImrān" is ʿImrān himself.

His saying ﴿offspring, some of them from others﴾: *dhurriyyatan* is in the accusative as a substitute (*badal*) for what precedes it, as said by al-Zajjaj, or in the accusative as a circumstantial (*ḥāl*), as said by al-Akhfash. The explanation of *dhurriyya* has already been given. *Baʿḍuhā min baʿḍ* (some of them from others) is in an accusative position as a qualifier of *dhurriyya*. Its meaning is: descended from one another, branching out, or supporting one another and strengthening each other in religion.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan through several chains, saying: Some people during the time of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, said: "By God, O Muhammad, we love our Lord!" Ibn Jarir related from Muhammad ibn Jaʿfar ibn al-Zubayr, regarding His saying ﴿Say: If you love God﴾: that is, if this is your saying about ʿIsā out of love for God and magnifying Him, ﴿then follow me, and God will love you and forgive you your sins﴾, that is, what has passed of your disbelief, ﴿and God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-Darda', regarding His saying: ﴿Say: If you love God, then follow me; God will love you﴾, he said: "upon righteousness, piety, humility, and the lowering of the self." It was also related by al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Abu Nuʿaym, al-Daylami, and Ibn ʿAsakir from him. Ibn ʿAsakir related the like from ʿĀʾisha. Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu Nuʿaym in *al-Ḥilya*, and al-Hakim related from ʿĀʾisha, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, said: "Polytheism is more hidden than the crawling of an ant on a rock on a dark night, and the least of it is that one loves in respect of some injustice and hates in respect of some justice. Is religion anything but love and hatred for the sake of God?" God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say: If you love God...﴾, the verse.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying ﴿the family of Abraham and the family of ʿImrān﴾, he said: They are the believers from the family of Abraham, the family of ʿImrān, the family of Yasin, and the family of Muhammad. ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatada, regarding His saying ﴿offspring, some of them from others﴾, he said: in intention, action, sincerity, and monotheism.

Al-ḥubb and al-maḥabba (love) mean the soul's inclination toward a thing. One says *aḥabbahu*, so he is *muḥibb* (one who loves), and *ḥabbahu yaḥibbuhu* with a kasra in the present tense, so he is *maḥbūb* (one who is loved). Al-Jawhari said: "This is anomalous (*shādhdh*), because the pattern *yafʿilu* with a kasra does not occur in the doubled (*muḍaʿʿaf*) verbs."

Ibn al-Dahhan said: For *ḥabba* there are two dialects, *ḥabba* and *aḥabba*. The root of *ḥabba* in this sense is *ḥababa*, like *ṭaraqa*. The love of God, glorified is He, has been interpreted as the will to obey Him. Al-Azhari said: The love of the servant for God and His Messenger is his obedience to them both and his following of their command, and the love of God for the servants is His bestowing favor upon them through forgiveness. Abu Raja al-ʿUtaridi read *fa-ittabaʿūnī* with a fatḥa on the *bāʾ* (i.e., *fa-ittabaʿūnī* as a verb form with a different vocalization, as recorded).

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verse 35–37:

His saying: ﴿إذْ قالَتِ﴾ [when the wife of ʿImrān said]. Abū ʿAmr said: "idh" is superfluous (zāʾida). Muḥammad ibn Yazīd said: it is connected to an omitted verb, its estimate being "remember when she said." Al-Zajjāj said: it is connected to the word "iṣṭafā" (chose). It was also said: it is connected to His saying "Sami'un ʿalīm" (All-Hearing, All-Knowing). The wife of ʿImrān was named Ḥannah, with an unpointed ḥāʾ (ḥ) and nūn, daughter of Fāqūd ibn Qubayl, mother of Maryam; so she was the grandmother of ʿĪsā. ʿImrān is the son of Māthān, the grandfather of ʿĪsā.

His saying: ﴿رَبِّ إنِّي نَذَرْتُ لَكَ ما في بَطْنِي﴾ [My Lord, I have vowed to You what is in my womb]. The fronting of the prepositional phrase ("laka," to You) is for the sake of emphasis on importance. This vow was permissible in their law. The meaning of "laka" is "for Your worship."

"Muḥarraran" (dedicated) is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl); i.e., freed, purely devoted to God, serving the church. The meaning here is freedom, which is the opposite of slavery. It was also said: the meaning of "muḥarrar" here is one purely devoted to God, Glorified is He, which nothing of worldly affairs mixes with. This was preferred on the grounds that there is no disagreement that ʿImrān and his wife were free.

His saying: ﴿فَتَقَبَّلْ مِنِّي﴾ [so accept from me]. "Taqabbul" is taking a thing with approval; i.e., accept from me my vow with what is in my womb. His saying: ﴿فَلَمّا وضَعَتْها﴾ [And when she gave birth to her]. The feminine pronoun is in accordance with what is known from the context, that what is in her womb is a female; or because it is female in God's knowledge; or by interpreting "what is in her womb" as "the soul" or "the living being" or something similar. His saying: ﴿قالَتْ رَبِّ إنِّي وضَعْتُها أُنْثى﴾ [She said: My Lord, I have given birth to her as a female]. She only said this statement because only a male was accepted in a vow, not a female. So it is as if she was grieved and saddened over what she had lost of that which she had hoped for and expected. "Unthā" is a confirmatory circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun, or a substitute (badal) for it.

His saying: ﴿واللَّهُ أعْلَمُ بِما وضَعَتْ﴾ [And God knows best what she gave birth to]. Abū Bakr and Ibn ʿĀmir read it with a ḍamma on the tāʾ (وضَعْتُ), so it is part of her speech and connected to what precedes it, and in it is the meaning of submission to God, humility, and affirmation of His transcendence that nothing is hidden from Him.

The majority read "waḍaʿat" (وضَعَتْ), so it is from the speech of God, Glorified is He, in a manner of magnifying what she gave birth to, exalting its status, and honouring her, since she experienced grief and sorrow; together with the fact that this female whom she gave birth to, God will make her and her son a sign for the worlds and a lesson for those who take heed, and will single her out with what He has not singled out anyone else with. Ibn ʿAbbās read "bi-mā waḍaʿt" (وضَعْتِ) with a kasra on the tāʾ, as an address from God to her; i.e., you do not know the worth of this gift and what God knows of it of matters that minds fall short of and intellects are bewildered by.

His saying: ﴿ولَيْسَ الذَّكَرُ كالأُنْثى﴾ [And the male is not like the female]. I.e., the male she sought is not like the female she gave birth to, for the utmost of what she wanted from it being male was that it would be a vow serving the church, whereas this female's matter is great and her status magnificent. This sentence is a parenthetical clause clarifying what is in the first sentence of magnifying the subject and raising its status and high rank. The "al" in "al-dhakar" and "al-unthā" is for a known reference; this is according to the reading of the majority and the reading of Ibn ʿAbbās. As for the reading of Abū Bakr and Ibn ʿĀmir, "walaysa al-dhakaru ka-al-unthā" is part of her speech and part of the completion of her grief and sorrow; i.e., the male I wanted to be a servant and fit for vowing is not like the female who is not fit for that, and it is as if she apologised to her Lord for what existed for her contrary to what she intended.

His saying: ﴿وإنِّي سَمَّيْتُها مَرْيَمَ﴾ [And I have named her Maryam]. It is conjoined to "innī waḍaʿtuhā unthā" and her purpose from this announcement of naming is drawing near to God, Glorified is He, and that her deed should correspond to the meaning of her name, for the meaning of Maryam in their language is "servant of the Lord." So even if she is not fit for serving the church, that does not prevent her from being among the female worshippers. His saying: ﴿وإنِّي أُعِيذُها بِكَ وذُرِّيَّتَها مِنَ الشَّيْطانِ الرَّجِيمِ﴾ [And I seek refuge for her in You, and for her offspring, from Satan the accursed]. This is conjoined to His saying "innī sammaytuhā Maryam." "Rajīm" means the expelled, and its origin is the one pelted with stones. She sought protection for her and her child from Satan and his helpers.

His saying: ﴿فَتَقَبَّلَها رَبُّها بِقَبُولٍ حَسَنٍ﴾ [So her Lord accepted her with good acceptance]. I.e., He was pleased with her as a vow, and set her on the path of the fortunate. Some said: the meaning of "taqabbul" is undertaking, nurturing, and taking charge of her affairs; "qabūl" is a verbal noun emphasizing the preceding verb, and the "bā'" is superfluous; the original is "taqabbulan." Similarly His saying: ﴿وأنْبَتَها نَباتًا حَسَنًا﴾ [And He made her grow with a good growth], whose original is "inbātan," so the superfluous letter was deleted. It was also said it is a verbal noun for an omitted verb; i.e., she grew a good growth.

The meaning is that He perfected her creation without excess or deficiency. It was said: she used to grow in a day what a child grows in a year. It was also said it is a metaphor for the good upbringing that benefits her, by which her affairs are set right in all her circumstances.

His saying: ﴿وكَفَّلَها زَكَرِيّا﴾ [And Zakariyyā took charge of her]. I.e., he took her under his care. Abū ʿUbayda said: he undertook the duty of caring for her. The Kufans read "wa-kaffalahā" with shaddah; i.e., God made him her guardian and one committed to her welfare, and its meaning is the same as in Ubayy's codex, "wa-akfalahā."

The rest read with the lightening (تخفيف), attributing the verb to Zakariyyā, and its meaning is what has preceded: that he took her under his care and undertook the duty of looking after her. ʿAmr ibn Mūsā narrated from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Muzanī "wa-kafilahā" with a kasra on the fāʾ. Al-Akhfash said: I have not heard "kafila." Mujāhid read "fa-taqabbalhā" with the lām sukūn as a request and supplication, and put "rabbahā" in the accusative as an annexed vocative. He also read "wa-anbitha" with sukūn on the tāʾ, "wa-kaffilhā" with shaddah on the kasra fāʾ and sukūn on the lām, and "Zakariyyā" in the accusative with madd.

Ḥafs, Ḥamza and al-Kisā'ī read "Zakariyyā" without madd, and the rest read it with madd. Al-Farrā' said: the people of the Ḥijāz pronounce "Zakariyyā" both with and without madd. Al-Akhfash said: it has dialects: madd and qaṣr, and "Zakariyy" with a shaddah on the yā', and this is impermissible under all estimates because of foreignness and definiteness along with the feminine ending (alif).

His saying: ﴿كُلَّما دَخَلَ عَلَيْها زَكَرِيّا المِحْرابَ﴾ [Every time Zakariyyā entered upon her in the sanctuary]. The adverbial phrase was fronted for emphasis on it. The word "kullamā" is an adverb of time, the time is omitted, and "mā" is either verbal (maṣdariyya) or an indefinite qualifying noun; the governing verb in that is "wajada" (he found), i.e., every time he entered upon her he found with her provision, i.e., a kind of provision.

"Miḥrāb" linguistically is the most honoured place in a gathering, as al-Qurṭubī said, and it is accusative by extension (tawassuʿ). It was said: Zakariyyā made for her a sanctuary that one could not ascend to except by a ladder, and he would lock her in until she grew old. Whenever he entered upon her he found with her winter fruit in summer and summer fruit in winter. So he said: ﴿يامَرْيَمُ أنّى لَكِ هَذا﴾ [O Maryam, from where is this for you?], i.e., from where does this provision come to you, which does not resemble the provisions of this world? ﴿قالَتْ هو مِن عِنْدِ اللَّهِ﴾ [She said: It is from God]. So that is not strange or outlandish. The clause ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ يَرْزُقُ مَن يَشاءُ بِغَيْرِ حِسابٍ﴾ [Indeed God provides for whom He wills without reckoning] is explanatory of what precedes it, and it is part of her speech; whoever said it is from Zakariyyā's speech makes the clause a new sentence.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His saying: ﴿إنِّي نَذَرْتُ لَكَ ما في بَطْنِي مُحَرَّرًا﴾ that he said: she had vowed to place him in the church to worship there, and she hoped that he would be male. Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him that he said: she vowed to make him dedicated to worship. ‌ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Mujāhid regarding His saying "muḥarraran" that he said: a servant of the church.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from him that he said: "muḥarraran" means purely devoted, nothing of worldly affairs mixing with it. al-Bukhārī, Muslim and others narrated from Abū Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "No child is born but that Satan touches him when he is born, so he cries out loudly from the touch of Satan, except Maryam and her son." Then Abū Hurayrah said: Recite, if you wish: ﴿وإنِّي أُعِيذُها بِكَ وذُرِّيَّتَها مِنَ الشَّيْطانِ الرَّجِيمِ﴾. There are other wordings of this ḥadīth from Abū Hurayrah, this being one of them, and it has been narrated from other narrators.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Ḥākim, who authenticated it, narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās who said: Zakariyyā took charge of her, and he entered upon her in the sanctuary and found with her grapes in a basket out of season. He said: "From where is this for you?" She said: "It is from God." He said: "Indeed He who provides you with grapes out of season is able to provide me with a child from the old, barren, sterile woman," ﴿هُنالِكَ دَعا زَكَرِيّا رَبَّهُ﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 38]. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Jarīr narrated from Qatādah who said: Maryam was the daughter of their chief and imam, and their rabbis disputed over her, so they drew lots with their arrows as to who would take charge of her; Zakariyyā was the husband of her sister, so he took charge of her, and she was with him and he nurtured her.

al-Bayhaqī in his Sunan narrated similarly from Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās and a group of the Companions. Ibn Jarīr narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding "wa-kaffalahā Zakariyyā" that he said: he placed her with him in his sanctuary.

The majority read "waḍaʿat" (وضَعَتْ), so it is from the speech of God, Glorified is He, in a manner of magnifying what she gave birth to, exalting its status, and honouring her, since she experienced grief and sorrow; together with the fact that this female whom she gave birth to, God will make her and her son a sign for the worlds and a lesson for those who take heed, and will single her out with what He has not singled out anyone else with. Ibn ʿAbbās read "bi-mā waḍaʿt" (وضَعْتِ) with a kasra on the tāʾ, as an address from God to her; i.e., you do not know the worth of this gift and what God knows of it of matters that minds fall short of and intellects are bewildered by.

His saying: ﴿ولَيْسَ الذَّكَرُ كالأُنْثى﴾ [And the male is not like the female]. I.e., the male she sought is not like the female she gave birth to, for the utmost of what she wanted from it being male was that it would be a vow serving the church, whereas this female's matter is great and her status magnificent. This sentence is a parenthetical clause clarifying what is in the first sentence of magnifying the subject and raising its status and high rank. The "al" in "al-dhakar" and "al-unthā" is for a known reference; this is according to the reading of the majority and the reading of Ibn ʿAbbās. As for the reading of Abū Bakr and Ibn ʿĀmir, "walaysa al-dhakaru ka-al-unthā" is part of her speech and part of the completion of her grief and sorrow; i.e., the male I wanted to be a servant and fit for vowing is not like the female who is not fit for that, and it is as if she apologised to her Lord for what existed for her contrary to what she intended.

His saying: ﴿وإنِّي سَمَّيْتُها مَرْيَمَ﴾ [And I have named her Maryam]. It is conjoined to "innī waḍaʿtuhā unthā" and her purpose from this announcement of naming is drawing near to God, Glorified is He, and that her deed should correspond to the meaning of her name, for the meaning of Maryam in their language is "servant of the Lord." So even if she is not fit for serving the church, that does not prevent her from being among the female worshippers. His saying: ﴿وإنِّي أُعِيذُها بِكَ وذُرِّيَّتَها مِنَ الشَّيْطانِ الرَّجِيمِ﴾ [And I seek refuge for her in You, and for her offspring, from Satan the accursed]. This is conjoined to His saying "innī sammaytuhā Maryam." "Rajīm" means the expelled, and its origin is the one pelted with stones. She sought protection for her and her child from Satan and his helpers.

His saying: ﴿فَتَقَبَّلَها رَبُّها بِقَبُولٍ حَسَنٍ﴾ [So her Lord accepted her with good acceptance]. I.e., He was pleased with her as a vow, and set her on the path of the fortunate. Some said: the meaning of "taqabbul" is undertaking, nurturing, and taking charge of her affairs; "qabūl" is a verbal noun emphasizing the preceding verb, and the "bā'" is superfluous; the original is "taqabbulan." Similarly His saying: ﴿وأنْبَتَها نَباتًا حَسَنًا﴾ [And He made her grow with a good growth], whose original is "inbātan," so the superfluous letter was deleted. It was also said it is a verbal noun for an omitted verb; i.e., she grew a good growth.

The meaning is that He perfected her creation without excess or deficiency. It was said: she used to grow in a day what a child grows in a year. It was also said it is a metaphor for the good upbringing that benefits her, by which her affairs are set right in all her circumstances.

His saying: ﴿وكَفَّلَها زَكَرِيّا﴾ [And Zakariyyā took charge of her]. I.e., he took her under his care. Abū ʿUbayda said: he undertook the duty of caring for her. The Kufans read "wa-kaffalahā" with shaddah; i.e., God made him her guardian and one committed to her welfare, and its meaning is the same as in Ubayy's codex, "wa-akfalahā."

The rest read with the lightening (تخفيف), attributing the verb to Zakariyyā, and its meaning is what has preceded: that he took her under his care and undertook the duty of looking after her. ʿAmr ibn Mūsā narrated from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Muzanī "wa-kafilahā" with a kasra on the fāʾ. Al-Akhfash said: I have not heard "kafila." Mujāhid read "fa-taqabbalhā" with the lām sukūn as a request and supplication, and put "rabbahā" in the accusative as an annexed vocative. He also read "wa-anbitha" with sukūn on the tāʾ, "wa-kaffilhā" with shaddah on the kasra fāʾ and sukūn on the lām, and "Zakariyyā" in the accusative with madd.

Ḥafs, Ḥamza and al-Kisā'ī read "Zakariyyā" without madd, and the rest read it with madd. Al-Farrā' said: the people of the Ḥijāz pronounce "Zakariyyā" both with and without madd. Al-Akhfash said: it has dialects: madd and qaṣr, and "Zakariyy" with a shaddah on the yā', and this is impermissible under all estimates because of foreignness and definiteness along with the feminine ending (alif).

His saying: ﴿كُلَّما دَخَلَ عَلَيْها زَكَرِيّا المِحْرابَ﴾ [Every time Zakariyyā entered upon her in the sanctuary]. The adverbial phrase was fronted for emphasis on it. The word "kullamā" is an adverb of time, the time is omitted, and "mā" is either verbal (maṣdariyya) or an indefinite qualifying noun; the governing verb in that is "wajada" (he found), i.e., every time he entered upon her he found with her provision, i.e., a kind of provision.

"Miḥrāb" linguistically is the most honoured place in a gathering, as al-Qurṭubī said, and it is accusative by extension (tawassuʿ). It was said: Zakariyyā made for her a sanctuary that one could not ascend to except by a ladder, and he would lock her in until she grew old. Whenever he entered upon her he found with her winter fruit in summer and summer fruit in winter. So he said: ﴿يامَرْيَمُ أنّى لَكِ هَذا﴾ [O Maryam, from where is this for you?], i.e., from where does this provision come to you, which does not resemble the provisions of this world? ﴿قالَتْ هو مِن عِنْدِ اللَّهِ﴾ [She said: It is from God]. So that is not strange or outlandish. Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His saying: ﴿إنِّي نَذَرْتُ لَكَ ما في بَطْنِي مُحَرَّرًا﴾ that he said: she had vowed to place him in the church to worship there, and she hoped that he would be male. Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him that he said: she vowed to make him dedicated to worship. ‌ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Mujāhid regarding His saying "muḥarraran" that he said: a servant of the church.
