The likeness of Jesus to Adam, in that he was created without a father as Adam was. That the compared thing (al-mushabbah bihi) includes an additional feature does not undermine the comparison: Adam had no mother either, just as he had no father. That is a matter outside the point of the comparison, even though the thing compared to is more extraordinary, more wonderful, and more striking in its expression than what is being compared. His saying ﴿He created him from dust﴾ is a clause explaining what was left vague in the parable, namely that Adam had neither a father nor a mother, but Allah created him from dust. This also answers those who denied the creation of Jesus without a father while acknowledging that Adam was created without either father or mother.

His saying ﴿Then He said to him, "Be," and he was﴾ means: "Be a human being," and he was a human being.

His saying "fa-yakunu" (and he was) is a report of a past state, and its explanation has already been given. His saying ﴿The truth is from your Lord﴾: al-Farra' said it is in the nominative by an implied "huwa" (it). Abu 'Ubayda said it is a new sentence, and its predicate is "from your Lord." It was also said that it is the subject of a deleted verb, meaning: "The truth has come to you from your Lord." His saying ﴿So do not be among the doubters﴾: the address is either to everyone among the people who is fit for it, meaning "let none of you be a doubter," or it is addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ). The prohibition to him is for the sake of greater reinforcement, since no doubt would ever come from him about this.

His saying ﴿Whoever argues with you about it﴾: although this is general in wording, what is meant is particular, namely the Christians who came to him (ﷺ) from Najran, as will be explained later. It is possible to say that it is general in application even though the occasion of revelation was specific. It therefore indicates the permissibility of mubahala (a mutual invocation of divine curse, a form of ritual challenge) for him (ﷺ) against anyone who argues with him about Jesus (peace be upon him), and his community follows his example. The pronoun "fihi" (about it) refers to Jesus. What is meant here by "the knowledge coming" is the coming of its cause, which is the clear signs. Al-muhajjah means dispute and argument.

His saying ("Come") means: come forward and approach. Its original sense is a request for the persons to approach, and it is used for opinion when the addressee is present, as you say to someone who is with you: "Come, let us look into this matter."

His saying ("Let us call our sons") and so on. Mention of the sons is given without the daughters, either because the women are included in the word "nisa'" (women), or because it is the sons who attend the scenes of dispute rather than the women. The meaning of the verse is: each of us and you should call their sons, their women, and themselves to mubahala. In this there is evidence that the sons of daughters are called sons, since the Prophet (ﷺ) meant by "sons" al-Hasanayn (the two grandsons), as will be explained later.

His saying ("Let us invoke") : the original meaning of ibtihal (earnest invocation) is striving in supplication, including invoking curse and other things. One says "bahalahu Allah," meaning Allah cursed him, and al-bahl means curse. Abu 'Ubayd and al-Kisa'i said: "nabtahil" means "let us invoke curses upon one another." It is also used for striving toward destruction, and from it is the verse of Labid:

*Among the chiefs, the lords of his people, upon whom fate looked and then destroyed them.*

That is, it strove for their destruction.

In al-Kashshaf it is said: then it was used for every supplication in which one strives earnestly, even if it is not a mutual curse. His saying ﴿Then let us lay the curse of Allah upon the liars﴾ is a conjunction with "nabtahil," explaining its meaning.

His saying: "Indeed, this" means: what Allah related to His Messenger about the account of Jesus ﴿is indeed the true narrative﴾. Al-qasas means succession, as one says: "So-and-so follows (yaqussu) the trace of so-and-so," meaning he follows him. It is then applied to speech in which one part follows another. The separating pronoun (damir al-fasl) is for restriction, and the entry of the particle of emphasis (al-lam) upon it is for additional emphasis. It is permissible for it to be the subject, with what follows being its predicate. The insertion of "min" in His saying ﴿there is no god but Allah﴾ is for emphasizing the generality, and this is a refutation of those Christians who held the doctrine of the Trinity.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others have narrated from Hudhayfah: "That al-'Aqib and al-Sayyid came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he intended to invoke a mutual curse upon them. One of them said to his companion: 'Do not invoke a curse upon him, for by Allah, if he is a prophet and he invokes a curse upon us, we shall never prosper, neither we nor our descendants after us.' They said to him: 'We will give you what you asked. Send with us a trustworthy man.' He said: 'Stand up, O Abu 'Ubayda.' When he stood, he said: 'This is the trustworthy one of this community.'"

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas: "A delegation from the people of Najran came to the Prophet (ﷺ), and among them were al-Sayyid and al-'Aqib. They said: 'What is your concern, mentioning our companion?' He said: 'Who is he?' They said: 'Jesus. You claim that he is the servant of Allah.' They said: 'Have you seen the like of Jesus, or have you been informed of him?' Then they left from his presence. Then Gabriel came and said: 'Say to them when they come to you: "Indeed, the likeness of Jesus with Allah is like the likeness of Adam"' up to the end of the verse." This story has been narrated in various forms from a number of the Successors (tabi'un).

Al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il narrated from Jabir, who said: "Al-'Aqib and al-Sayyid came to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he invited them to Islam. They said: 'We have submitted, O Muhammad.' He said: 'You are lying. If you wish, I will tell you what prevents you from Islam.' They said: 'Speak.' He said: 'Love of the cross, drinking wine, and eating the flesh of swine.' Jabir said: He then invited them to mutual cursing (mula'anah), and they agreed to meet him the next day. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out in the morning, took hold of the hand of 'Ali, Fatimah, al-Hasan and al-Husayn, and then sent for them, but they refused to answer and admitted (their rejection). He said: 'By Him who sent me with the truth, if they had done it, the valley would have rained fire upon them.' Jabir said: It was about them that ﴿Come, let us call our sons﴾ up to the end of the verse was revealed."

Jabir said: "Ourselves and yourselves" refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and 'Ali; "our sons" refers to al-Hasan and al-Husayn; "our women" refers to Fatimah. Al-Hakim also narrated it from another route from Jabir and authenticated it, and in it they said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Is it acceptable to you that we curse you (mutually)?"

Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: "When this verse ﴿Say: Come﴾ was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called 'Ali, Fatimah, Hasan and Husayn, and said: 'O Allah, these are my family (ahl).'"

Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Ja'far ibn Muhammad from his father, regarding ﴿Come, let us call our sons﴾ up to the end of the verse, that he said: "He brought Abu Bakr and his son, 'Umar and his son, 'Uthman and his son, and 'Ali and his son."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through Ibn Jurayj from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿then let us invoke﴾ that it means "let us strive (in supplication)."

Al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "This is the sincerity (al-ikhlas)," pointing with his finger next to the thumb, "and this is the supplication," and he raised his hands level with his shoulders, "and this is the ibtihal," and he raised his hands outstretched.

Al-Shawkani, *Fath al-Qadir*, on Surah 3, verse 64:

It has been said: the address is to the people of Najran, as indicated by what precedes this verse. It has also been said: it is to the Jews of Medina. And it has been said: it is to the Jews and Christians together, which is the apparent sense of the Qur'anic wording. There is no basis for restricting it to some of them, since this is a general call that is not specific to those who disputed with the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Al-sawa' (the equitable word, the common ground) means justice ('adl).

Al-Farra' said: It is said in meaning that 'adl can be *siwan* and *sawa'*. If you pronounce the *sin* with a fatha, you lengthen it (*sawa'*); if you pronounce it with a damma or a kasra, you shorten it (*siwan*). Zuhayr said:

*"I irrigate a plot in which there is no wrong, and its plants are watered by the equitable rain within it."*

In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: *"to a word of justice between us and you."* The meaning is: come to what you have been called to, which is the just and upright word in which there is no deviation from the truth. He explained it with His saying: ﴿That we worship none but God﴾. This phrase is in the genitive position as an apposition (*badal*) to *kalimah* (word), or in the nominative position by implying a subject (*mubtada'*), i.e., it is: that we do not worship. It is also permissible for *an* to be explanatory (*mufassirah*), in which case the clause it introduces has no grammatical position.

His saying: ﴿And that some of us do not take others as lords﴾ is a rebuke to those who believed in the lordship of the Messiah and 'Uzayr, and an indication that these are of the human kind and among its members. It is also a censure of those who imitate men in the religion of God, permitting what they permit and forbidding what they forbid. Whoever does this has indeed taken the one he imitates as a lord. From this is His saying: ﴿They took their rabbis and their monks as lords besides God﴾ [al-Tawbah: 84]. Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' permitted the jussive (*jazm*) in *wa-la nushrika* and *wa-la yattakhidha* by way of assumed (*tawahhum*) analogy.

His saying: ﴿But if they turn away﴾, that is, if they turn away from what they were called to, ﴿then say: Bear witness that we are Muslims﴾, that is: submitting to His rulings, content with Him, acknowledging what God has bestowed upon us of this upright religion.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and al-Nasa'i reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Abu Sufyan told me that Heraclius (Hiraql) called for the letter of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and read it. In it was: *In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. From Muhammad, the Messenger of God, to Heraclius, the great one of the Romans: Peace be upon him who follows guidance. To proceed: I call you with the call of Islam. Embrace Islam and you will be safe; God will give you your reward twice. But if you turn away, the sin of the Arisiyyin (peasants/subjects) will be upon you. "O People of the Scripture, come to a word that is common between us and you," up to His saying: "that we are Muslims."*"

Al-Tabarani reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the letter of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to the disbelievers contained: ﴿Come to a word﴾, the verse.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Jurayj, who said: "It reached me that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) called the Jews of Medina to what is in this verse, but they refused him, so he fought them until they acknowledged the *jizya* (poll tax)."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Qatadah, who said: "It was mentioned to us that the Prophet (ﷺ) called the Jews of Medina to the common word." Ibn Jarir reported similarly from al-Rabi'.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Qatadah concerning ﴿to a word common between us and you﴾, he said: "Just (*'adl*)." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported the like from al-Rabi'.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jurayj concerning His saying: ﴿And that some of us do not take others as lords﴾, he said: "That some of us do not obey others in disobedience to God." It is also said: that lordship is that people obey their masters and leaders in what is not worship, even if they do not pray to them. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from 'Ikrimah concerning His saying: ﴿And that some of us do not take others as lords﴾, he said: "It is the prostration of some of them to others."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verses 65–68:

When each of the two groups, the Jews and the Christians, claimed that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was upon their religion, Allah, glorified is He, refuted that claim against them and made clear that the Jewish religion (al-milla al-yahudiyya) and the Christian religion (al-milla al-nasraniyya) came into being only after him. Al-Zajjaj said: "This verse is the clearest proof against the Jews and the Christians that the Torah and the Gospel were revealed after him, and neither of them contains the name of any of the religions, while the name Islam is in every book." End of quotation.

But this is open to question. The Gospel is full of verses from the Torah and of mention of the law of Musa, and of arguing with it against the Jews. Likewise the Psalms contain, in many places, mention of the law of Musa, and at its beginning there is good news of Isa. Furthermore, the Torah mentions many of the earlier laws. Everyone who knows these revealed books recognises this. The scholars have differed over the length of the period between Ibrahim and Musa, and the period between Musa and Isa.

Al-Qurtubi said: It is said that between Ibrahim and Musa there were a thousand years, and between Musa and Isa there were two thousand years. Likewise in al-Kashshaf.

His saying: ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ means: will you not reflect on the refutation of your argument and the falsehood of your claim?

His saying: ﴿Here you are, you are those who argued about what you have knowledge of﴾. The original form of "ha antum" is "a antum"; the first hamza was changed into a ha because it is a cognate of it (ukhtuha). This was said by Abu Amr ibn al-Ala' and al-Akhfash.

Al-Nahhas said: This is a good view. Qunbul recited "hantum". It is also said that the ha is an interjection (li-l-tanbih) that enters the sentence that follows it; i.e., "Here you are, these foolish people, you argued", and in "ha'ulaa" there are two dialects: the lengthened (al-madd) and the shortened (al-qasr).

What is meant by "what you have knowledge of" is what was in the Torah, even though they opposed its requirement and disputed about it with falsehood. What they have no knowledge of is their claim that Ibrahim was upon their religion, due to their ignorance of the time in which he lived. The verse is evidence for the prohibition of disputing with falsehood. Rather, encouragement to abandon disputation even by one who is right has come, as in the hadith: "Whoever abandons argument, even when he is right, I guarantee him a house in the outskirts of Paradise."

Disputing in the best manner has been permitted, due to His saying: ﴿And argue with them in the best manner﴾ [al-Nahl: 125], ﴿And do not argue with the People of the Book except in the best manner﴾ [al-Ankabut: 46], and similar. So its permissibility should be restricted to the situations in which the benefit of doing it outweighs the harm, or to the situations in which the argument is conducted with gentleness rather than harshness.

His saying: ﴿And Allah knows﴾ means He knows every thing, and so this includes what they argued with. The explanation of "hanif" has already been given.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, the people most worthy of Ibrahim﴾ means: the ones most entitled to him and most specially connected to him are ﴿those who followed him﴾, who adhered to his religion and imitated his faith; ﴿and this Prophet﴾, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ), whom He singled out for mention to glorify and honour him. His (ﷺ) being most worthy of Ibrahim is both by way of his being of Ibrahim's descendants and by way of his agreement with Ibrahim's religion in much of the law, and ﴿those who believed﴾ are the community of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Christians of Najran and the rabbis of the Jews gathered before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and disputed in his presence. The rabbis said: "Ibrahim was none other than a Jew," and the Christians said: "Ibrahim was none other than a Christian." So there was revealed concerning them ("O People of the Book, why do you argue about Ibrahim") — the verse. Something similar has been related from a group of the early generations (al-salaf).

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu al-Aliyah regarding ﴿Here you are, you are those who argued about what you have knowledge of﴾, that he said: "about what you witnessed, saw and observed," ﴿So why do you argue about what you have no knowledge of﴾, he said: "about what you did not witness, did not see and did not observe." Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported similarly from Qatada.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Suddi concerning the verse, that he said: "As for what they have knowledge of, it is what was forbidden to them and what they were commanded. As for what they have no knowledge of, it is the matter of Ibrahim." Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Hasan, who said: "One who argues with knowledge is excused; one who argues with ignorance is not excused."

Ibn Jarir reported from him, from al-Sha'bi, regarding His saying ﴿Ibrahim was not﴾, that he said: "Allah refuted them and dismissed their argument." He also reported similarly from al-Rabi'.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported similarly from Muqatil ibn Hibban. Abd ibn Humayd reported through the route of Shahr ibn Hawshab, who said: "Ibn Ghanm related to me that when the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out to the Negus, he mentioned their story with him and what they said to him when Amr ibn al-As said to him: 'They revile Isa'; and it is a well-known story." Then he said: "So there was revealed on that day, their dispute before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was in Medina: ﴿Indeed, the people most worthy of Ibrahim﴾ — the verse."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, reported from Ibn Mas'ud that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Every prophet has allies (wulat) among the prophets, and my ally among them is my father Khalil (Ibrahim) — my Lord's friend," then he recited ﴿Indeed, the people most worthy of Ibrahim﴾ — the verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Hakam ibn Mina' that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O assembly of Quraysh, indeed the people most worthy of the Prophet are the God-fearing (al-muttaqun), so be you the way to that. Take care that people do not come to me bearing deeds while you come to me bearing this world, so that I turn my face away from you." Then he recited to them: ﴿Indeed, the people most worthy of Ibrahim﴾ — the verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Hasan concerning the verse that he said: "Every believer is an ally (wali) of Ibrahim, of those who passed away and of those who remain."

Take care that people do not come to me bearing deeds while you come to me bearing this world, so that I turn my face away from you." Then he recited to them: ﴿Indeed, the people most worthy of Ibrahim﴾ — the verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Hasan concerning the verse that he said: "Every believer is an ally (wali) of Ibrahim, of those who passed away and of those who remain."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verses 65–68:

When each of the two groups, the Jews and the Christians, claimed that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was upon their religion, Allah, glorified is He, refuted that claim against them and made clear that the Jewish religion (al-milla al-yahudiyya) and the Christian religion (al-milla al-nasraniyya) came into being only after him. Al-Zajjaj said: "This verse is the clearest proof against the Jews and the Christians that the Torah and the Gospel were revealed after him, and neither of them contains the name of any of the religions, while the name Islam is in every book." End of quotation.

But this is open to question. The Gospel is full of verses from the Torah and of mention of the law of Musa, and of arguing with it against the Jews. Likewise the Psalms contain, in many places, mention of the law of Musa, and at its beginning there is good news of Isa. Furthermore, the Torah mentions many of the earlier laws. Everyone who knows these revealed books recognises this. The scholars have differed over the length of the period between Ibrahim and Musa, and the period between Musa and Isa.

Al-Qurtubi said: It is said that between Ibrahim and Musa there were a thousand years, and between Musa and Isa there were two thousand years. Likewise in al-Kashshaf.

(p. 225) The "group of the People of the Book" (al-Ta'ifah min Ahl al-Kitab) refers to the Jews of Banu al-Nadir, Banu Qurayzah and Banu Qaynuqa', when they invited a group of the Muslims to their religion, and this will come later. It is also said that it refers to all the People of the Book, in which case "min" (from) is explanatory (li-bayan al-jins, "to specify the kind").

His saying ﴿and they lead astray none but themselves﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah), indicating the firmness of the believers in faith, so that the harm of whoever intends to tempt them returns only upon himself. By "the signs of Allah" is meant what is in their books of the proofs of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿While you witness﴾ means what is in your books of that, or that you bear witness to the like of it from the signs of the prophets whose prophethood you acknowledge. Or the meaning is concealing all the signs out of obstinacy, while you know that they are true.

"Confusing the truth with falsehood" (labs al-haqq bi'l-batil) means mixing it with what they deliberately distort. ﴿While you know﴾ is a circumstantial clause.

His saying ﴿And a group of the People of the Book said﴾: they were their leaders and nobles, who said this statement to the common people among their folk. "The face of the day" (wajh al-nahar) is its beginning, and it was called "face" because it is its best part. He (the poet) said:

"And it shines at the face of the day, luminous, like a pearl of the sea whose string has been drawn out."

It is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarf). They commanded them to this in order to introduce doubt among the believers, because they believed that the People of the Book possess knowledge; so when they disbelieved after believing, doubt would fall upon others and seize them, while they did not know that Allah had made firm the hearts of the believers and established their feet, so the rumours of Allah's enemies do not shake them, nor does the wind of the obstinate move them.

His saying ﴿And do not believe except in one who follows your religion﴾ is from the speech of the Jews to one another; that is, the leaders said this to the common people: do not give true belief except to one who follows your religion, the community to which you belong. As for others who have become Muslim, they displayed belief to them as deception ﴿the face of the day, and disbelieve at its end﴾, in order to lead them into temptation. His saying ﴿that anyone be given the like of what you were given﴾, according to this, is connected to an omitted element; that is, you did that so that anyone would be given the like of what you were given: meaning that the envy and rebellion within you, that anyone be given the like of what you were given of the excellence of knowledge and the Book, prompted you to say what you said.

His saying ﴿or they argue with you﴾ is coordinated with "that anyone be given"; that is, do not believe with true belief and do not affirm what is in your breasts with sincere affirmation except to one who follows your religion. You did that and planned it so that the Muslims would argue with you before Allah on the Day of Resurrection with the truth. His saying ﴿Indeed, guidance is the guidance of Allah﴾ is a parenthetical clause (jumlah i'tiradiyyah).

Al-Akhfash said: the meaning is "And do not believe except in one who follows your religion, and do not believe that anyone be given the like of what you were given, and do not affirm that they argue with you." He went to the view that it is coordinated. It is also said: the meaning is "Do not believe, at the face of the day, and disbelieve at its end, except in one who follows your religion"; that is, one who entered Islam and was of your religion before his Islam, because the Islam of those who were from among them is what killed them with rage and caused them to die of grief and sorrow. According to this, his saying "that anyone be given" is connected to an omitted element, as in the first case.

It is also said that his saying "that anyone be given" is connected to his saying "do not believe," meaning do not manifest your belief, ﴿that anyone be given the like of what you were given﴾; that is, keep secret your affirmation that the Muslims have been given from the books of Allah the like of what you were given, and do not disclose it except to the followers of your religion. It is also said: the meaning is "And do not believe except in one who follows your religion, that anyone be given the like of what they were given." In this case, "that" and what follows it are in the nominative position as a subject (mubtada'), and the predicate (khabar) is omitted, its estimated form being "you affirm this." It is permissible that it be in the accusative position, with an omitted verb estimated as "you affirm that anyone be given."

Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin and Humayd recited "a'n yu'ta" with the elongated alif (i.e., "an" as an interrogative/emphatic variant). Al-Khalil said: "an" is in the genitive position, with an omitted governing particle.

Ibn Juraij said: the meaning is "And do not believe except in one who follows your religion, out of dislike that anyone be given." It is also said the meaning is: do not inform (the Muslims) of what is in your Book concerning the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) except to one who follows your religion, lest that become a cause for the belief of others in Muhammad (ﷺ). Al-Farra' said: it is possible that the speech of the Jews ended at his saying ﴿except in one who follows your religion﴾, then He said to Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿Say: indeed, guidance is the guidance of Allah﴾; that is, the true explanation is the explanation of Allah, who made clear that no one should be given the like of what you were given, on the assumption of a negative "la" (not), like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah makes clear to you that you may not go astray﴾ [al-Nisa': 176], that is, lest you go astray. The "aw" (or) in His saying ﴿or they argue with you﴾ means "until" (hatta), and so said al-Kisa'i. According to al-Akhfash it is coordinating, as was mentioned earlier.

It is also said: "guidance of Allah" is an apposition (badal) for "guidance," and "that anyone be given" is the predicate of "indeed" (inna), with the meaning: "Say: indeed the guidance of Allah is that anyone be given the like of what you were given." It has been said that this verse is the most difficult of the verses of this surah in its interpretation, and that is correct.

Al-Hasan recited "yu'ti" with a kasrah on the upper ta' (i.e., "yu'ti" as the verb in the active form with the second person address, read with kasrah). Sa'id ibn Jubayr recited "in yu'ta" with a kasrah on the hamzah, taking it as the negative particle "in" (not).

His saying ﴿He singles out for His mercy whom He wills﴾: it is said this is prophethood, and it is said it is more general than that. It is a refutation of them and a rejection of what they said and planned. Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Sufyan, who said: "Everything in Al 'Imran that mentions the People of the Book refers to the Christians." This is refuted by the fact that many of the addresses to the People of the Book mentioned in this surah cannot be applied to the Christians at all, and among them are these verses that we are now explaining, for the group that wished to lead the Muslims astray, and likewise the group saying ﴿Believe in what has been revealed to those who believed, at the face of the day﴾ are from the Jews specifically.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Qatadah concerning His saying ﴿O People of the Book, why do you disbelieve in the signs of Allah while you witness﴾ that he said: "You witness that the description of the Prophet of Allah Muhammad is in your book; then you disbelieve in him and deny him, and you do not believe in him, while you find him written with you in the Torah and the Gospel, the unlettered Prophet." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded the same from al-Rabi'. They also recorded the like of it from al-Suddi, and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded something similar from Muqatil.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn Juraij concerning ﴿while you witness﴾ that it is "that the religion with Allah is Islam; there is no religion with Allah other than it." They (Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim) also recorded from al-Rabi' concerning His saying ﴿Why do you confuse the truth with falsehood﴾: he said: "You mix Judaism and Christianity with Islam, while you know that the religion of Allah, which He does not accept from anyone other than it, is Islam." ﴿And you conceal the truth﴾: he said: "You conceal the matter of Muhammad while you find him written with you in the Torah and the Gospel." Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir recorded the like of it from Qatadah.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Abdullah ibn al-Sayf, Adi ibn Zayd and al-Harith ibn 'Awf said to one another: 'Come, let us believe in what has been revealed to Muhammad and his companions in the morning, and disbelieve in it in the evening, until we confuse their religion for them, perhaps they will do as we do and turn back from their religion.' So Allah revealed concerning them: ﴿O People of the Book, why do you confuse the truth with falsehood﴾ up to His saying ﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾." Something similar has been related from a group of the early generation (al-salaf).

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah recorded through the route of Abu Zabyan from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿And a group said﴾, the verse, that he said: "They used to be with them at the beginning of the day, sitting with them and speaking with them; then when they reached the evening and the prayer time came, they disbelieved in it and abandoned it." Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Qatadah concerning His saying ﴿And do not believe except in one who follows your religion﴾ that he said: "This is the saying of some of them to others." Ibn Jarir recorded the like of it from al-Rabi', and also recorded something similar from al-Suddi.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Mujahid concerning ﴿that anyone be given the like of what you were given﴾: out of envy from the Jews that prophethood should be in others besides them, and their desire that they (the others) be made to follow their religion. Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Abu Malik and Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning ﴿that anyone be given the like of what you were given﴾ that he said: "It is the community of Muhammad (ﷺ)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from al-Suddi that Allah said to Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿Indeed, guidance is the guidance of Allah, that anyone be given the like of what you were given﴾, (addressing) O community of Muhammad, ﴿or they argue with you before your Lord﴾. The Jews say: "Allah has done such and such honour to us, until He sent down upon us the manna and the quail. So if what I have given you is superior, then say: ﴿Say: indeed, bounty is in the hand of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills﴾."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Qatadah concerning ﴿Say: indeed, guidance is the guidance of Allah, that anyone be given the like of what you were given﴾ that he said: "When Allah sent down a Book like your Book and sent a prophet like your prophet, you envied them for that, ﴿Say: indeed, bounty is in the hand of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills﴾."

Ibn Jarir recorded the like of it from al-Rabi'. Ibn Jarir recorded from Ibn Juraij concerning ﴿Say: indeed, guidance is the guidance of Allah, that anyone be given the like of what you were given﴾ that he said: "This is the matter with which Allah has bestowed favour: ﴿that anyone be given the like of what you were given, or they argue with you before your Lord﴾." He said: "Some of them said to others: 'Do not inform them of what Allah has made clear to you in His Book,' ﴿so that they may argue with you﴾," he said: "so that they may dispute with you, ﴿before your Lord﴾, so that they would have a proof against you." ﴿Say: indeed, bounty is in the hand of Allah﴾, he said: "It is Islam." ﴿He singles out for His mercy whom He wills﴾, he said: "It is the Qur'an and Islam."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Mujahid concerning ﴿He singles out for His mercy whom He wills﴾ that he said: "It is prophethood." Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from al-Hasan who said: "His mercy is Islam, with which He singles out whom He wills."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verses 79–80:

Meaning: it is not fitting nor proper for a human being to say this statement while possessing that attribute. In it is a clarification from Allah, glorified is He, to His servants that the Christians fabricated against Jesus, peace be upon him, what was not authentically transmitted from him, and it is not fitting that he should say it. And "al-hukm" (judgment, wisdom) means understanding and knowledge.

His saying: ﴿But be ones who are rabbaniyyin﴾ — i.e., rather, the Prophet would say: "Be rabbaniyyin." The rabbani (ribbi, one devoted to the Lord) is a relative noun derived from "rabb" (Lord) with the addition of the alif and nun for emphasis (mubalagha), as one says of a man with a large beard "lihyani," of one with a great quantity "jammani," and of one with a thick neck "raqbani." It has been said: the rabbani is one who trains people in the minor aspects of knowledge before its major aspects, as if he emulates the Lord, glorified is He, in facilitating matters. Al-Mubarrad said: the rabbaniyyun are masters of knowledge; its singular is rabbani, from the verb "rabbahu, yurabbihi, fa-huwa rabban," meaning when he manages and reforms him, and the ya' is for the relative (nisba). So the meaning of rabbani is one who knows the religion of the Lord, strong, adhering to obedience to Allah. It has also been said: the knowledgeable and wise one.

His saying: ﴿by what you have been teaching﴾ — i.e., because of your being knowledgeable; that is, be rabbaniyyin by this cause. For the attainment of knowledge by a person and his studying of it result in rabbaniyya, which is teaching knowledge and strength in adhering to the obedience of Allah. Ibn 'Abbas and the people of Kufa read ﴿bima kuntum tu'allimun﴾ with tashdid (doubling of the 'ayn, from ʿallama).

Abu 'Amr and the people of Medina read it with takhfif (without doubling, from ʿalima / darasa-type form), and Abu 'Ubayd chose the first reading. He said: "Because it combines both meanings." Makki said: "The tashdid is more eloquent, because the knowledgeable person may be knowledgeable without being a teacher; the tashdid indicates both knowledge and teaching, whereas the takhfif indicates only knowledge." Abu Hatim chose the second reading.

Abu 'Amr said: "Its corroboration is ﴿tadrusun﴾ (you study) with takhfif rather than tashdid," and he concluded. The summary is that whoever reads with tashdid is obliged to interpret rabbani as something beyond knowledge and teaching, namely that he be together with that sincere, or wise, or forbearing, so that the causality becomes evident; and whoever reads with takhfif may interpret rabbani as the scholar who teaches people, so the meaning becomes: be teachers because you are scholars and because you study knowledge.

In this verse is the greatest incentive for whoever teaches to act, and among the greatest acts of acting upon knowledge is teaching it and sincerity to Allah, glorified is He.

His saying: ﴿Nor would He command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords﴾

With the accusative (naṣb), coordinated with "thumma yaqula" (then he would say); and "wa-la" is extra for emphasis of negation. That is: it is not for him to command the worship of himself, nor to command taking the angels and prophets as lords, but rather he forbids it. It is also permissible to coordinate it with "an yu'tiyahu" (that He should give him), meaning: it was not for a human that he should command you to take the angels and prophets as lords. Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and Hamza read with naṣb, while the rest read with raf' (nominative), as a new and separate sentence from the first discourse; that is: "Nor would Allah command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords." This is supported by the fact that in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud it reads "wa-lan yaʾmurakum" (and he will never command you).

The hamza in His saying ﴿a-yaʾmurukum﴾ (would He command you?) is for denying what was negated of humans. Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verses 79–80:

Meaning: it is not fitting nor proper for a human being to say this statement while possessing that attribute. In it is a clarification from Allah, glorified is He, to His servants that the Christians fabricated against Jesus, peace be upon him, what was not authentically transmitted from him, and it is not fitting that he should say it. And "al-hukm" (judgment, wisdom) means understanding and knowledge.

His saying: ﴿But be ones who are rabbaniyyin﴾ — i.e., rather, the Prophet would say: "Be rabbaniyyin." The rabbani (ribbi, one devoted to the Lord) is a relative noun derived from "rabb" (Lord) with the addition of the alif and nun for emphasis (mubalagha), as one says of a man with a large beard "lihyani," of one with a great quantity "jammani," and of one with a thick neck "raqbani." It has been said: the rabbani is one who trains people in the minor aspects of knowledge before its major aspects, as if he emulates the Lord, glorified is He, in facilitating matters. Al-Mubarrad said: the rabbaniyyun are masters of knowledge; its singular is rabbani, from the verb "rabbahu, yurabbihi, fa-huwa rabban," meaning when he manages and reforms him, and the ya' is for the relative (nisba). So the meaning of rabbani is one who knows the religion of the Lord, strong, adhering to obedience to Allah. It has also been said: the knowledgeable and wise one.

His saying: ﴿by what you have been teaching﴾ — i.e., because of your being knowledgeable; that is, be rabbaniyyin by this cause. For the attainment of knowledge by a person and his studying of it result in rabbaniyya, which is teaching knowledge and strength in adhering to the obedience of Allah. Ibn 'Abbas and the people of Kufa read ﴿bima kuntum tu'allimun﴾ with tashdid (doubling of the 'ayn, from ʿallama).

Abu 'Amr and the people of Medina read it with takhfif (without doubling, from ʿalima / darasa-type form), and Abu 'Ubayd chose the first reading. He said: "Because it combines both meanings." Makki said: "The tashdid is more eloquent, because the knowledgeable person may be knowledgeable without being a teacher; the tashdid indicates both knowledge and teaching, whereas the takhfif indicates only knowledge." Abu Hatim chose the second reading.

Abu 'Amr said: "Its corroboration is ﴿tadrusun﴾ (you study) with takhfif rather than tashdid," and he concluded. The summary is that whoever reads with tashdid is obliged to interpret rabbani as something beyond knowledge and teaching, namely that he be together with that sincere, or wise, or forbearing, so that the causality becomes evident; and whoever reads with takhfif may interpret rabbani as the scholar who teaches people, so the meaning becomes: be teachers because you are scholars and because you study knowledge.

In this verse is the greatest incentive for whoever teaches to act, and among the greatest acts of acting upon knowledge is teaching it and sincerity to Allah, glorified is He.

His saying: ﴿Nor would He command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords﴾

With the accusative (naṣb), coordinated with "thumma yaqula" (then he would say); and "wa-la" is extra for emphasis of negation. That is: it is not for him to command the worship of himself, nor to command taking the angels and prophets as lords, but rather he forbids it. It is also permissible to coordinate it with "an yu'tiyahu" (that He should give him), meaning: it was not for a human that he should command you to take the angels and prophets as lords. Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and Hamza read with naṣb, while the rest read with raf' (nominative), as a new and separate sentence from the first discourse; that is: "Nor would Allah command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords." This is supported by the fact that in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud it reads "wa-lan yaʾmurakum" (and he will never command you).

Al-Shawkani, *Fath al-Qadir*, commentary on Surah Al ʿImran, verses 81–82:

There is disagreement over the meaning of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when God took the covenant of the Prophets﴾. Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, Tawus, al-Hasan and al-Suddi said: God took the covenant of the prophets that each of them would affirm the faith of the others and would command one another to do so. This is the meaning of supporting him and believing in him, and it is the apparent sense of the verse. Its upshot is that God took the covenant from the earlier prophets that they would believe in what the later one brought and support him.

Al-Kisa'i said: it is possible that the meaning of ﴿And when God took the covenant of the Prophets﴾ is "And when God took the covenant of those who are with the Prophets." This is supported by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "And when God took the covenant of those who were given the Book" (wa-idh akhadha Allahu mithaqa alladhina utu al-kitab). It has also been said that there is an ellipsis (hadhf) in the speech. The meaning is: "And when God took the covenant of the Prophets: 'Whatever I have given you of Book and wisdom, then (there will come to you a Messenger confirming what is with you), you will surely believe in him and surely support him.'" This ellipsis is indicated by His words: ﴿And have you accepted My burden on that condition?﴾ and by the word in His words ﴿what I have given you﴾ which means "that which" (alladhi).

Sibawayh said: I asked al-Khalil about His words, ﴿And when God took the covenant of the Prophets, [saying] "Whatever I have given you"﴾, and he said: "ma" here means "alladhi" (that which). Al-Nahhas said: the estimated form, according to al-Khalil's view, is "alladhi ataytukumuhu" (that which I gave you), and then the pronoun (ha') was deleted because the noun was long. The lam is the lam of the inceptive (lam al-ibtida'). This is also the view of al-Akhfash, and "ma" is then in the nominative position as a subject (mubtada'), its predicate being "of Book and wisdom."

His words: "Then there comes to you" and what follows it form a clause conjoined to the relative clause (sila), and the returning pronoun is deleted, i.e., "confirming it" (musaddiq bihi). Al-Mubarrad, al-Zajjaj and al-Kisa'i said: "ma" is conditional (shartiyya), and the lam of confirmation (lam al-tahqiq) has entered upon it, as it enters upon "in." "You will surely believe in him" is the answer to the oath, which is the taking of the covenant, since it is in the position of an oath, as you would say, "I have taken your pledge that you will surely do such-and-such." It stands in place of the answer to the condition (jaza').

Al-Kisa'i also said: the answer to the condition is His words, ﴿Then whoever turns away﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: the lam in His words ﴿what I have given you﴾ is the preparatory lam (lam al-tawti'a), and the lam in His words "you will surely believe" is the answer to the oath. "Ma" may be one that includes the meaning of the condition, and "you will surely believe" stands in place of the answer to both the oath and the condition together. It may also be that "ma" is a relative pronoun meaning "to that which I have given you, you will surely believe in him." End of quotation.

Hamzah read "li-ma ataytukum" with a kasrah on the lam, and "ma" means "alladhi," and the phrase is connected to akhadha (took). The people of Madinah read "ataynakum" (in the plural of majesty, honouring). The rest read "ataytukum" (in the singular). It has also been said that "ma" in the reading of the one who read with a kasrah on the lam is a verbal-source particle (masdariyya). Its meaning is: "because of My giving you some of the Book and wisdom, and then because of the coming of a Messenger confirming what is with you." The lam is the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil), i.e., "because of that God took the covenant of those who were given the Book, that you will surely believe in him."

His words, "(agreed) you have acknowledged" (aqrartum), are from iqrar (acknowledgement). In the language, al-isr means a burden. The covenant was called isr because of the strictness it contains. The meaning is: "And you accepted My covenant on that condition."

His words, ﴿They said: We acknowledge﴾, form a resumptive clause (jumla istinafiyya), as if it were said: "What did they say at that?" and it was answered: "They said: We acknowledge." He did not mention isr (burden) by any of them, being content with that.

His words, ﴿He said: Then bear witness﴾, mean: God, glorified is He, said: "Then bear witness," i.e., let some of them bear witness against others. ﴿And I am with you among the witnesses﴾, i.e., I am, over your acknowledgement and the testimony of some of you against others, among the witnesses.

His words, ﴿Then whoever turns away﴾, mean: whoever turns away from what was mentioned after that covenant, ﴿those are the defiantly disobedient﴾, i.e., those who depart from obedience.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Saʿid ibn Jubayr who said: I said to Ibn ʿAbbas: "The companions of ʿAbd Allah read: 'And when God took the covenant of those who were given the Book, [about] what I have given you of Book and wisdom,' while we read: 'the covenant of the Prophets.'" Ibn ʿAbbas said: "God only took the covenant of the Prophets concerning their peoples."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Tawus concerning the verse, who said: God took the covenant of the Prophets that each would affirm the others.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Mujahid concerning His words, ﴿And when God took the covenant of the Prophets﴾ (p. 229), who said: "It is an error of the scribes, and in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is: 'the covenant of those who were given the Book.'"

Ibn Jarir transmitted from ʿAli who said: God did not send any prophet, from Adam onward, without taking from him the covenant concerning Muhammad: "If he is sent while you are alive, you will surely believe in him and surely support him," and he commanded him to take the covenant from his people. Then he recited: ﴿And when God took the covenant of the Prophets﴾, the verse.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Suddi something similar concerning the verse. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas something similar. Ibn Jarir transmitted through al-ʿAwfi from him, concerning His words, ﴿My burden (isri)﴾, that he said: "My covenant (ahdi)." Ibn Jarir transmitted from ʿAli concerning His words, ﴿He said: Then bear witness﴾, that he said: "Bear witness against your nations with that," ﴿and I am with you among the witnesses﴾ "over you and over them," ﴿Then whoever turns away﴾ "from you, O Muhammad, after this covenant, from all the nations," ﴿those are the defiantly disobedient﴾, "they are the ones who disobey in unbelief."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verses 83–85:

His saying: "Afa-ghayra" (﴿أفَغَيْرَ﴾) is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on something implied, meaning: "Do you turn away, then seek other than the religion of Allah?" The object is placed first because it is the focus of the denunciation. Abu ʿAmr alone read "yabghūna" (يَبْغُونَ) with the letter yāʾ (the third-person form) and "tarjiʿūna" (تَرْجِعُونَ) with the letter tāʾ (the second-person form). He said: "Because the first is specific and the second is general, so he differentiated between them, since they differ in meaning."

Ḥafṣ read with yāʾ in both places. The rest read with tāʾ in both. "Ṭawʿan wa-karhan" (﴿طَوْعًا وكَرْهًا﴾) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning: willingly and unwillingly. Ṭawʿ (طَوْعٌ) is submission and following with ease; karh (كُرْهٌ) is that which involves hardship, and it comes from aslama (أسلم) out of fear of being killed; his submission is then a surrender from him.

His saying: "Āmannā" (﴿آمَنّا﴾) is a report from him, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, about himself and his community: ﴿لا نُفَرِّقُ بَيْنَ أحَدٍ مِنهُمْ﴾ ("We make no distinction between any of them"), unlike the Jews and Christians, who made distinctions, believing in some and disbelieving in others.

The explanation of this verse has already been given: ﴿ونَحْنُ لَهُ مُسْلِمُونَ﴾ ("and to Him we are submitting"), that is, submitting sincerely. His saying: "dīnan" (دِينًا) is the object of the verb; that is, "yabtaghi dīnan" (whoever seeks a religion) being other than Islam. It is also permissible that "ghayra al-Islām" (غَيْرَ الإسْلامِ) be in the accusative as the object of the verb, and "dīnan" is either a specification (tamyīz) or a circumstantial state (ḥāl) if it is interpreted as a derived noun, or an appositive (badal) of "ghayra."

His saying: ﴿وهُوَ في الآخِرَةِ مِنَ الخاسِرِينَ﴾ ("and he in the Hereafter will be among the losers") is either in the accusative position as a circumstantial state, or a resumptive independent clause; that is, among those who fall into loss on the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Ṭabarānī narrated with a weak chain (isnād) from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His saying: ﴿ولَهُ أسْلَمَ مَن في السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ﴾ ("To Him submits whoever is in the heavens and the earth"), that he said: "As for those in the heavens, they are the angels. As for those on the earth, they are those born upon Islam. As for 'unwillingly,' they are those brought from the captive nations in chains and shackles, led to Paradise while they are unwilling."

Al-Daylamī narrated from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said concerning the verse: "The angels obeyed Him in the heavens, and the Anṣār and ʿAbd al-Qays obeyed Him on the earth."

Ibn Jarīr narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said concerning the verse ﴿أسْلَمَ مَن في السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ﴾: "When the covenant was taken from them."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from him concerning His saying: ﴿ولَهُ أسْلَمَ﴾: "It is recognition (maʿrifah)."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Qatādah concerning the verse, who said: "As for the believer, he submitted willingly, and that benefited him and was accepted from him. As for the disbeliever, he submitted when he saw the might of Allah, and that did not benefit him and was not accepted from him: ﴿فَلَمْ يَكُ يَنْفَعُهم إيمانُهم لَمّا رَأوْا بَأْسَنا﴾" ("But their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our might," Ghāfir: 85).

Al-Ṭabarānī in al-Awsaṭ narrated from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever among slaves, animals or children has bad character, then recite into his ear: ﴿أفَغَيْرَ دِينِ اللَّهِ يَبْغُونَ﴾."

Ibn al-Sunnī in ʿAmal al-Yawm wa-al-Laylah narrated from Yūnus ibn ʿUbayd, who said: "No man who is on a difficult animal recites into its ear ﴿أفَغَيْرَ دِينِ اللَّهِ يَبْغُونَ﴾ and the rest of the verse, except that it is subdued by the permission of Allah, Mighty and Majestic."

Aḥmad and al-Ṭabarānī in al-Awsaṭ narrated from Abū Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "On the Day of Resurrection, the deeds will come. Prayer will come and say: 'O Lord, I am prayer!' He will say: 'You are upon good.' Charity will come and say: 'O Lord, I am charity!' He will say: 'You are upon good.' Fasting will come and say: 'I am fasting!' He will say: 'You are upon good.' Then all the deeds will come, and to each Allah says: 'You are upon good.' Allah the Exalted said in His Book: ﴿ومَن يَبْتَغِ غَيْرَ الإسْلامِ دِينًا فَلَنْ يُقْبَلَ مِنهُ وهو في الآخِرَةِ مِنَ الخاسِرِينَ﴾."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verses 83–85:

His saying: "Afa-ghayra" (﴿أفَغَيْرَ﴾) is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on something implied, meaning: "Do you turn away, then seek other than the religion of Allah?" The object is placed first because it is the focus of the denunciation. Abu ʿAmr alone read "yabghūna" (يَبْغُونَ) with the letter yāʾ (the third-person form) and "tarjiʿūna" (تَرْجِعُونَ) with the letter tāʾ (the second-person form). He said: "Because the first is specific and the second is general, so he differentiated between them, since they differ in meaning."

Ḥafṣ read with yāʾ in both places. The rest read with tāʾ in both. "Ṭawʿan wa-karhan" (﴿طَوْعًا وكَرْهًا﴾) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning: willingly and unwillingly. Ṭawʿ (طَوْعٌ) is submission and following with ease; karh (كُرْهٌ) is that which involves hardship, and it comes from aslama (أسلم) out of fear of being killed; his submission is then a surrender from him.

His saying: "Āmannā" (﴿آمَنّا﴾) is a report from him, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, about himself and his community: ﴿لا نُفَرِّقُ بَيْنَ أحَدٍ مِنهُمْ﴾ ("We make no distinction between any of them"), unlike the Jews and Christians, who made distinctions, believing in some and disbelieving in others.

The explanation of this verse has already been given: ﴿ونَحْنُ لَهُ مُسْلِمُونَ﴾ ("and to Him we are submitting"), that is, submitting sincerely. Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verses 86–91:

His saying: ﴿How will Allah guide a people﴾. This interrogative (istifham) means denial: that is, Allah does not guide them. A parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿How can there be a covenant for the polytheists with Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 71], meaning there is no covenant for them. Similar to it is the saying of the poet:

*How can I sleep upon the bed, when a fierce raid has not yet struck Syria?*

meaning: I cannot sleep.

The meaning of the verse: Allah does not guide to the truth a people who disbelieved after their belief, and after they had testified that the Messenger is true, and after the clear proofs had come to them from the Book of Allah, the Exalted, and the miracles of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). His saying: ﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumlah ḥāliyyah, a clause describing the state of the subject); that is: how would He guide the apostates, when the state is that He does not guide those among them who have done nothing but wrong themselves, and among them are those who remain upon disbelief? There is no doubt that the sin of the apostate is greater than the sin of one who remains upon disbelief, because the apostate has known the truth and then turned away out of obstinacy and rebellion.

His saying: (p-230) ﴿Those﴾ is a reference to the people characterized by those previously mentioned qualities, and it is a mubtadaʾ (subject of a nominal sentence), whose predicate (khabar) is the clause that follows it. The explanation of "curse" (laʿn) has already been given.

His saying: ﴿Nor will they be reprieved﴾ means: they will not be delayed or given respite. Then He excepted the penitent, saying: ﴿except those who repent after that﴾; that is, after the apostasy, and they correct with Islam what they had corrupted of their religion through apostasy. In this there is evidence for the acceptance of the repentance of an apostate when he returns to Islam sincerely, and there is no disagreement on this as far as I know.

His saying: ﴿Then they increased in disbelief﴾. Qatadah, ʿAtaʾ al-Khurasani and al-Hasan said: it was revealed concerning the Jews and the Christians who disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ) after their belief, through his description and attributes, ﴿then they increased in disbelief﴾ by persisting in their disbelief. It was also said: they increased in disbelief through the sins they committed. Ibn Jarir al-Tabari preferred this view and restricted it to the Jews alone. A group of exegetes found difficulty with His saying: ﴿their repentance will never be accepted﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 18], given that repentance is accepted, as in the first verse, and as in His saying: ﴿And it is He who accepts repentance from His servants﴾ [al-Shura: 25], and other such verses. So it was said: the meaning is that their repentance will not be accepted at the time of death.

Al-Nahhas said: this is a fine view, as Allah says: ﴿And repentance is not for those who do evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have now repented"﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 18]. This was also the view of al-Hasan, Qatadah and ʿAtaʾ, and from it is the hadith: "Allah accepts the repentance of the servant as long as he has not yet reached the death rattle (lam yughargir)." It was also said: the meaning is that their repentance which they had before they disbelieved will not be accepted, because disbelief nullifies (aḥbaṭa) what precedes it. It was also said: their repentance will not be accepted if they repent from one disbelief to another disbelief. The more preferable view is to interpret the non-acceptance of their repentance in this verse as referring to one who died as a disbeliever without repenting; it is as if He expressed dying in disbelief by the non-acceptance of repentance. The verse mentioned after this one, His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved and died while they were disbelievers﴾, serves as an explanation of it.

His saying: ﴿the earth full of gold﴾. Al-milʾ (with a kasra) is the quantity that fills a thing, and al-malʾ (with a fatḥa) is the verbal noun of "I filled the thing." ﴿Gold﴾ (dhahaban) is a tamyīz (specification accusative), as said by al-Farraʾ and others. Al-Kisaʾi said: it is put in the accusative by an implied "min dhahab" (of gold), like His saying: ﴿or its equivalent in fasting﴾ [al-Maʾidah: 95], meaning "of fasting." Al-Aʿmash read dhahabun in the nominative, as a badal (substitution) for milʾ. The waw in His saying: ﴿even if he offered it in ransom﴾ is said to be superfluous and extra (muqḥamah zāʾidah), meaning: even if he offered it in ransom. It was also said: there is in it an attribution to the wealthy, as if it were said: no ransom will be accepted from any one of them, even if he were to ransom himself with the earth full of gold. It was also said: it is a conjunction upon an implied element; that is: the earth full of gold will not be accepted from any one of them, even if he gave it in charity in this world, and even if he ransomed himself with it from the punishment; that is, with its equivalent.

Al-Nasaʾi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan have related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "A man from the Ansar had embraced Islam, then apostatized and joined the polytheists. Then he regretted and sent to his people: 'Send to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asking: Is there any repentance for me?' Then it was revealed: ﴿How will Allah guide a people who disbelieved after their belief﴾ until His saying: ﴿Forgiving, Merciful﴾. So his people sent to him and he embraced Islam." ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Mujahid something similar, and he said: it was al-Harith ibn Suwayd. ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from al-Suddi something similar. Ibn Ishaq and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn ʿAbbas something similar also, and it has been related from a group something similar too.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related, through al-ʿAwfi, from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying: ﴿How will Allah guide a people who disbelieved after their belief﴾, that he said: they are the People of the Book among the Jews, who recognized Muhammad and then disbelieved in him. ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from al-Hasan, who said: they are the People of the Book among the Jews and Christians, and he mentioned something similar to what was mentioned before from him. Al-Bazzar related from Ibn ʿAbbas that a people embraced Islam, then apostatized, then embraced Islam, then apostatized; so they sent to their people asking on their behalf, and this was mentioned to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and then this verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved after their belief and then increased in disbelief﴾. Al-Suyuti said: this is an error on the part of al-Bazzar.

Ibn Jarir related from al-Hasan concerning the verse, who said: the Jews and the Christians, their repentance will not be accepted at the time of death. ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah concerning the verse, who said: they are the Jews who disbelieved in the Gospel and in Jesus, then increased in disbelief by disbelieving in Muhammad (ﷺ) and the Qur'an. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-ʿAliyah concerning the verse, who said: it was only revealed concerning the Jews and the Christians who disbelieved after their belief, then increased in disbelief through sins they committed; then they went to repent from those sins while still in their disbelief. Had they been upon guidance, their repentance would have been accepted, but they were upon error.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿then they increased in disbelief﴾, that he said: they grew upon their disbelief. Ibn Jarir related from al-Suddi concerning His saying: ﴿then they increased in disbelief﴾, that he said: they died while they were disbelievers. ﴿Their repentance will not be accepted﴾: he said: if one repents at his death, his repentance will not be accepted.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-ʿAliyah concerning His saying: ﴿their repentance will never be accepted﴾, that he said: they repented from sins but did not repent from the root (of disbelief). Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan concerning His saying: ﴿and they died while they were disbelievers﴾, that he said: it refers to every disbeliever.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The disbeliever will be brought on the Day of Resurrection and it will be said to him: 'Tell me, if you had the earth full of gold, would you have ransomed yourself with it?' He will say: 'Yes.' It will be said to him: 'You were asked for what is easier than that.' That is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved and died while they were disbelievers﴾, the verse."

meaning: I cannot sleep.

His saying: ﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumlah ḥāliyyah, a clause describing the state of the subject); that is: how would He guide the apostates, when the state is that He does not guide those among them who have done nothing but wrong themselves, and among them are those who remain upon disbelief? There is no doubt that the sin of the apostate is greater than the sin of one who remains upon disbelief, because the apostate has known the truth and then turned away out of obstinacy and rebellion.

Al-Bazzar related from Ibn ʿAbbas that a people embraced Islam, then apostatized, then embraced Islam, then apostatized; so they sent to their people asking on their behalf, and this was mentioned to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and then this verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved after their belief and then increased in disbelief﴾. Al-Suyuti said: this is an error on the part of al-Bazzar.

Ibn Jarir related from al-Hasan concerning the verse, who said: the Jews and the Christians, their repentance will not be accepted at the time of death. ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah concerning the verse, who said: they are the Jews who disbelieved in the Gospel and in Jesus, then increased in disbelief by disbelieving in Muhammad (ﷺ) and the Qur'an. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-ʿAliyah concerning the verse, who said: it was only revealed concerning the Jews and the Christians who disbelieved after their belief, then increased in disbelief through sins they committed; then they went to repent from those sins while still in their disbelief. Had they been upon guidance, their repentance would have been accepted, but they were upon error.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿then they increased in disbelief﴾, that he said: they grew upon their disbelief. Ibn Jarir related from al-Suddi concerning His saying: ﴿then they increased in disbelief﴾, that he said: they died while they were disbelievers. ﴿Their repentance will not be accepted﴾: he said: if one repents at his death, his repentance will not be accepted.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-ʿAliyah concerning His saying: ﴿their repentance will never be accepted﴾, that he said: they repented from sins but did not repent from the root (of disbelief). Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan concerning His saying: ﴿and they died while they were disbelievers﴾, that he said: it refers to every disbeliever.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The disbeliever will be brought on the Day of Resurrection and it will be said to him: 'Tell me, if you had the earth full of gold, would you have ransomed yourself with it?' He will say: 'Yes.' It will be said to him: 'You were asked for what is easier than that.' That is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved and died while they were disbelievers﴾, the verse."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verses 86–91:

His saying: ﴿How will Allah guide a people﴾. This interrogative (istifham) means denial: that is, Allah does not guide them. A parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿How can there be a covenant for the polytheists with Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 71], meaning there is no covenant for them. Similar to it is the saying of the poet:

*How can I sleep upon the bed, when a fierce raid has not yet struck Syria?*

meaning: I cannot sleep.

The meaning of the verse: Allah does not guide to the truth a people who disbelieved after their belief, and after they had testified that the Messenger is true, and after the clear proofs had come to them from the Book of Allah, the Exalted, and the miracles of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). His saying: ﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumlah ḥāliyyah, a clause describing the state of the subject); that is: how would He guide the apostates, when the state is that He does not guide those among them who have done nothing but wrong themselves, and among them are those who remain upon disbelief? There is no doubt that the sin of the apostate is greater than the sin of one who remains upon disbelief, because the apostate has known the truth and then turned away out of obstinacy and rebellion.

His saying: (p-230) ﴿Those﴾ is a reference to the people characterized by those previously mentioned qualities, and it is a mubtadaʾ (subject of a nominal sentence), whose predicate (khabar) is the clause that follows it. The explanation of "curse" (laʿn) has already been given.

His saying: ﴿Nor will they be reprieved﴾ means: they will not be delayed or given respite. Then He excepted the penitent, saying: ﴿except those who repent after that﴾; that is, after the apostasy, and they correct with Islam what they had corrupted of their religion through apostasy. In this there is evidence for the acceptance of the repentance of an apostate when he returns to Islam sincerely, and there is no disagreement on this as far as I know.

His saying: ﴿Then they increased in disbelief﴾. Qatadah, ʿAtaʾ al-Khurasani and al-Hasan said: it was revealed concerning the Jews and the Christians who disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ) after their belief, through his description and attributes, ﴿then they increased in disbelief﴾ by persisting in their disbelief. It was also said: they increased in disbelief through the sins they committed. Ibn Jarir al-Tabari preferred this view and restricted it to the Jews alone. A group of exegetes found difficulty with His saying: ﴿their repentance will never be accepted﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 18], given that repentance is accepted, as in the first verse, and as in His saying: ﴿And it is He who accepts repentance from His servants﴾ [al-Shura: 25], and other such verses. So it was said: the meaning is that their repentance will not be accepted at the time of death.

Al-Nahhas said: this is a fine view, as Allah says: ﴿And repentance is not for those who do evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have now repented"﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 18]. This was also the view of al-Hasan, Qatadah and ʿAtaʾ, and from it is the hadith: "Allah accepts the repentance of the servant as long as he has not yet reached the death rattle (lam yughargir)." It was also said: the meaning is that their repentance which they had before they disbelieved will not be accepted, because disbelief nullifies (aḥbaṭa) what precedes it. It was also said: their repentance will not be accepted if they repent from one disbelief to another disbelief. The more preferable view is to interpret the non-acceptance of their repentance in this verse as referring to one who died as a disbeliever without repenting; it is as if He expressed dying in disbelief by the non-acceptance of repentance. The verse mentioned after this one, His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved and died while they were disbelievers﴾, serves as an explanation of it.

His saying: ﴿the earth full of gold﴾. Al-milʾ (with a kasra) is the quantity that fills a thing, and al-malʾ (with a fatḥa) is the verbal noun of "I filled the thing." ﴿Gold﴾ (dhahaban) is a tamyīz (specification accusative), as said by al-Farraʾ and others. Al-Kisaʾi said: it is put in the accusative by an implied "min dhahab" (of gold), like His saying: ﴿or its equivalent in fasting﴾ [al-Maʾidah: 95], meaning "of fasting." Al-Aʿmash read dhahabun in the nominative, as a badal (substitution) for milʾ. The waw in His saying: ﴿even if he offered it in ransom﴾ is said to be superfluous and extra (muqḥamah zāʾidah), meaning: even if he offered it in ransom. It was also said: there is in it an attribution to the wealthy, as if it were said: no ransom will be accepted from any one of them, even if he were to ransom himself with the earth full of gold. It was also said: it is a conjunction upon an implied element; that is: the earth full of gold will not be accepted from any one of them, even if he gave it in charity in this world, and even if he ransomed himself with it from the punishment; that is, with its equivalent.

Al-Nasaʾi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan have related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "A man from the Ansar had embraced Islam, then apostatized and joined the polytheists. Then he regretted and sent to his people: 'Send to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asking: Is there any repentance for me?' Then it was revealed: ﴿How will Allah guide a people who disbelieved after their belief﴾ until His saying: ﴿Forgiving, Merciful﴾. So his people sent to him and he embraced Islam." ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Mujahid something similar, and he said: it was al-Harith ibn Suwayd. ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from al-Suddi something similar. Ibn Ishaq and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn ʿAbbas something similar also, and it has been related from a group something similar too.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related, through al-ʿAwfi, from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying: ﴿How will Allah guide a people who disbelieved after their belief﴾, that he said: they are the People of the Book among the Jews, who recognized Muhammad and then disbelieved in him. ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from al-Hasan, who said: they are the People of the Book among the Jews and Christians, and he mentioned something similar to what was mentioned before from him. Al-Bazzar related from Ibn ʿAbbas that a people embraced Islam, then apostatized, then embraced Islam, then apostatized; so they sent to their people asking on their behalf, and this was mentioned to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and then this verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved after their belief and then increased in disbelief﴾. Al-Suyuti said: this is an error on the part of al-Bazzar.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan concerning His saying: ﴿and they died while they were disbelievers﴾, that he said: it refers to every disbeliever.
