He will say: 'Yes.' It will be said to him: 'You were asked for what is easier than that.' That is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved and died while they were disbelievers﴾, the verse."

This is a new statement, an address to the believers following the mention of what does not benefit the disbelievers.

His saying: ﴿You will never attain righteousness﴾. It is said: "Ma'ruf reached me (nalani) from so-and-so," meaning it arrived to me. Al-nawal is the gift, from your saying "nawwaltuhu tanwilan," meaning I gave it to him. Al-birr (righteousness): it is good deeds. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, 'Ata', Mujahid, 'Amr ibn Maymun and al-Suddi said: it is Paradise. So the meaning of the verse is: "You will never attain good deeds or Paradise," i.e., you will not reach that nor arrive at it, ﴿until you spend of what you love﴾, i.e., until your spending is from your wealth that you love. The word (min) here is partitive (tab'idiyyah), and this is supported by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "until you spend some of what (p-231) you love." It has also been said that it is explanatory (bayaniyyah), and (ma) is a relative pronoun or a qualifying noun. The intended meaning is spending in the way of good, whether charity or other acts of obedience. It has also been said that the intended meaning is the obligatory zakat.

His saying: "of anything" is an explanation of His saying "what you spend," i.e., whatever you spend, of any kind, whether good or bad. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of it﴾. Here "ma" is a conditional particle that jazms (apocopates). His saying ﴿indeed, Allah is Knowing of it﴾ is a justification for the apodosis of the condition, occupying its place.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others have related from Anas that when this verse was revealed, Abu Talhah came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, the dearest of my property to me is Bayruha, and it is a charity..." The hadith. It has been narrated with different wordings.

'Abd ibn Humayd and al-Bazzar related from Ibn Umar that he said: "This verse came to my mind: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend of what you love﴾, so I considered what Allah had given me, and I found nothing dearer to me than Marjanah, a Roman slave-girl of mine. So I said: she is free for the sake of Allah. Then, if I were to return to something I had dedicated to Allah, I would marry her." So he married her to Nafi'.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Umar ibn al-Khattab that he wrote to Abu Musa al-Ash'ari asking him to buy for him a slave-girl from the captives of Jalula'. Umar summoned her and said: "Indeed Allah says: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend of what you love﴾," and then Umar freed her.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related that when the verse was revealed, Zayd ibn Harithah came with a horse of his called Subul, which was the dearest of his property to him, and said: "It is a charity."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Mas'ud, regarding His saying ﴿You will never attain righteousness﴾, that he said: "Paradise." Ibn Jarir related from 'Amr ibn Maymun and al-Suddi the like of it. Ibn al-Mundhir related from Masruq the like of it.

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verses 93–95:

His statement, ﴿All food﴾, means all that is eaten. *Hill* (lawful) is a verbal noun that is used in the same form for the singular and plural, and the masculine and feminine, and it means *halal* (lawful). Israel is Ya'qub (Jacob), as its verification has already been discussed. The meaning of the verse is that all foods were lawful for the Children of Ya'qub, and nothing was made unlawful for them except what Israel made unlawful for himself.

The explanation of what he made unlawful for himself will come later. This exception is *muttasil* (connected) to the subject of *kana* (was). His statement, ﴿before the Torah was revealed﴾, is connected to his statement "was lawful" (*kana hillan*). That is, all foods were lawful, ﴿before the Torah was revealed﴾. That is, what was other than the excepted item was lawful for them ﴿before the Torah was revealed﴾. The Torah contains the prohibition of what God made unlawful for them because of their wrongdoing. This is a refutation of the Jews, when they denied what God, glorified is He, related to His Messenger, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, that the cause of what God made unlawful for them was their wrongdoing and their transgression, as in His statement: ﴿For the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We made unlawful for them good things that had been lawful for them﴾ [An-Nisa: 160], and so on.

His statement: ﴿And to those who were Jews We made unlawful every animal with claws; and of cattle and sheep We made unlawful for them their fat, except what is on their backs or entrails or what is mixed with bone. That was Our repayment to them for their rebellion﴾ [Al-An'am: 146], up to His statement ﴿That We repaid them for their rebellion﴾. They said that these prohibitions were a mercy upon those prophets who came before them. By this they intended to deny what God related to our Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, in His Noble Book. Then God, glorified is He, commanded him to argue with them using their own Book, and to make between himself and them a judgement by what God revealed to them, not by what He revealed to him. So He said: ﴿Say, "Bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful"﴾, so that you may know the truth of what God related in the Qur'an, that nothing was made unlawful for the Children of Israel before the revelation of the Torah except what Ya'qub made unlawful for himself. In this there is such fairness toward opponents that its measure cannot be estimated and its extent cannot be reached.

Then He said: ﴿Then whoever fabricates falsehood against God after that﴾, that is, after the presentation of the Torah and its recitation, ﴿those are the wrongdoers﴾, that is, those who go to extremes in wrongdoing and exceed its bounds, for there is no greater wrongdoer than one who is judged by his own Book and by what he believes to be valid law. Then he argued, after that, fabricating falsehood against God. Then, since what they fabricated of falsehood after the proof had been established against them by their own Book was baseless and rejected, and since what God, glorified is He, related in the Qur'an and what the Torah confirmed was true and sincere, and since the establishment of this truthfulness was by a clear proof that the opponent cannot repel, God, glorified is He, commanded His Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, to proclaim the truthfulness of God after He had recorded falsehood against them. So He said: ﴿Say, "God has spoken the truth; so follow the religion of Ibrahim, a *hanif* (one upright in faith), and he was not of the polytheists"﴾. That is, the religion of Islam, which I follow. The meaning of *hanif* has already been explained. It is as if He said to them: when my truthfulness and the truthfulness of what I brought become clear to you, then enter my religion, for among what God revealed to me is: ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 85].

Al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sound (*hasan*), narrated from Ibn Abbas that: "The Jews said to the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace: Inform us what Israel made unlawful for himself. He said: He used to live in the desert, and he suffered from sciatica (*irq al-nasa'*), and he found nothing that suited him except forbidding camels and their milk, so for that reason he forbade them." They said: "You have spoken the truth." And he mentioned the hadith. It was also narrated by Ahmad and al-Nasa'i.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who graded it sound, narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding the verse that he said: "The vein (*irq*) that I find is the sciatic vein. He used to spend the night with a *zuqq*, meaning screaming. So he made a vow to God that if He healed him, he would not eat any meat containing a vein. Therefore the Jews forbade it." Al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh*, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, from his own words, what al-Tirmidhi had earlier narrated from him as a raised (*marfu'*) report.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through the chain of Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, that he used to say: "What Israel made unlawful for himself was the two extra lobes of the liver, the two kidneys, and the fat, except what was on the back." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he said: "The Jews said to the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace: The Torah was revealed with the prohibition of what Israel made unlawful. So God said to Muhammad, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace: ﴿Say, 'Bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful'﴾." And they lied, for it is not in the Torah.

Then He said: ﴿Then whoever fabricates falsehood against God after that﴾, that is, after the presentation of the Torah and its recitation, ﴿those are the wrongdoers﴾, that is, those who go to extremes in wrongdoing and exceed its bounds, for there is no greater wrongdoer than one who is judged by his own Book and by what he believes to be valid law. Then he argued, after that, fabricating falsehood against God. Then, since what they fabricated of falsehood after the proof had been established against them by their own Book was baseless and rejected, and since what God, glorified is He, related in the Qur'an and what the Torah confirmed was true and sincere, and since the establishment of this truthfulness was by a clear proof that the opponent cannot repel, God, glorified is He, commanded His Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, to proclaim the truthfulness of God after He had recorded falsehood against them. So He said: ﴿Say, "God has spoken the truth; so follow the religion of Ibrahim, a *hanif* (one upright in faith), and he was not of the polytheists"﴾. That is, the religion of Islam, which I follow. The meaning of *hanif* has already been explained. It is as if He said to them: when my truthfulness and the truthfulness of what I brought become clear to you, then enter my religion, for among what God revealed to me is: ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 85].

Al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sound (*hasan*), narrated from Ibn Abbas that: "The Jews said to the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace: Inform us what Israel made unlawful for himself. He said: He used to live in the desert, and he suffered from sciatica (*irq al-nasa'*), and he found nothing that suited him except forbidding camels and their milk, so for that reason he forbade them." They said: "You have spoken the truth." And he mentioned the hadith. It was also narrated by Ahmad and al-Nasa'i.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who graded it sound, narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding the verse that he said: "The vein (*irq*) that I find is the sciatic vein. He used to spend the night with a *zuqq*, meaning screaming. So he made a vow to God that if He healed him, he would not eat any meat containing a vein. Therefore the Jews forbade it." Al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh*, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, from his own words, what al-Tirmidhi had earlier narrated from him as a raised (*marfu'*) report.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through the chain of Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, that he used to say: "What Israel made unlawful for himself was the two extra lobes of the liver, the two kidneys, and the fat, except what was on the back." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he said: "The Jews said to the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace: The Torah was revealed with the prohibition of what Israel made unlawful. So God said to Muhammad, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace: ﴿Say, 'Bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful'﴾." And they lied, for it is not in the Torah.

This is the start of an explanation of another matter about which the Jews argued falsely. They said that Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem's sanctuary) is more excellent and greater than the Ka'bah, because it is the place of emigration of the prophets and because it is in the holy land. God refuted this with His words: ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind﴾ (the verse continues). The phrase "established" (wudi'a) is an attributive description of "House," and the predicate of "indeed" is His words: ﴿that which is at Bakkah﴾. By describing it as the first place of worship, God pointed out that it is more excellent than others. There is disagreement about who first built it. It was said to be the angels; it was said to be Adam; and it was said to be Abraham. These can be reconciled by saying that the first to build it was the angels, then Adam renewed it, then Abraham.

Bakkah is a proper name for the sacred city, as is Makkah, and they are two dialects of the same name. It was said that Bakkah is the name of the site of the House, while Makkah is the name of the sacred city. It was also said that Bakkah refers to the Mosque and Makkah to the whole Haram. It was said that it was called Bakkah because of the crowding of people during circumambulation (tawaf); one says "bakka al-qawm" meaning "they crowded." It was also said that al-bakk means breaking the neck, and it was so named because it breaks the necks of tyrants.

As for its name Makkah, it was said that it was so called because of the scarcity of its water. It was also said that it is because it extracts the marrow from the bone, by the hardship that befalls its inhabitants. From this comes "makktu al-'azm," when you extract what is in the bone; and "makka al-fasil dar'a ummihi" (the young camel sucked its mother's udder), and "imtakkahu" when he sucked it. It was also said that it was so named because it destroys whoever wrongs in it, i.e., it ruins him.

His words "mubarakan" (blessed) are a circumstantial clause (hal) either from the pronoun in "wudi'a" or from the adverbial complement, because the implied meaning is "that which settled at Bakkah, blessed." Blessing (barakah) is the abundance of good that comes to whoever settles in it or visits it, i.e., the multiplied reward.

The "clear signs" (al-ayat al-bayyinat) and the evident ones include: al-Safa and al-Marwah; the trace of a foot on the hard rock; that when rain falls on the side of the Yemeni Corner, fertility is in Yemen, and if it falls on the Syrian side, fertility is in Syria, and when it covers the House, fertility is in all the lands; the deflection of birds from flying over its airspace at all times; and the destruction of the tyrants who intend it, among others. His words ﴿the station of Abraham﴾ are a substitution (badal) from "signs." This was said by Muhammad ibn Yazid al-Mubarrad.

In al-Kashshaf (by al-Zamakhshari) it is said to be an explanatory apposition (atf bayan). Al-Akhfash said it is a subject whose predicate is omitted, the implied meaning being "among them is the station of Abraham." It was also said that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "they are the station of Abraham." The author of al-Kashshaf raised a difficulty about explaining "signs" by it, since "signs" is plural while "the station" is singular. He answered that the station was treated as a single thing equal to multiple signs because of its great status, or that it contains several signs. He said: it is also permissible to mean by it: clear signs, namely the station of Abraham and the safety of whoever enters it, because two things are a type of plurality.

His words ﴿And whoever enters it is safe﴾ form a new independent sentence to explain a ruling of the Haram: whoever enters it is safe. By this, those who said that whoever takes refuge in the Haram after committing a prescribed penalty (hadd) is not punished until he leaves it argued; this is the view of Abu Hanifah and those who followed him. The majority disagreed and said that the prescribed penalties are carried out within the Haram. Some scholars said that the verse is a report in the sense of a command, i.e., "whoever enters it, grant him safety," like His words: ﴿so there shall be no obscenity, no wickedness, and no disputing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 197], meaning: do not be obscene, do not be wicked, and do not dispute.

His words ﴿And pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to God by the people﴾: the "li" in "lillah" is what is called the "lam of obligation and binding." Then the meaning was further emphasized by the particle "ʿala" (upon), for it is among the clearest indications of obligation for the Arabs, as when a speaker says: "So-and-so has such-and-such upon me." God mentioned pilgrimage in the most emphatic way of indicating obligation, to affirm His right and to magnify its sanctity. This address includes all people and nobody is excluded except those specified by evidence, such as the child and the slave. His words ﴿for whoever is able to find a way thereto﴾ are in the genitive position as a partial substitute (badl ba'd) for "the people." Most grammarians held this view. Al-Kisa'i permitted that it be in the nominative position as the agent of "hajj."

The implied meaning is: that whoever is able to find a way to it should make pilgrimage to the House. It was also said that "man" is a conditional particle, and the answer (jaza') is omitted, meaning: whoever is able to find a way to it, then pilgrimage is incumbent upon him. The scholars differed about what "ability" (istita'ah) is. It was said to be provisions and a riding animal. This view was adopted by a group of the Companions, and al-Tirmidhi reported it from most scholars, and it is the correct view.

Malik said: if a man trusts in his strength, pilgrimage becomes obligatory for him even if he has no provisions or mount, provided he is able to earn a living. This was also the view of Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, al-Sha'bi and 'Ikrimah. al-Dahhak said: if he is a young, strong, healthy man and has no wealth, he must hire himself out until he pays for his pilgrimage. Among the things that fall under ability by primary inclusion is that the road to pilgrimage be safe, such that the pilgrim is secure for his person and his property, the property he has no provisions other than. But if the road is not safe, there is no ability, because God, glorified is He, says: ﴿for whoever is able to find a way thereto﴾, and one who fears for his person or property has not found a way thereto, without doubt or ambiguity.

The scholars differed when on the road there are oppressors who take some wealth in a manner that does not consume the pilgrimage provisions. Al-Shafi'i said: he should not give even a grain, and the obligation of pilgrimage falls from him. A group agreed with him and others disagreed. The apparent view is that whoever is able to obtain provisions and a mount, and the road is safe in such a way that he can pass through it even by placating some oppressors with a portion of wealth, through which the pilgrim can manage without reducing his provisions or being ruined, then pilgrimage is not dropped from him; rather it is obligatory upon him, because he has found a way by giving up some wealth. But this wealth paid on the road is among the things upon which ability depends. So if a man has provisions and a mount but does not have what he can pay to the toll-collector on the road, pilgrimage is not obligatory upon him, because he has not found a way thereto, and this is indispensable. This does not contradict interpreting ability as provisions and a mount, for passage on the pilgrimage road is impossible for one who has provisions and a mount except by paying that amount which the toll-collectors take. Perhaps the basis of al-Shafi'i's view that pilgrimage is dropped is that this toll is an evil, and it is not obligatory for the pilgrim to enter into an evil, and that by it he is not able.

Among the things that fall under ability is that the pilgrim be physically sound in a way that enables him to ride. If he is so disabled that he can neither walk nor ride, then even if he finds provisions and a mount, he has not found a way.

His words ﴿And whoever disbelieves, then indeed God is free of need of the worlds﴾ (p-233) — it was said: He used the word "disbelief" to refer to abandoning pilgrimage, to emphasize its obligation and to be severe toward the one who abandons it. It was also said the meaning is: whoever disbelieves in the obligation of pilgrimage and does not consider it obligatory. It was said: whoever abandons pilgrimage while able to perform it is a disbeliever.

In His words ﴿indeed God is free of need of the worlds﴾ there is an indication of the severe displeasure toward one who abandons pilgrimage despite having the ability, and of his forsakenness and distance from God, glorified is He, such that whoever hears it is overwhelmed and his heart trembles. God, glorified is He, only prescribed these laws for His servants for their benefit and welfare, and He, exalted is His majesty and sanctified His sovereignty, is free of need: the acts of obedience of His servants all return to Him with no benefit whatsoever.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ali ibn Abi Talib regarding His words ﴿Indeed, the first House﴾ (the verse), that he said: there were houses before it, but it was the first House established for the worship of God.

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others reported from Abu Dharr who said: "I said: O Messenger of God, which mosque was established first? He said: the Sacred Mosque. I said: then which? He said: the Farthest Mosque. I said: how long between them? He said: forty years." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman reported from Ibn 'Umar who said: "God created the House two thousand years before the earth, when His Throne was upon the water as a white foam, and the earth was beneath it like a shrivelled piece, then the earth was spread out from beneath it."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported something similar from Abu Hurayrah. Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Azraqi reported from Ibn Jurayj who said: "We have been told that the Jews said: Bayt al-Maqdis is greater than the Ka'bah because it is the place of emigration of the prophets and because it is in the holy land. The Muslims said: rather the Ka'bah is greater. This reached the Prophet (ﷺ), and then the verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, the first House﴾ up to His words: ﴿in it are clear signs, the station of Abraham﴾, and this is not in Bayt al-Maqdis; ﴿and whoever enters it is safe﴾, and this is not in Bayt al-Maqdis; ﴿and pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to God by the people﴾, and this is not in Bayt al-Maqdis."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr who said: "Bakkah was only so named because people come to it from every side as pilgrims." Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi related from Mujahid: "Bakkah was only so named because people crowd together in it," i.e., they throng.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Muqatil ibn Hayyan regarding His words ﴿blessed﴾ that he said: good and blessing were placed in it, ﴿and a guidance for the worlds﴾, meaning: by guidance, their qiblah. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported through al-Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿in it are clear signs﴾ that among them are the station of Abraham and al-Mash'ar.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from al-Hasan regarding His words ﴿in it are clear signs﴾ that he said: the station of Abraham, ﴿and whoever enters it is safe, and pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to God by the people﴾. al-Azraqi reported similarly from Zayd ibn Aslam.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah regarding His words ﴿and whoever enters it is safe﴾ that he said: this was in the pre-Islamic period. A man who committed every crime against himself and then took refuge in the Haram would not be touched or pursued. But in Islam, it does not protect from God's prescribed penalties: whoever steals within it has his hand cut off, whoever fornicates within it has the prescribed punishment carried out upon him, and whoever kills within it is killed. Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Azraqi reported from Umar ibn al-Khattab who said: "If I found the slayer of al-Khattab within it, I would not touch him until he leaves it."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿and whoever enters it is safe﴾ that he said: whoever seeks refuge in the House, the House will protect him; but he will not be sheltered, fed or given drink; and when he leaves, he is taken for his sin. This meaning has been related from him through several chains.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him that he said: "If I found the killer of my father within the Haram, I would not approach him." Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Umar who said: "If I found the killer of my father within the Haram, I would not provoke him."

al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and others reported from Abu Shurayh al-'Adawi who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) stood on the day after the Conquest and said: Indeed Makkah was made sacred by God, and it was not made sacred by people. So it is not lawful for a person who believes in God and the Last Day to shed blood in it or cut down a tree in it. If anyone takes permission to fight in it on the basis of the Messenger of God's fighting, say to him: God permitted His Messenger but did not permit you. He permitted me only for an hour of the day, and then its sanctity returned today as it was yesterday." al-Daraqutni and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, reported from Anas that "the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked about His words ﴿for whoever is able to find a way thereto﴾, and it was said: what is the way? He said: provisions and a riding animal."

Al-Shafi'i, 'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn 'Adi, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn 'Umar, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) (marfu'): "A man stood up and said: What is the sabil (way/means)? He said: Provision and a mount."

al-Daraqutni and al-Bayhaqi in their Sunan narrated through the route of al-Hasan, from his mother, from 'A'ishah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked: What is the sabil to the Hajj? He said: Provision and a mount."

al-Daraqutni in his Sunan narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), the same. al-Daraqutni narrated from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), the same.

al-Daraqutni narrated from Jabir, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), the same. This hadith has been related through multiple routes; at its lowest it is hasan li-ghayrihi (good by virtue of corroboration), so the criticisms directed at some of its routes do no harm, as is well known.

al-Daraqutni narrated from 'Ali, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding the verse: "He was asked, the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: You find the back of a camel (i.e., a mount)."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Jarir narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab concerning His saying: ﴿Whoever is able to make his way to it﴾, that he said: Provision and a mount. They both also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas the same. Ibn Majah, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from him traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi narrated from him that he said: The sabil is that the servant's body be sound and that he have the price of provision and a mount without it ruining him. Ibn Abi Shaybah and 'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from him that he said: "Sabilan (a way): whoever finds in it sufficiency, and nothing stands between him and it."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr that he said: al-Istita'ah (ability) is al-quwwah (strength). Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Nakha'i that he said: Indeed, the mahram (unmarriageable male relative) for a woman is of the sabil which Allah mentioned.

It has been established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that a woman is forbidden to travel without a mahram. The hadiths differ regarding the duration (of such travel): in one wording three days, in another a day and a night, and in another a barid (postal stage).

Hadiths have also come with severe warnings against whoever possesses provision and a mount and does not perform Hajj. al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever possesses provision and a mount that carries him to the House of Allah, and does not perform Hajj to the House of Allah, then it makes no difference whether he dies a Jew or a Christian; that is because Allah says: ﴿And for Allah, on mankind, is the pilgrimage to the House — for whoever is able to make his way to it. And whoever disbelieves, then indeed Allah is free of need from the worlds﴾." In its chain is Hilal al-Khurasani, Abu Hashim.

al-Bukhari said: "Munkar al-hadith" (one whose narrations are rejected). It was said: "Majhul" (unknown).

Ibn 'Adi said: "This hadith is not preserved (mahfuz), and in its chain also is al-Harith al-A'war, and in him there is weakness."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ahmad in Kitab al-Iman, Abu Ya'la and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Umamah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever dies without performing the Hajj of Islam, and was not prevented by a restraining illness, or an oppressive ruler, or an apparent need, then let him die in whatever state he wishes, a Jew or a Christian."

Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) as mursal (a hadith whose chain omits a Companion), the same.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, al-Suyuti said: with a sound chain, from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: "I had resolved to send men to these cities so that they might examine every person who had wealth (jiddah) but did not perform Hajj, and then impose the jizya (poll tax) upon them; they are not Muslims, they are not Muslims."

al-Isma'ili narrated from him, saying: "Whoever is able to perform Hajj but does not perform it, it makes no difference whether he dies a Jew or a Christian." Ibn Kathir said after citing its chain: "This is a sound chain." Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from him something similar.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Umar: "Whoever dies while he is wealthy (musir) and has not performed Hajj, will come on the Day of Resurrection with the word 'disbeliever' written between his eyes." Sa'id ibn Mansur narrated from him: "Whoever finds a way (sabil) to Hajj, for a year, then another year, then another year, then dies without performing Hajj, he shall not be prayed over, and it is not known whether he died a Jew or a Christian."

Sa'id ibn Mansur narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: "If the people abandoned Hajj, I would fight them over it just as we fight them over the Salah and the Zakah."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And whoever disbelieves, then indeed Allah is free of need﴾, that he said: "Whoever claims that it is not obligatory upon him."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the verse, that he said: "Whoever disbelieves in the Hajj, does not regard his Hajj as righteousness, nor his abandoning it as sinful."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ikrimah, who said: "When the verse was revealed: ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as religion﴾ [Al 'Imran: 85], the Jews said: 'We are Muslims.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said to them: 'Indeed Allah has enjoined upon the Muslims the Hajj to the House.' They said: 'It was not prescribed for us,' and they refused to perform Hajj. Allah said: ﴿And whoever disbelieves, then indeed Allah is free of need from the worlds﴾."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ikrimah something similar. Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Dahhak, who said: "When the verse of Hajj was revealed: ﴿And for Allah, on mankind, is the pilgrimage to the House﴾, to the end of the verse, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gathered the people of the religions: the polytheist Arabs, the Christians, the Jews, the Magians and the Sabians, and said: 'Indeed Allah has enjoined upon you the Hajj, so perform Hajj to the House.' None accepted it except the Muslims, and five religions disbelieved in it. They said: 'We do not believe in it, nor do we pray towards it, nor do we face it.' So Allah revealed: ﴿And whoever disbelieves, then indeed Allah is free of need from the worlds﴾."

'Abd ibn Humayd and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Mujahid something similar. 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu Dawud Nufay' who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿And for Allah, on mankind, is the pilgrimage to the House﴾, to the end of the verse. A man from Hudhayl stood up and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, whoever abandons it, has he disbelieved?' He said: 'Whoever abandons it, not fearing its punishment; and whoever performs it, not hoping for its reward, then he is that (i.e., a disbeliever).'"

Ibn Jarir narrated from 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah concerning the verse, that he said: "Whoever disbelieves in the House." Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Ibn 'Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), "concerning the saying of Allah: ﴿And whoever disbelieves﴾, he said: Whoever disbelieves in Allah and the Last Day." 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid the same, from his own saying. Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Zayd that he was asked about this, so he recited: ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind﴾ up to His saying: ﴿a way﴾, and then said: "And whoever disbelieves in these verses." Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Mas'ud concerning the verse, that he said: "And whoever disbelieves, so he does not believe in it: then he is the disbeliever."

This is the start of an explanation of another matter about which the Jews argued falsely. It was also said that it is because it extracts the marrow from the bone, by the hardship that befalls its inhabitants. From this comes "makktu al-'azm," when you extract what is in the bone; and "makka al-fasil dar'a ummihi" (the young camel sucked its mother's udder), and "imtakkahu" when he sucked it. The "clear signs" (al-ayat al-bayyinat) and the evident ones include: al-Safa and al-Marwah; the trace of a foot on the hard rock; that when rain falls on the side of the Yemeni Corner, fertility is in Yemen, and if it falls on the Syrian side, fertility is in Syria, and when it covers the House, fertility is in all the lands; the deflection of birds from flying over its airspace at all times; and the destruction of the tyrants who intend it, among others. His words ﴿the station of Abraham﴾ are a substitution (badal) from "signs." This was said by Muhammad ibn Yazid al-Mubarrad.

In al-Kashshaf (by al-Zamakhshari) it is said to be an explanatory apposition (atf bayan). Al-Akhfash said it is a subject whose predicate is omitted, the implied meaning being "among them is the station of Abraham." It was also said that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "they are the station of Abraham." The author of al-Kashshaf raised a difficulty about explaining "signs" by it, since "signs" is plural while "the station" is singular. He answered that the station was treated as a single thing equal to multiple signs because of its great status, or that it contains several signs. He said: it is also permissible to mean by it: clear signs, namely the station of Abraham and the safety of whoever enters it, because two things are a type of plurality.

His words ﴿And whoever enters it is safe﴾ form a new independent sentence to explain a ruling of the Haram: whoever enters it is safe. By this, those who said that whoever takes refuge in the Haram after committing a prescribed penalty (hadd) is not punished until he leaves it argued; this is the view of Abu Hanifah and those who followed him. The majority disagreed and said that the prescribed penalties are carried out within the Haram. Some scholars said that the verse is a report in the sense of a command, i.e., "whoever enters it, grant him safety," like His words: ﴿so there shall be no obscenity, no wickedness, and no disputing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 197], meaning: do not be obscene, do not be wicked, and do not dispute.

His words ﴿And pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to God by the people﴾: the "li" in "lillah" is what is called the "lam of obligation and binding." Then the meaning was further emphasized by the particle "ʿala" (upon), for it is among the clearest indications of obligation for the Arabs, as when a speaker says: "So-and-so has such-and-such upon me." God mentioned pilgrimage in the most emphatic way of indicating obligation, to affirm His right and to magnify its sanctity. This address includes all people and nobody is excluded except those specified by evidence, such as the child and the slave. His words ﴿for whoever is able to find a way thereto﴾ are in the genitive position as a partial substitute (badl ba'd) for "the people." Most grammarians held this view. Al-Kisa'i permitted that it be in the nominative position as the agent of "hajj."

The implied meaning is: that whoever is able to find a way to it should make pilgrimage to the House. It was also said that "man" is a conditional particle, and the answer (jaza') is omitted, meaning: whoever is able to find a way to it, then pilgrimage is incumbent upon him. The scholars differed about what "ability" (istita'ah) is. It was said to be provisions and a riding animal. This view was adopted by a group of the Companions, and al-Tirmidhi reported it from most scholars, and it is the correct view.

Malik said: if a man trusts in his strength, pilgrimage becomes obligatory for him even if he has no provisions or mount, provided he is able to earn a living. This was also the view of Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, al-Sha'bi and 'Ikrimah. al-Dahhak said: if he is a young, strong, healthy man and has no wealth, he must hire himself out until he pays for his pilgrimage. Among the things that fall under ability by primary inclusion is that the road to pilgrimage be safe, such that the pilgrim is secure for his person and his property, the property he has no provisions other than. But if the road is not safe, there is no ability, because God, glorified is He, says: ﴿for whoever is able to find a way thereto﴾, and one who fears for his person or property has not found a way thereto, without doubt or ambiguity.

The scholars differed when on the road there are oppressors who take some wealth in a manner that does not consume the pilgrimage provisions. Al-Shafi'i said: he should not give even a grain, and the obligation of pilgrimage falls from him. A group agreed with him and others disagreed. The apparent view is that whoever is able to obtain provisions and a mount, and the road is safe in such a way that he can pass through it even by placating some oppressors with a portion of wealth, through which the pilgrim can manage without reducing his provisions or being ruined, then pilgrimage is not dropped from him; rather it is obligatory upon him, because he has found a way by giving up some wealth. But this wealth paid on the road is among the things upon which ability depends. So if a man has provisions and a mount but does not have what he can pay to the toll-collector on the road, pilgrimage is not obligatory upon him, because he has not found a way thereto, and this is indispensable. This does not contradict interpreting ability as provisions and a mount, for passage on the pilgrimage road is impossible for one who has provisions and a mount except by paying that amount which the toll-collectors take. Perhaps the basis of al-Shafi'i's view that pilgrimage is dropped is that this toll is an evil, and it is not obligatory for the pilgrim to enter into an evil, and that by it he is not able.

Among the things that fall under ability is that the pilgrim be physically sound in a way that enables him to ride. If he is so disabled that he can neither walk nor ride, then even if he finds provisions and a mount, he has not found a way.

His words ﴿And whoever disbelieves, then indeed God is free of need of the worlds﴾ (p-233) — it was said: He used the word "disbelief" to refer to abandoning pilgrimage, to emphasize its obligation and to be severe toward the one who abandons it. It was also said the meaning is: whoever disbelieves in the obligation of pilgrimage and does not consider it obligatory. It was said: whoever abandons pilgrimage while able to perform it is a disbeliever.

In His words ﴿indeed God is free of need of the worlds﴾ there is an indication of the severe displeasure toward one who abandons pilgrimage despite having the ability, and of his forsakenness and distance from God, glorified is He, such that whoever hears it is overwhelmed and his heart trembles. God, glorified is He, only prescribed these laws for His servants for their benefit and welfare, and He, exalted is His majesty and sanctified His sovereignty, is free of need: the acts of obedience of His servants all return to Him with no benefit whatsoever.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ali ibn Abi Talib regarding His words ﴿Indeed, the first House﴾ (the verse), that he said: there were houses before it, but it was the first House established for the worship of God.

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others reported from Abu Dharr who said: "I said: O Messenger of God, which mosque was established first? He said: the Sacred Mosque. I said: then which? He said: the Farthest Mosque. I said: how long between them? He said: forty years." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman reported from Ibn 'Umar who said: "God created the House two thousand years before the earth, when His Throne was upon the water as a white foam, and the earth was beneath it like a shrivelled piece, then the earth was spread out from beneath it."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported something similar from Abu Hurayrah. Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Azraqi reported from Ibn Jurayj who said: "We have been told that the Jews said: Bayt al-Maqdis is greater than the Ka'bah because it is the place of emigration of the prophets and because it is in the holy land. The Muslims said: rather the Ka'bah is greater. This reached the Prophet (ﷺ), and then the verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, the first House﴾ up to His words: ﴿in it are clear signs, the station of Abraham﴾, and this is not in Bayt al-Maqdis; ﴿and whoever enters it is safe﴾, and this is not in Bayt al-Maqdis; ﴿and pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to God by the people﴾, and this is not in Bayt al-Maqdis."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr who said: "Bakkah was only so named because people come to it from every side as pilgrims." Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi related from Mujahid: "Bakkah was only so named because people crowd together in it," i.e., they throng.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Muqatil ibn Hayyan regarding His words ﴿blessed﴾ that he said: good and blessing were placed in it, ﴿and a guidance for the worlds﴾, meaning: by guidance, their qiblah. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported through al-Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿in it are clear signs﴾ that among them are the station of Abraham and al-Mash'ar.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from al-Hasan regarding His words ﴿in it are clear signs﴾ that he said: the station of Abraham, ﴿and whoever enters it is safe, and pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to God by the people﴾. al-Azraqi reported similarly from Zayd ibn Aslam.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah regarding His words ﴿and whoever enters it is safe﴾ that he said: this was in the pre-Islamic period. A man who committed every crime against himself and then took refuge in the Haram would not be touched or pursued. But in Islam, it does not protect from God's prescribed penalties: whoever steals within it has his hand cut off, whoever fornicates within it has the prescribed punishment carried out upon him, and whoever kills within it is killed. Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Azraqi reported from Umar ibn al-Khattab who said: "If I found the slayer of al-Khattab within it, I would not touch him until he leaves it."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿and whoever enters it is safe﴾ that he said: whoever seeks refuge in the House, the House will protect him; but he will not be sheltered, fed or given drink; and when he leaves, he is taken for his sin. This meaning has been related from him through several chains.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him that he said: "If I found the killer of my father within the Haram, I would not approach him." Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Umar who said: "If I found the killer of my father within the Haram, I would not provoke him."

al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and others reported from Abu Shurayh al-'Adawi who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) stood on the day after the Conquest and said: Indeed Makkah was made sacred by God, and it was not made sacred by people. So it is not lawful for a person who believes in God and the Last Day to shed blood in it or cut down a tree in it. If anyone takes permission to fight in it on the basis of the Messenger of God's fighting, say to him: God permitted His Messenger but did not permit you. He permitted me only for an hour of the day, and then its sanctity returned today as it was yesterday." al-Daraqutni and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, reported from Anas that "the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked about His words ﴿for whoever is able to find a way thereto﴾, and it was said: what is the way? He said: provisions and a riding animal."

Al-Shafi'i, 'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn 'Adi, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn 'Umar, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) (marfu'): "A man stood up and said: What is the sabil (way/means)? He said: Provision and a mount."

al-Daraqutni and al-Bayhaqi in their Sunan narrated through the route of al-Hasan, from his mother, from 'A'ishah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked: What is the sabil to the Hajj? He said: Provision and a mount."

al-Daraqutni in his Sunan narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), the same. al-Daraqutni narrated from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), the same.

al-Daraqutni narrated from Jabir, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), the same. This hadith has been related through multiple routes; at its lowest it is hasan li-ghayrihi (good by virtue of corroboration), so the criticisms directed at some of its routes do no harm, as is well known.

al-Daraqutni narrated from 'Ali, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding the verse: "He was asked, the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: You find the back of a camel (i.e., a mount)."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Jarir narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab concerning His saying: ﴿Whoever is able to make his way to it﴾, that he said: Provision and a mount. They both also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas the same. Ibn Majah, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from him traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi narrated from him that he said: The sabil is that the servant's body be sound and that he have the price of provision and a mount without it ruining him. Ibn Abi Shaybah and 'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from him that he said: "Sabilan (a way): whoever finds in it sufficiency, and nothing stands between him and it."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr that he said: al-Istita'ah (ability) is al-quwwah (strength). Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Nakha'i that he said: Indeed, the mahram (unmarriageable male relative) for a woman is of the sabil which Allah mentioned.

It has been established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that a woman is forbidden to travel without a mahram. The hadiths differ regarding the duration (of such travel): in one wording three days, in another a day and a night, and in another a barid (postal stage).

Hadiths have also come with severe warnings against whoever possesses provision and a mount and does not perform Hajj. al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever possesses provision and a mount that carries him to the House of Allah, and does not perform Hajj to the House of Allah, then it makes no difference whether he dies a Jew or a Christian; that is because Allah says: ﴿And for Allah, on mankind, is the pilgrimage to the House — for whoever is able to make his way to it. And whoever disbelieves, then indeed Allah is free of need from the worlds﴾." In its chain is Hilal al-Khurasani, Abu Hashim.

al-Bukhari said: "Munkar al-hadith" (one whose narrations are rejected). It was said: "Majhul" (unknown).

Ibn 'Adi said: "This hadith is not preserved (mahfuz), and in its chain also is al-Harith al-A'war, and in him there is weakness."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ahmad in Kitab al-Iman, Abu Ya'la and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Umamah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever dies without performing the Hajj of Islam, and was not prevented by a restraining illness, or an oppressive ruler, or an apparent need, then let him die in whatever state he wishes, a Jew or a Christian."

Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) as mursal (a hadith whose chain omits a Companion), the same.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, al-Suyuti said: with a sound chain, from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: "I had resolved to send men to these cities so that they might examine every person who had wealth (jiddah) but did not perform Hajj, and then impose the jizya (poll tax) upon them; they are not Muslims, they are not Muslims."

al-Isma'ili narrated from him, saying: "Whoever is able to perform Hajj but does not perform it, it makes no difference whether he dies a Jew or a Christian." Ibn Kathir said after citing its chain: "This is a sound chain." Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from him something similar.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Umar: "Whoever dies while he is wealthy (musir) and has not performed Hajj, will come on the Day of Resurrection with the word 'disbeliever' written between his eyes." Sa'id ibn Mansur narrated from him: "Whoever finds a way (sabil) to Hajj, for a year, then another year, then another year, then dies without performing Hajj, he shall not be prayed over, and it is not known whether he died a Jew or a Christian."

Sa'id ibn Mansur narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: "If the people abandoned Hajj, I would fight them over it just as we fight them over the Salah and the Zakah."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And whoever disbelieves, then indeed Allah is free of need﴾, that he said: "Whoever claims that it is not obligatory upon him."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the verse, that he said: "Whoever disbelieves in the Hajj, does not regard his Hajj as righteousness, nor his abandoning it as sinful."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ikrimah, who said: "When the verse was revealed: ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as religion﴾ [Al 'Imran: 85], the Jews said: 'We are Muslims.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said to them: 'Indeed Allah has enjoined upon the Muslims the Hajj to the House.' They said: 'It was not prescribed for us,' and they refused to perform Hajj. Allah said: ﴿And whoever disbelieves, then indeed Allah is free of need from the worlds﴾."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ikrimah something similar. Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Dahhak, who said: "When the verse of Hajj was revealed: ﴿And for Allah, on mankind, is the pilgrimage to the House﴾, to the end of the verse, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gathered the people of the religions: the polytheist Arabs, the Christians, the Jews, the Magians and the Sabians, and said: 'Indeed Allah has enjoined upon you the Hajj, so perform Hajj to the House.' None accepted it except the Muslims, and five religions disbelieved in it. They said: 'We do not believe in it, nor do we pray towards it, nor do we face it.' So Allah revealed: ﴿And whoever disbelieves, then indeed Allah is free of need from the worlds﴾."

'Abd ibn Humayd and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Mujahid something similar. 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu Dawud Nufay' who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿And for Allah, on mankind, is the pilgrimage to the House﴾, to the end of the verse. A man from Hudhayl stood up and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, whoever abandons it, has he disbelieved?' He said: 'Whoever abandons it, not fearing its punishment; and whoever performs it, not hoping for its reward, then he is that (i.e., a disbeliever).'"

Ibn Jarir narrated from 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah concerning the verse, that he said: "Whoever disbelieves in the House." Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Ibn 'Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), "concerning the saying of Allah: ﴿And whoever disbelieves﴾, he said: Whoever disbelieves in Allah and the Last Day." 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid the same, from his own saying. Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Zayd that he was asked about this, so he recited: ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind﴾ up to His saying: ﴿a way﴾, and then said: "And whoever disbelieves in these verses." Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Mas'ud concerning the verse, that he said: "And whoever disbelieves, so he does not believe in it: then he is the disbeliever."

**Al-Shawkani, Fath al-Qadir, on Surah Al ʿImran, verses 98–103**

[Commentary on the verse ﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the signs of Allah while Allah is witness over what you do?"﴾]

His saying ﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture"﴾ is addressed to the Jews and the Christians. The interrogative in His saying ﴿why do you disbelieve﴾ is for denunciation and reproach.

His saying ﴿while Allah is witness over what you do﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*jumlah ḥāliyyah*) that reinforces the reproach and denunciation. Likewise, the use of the intensive form in *shahīd* (witness) conveys greater emphasis and dread. The interrogative in His saying ﴿why do you bar﴾ conveys what the first interrogative conveyed.

Al-Ḥasan read *taṣuddūna* from *aṣadda*, and both are dialectal forms, like *ṣadda al-laḥmu* and *aṣadda*, meaning the meat decayed and became foul. "The way of Allah" is His religion which He approved for His servants, namely the religion of Islam. *ʿIwaj* (crookedness) means inclination and deviation. It is said *ʿiwaj* with a kasra when it refers to religion, speech, and action, and with a fatḥa when it refers to physical things such as a wall and the like. This was related from Abū ʿUbaydah and others. The position of His saying ﴿seeking to make it crooked﴾ is accusative as a circumstantial state. The meaning is: you seek for it crookedness and deviation from the right course and uprightness, by your casting doubt upon the people that it is so, in order to distort it and to make your false claims appear straight.

His saying ﴿while you are witnesses﴾ is a circumstantial clause; that is: how do you seek that while you are witnesses that it is the religion of Islam, the religion of Allah which accepts no other, and that in it is the description of Muhammad (ﷺ)? It was also said that the meaning of ﴿while you are witnesses﴾ is: "intelligent." It was also said that the meaning is: "while you are witnesses among the people of your religion, accepted by them. So how do you bring falsehood that opposes what you are upon among the people of your religion?" Then He, glory be to Him, warned them with His saying ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾.

Then He, glory be to Him, addressed the believers, warning them against obeying the Jews and the Christians, and explaining to them that such obedience leads to their returning them to disbelief after their faith. The occasion of revelation of the verse will come.

The interrogative in His saying ﴿how do you disbelieve﴾ is for denunciation; that is: from where would that come to you when you have what prevents it and cuts off its trace, namely the recitation of the signs of Allah upon you and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) being among you? The position of His saying ﴿while you [have]﴾ and what follows it is accusative as a circumstantial state.

Then He guided them to hold fast to Allah, so that they might thereby attain guidance to the straight path, which is Islam. In describing the path as upright is a refutation of what they claimed of crookedness. Al-Zajjāj said: It is possible that this address is specifically to the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), since the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was among them and they witnessed him. And it is possible that this address is to the entire community, since his traces, his sign, and the Qur'an given to him are among us, so it is as if the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is among us even if we do not witness him. End of quote.

The meaning of *iʿtiṣām bi-Allāh* (holding fast to Allah) is adhering to His religion and obeying Him. It was also said: [it means] adhering to the Qur'an. It is said: *iʿtaṣama bihi*, *istaʿṣama*, *tamassaka*, and *istamsaka*, meaning he sought refuge in it from others. And *ʿaṣamahu al-ṭaʿām* means hunger was prevented from him by food.

His saying ﴿Be mindful of Allah with the mindfulness due to Him﴾: that is, the mindfulness that is due to Him, which is that the servant does not abandon anything that is obligatory for him to do, does not do anything that is obligatory for him to abandon, and exerts his effort and capacity in that.

Al-Qurṭubī said: The commentators mentioned that when this verse was revealed, they said, "O Messenger of Allah, who can be strong enough for this?" and it was difficult for them. So Allah revealed ﴿So be mindful of Allah as much as you are able﴾ [al-Taghābun: 16], and this verse was thereby abrogated (*nusikhat*). This was related from Qatādah, al-Rabīʿ, and Ibn Zayd.

Muqātil said: In Āl ʿImrān there is nothing abrogated except this. It was also said that His saying ﴿Be mindful of Allah with the mindfulness due to Him﴾ is clarified by His saying ﴿So be mindful of Allah as much as you are able﴾, and the meaning is: be mindful of Allah with the mindfulness due to Him as much as you are able.

He said: This is more correct, because abrogation (*naskh*, the cancelling of one ruling by a later one) occurs only when reconciliation is impossible, and reconciliation is possible, so it is preferable.

His saying ﴿And do not die except while you are Muslims﴾: that is, do not be in any state other than the state of Islam. The exception here is an exception from a negated context (*istithnāʾ mufarragh*, an exception where the excepted element is left unstated). The clause, namely His saying ﴿while you are Muslims﴾, is accusative as a circumstantial state. The explanation of a similar verse has already been given in al-Baqarah.

His saying ﴿And hold fast, all of you, to the rope of Allah﴾: *al-ḥabl* (the rope) is a homonymous word. Its original meaning in the language is the means by which one reaches the desired goal, and it is either a metaphor or a figurative usage. He, glory be to Him, commanded them to unite in holding to the religion of Islam or to the Qur'an, and forbade them from division arising from disagreement in religion. Then He commanded them to remember the blessing of Allah upon them, and He explained to them from this blessing what is appropriate to the situation: that they had been enemies, divided, killing one another and plundering one another. Then through this blessing they became brothers, and they had been on the brink of a pit of the Fire because of their disbelief, so Allah rescued them from this pit through Islam.

The meaning of His saying ﴿you became﴾ is "you became," and it does not mean its original sense, which is entering the time of morning. *Shafā* (brink) of everything is its edge, and likewise its rim. *Ashfā ʿalā al-shayʾ* means he overlooked it. It is a metaphor for the state they were in during the Jāhiliyyah (the time of ignorance). His saying ﴿thus﴾ refers to the verbal noun of the verb that follows it; that is: like that eloquent clarification, Allah makes clear to you.

His saying ﴿so that you may be guided﴾ is an exhortation to them to remain steadfast upon guidance and to increase in it.

Ibn Isḥāq, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and Abū al-Shaykh related from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: Shās ibn Qays passed by a group of the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), from the Aws and the Khazraj, in a gathering in which they had come together to converse. He was an old man who had reached great age in the Jāhiliyyah, extremely disbelieving, harshly maligning the Muslims, and intensely envious of them. He was angered by what he saw of their affection, their unity, and the good relations among them in Islam, after the enmity that had existed between them in the Jāhiliyyah. So he said: "The chiefs of the Banū Qaylah have gathered in this land. By Allah, we have no place among them if their chiefs gather here." Then he ordered a young man with him from among the Jews, saying: "Go to them, sit with them, then remind them of the Day of Buʿāth and what preceded it, and recite to them some of the poetry they used to exchange about it." The Day of Buʿāth was a day in which the Aws and the Khazraj fought, and victory on it was for the Aws over the Khazraj. So he did that. The people then spoke, disputed, and boasted at that moment, until two men from the two clans leapt up before the assembly: Aws ibn Qayẓī of the Banū Ḥārithah from the Aws, and Jabbār ibn Ṣakhr of the Banū Salamah from the Khazraj. They quarreled, then one of them said to his companion: "If you wish, by Allah, we can restore it now as it was at its beginning." Both groups became angry and said: "We have done so. The weapons! The weapons! Our appointment is al-Ẓāhirah," and al-Ẓāhirah was al-Ḥarrah. So they threw the weapons from their hands and wept, and men embraced one another. Then they departed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), listening and obeying, after Allah had extinguished from them the plot of the enemy of Allah, Shās. Allah revealed concerning Shās ibn Qays and what he did: ﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the signs of Allah while Allah is witness over what you do?"﴾ up to His saying ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾. And He revealed concerning Aws ibn Qayẓī, Jabbār ibn Ṣakhr, and those who were with them from their people, who did what they did: ﴿O you who have believed, if you obey a faction of those who were given the Scripture﴾ up to His saying ﴿and for them is a great punishment﴾. This story has been related in brief and in detail through various chains.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from al-Suddī concerning His saying ﴿Why do you bar from the way of Allah﴾, who said: They used to say, when someone asked them: "Do you find Muhammad?" They said: "No." So they barred the people from him, and sought to make Muhammad crooked, that is, to destroy him. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Jarīr related from Qatādah: "Why do you bar from Islam and from the Prophet of Allah those who believe in Allah, while you are witnesses in what you read of the Book of Allah, that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and that Islam is the religion of Allah which accepts no other and rewards only through it? You find it written with you in the Torah and the Gospel."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Ibn Jurayj concerning His saying ﴿And whoever holds fast to Allah﴾, who said: "He believes in Him." Al-Ḥākim graded it sound, and Ibn Mardawayh related it through another chain from him, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ), without the words "and thanked and not denied."

Traditions have indeed been related that the Book of Allah is the stretched-out rope of Allah. Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Abū al-ʿĀliyah who said: "And hold fast to the rope of Allah" means by sincerity to Allah alone.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from al-Ḥasan who said: "By obedience to Him." He also related from Qatādah who said: "By His covenant and His command."

Ibn Jarīr related from Ibn Zayd who said: "By Islam." Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Ibn Jurayj concerning His saying ﴿when you were enemies﴾, who said: "[It refers to] what was between the Aws and the Khazraj concerning the affair of ʿĀʾishah."

Ibn Isḥāq said: The war between the Aws and the Khazraj lasted a hundred and twenty years, until Islam came and Allah extinguished that and united them. Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from al-Suddī concerning His saying ﴿and you were on the brink of a pit of the Fire﴾, who said: "You were on the edge of the Fire; whoever of you died would fall into the Fire, so Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ) and rescued you through him from that pit."

**Al-Shawkani, Fath al-Qadir, on Surah Al ʿImran, verses 98–103**

[Commentary on the verse ﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the signs of Allah while Allah is witness over what you do?"﴾]

His saying ﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture"﴾ is addressed to the Jews and the Christians. The interrogative in His saying ﴿why do you disbelieve﴾ is for denunciation and reproach.

His saying ﴿while Allah is witness over what you do﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*jumlah ḥāliyyah*) that reinforces the reproach and denunciation. Likewise, the use of the intensive form in *shahīd* (witness) conveys greater emphasis and dread. The interrogative in His saying ﴿why do you bar﴾ conveys what the first interrogative conveyed.

Al-Ḥasan read *taṣuddūna* from *aṣadda*, and both are dialectal forms, like *ṣadda al-laḥmu* and *aṣadda*, meaning the meat decayed and became foul. "The way of Allah" is His religion which He approved for His servants, namely the religion of Islam. *ʿIwaj* (crookedness) means inclination and deviation. It is said *ʿiwaj* with a kasra when it refers to religion, speech, and action, and with a fatḥa when it refers to physical things such as a wall and the like. This was related from Abū ʿUbaydah and others. The position of His saying ﴿seeking to make it crooked﴾ is accusative as a circumstantial state. The meaning is: you seek for it crookedness and deviation from the right course and uprightness, by your casting doubt upon the people that it is so, in order to distort it and to make your false claims appear straight.

His saying ﴿while you are witnesses﴾ is a circumstantial clause; that is: how do you seek that while you are witnesses that it is the religion of Islam, the religion of Allah which accepts no other, and that in it is the description of Muhammad (ﷺ)? It was also said that the meaning of ﴿while you are witnesses﴾ is: "intelligent." It was also said that the meaning is: "while you are witnesses among the people of your religion, accepted by them. So how do you bring falsehood that opposes what you are upon among the people of your religion?" Then He, glory be to Him, warned them with His saying ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾.

Then He, glory be to Him, addressed the believers, warning them against obeying the Jews and the Christians, and explaining to them that such obedience leads to their returning them to disbelief after their faith. The occasion of revelation of the verse will come.

The interrogative in His saying ﴿how do you disbelieve﴾ is for denunciation; that is: from where would that come to you when you have what prevents it and cuts off its trace, namely the recitation of the signs of Allah upon you and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) being among you? The position of His saying ﴿while you [have]﴾ and what follows it is accusative as a circumstantial state.

Then He guided them to hold fast to Allah, so that they might thereby attain guidance to the straight path, which is Islam. In describing the path as upright is a refutation of what they claimed of crookedness. Al-Zajjāj said: It is possible that this address is specifically to the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), since the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was among them and they witnessed him. And it is possible that this address is to the entire community, since his traces, his sign, and the Qur'an given to him are among us, so it is as if the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is among us even if we do not witness him. End of quote.

The meaning of *iʿtiṣām bi-Allāh* (holding fast to Allah) is adhering to His religion and obeying Him. It was also said: [it means] adhering to the Qur'an. It is said: *iʿtaṣama bihi*, *istaʿṣama*, *tamassaka*, and *istamsaka*, meaning he sought refuge in it from others. And *ʿaṣamahu al-ṭaʿām* means hunger was prevented from him by food.

His saying ﴿Be mindful of Allah with the mindfulness due to Him﴾: that is, the mindfulness that is due to Him, which is that the servant does not abandon anything that is obligatory for him to do, does not do anything that is obligatory for him to abandon, and exerts his effort and capacity in that.

Al-Qurṭubī said: The commentators mentioned that when this verse was revealed, they said, "O Messenger of Allah, who can be strong enough for this?" and it was difficult for them. So Allah revealed ﴿So be mindful of Allah as much as you are able﴾ [al-Taghābun: 16], and this verse was thereby abrogated (*nusikhat*). This was related from Qatādah, al-Rabīʿ, and Ibn Zayd.

Muqātil said: In Āl ʿImrān there is nothing abrogated except this. It was also said that His saying ﴿Be mindful of Allah with the mindfulness due to Him﴾ is clarified by His saying ﴿So be mindful of Allah as much as you are able﴾, and the meaning is: be mindful of Allah with the mindfulness due to Him as much as you are able.

He said: This is more correct, because abrogation (*naskh*, the cancelling of one ruling by a later one) occurs only when reconciliation is impossible, and reconciliation is possible, so it is preferable.

His saying ﴿And do not die except while you are Muslims﴾: that is, do not be in any state other than the state of Islam. The exception here is an exception from a negated context (*istithnāʾ mufarragh*, an exception where the excepted element is left unstated). The clause, namely His saying ﴿while you are Muslims﴾, is accusative as a circumstantial state. The explanation of a similar verse has already been given in al-Baqarah.

His saying ﴿And hold fast, all of you, to the rope of Allah﴾: *al-ḥabl* (the rope) is a homonymous word. Its original meaning in the language is the means by which one reaches the desired goal, and it is either a metaphor or a figurative usage. He, glory be to Him, commanded them to unite in holding to the religion of Islam or to the Qur'an, and forbade them from division arising from disagreement in religion. Then He commanded them to remember the blessing of Allah upon them, and He explained to them from this blessing what is appropriate to the situation: that they had been enemies, divided, killing one another and plundering one another. Then through this blessing they became brothers, and they had been on the brink of a pit of the Fire because of their disbelief, so Allah rescued them from this pit through Islam.

The meaning of His saying ﴿you became﴾ is "you became," and it does not mean its original sense, which is entering the time of morning. *Shafā* (brink) of everything is its edge, and likewise its rim. *Ashfā ʿalā al-shayʾ* means he overlooked it. It is a metaphor for the state they were in during the Jāhiliyyah (the time of ignorance). His saying ﴿thus﴾ refers to the verbal noun of the verb that follows it; that is: like that eloquent clarification, Allah makes clear to you.

His saying ﴿so that you may be guided﴾ is an exhortation to them to remain steadfast upon guidance and to increase in it.

Ibn Isḥāq, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and Abū al-Shaykh related from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: Shās ibn Qays passed by a group of the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), from the Aws and the Khazraj, in a gathering in which they had come together to converse. He was an old man who had reached great age in the Jāhiliyyah, extremely disbelieving, harshly maligning the Muslims, and intensely envious of them. He was angered by what he saw of their affection, their unity, and the good relations among them in Islam, after the enmity that had existed between them in the Jāhiliyyah.
