**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verses 104–109:**

His saying, ﴿وَلْتَكُن﴾ (*wa-l-takun*, "let there be"): the majority (*al-jumhur*) read the lam with a sukun (*bi-iskan al-lam*). It was also read with a kasra on the lam, according to the original form (*'ala al-asl*). The *min* in His saying, ﴿مِنكُمْ﴾ (*minkum*, "from among you"), is partitive (*li-l-tab'idh*). It was also said that it is explanatory of the kind (*li-bayan al-jins*). The first reading was preferred on the grounds that enjoining good and forbidding evil are collective obligations (*furud al-kifayat*), which are restricted to the people of knowledge (*ahl al-'ilm*), who recognise that what they enjoin is good (*ma'ruf*) and what they forbid is evil (*munkar*).

Al-Qurtubi said: The first reading is more sound, for it indicates that enjoining good and forbidding evil is a collective obligation. God, glory be to Him, has specified them by His saying: ﴿those who, if We establish them in the land...﴾ [al-Hajj: 41], and so on.

Ibn al-Zubayr read: "Let there be from among you a community that calls to good, enjoins what is right, forbids what is wrong, and seeks help from God against what afflicts them." Abu Bakr ibn al-Anbari said: This addition is an explanation (*tafsir*) by Ibn al-Zubayr and a statement of his own speech, which some transmitters mistook and attached to the words of the Qur'an.

It has been narrated that Uthman recited it in this way but did not write it in his codex (*mushaf*), which indicates that it is not part of the Qur'an.

In the verse there is evidence for the obligation of enjoining good and forbidding evil. Its obligation is established by the Book and the Sunnah, and it is one of the greatest obligations of the pure Shari'a, a great foundation of its principles, and a firmly established pillar of its pillars. Through it its order is completed and its summit is raised.

His saying, ﴿يَأْمُرُونَ بِالْمَعْرُوفِ وَيَنْهَوْنَ عَنِ الْمُنكَرِ﴾ ("they enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong"), is of the type of the specific being conjoined to the general (*'atf al-khass 'ala al-'amm*), to show their nobility, and that they are the two complete individual instances (*al-fardan al-kamilan*) of the good to which God commanded His servants to call. This is like what was said regarding the conjunction of Jibril and Mika'il with the angels. The object of the three verbs is omitted, for the purpose of generality; that is, they call, enjoin, and forbid, meaning: everyone from whom there arises a cause that requires that. The reference in His saying, ﴿وَأُوْلَئِكَ﴾ ("and those"), returns to the community by virtue of its being characterised by what is mentioned after it: ﴿هُمُ الْمُفْلِحُونَ﴾ ("they are the successful"), i.e., those specially characterised by success. The definite article in *al-muflihun* is for a known reference (*li-l-'ahd*) or for the reality (*li-l-haqiqa*) that everyone recognises.

His saying: ﴿وَلَا تَكُونُوا كَالَّذِينَ تَفَرَّقُوا﴾ ("And do not be like those who divided"): according to the majority of the exegetes (*jumhur al-mufassirin*) they are the Jews and the Christians. It was also said that they are the innovators (*al-mubtadi'a*) of this community, and it was said they are the Harurites (*al-harûriyya*). The apparent meaning is the first.

The clear signs (*al-bayyinat*) are the manifest verses that make the truth clear and necessitate the absence of disagreement. It was said: This prohibition of division and disagreement is restricted to the fundamental matters (*al-masa'il al-usuliyya*). As for the derivative juristic matters (*al-masa'il al-furu'iyya al-ijtihadiyya*), disagreement regarding them is permissible, and the Companions and those after them among the Successors (*tabi'un*) and their followers (*tabi' al-tabi'in*) continued to differ regarding the rulings of new events. This requires examination, for in those eras there continued to exist those who denied disagreement, and restricting some matters of religion to permissibility of disagreement while not others is not correct. (p-237) Rather, legislative matters are equal in their attachment to the Shari'a.

His saying: ﴿يَوْمَ تَبْيَضُّ وُجُوهٌ﴾ ("on the day when faces turn white") is in the accusative, governed by a hidden verb: "Remember." It was also said that it is governed by what His saying indicates: ﴿لَهُمْ عَذَابٌ عَظِيمٌ﴾ ("for them is a great punishment"), for its implied sense is: "A great punishment will be established for them on the day when faces turn white," that is, on the Day of Resurrection, when they are raised from their graves: the faces of the believers will be white and the faces of the disbelievers will be black. It is said that this occurs at the reading of the Book: when the believer reads his book and sees his good deeds, he rejoices and his face turns white; and when the disbeliever reads his book and sees his evil deeds, he grieves and his face turns black.

The indefiniteness in *wujuh* ("faces") is for multiplicity, that is, many faces. Yahya ibn Wathhab read *tabyaddu* and *taswaddu* with a kasra on both the taʼs.

Al-Zuhri read *tabyaadd* and *taswaadd*.

His saying: ﴿أَكَفَرْتُم﴾ ("Did you disbelieve...?"): that is, it will be said to them: "Did you disbelieve?" The hamza is for rebuke and for marvelling at their condition. This is a detailed account of the states of the two groups after a general statement. He mentioned the state of the disbelievers first, because the context is one of warning and intimidation. It was said: they are the People of the Book; it was said: the apostates; it was said: the hypocrites; it was said: the innovators.

His saying: ﴿فَفِي رَحْمَةِ اللَّهِ﴾ ("then in the mercy of God"), that is, in His Paradise and the abode of His honour. He expressed this by "mercy" as an indication that deeds alone do not secure their doer's entry into Paradise; rather, mercy is necessary. From this is the hadith: "No one will enter Paradise by his deeds," and it is in the Sahih. His saying: ﴿هُمْ فِيهَا خَالِدُونَ﴾ ("they will abide therein eternally") is a resumptive sentence (*jumla isti'nafiyya*), an answer to a presumed question.

﴿تِلْكَ﴾ ("These") is a reference to what preceded of the punishment of the disbelievers and the bliss of the believers. His saying: ﴿نَتْلُوهَا عَلَيْكَ بِالْحَقِّ﴾ ("We recite them to you in truth") is a circumstantial clause (*jumla haliyya*), and *bil-haqq* is attached to an omitted element, that is: "clothed with truth," which is justice (*al-'adl*).

His saying: ﴿وَمَا اللَّهُ يُرِيدُ ظُلْمًا لِّلْعَالَمِينَ﴾ ("And God does not intend any injustice to the worlds") is a concluding sentence (*jumla tadhyiliyya*), confirming the content of what precedes it. In directing the negation to the will that falls upon an indefinite noun, there is evidence that He, glory be to Him, does not will any single instance of injustice falling upon any single member of the worlds. What is meant by ﴿مَا فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَمَا فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾ ("what is in the heavens and what is in the earth") is His creatures, glory be to Him; that is, to Him belongs all of that, and He disposes of it as He wills and in accordance with what He desires. He expressed it with *ma* (which is used for non-rational beings) by way of predominance of non-rational beings over rational ones, because of their great number, or because rational beings are treated as the same as others.

Al-Mahdawi said: The connection of this with what precedes it is that, when He mentioned the states of the believers and the disbelievers, and that He does not intend injustice to the worlds, He linked it to the mention of the vastness of His power and His independence from injustice, since all that is in the heavens and the earth is in His grip. It was also said: it is the beginning of a speech that includes a clarification to His servants that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him, so that they may ask Him and worship Him and not worship anything else.

His saying: ﴿وَإِلَى اللَّهِ تُرْجَعُ الْأُمُورُ﴾ ("And to God all matters are returned"), that is, not to anyone else, neither as partners nor independently.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Ja'far al-Baqir, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited: ﴿وَلْتَكُن مِّنكُمْ أُمَّةٌ يَدْعُونَ إِلَى الْخَيْرِ﴾ and said: 'The good is following the Qur'an and my Sunnah.'" It was also read with a kasra on the lam, according to the original form (*'ala al-asl*). The *min* in His saying, ﴿مِنكُمْ﴾ (*minkum*, "from among you"), is partitive (*li-l-tab'idh*). It was also said that it is explanatory of the kind (*li-bayan al-jins*). The first reading was preferred on the grounds that enjoining good and forbidding evil are collective obligations (*furud al-kifayat*), which are restricted to the people of knowledge (*ahl al-'ilm*), who recognise that what they enjoin is good (*ma'ruf*) and what they forbid is evil (*munkar*).

Al-Qurtubi said: The first reading is more sound, for it indicates that enjoining good and forbidding evil is a collective obligation. God, glory be to Him, has specified them by His saying: ﴿those who, if We establish them in the land...﴾ [al-Hajj: 41], and so on.

Ibn al-Zubayr read: "Let there be from among you a community that calls to good, enjoins what is right, forbids what is wrong, and seeks help from God against what afflicts them." Abu Bakr ibn al-Anbari said: This addition is an explanation (*tafsir*) by Ibn al-Zubayr and a statement of his own speech, which some transmitters mistook and attached to the words of the Qur'an.

It has been narrated that Uthman recited it in this way but did not write it in his codex (*mushaf*), which indicates that it is not part of the Qur'an.

In the verse there is evidence for the obligation of enjoining good and forbidding evil. Its obligation is established by the Book and the Sunnah, and it is one of the greatest obligations of the pure Shari'a, a great foundation of its principles, and a firmly established pillar of its pillars. Through it its order is completed and its summit is raised.

His saying, ﴿يَأْمُرُونَ بِالْمَعْرُوفِ وَيَنْهَوْنَ عَنِ الْمُنكَرِ﴾ ("they enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong"), is of the type of the specific being conjoined to the general (*'atf al-khass 'ala al-'amm*), to show their nobility, and that they are the two complete individual instances (*al-fardan al-kamilan*) of the good to which God commanded His servants to call. This is like what was said regarding the conjunction of Jibril and Mika'il with the angels. The object of the three verbs is omitted, for the purpose of generality; that is, they call, enjoin, and forbid, meaning: everyone from whom there arises a cause that requires that. The reference in His saying, ﴿وَأُوْلَئِكَ﴾ ("and those"), returns to the community by virtue of its being characterised by what is mentioned after it: ﴿هُمُ الْمُفْلِحُونَ﴾ ("they are the successful"), i.e., those specially characterised by success. The definite article in *al-muflihun* is for a known reference (*li-l-'ahd*) or for the reality (*li-l-haqiqa*) that everyone recognises.

His saying: ﴿وَلَا تَكُونُوا كَالَّذِينَ تَفَرَّقُوا﴾ ("And do not be like those who divided"): according to the majority of the exegetes (*jumhur al-mufassirin*) they are the Jews and the Christians. It was also said that they are the innovators (*al-mubtadi'a*) of this community, and it was said they are the Harurites (*al-harûriyya*). The apparent meaning is the first.

The clear signs (*al-bayyinat*) are the manifest verses that make the truth clear and necessitate the absence of disagreement. It was said: This prohibition of division and disagreement is restricted to the fundamental matters (*al-masa'il al-usuliyya*). As for the derivative juristic matters (*al-masa'il al-furu'iyya al-ijtihadiyya*), disagreement regarding them is permissible, and the Companions and those after them among the Successors (*tabi'un*) and their followers (*tabi' al-tabi'in*) continued to differ regarding the rulings of new events. This requires examination, for in those eras there continued to exist those who denied disagreement, and restricting some matters of religion to permissibility of disagreement while not others is not correct. (p-237) Rather, legislative matters are equal in their attachment to the Shari'a.

His saying: ﴿يَوْمَ تَبْيَضُّ وُجُوهٌ﴾ ("on the day when faces turn white") is in the accusative, governed by a hidden verb: "Remember." It was also said that it is governed by what His saying indicates: ﴿لَهُمْ عَذَابٌ عَظِيمٌ﴾ ("for them is a great punishment"), for its implied sense is: "A great punishment will be established for them on the day when faces turn white," that is, on the Day of Resurrection, when they are raised from their graves: the faces of the believers will be white and the faces of the disbelievers will be black. It is said that this occurs at the reading of the Book: when the believer reads his book and sees his good deeds, he rejoices and his face turns white; and when the disbeliever reads his book and sees his evil deeds, he grieves and his face turns black.

The indefiniteness in *wujuh* ("faces") is for multiplicity, that is, many faces. Yahya ibn Wathhab read *tabyaddu* and *taswaddu* with a kasra on both the taʼs.

Al-Zuhri read *tabyaadd* and *taswaadd*.

His saying: ﴿أَكَفَرْتُم﴾ ("Did you disbelieve...?"): that is, it will be said to them: "Did you disbelieve?" The hamza is for rebuke and for marvelling at their condition. This is a detailed account of the states of the two groups after a general statement. He mentioned the state of the disbelievers first, because the context is one of warning and intimidation. It was said: they are the People of the Book; it was said: the apostates; it was said: the hypocrites; it was said: the innovators.

This is like what was said regarding the conjunction of Jibril and Mika'il with the angels. The object of the three verbs is omitted, for the purpose of generality; that is, they call, enjoin, and forbid, meaning: everyone from whom there arises a cause that requires that. Al-Qurtubi said: The first reading is more sound, for it indicates that enjoining good and forbidding evil is a collective obligation. God, glory be to Him, has specified them by His saying: ﴿those who, if We establish them in the land...﴾ [al-Hajj: 41], and so on.

Ibn al-Zubayr read: "Let there be from among you a community that calls to good, enjoins what is right, forbids what is wrong, and seeks help from God against what afflicts them." Abu Bakr ibn al-Anbari said: This addition is an explanation (*tafsir*) by Ibn al-Zubayr and a statement of his own speech, which some transmitters mistook and attached to the words of the Qur'an.

It has been narrated that Uthman recited it in this way but did not write it in his codex (*mushaf*), which indicates that it is not part of the Qur'an.

In the verse there is evidence for the obligation of enjoining good and forbidding evil. Its obligation is established by the Book and the Sunnah, and it is one of the greatest obligations of the pure Shari'a, a great foundation of its principles, and a firmly established pillar of its pillars. Through it its order is completed and its summit is raised.

His saying, ﴿يَأْمُرُونَ بِالْمَعْرُوفِ وَيَنْهَوْنَ عَنِ الْمُنكَرِ﴾ ("they enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong"), is of the type of the specific being conjoined to the general (*'atf al-khass 'ala al-'amm*), to show their nobility, and that they are the two complete individual instances (*al-fardan al-kamilan*) of the good to which God commanded His servants to call. This is like what was said regarding the conjunction of Jibril and Mika'il with the angels. The object of the three verbs is omitted, for the purpose of generality; that is, they call, enjoin, and forbid, meaning: everyone from whom there arises a cause that requires that. The reference in His saying, ﴿وَأُوْلَئِكَ﴾ ("and those"), returns to the community by virtue of its being characterised by what is mentioned after it: ﴿هُمُ الْمُفْلِحُونَ﴾ ("they are the successful"), i.e., those specially characterised by success. The definite article in *al-muflihun* is for a known reference (*li-l-'ahd*) or for the reality (*li-l-haqiqa*) that everyone recognises.

His saying: ﴿وَلَا تَكُونُوا كَالَّذِينَ تَفَرَّقُوا﴾ ("And do not be like those who divided"): according to the majority of the exegetes (*jumhur al-mufassirin*) they are the Jews and the Christians. It was also said that they are the innovators (*al-mubtadi'a*) of this community, and it was said they are the Harurites (*al-harûriyya*). The apparent meaning is the first.

The clear signs (*al-bayyinat*) are the manifest verses that make the truth clear and necessitate the absence of disagreement. It was said: This prohibition of division and disagreement is restricted to the fundamental matters (*al-masa'il al-usuliyya*). As for the derivative juristic matters (*al-masa'il al-furu'iyya al-ijtihadiyya*), disagreement regarding them is permissible, and the Companions and those after them among the Successors (*tabi'un*) and their followers (*tabi' al-tabi'in*) continued to differ regarding the rulings of new events. This requires examination, for in those eras there continued to exist those who denied disagreement, and restricting some matters of religion to permissibility of disagreement while not others is not correct. (p-237) Rather, legislative matters are equal in their attachment to the Shari'a.

His saying: ﴿يَوْمَ تَبْيَضُّ وُجُوهٌ﴾ ("on the day when faces turn white") is in the accusative, governed by a hidden verb: "Remember." It was also said that it is governed by what His saying indicates: ﴿لَهُمْ عَذَابٌ عَظِيمٌ﴾ ("for them is a great punishment"), for its implied sense is: "A great punishment will be established for them on the day when faces turn white," that is, on the Day of Resurrection, when they are raised from their graves: the faces of the believers will be white and the faces of the disbelievers will be black. It is said that this occurs at the reading of the Book: when the believer reads his book and sees his good deeds, he rejoices and his face turns white; and when the disbeliever reads his book and sees his evil deeds, he grieves and his face turns black.

The indefiniteness in *wujuh* ("faces") is for multiplicity, that is, many faces. Yahya ibn Wathhab read *tabyaddu* and *taswaddu* with a kasra on both the taʼs.

Al-Zuhri read *tabyaadd* and *taswaadd*.

His saying: ﴿أَكَفَرْتُم﴾ ("Did you disbelieve...?"): that is, it will be said to them: "Did you disbelieve?" The hamza is for rebuke and for marvelling at their condition. This is a detailed account of the states of the two groups after a general statement. He mentioned the state of the disbelievers first, because the context is one of warning and intimidation. It was said: they are the People of the Book; it was said: the apostates; it was said: the hypocrites; it was said: the innovators.

His saying: ﴿فَفِي رَحْمَةِ اللَّهِ﴾ ("then in the mercy of God"), that is, in His Paradise and the abode of His honour. He expressed this by "mercy" as an indication that deeds alone do not secure their doer's entry into Paradise; rather, mercy is necessary. From this is the hadith: "No one will enter Paradise by his deeds," and it is in the Sahih. His saying: ﴿هُمْ فِيهَا خَالِدُونَ﴾ ("they will abide therein eternally") is a resumptive sentence (*jumla isti'nafiyya*), an answer to a presumed question.

﴿تِلْكَ﴾ ("These") is a reference to what preceded of the punishment of the disbelievers and the bliss of the believers. His saying: ﴿نَتْلُوهَا عَلَيْكَ بِالْحَقِّ﴾ ("We recite them to you in truth") is a circumstantial clause (*jumla haliyya*), and *bil-haqq* is attached to an omitted element, that is: "clothed with truth," which is justice (*al-'adl*).

His saying: ﴿وَمَا اللَّهُ يُرِيدُ ظُلْمًا لِّلْعَالَمِينَ﴾ ("And God does not intend any injustice to the worlds") is a concluding sentence (*jumla tadhyiliyya*), confirming the content of what precedes it. In directing the negation to the will that falls upon an indefinite noun, there is evidence that He, glory be to Him, does not will any single instance of injustice falling upon any single member of the worlds. What is meant by ﴿مَا فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَمَا فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾ ("what is in the heavens and what is in the earth") is His creatures, glory be to Him; that is, to Him belongs all of that, and He disposes of it as He wills and in accordance with what He desires. He expressed it with *ma* (which is used for non-rational beings) by way of predominance of non-rational beings over rational ones, because of their great number, or because rational beings are treated as the same as others.

Al-Mahdawi said: The connection of this with what precedes it is that, when He mentioned the states of the believers and the disbelievers, and that He does not intend injustice to the worlds, He linked it to the mention of the vastness of His power and His independence from injustice, since all that is in the heavens and the earth is in His grip. It was also said: it is the beginning of a speech that includes a clarification to His servants that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him, so that they may ask Him and worship Him and not worship anything else.

His saying: ﴿وَإِلَى اللَّهِ تُرْجَعُ الْأُمُورُ﴾ ("And to God all matters are returned"), that is, not to anyone else, neither as partners nor independently.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Ja'far al-Baqir, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited: ﴿وَلْتَكُن مِّنكُمْ أُمَّةٌ يَدْعُونَ إِلَى الْخَيْرِ﴾ and said: 'The good is following the Qur'an and my Sunnah.'" Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu al-'Aliyah, who said: "Every verse that God has mentioned in the Qur'an concerning enjoining what is right is Islam, and forbidding what is wrong is worship of idols and of Satan," end of quote.

This is a restriction without a restricting indicator, for neither in the language of the Arabs nor in the usage of the Shari'a is there anything that indicates that.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Muqatil ibn Hayyan, who said: ﴿يَدْعُونَ إِلَى الْخَيْرِ﴾ means Islam; ﴿وَيَأْمُرُونَ بِالْمَعْرُوفِ﴾ means obedience to their Lord; ﴿وَيَنْهَوْنَ عَنِ الْمُنكَرِ﴾ means disobedience to their Lord.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Dahhak regarding the verse, who said: "They are exclusively the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), and they are the transmitters," end of quote. I do not know what the basis of this restriction is, for the address in this verse is like the address in all the other matters which God has legislated for His servants and imposed upon them.

Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The Jews split into seventy-one sects, the Christians split into seventy-two sects, and my community will split into seventy-three sects." Ahmad, Abu Dawud, and al-Hakim narrated from Mu'awiya, marfu', something similar, and added: "All of them are in the Fire except one, and it is the Jama'a (community)."

Al-Hakim narrated from Abd Allah ibn Amr, marfu', something similar as well, and added: "All of them are in the Fire except one religious community (*milla*). It was asked: 'What is the one?' He said: 'That which I and my Companions are upon today.'" Ibn Majah narrated from Awf ibn Malik, marfu', something similar, and in it: "One is in Paradise and seventy-two are in the Fire. It was asked: 'O Messenger of God, who are they?' He said: 'The Jama'a.'" Ahmad narrated it from the hadith of Anas, and in it: "It was asked: 'O Messenger of God, who is that sect?' He said: 'The Jama'a.'"

Many verses and hadiths have come concerning enjoining good and forbidding evil, and concerning remaining in the community (*al-jama'a*) and forbidding division. Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Khatib narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿يَوْمَ تَبْيَضُّ وُجُوهٌ﴾, he said: "The faces of the People of the Sunnah and the Jama'a will turn white, and the faces of the people of innovations (*bida'*) and misguidance will turn black."

Al-Khatib and al-Daylami narrated it from Ibn Umar, marfu'; and Abu Nasr al-Sijzi also narrated it, marfu', in al-Ibana, from Abu Sa'id. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b regarding the verse, who said: "They will become two groups on the Day of Resurrection. It will be said to the one whose face has turned black: 'Did you disbelieve after your faith?' This is the faith that was in the loins of Adam when they were one community. As for those whose faces turned white, they are those who remained steadfast in their faith and sincerely devoted their religion to Him; so God whitened their faces and admitted them into His good pleasure and His Paradise." Other than this has also been narrated.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 3, verses 110–112**

His statement, ﴿You were the best nation﴾, is a resumptive sentence (*kalam mustaʾnaf*, a new clause not grammatically tied to what precedes it) that includes an explanation of the state of this nation in excellence over other nations. It was said that *kuntum* here is the complete (*tammah*) verb, meaning: you came into existence and were created as the best nation. Similar to this is what Sibawayh recited:

*"And neighbours of ours who were noble."*

And from the same usage is His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿How can we speak to one who is in the cradle, a child?﴾ [Maryam: 29], and His statement: ﴿Remember when you were few and He multiplied you﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 86]. Al-Akhfash said: He means the people of a nation, i.e., the best people of a religion, and he recited:

*"I swore, and I left no suspicion of you in your self, and would one of a nation sin while he is obedient?"*

It was also said that the meaning is: you were in the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawh al-mahfuz*). It was said: you have been so since you believed. In this is evidence that this Islamic nation is the best of nations absolutely, and that this excellence is shared among the first and last of this nation in comparison with other nations, even though they differ in rank among themselves, as has been reported concerning the virtue of the Companions over others.

His statement, ﴿brought forth for mankind﴾, means: made manifest to them. His statement, ﴿you enjoin what is right﴾, and what follows, is a resumptive sentence that explains their being the best nation, together with what this entails: that they are the best nation so long as they uphold this and are characterised by it. When they abandon enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, that excellence departs from them. For this reason Mujahid said: they are the best nation on the conditions mentioned in the verse. This implies that *tamurūna* and what follows it are in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), meaning: you were the best nation while you were enjoining, forbidding, and believing in Allah and in what it is obligatory for you to believe in, from His Book, His Messenger, and what He has legislated for His servants, for faith in Allah, glory be to Him, is not complete except by believing in these matters.

His statement, ﴿And if the People of the Book had believed﴾, means: the Jews, believing as the Muslims believe in Allah, His messengers, and His books, ﴿it would have been better for them﴾. But they did not do so; rather they said: "We believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part." Then He explained the state of the People of the Book with His statement: ﴿Among them are believers﴾, and they are those among them who believed in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), for they believed in what was revealed to him and what was revealed before him. ﴿And most of them are defiant transgressors﴾, meaning: those who have departed from the path of truth, who are obstinate in their falsehood, who deny the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and what he brought. Accordingly, this detail is, on this reading, a resumptive statement answering an assumed question, as if it were said: "Is there among them anyone who believed and thereby deserved what Allah promised?"

His statement, ﴿They will not harm you except with some injury﴾, means: they will not harm you with any kind of harm except with a kind of hurt, namely lying, distortion, and slander. They are not able to inflict the harm that is genuine harm, such as war, plunder, and the like. The exception here is therefore an exception from a negated general (*mufarragh*), and this is a promise from Allah to His Messenger and to the believers that the People of the Book will not overcome them, and that they will be victorious over them. It was also said that the exception is disjunctive (*munqaṭiʿ*).

The meaning is: they will not harm you at all, but they will hurt you. Then He, glory be to Him, explained what He had negated of harm with His statement: ﴿And if they fight you, they will turn their backs to you﴾, meaning: they will be routed and will not be able to resist you, let alone harm you. His statement, ﴿then they will not be helped﴾, is coordinated (*ʿaṭf*) with the conditional sentence; that is: then no help will be found for them, and no victory will be established for them in any circumstance. Rather, their condition is abandonment so long as they remain.

We have indeed found what He, glory be to Him, promised to be true, for the Jews have never had the banner of victory raised for them, nor has an army gathered for them that prevailed, since the revelation of this verse, so it is one of the miracles of prophethood. His statement, ﴿Humiliation is stamped upon them﴾, has already been explained in al-Baqarah, the meaning of this construction.

The meaning is: humiliation has become encompassing them in every state, under every circumstance, wherever they are found, ﴿except with a rope from Allah﴾, meaning: except that they hold fast to a rope from Allah, as al-Farra' said, i.e., to the protection (*dhimma*) of Allah or to His Book, ﴿and a rope from mankind﴾, meaning: to a protection from people, who are the Muslims. It was also said that by "people" is meant the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿And they have returned with anger from Allah﴾. It was said: they have incurred it. The basic meaning of this word in the language is necessity and entitlement, i.e., anger from Allah has become binding upon them, and they deserve it. The meaning of the stamping of destitution (*maskana*) is its encompassing them from all sides. This is indeed the condition of the Jews, for they are under extreme poverty and severe destitution, except for a rare exception among them.

The demonstrative in His statement ﴿that﴾ refers to what preceded: the stamping of humiliation, destitution, and anger. That is, this befell them because they disbelieved in the signs of Allah and killed the prophets without right. The demonstrative ﴿that﴾ here refers to disbelief and the killing of prophets, which resulted from their disobedience to Allah and their transgression of His limits. The meaning of the verse is: Allah stamped upon them humiliation, destitution, and the return with anger from Him, because they disbelieved in His signs and killed His prophets, through their disobedience and transgression.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim (who authenticated it) have related from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His statement ﴿You were the best nation﴾, that he said: "They are those who emigrated with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim have related from al-Suddi concerning the verse that he said: "ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab said: 'If Allah had willed, He would have said: you (plural), and we would all have been included. But He said: you were among the special Companions of Muhammad, and whoever does as they did, will be like them: they were the best nation brought forth for mankind.'"

In another wording from him, it is that he said: "It applies to our first generation and does not apply to our last generation." Ibn Jarir has related from Qatada that he said: "It has been mentioned to us that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab recited this verse, then said: 'O people, whoever is pleased to be of that nation, let him fulfil the condition of Allah concerning it.'"

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir have related from ʿIkrima concerning the verse that he said: "It was revealed concerning Ibn Masʿud, ʿAmmar ibn Yasir, Salim the client of Abu Hudhayfa, Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, and Muʿadh ibn Jabal." Al-Bukhari and others have related from Abu Hurayra concerning the verse that he said: "The best of people for people are those who bring them in chains around their necks until they enter Islam."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it good), Ibn Majah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim (who authenticated it) have related from Muʿawiya ibn Haydah that he heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say concerning the verse: "Indeed you will complete seventy nations, you are the best of them and the most honourable of them." It has been related from the hadith of Muʿadh and Abu Saʿid with similar meaning.

Many hadiths have been reported in the two Sahihs and other collections that seventy thousand of this nation will enter Paradise without reckoning and without punishment, and this is one of the benefits of its being the best of nations. Ibn Jarir has related from al-Hasan concerning ﴿They will not harm you except with some injury﴾ that he said: "You will hear from them lies about Allah, calling you to misguidance."

He also related from Ibn Jurayj who said: "Their association (of partners with Allah) concerning ʿUzayr, ʿIsa, and the cross." Ibn Abi Hatim has related from al-Hasan and Qatada concerning ﴿Humiliation is stamped upon them﴾ that they both said: "They give the jizya (poll tax, levied on non-Muslim subjects) from the hand (in submission) (p. 239) while they are humbled."

Ibn al-Mundhir related a similar report from al-Dahhak. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim have related from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning ﴿except with a rope from Allah and a rope from mankind﴾ that he said: "With a covenant from Allah and a covenant from people."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it good), Ibn Majah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim (who authenticated it) have related from Muʿawiya ibn Haydah that he heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say concerning the verse: "Indeed you will complete seventy nations, you are the best of them and the most honourable of them." It has been related from the hadith of Muʿadh and Abu Saʿid with similar meaning.

Many hadiths have been reported in the two Sahihs and other collections that seventy thousand of this nation will enter Paradise without reckoning and without punishment, and this is one of the benefits of its being the best of nations. Ibn Jarir has related from al-Hasan concerning ﴿They will not harm you except with some injury﴾ that he said: "You will hear from them lies about Allah, calling you to misguidance."

He also related from Ibn Jurayj who said: "Their association (of partners with Allah) concerning ʿUzayr, ʿIsa, and the cross." Ibn Abi Hatim has related from al-Hasan and Qatada concerning ﴿Humiliation is stamped upon them﴾ that they both said: "They give the jizya (poll tax, levied on non-Muslim subjects) from the hand (in submission) (p. 239) while they are humbled."

Ibn al-Mundhir related a similar report from al-Dahhak. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim have related from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning ﴿except with a rope from Allah and a rope from mankind﴾ that he said: "With a covenant from Allah and a covenant from people."

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 3, verses 110–112**

His statement, ﴿You were the best nation﴾, is a resumptive sentence (*kalam mustaʾnaf*, a new clause not grammatically tied to what precedes it) that includes an explanation of the state of this nation in excellence over other nations. It was said that *kuntum* here is the complete (*tammah*) verb, meaning: you came into existence and were created as the best nation. Similar to this is what Sibawayh recited:

*"And neighbours of ours who were noble."*

And from the same usage is His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿How can we speak to one who is in the cradle, a child?﴾ [Maryam: 29], and His statement: ﴿Remember when you were few and He multiplied you﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 86]. Al-Akhfash said: He means the people of a nation, i.e., the best people of a religion, and he recited:

*"I swore, and I left no suspicion of you in your self, and would one of a nation sin while he is obedient?"*

It was also said that the meaning is: you were in the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawh al-mahfuz*). It was said: you have been so since you believed. In this is evidence that this Islamic nation is the best of nations absolutely, and that this excellence is shared among the first and last of this nation in comparison with other nations, even though they differ in rank among themselves, as has been reported concerning the virtue of the Companions over others.

His statement, ﴿brought forth for mankind﴾, means: made manifest to them. His statement, ﴿you enjoin what is right﴾, and what follows, is a resumptive sentence that explains their being the best nation, together with what this entails: that they are the best nation so long as they uphold this and are characterised by it. When they abandon enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, that excellence departs from them. For this reason Mujahid said: they are the best nation on the conditions mentioned in the verse. This implies that *tamurūna* and what follows it are in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), meaning: you were the best nation while you were enjoining, forbidding, and believing in Allah and in what it is obligatory for you to believe in, from His Book, His Messenger, and what He has legislated for His servants, for faith in Allah, glory be to Him, is not complete except by believing in these matters.

His statement, ﴿And if the People of the Book had believed﴾, means: the Jews, believing as the Muslims believe in Allah, His messengers, and His books, ﴿it would have been better for them﴾. But they did not do so; rather they said: "We believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part." Then He explained the state of the People of the Book with His statement: ﴿Among them are believers﴾, and they are those among them who believed in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), for they believed in what was revealed to him and what was revealed before him. ﴿And most of them are defiant transgressors﴾, meaning: those who have departed from the path of truth, who are obstinate in their falsehood, who deny the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and what he brought. Accordingly, this detail is, on this reading, a resumptive statement answering an assumed question, as if it were said: "Is there among them anyone who believed and thereby deserved what Allah promised?"

His statement, ﴿They will not harm you except with some injury﴾, means: they will not harm you with any kind of harm except with a kind of hurt, namely lying, distortion, and slander. They are not able to inflict the harm that is genuine harm, such as war, plunder, and the like. The exception here is therefore an exception from a negated general (*mufarragh*), and this is a promise from Allah to His Messenger and to the believers that the People of the Book will not overcome them, and that they will be victorious over them. It was also said that the exception is disjunctive (*munqaṭiʿ*).

The meaning is: they will not harm you at all, but they will hurt you. Then He, glory be to Him, explained what He had negated of harm with His statement: ﴿And if they fight you, they will turn their backs to you﴾, meaning: they will be routed and will not be able to resist you, let alone harm you. His statement, ﴿then they will not be helped﴾, is coordinated (*ʿaṭf*) with the conditional sentence; that is: then no help will be found for them, and no victory will be established for them in any circumstance. Rather, their condition is abandonment so long as they remain.

We have indeed found what He, glory be to Him, promised to be true, for the Jews have never had the banner of victory raised for them, nor has an army gathered for them that prevailed, since the revelation of this verse, so it is one of the miracles of prophethood. His statement, ﴿Humiliation is stamped upon them﴾, has already been explained in al-Baqarah, the meaning of this construction.

The meaning is: humiliation has become encompassing them in every state, under every circumstance, wherever they are found, ﴿except with a rope from Allah﴾, meaning: except that they hold fast to a rope from Allah, as al-Farra' said, i.e., to the protection (*dhimma*) of Allah or to His Book, ﴿and a rope from mankind﴾, meaning: to a protection from people, who are the Muslims. It was also said that by "people" is meant the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿And they have returned with anger from Allah﴾. It was said: they have incurred it. The basic meaning of this word in the language is necessity and entitlement, i.e., anger from Allah has become binding upon them, and they deserve it. The meaning of the stamping of destitution (*maskana*) is its encompassing them from all sides. This is indeed the condition of the Jews, for they are under extreme poverty and severe destitution, except for a rare exception among them.

The demonstrative in His statement ﴿that﴾ refers to what preceded: the stamping of humiliation, destitution, and anger. That is, this befell them because they disbelieved in the signs of Allah and killed the prophets without right. The demonstrative ﴿that﴾ here refers to disbelief and the killing of prophets, which resulted from their disobedience to Allah and their transgression of His limits. The meaning of the verse is: Allah stamped upon them humiliation, destitution, and the return with anger from Him, because they disbelieved in His signs and killed His prophets, through their disobedience and transgression.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim (who authenticated it) have related from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His statement ﴿You were the best nation﴾, that he said: "They are those who emigrated with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim have related from al-Suddi concerning the verse that he said: "ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab said: 'If Allah had willed, He would have said: you (plural), and we would all have been included. But He said: you were among the special Companions of Muhammad, and whoever does as they did, will be like them: they were the best nation brought forth for mankind.'"

In another wording from him, it is that he said: "It applies to our first generation and does not apply to our last generation." Ibn Jarir has related from Qatada that he said: "It has been mentioned to us that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab recited this verse, then said: 'O people, whoever is pleased to be of that nation, let him fulfil the condition of Allah concerning it.'"

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir have related from ʿIkrima concerning the verse that he said: "It was revealed concerning Ibn Masʿud, ʿAmmar ibn Yasir, Salim the client of Abu Hudhayfa, Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, and Muʿadh ibn Jabal."
