"Adhillah" is the plural of paucity (jam' qillah), and its meaning is that they were, because of their paucity, "adhillah" (humbled); it is the plural of "dhalil" used metaphorically for paucity, since they were not in themselves humbled, rather they were honored. "Al-nasr" is help.

The historians and biographers have explained the battles of Badr and Uhud in the most complete explanation, so there is no need for us to recount that here. His words: ﴿when you said to the believers﴾ are connected to His words "helped you," and the hamza in His words "Is it not sufficient for you" is for denial from him (ﷺ) of their not being content with that support from the angels. The meaning of "kifayah" (sufficiency) is filling the need and sustaining the matter; "imdad" in origin is giving a thing in successive states (hal ba'd hal), and the use of "lan" is to emphasize negation.

The origin of "fawr" is intending a thing and taking up with it in earnest; it is from the saying of the people: "faratil-qidr taphuru fawran wa fawaran" (the pot boiled) when it boils; "al-fawr" is boiling, and "fara ghadabuhu" (his anger surged) when it rose up; and "fa'alahu min fawrihi" means before it calmed down. "Al-fawwarah" is what boils out of the pot, and it is used metaphorically for speed. That is: if they come upon you at this very moment, your Lord will reinforce you with angels while they are coming, without delay.

His words: "(musawwamin)" with a fatha on the waw is a passive participle, and this is the reading of Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Nafi'; that is, marked with signs.

Ibn 'Amr, Ibn Kathir and 'Asim read "musawwimin" with a kasra on the waw, an active participle; that is, marking themselves with a sign. Ibn Jarir preferred this reading. Taswim is showing the distinguishing mark of a thing.

Many commentators said: "(musawwimin)" means sending their horses in the raid. It was also said that the angels wore white turbans, and it was said red, and it was said green, and it was said yellow; these are the signs by which they marked themselves. This is related from al-Zajjaj. It was also said that they were upon piebald horses, and it was said other than that.

His words: ﴿And Allah did not make it except as good tidings for you﴾ are an independent statement, not included in the content of the speech; the pronoun in "ja'alahu" refers either to the reinforcement understood from the verb, or to the marking, or to the sending down. Al-Zajjaj and the author of al-Kashshaf preferred the first.

His words "illa bushra" (except as good tidings) are an exceptive construction (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general of generals; "bushra" is a noun from "bishara" (good news); that is: only so that you be given good news that you will be helped, and so that your hearts be reassured by it, that is, by the reinforcement. The "lam" is the lam of purpose (lam kay). Allah made that reinforcement good news of victory and tranquility for the hearts. In restricting the reinforcement to these two there is an indication that the angels did not directly engage in fighting that day, and that victory is only from Allah, not from anyone else; so the multitude of fighters and the abundance of equipment avail nothing.

His words: ﴿that He might cut off a part of those who disbelieved﴾ are connected to His words "And Allah had already helped you at Badr." It was also said: they are connected to His words "And victory is only from Allah," and it was said: they are connected to His words "your Lord will reinforce you." "Tarf" is a group. The meaning: Allah helped you at Badr so that He might cut off a group of the disbelievers, namely those who were killed on the Day of Badr; or: "And victory is only from Allah" so that He might cut off that group, or "will reinforce you" so that He might cut off.

"Yakbitahum" means to grieve them, and "al-makbut" is the grieved one. Some lexicographers said its meaning is "yakidahum," that is, He afflicts them with sorrow and rage in their livers; but this is not correct, for the meaning of "kabata" is to grieve, to enrage and to humble, and the meaning of "kabida" is to strike the liver. ﴿So that they return disappointed﴾, that is, not victorious in their aim.

In His words: ﴿And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ is an indication that His mercy precedes His wrath, and good news to His servants that He is characterized by forgiveness and mercy in the highest degree. How sublime this great closing is, and how beloved to the hearts of those who know the secrets of revelation!

Among what was revealed of the Qur'an concerning the Day of Uhud were sixty verses of Al 'Imran, in which is a description of what happened on that day and a rebuke of those among them who were rebuked. Allah says to His Prophet: ﴿And when you went out early from your family﴾, the verse.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan that the verse concerns the Day of the Confederates (al-Ahzab). It is recorded in the books of biography and history how the consultation with the Prophet (ﷺ) on the Day of Uhud differed: some said, "We go out to them," and some said, "We remain in Medina." So he went out. Among those who advised was 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, the chief of the hypocrites, whose opinion was to remain in Medina and fight there. Then, when his opinion was opposed, he withdrew with those of the hypocrites who were with him, and they were about a third of the people with whom the Prophet (ﷺ) had gone out.

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from Jabir who said: "Concerning us were revealed the words about Banu Harithah and Banu Salamah: ﴿When two parties among you were about to lose heart﴾, and it does not please me that it was not revealed, because of His words: ﴿And Allah is their protector﴾." 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Qatadah regarding His words ﴿When two parties were about to lose heart﴾ that he said: "That is the Day of Uhud."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "They are Banu Harithah and Banu Salamah." 'Abd ibn Humayd related from Mujahid regarding ﴿And Allah had already helped you at Badr﴾: "up to three thousand angels sent down in the account of Badr."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan regarding His words: ﴿while you were humble﴾, he says: "while you were few, and they that day were some ten and three hundred." Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Sha'bi that the Muslims were informed on the Day of Badr that Kurz ibn Jabir al-Muharibi was supplying the polytheists, which distressed them, so Allah revealed ﴿Is it not sufficient for you that your Lord reinforce you with three thousand [angels]﴾ to His words "marked." He said: "Kurz learned of this and did not supply the polytheists, and the Muslims were not supplied with the five thousand."

Ibn Jarir related from al-Sha'bi: "When the Day of Badr came, news reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)," and then he mentioned something similar, except that he said: ﴿And they come upon you from this very moment﴾, meaning Kurz and his companions, ﴿your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels marked﴾. Then Kurz and his companions were defeated, so He did not reinforce them, and the five thousand did not descend, and they were reinforced afterward (p-243) with a thousand, so they were four thousand. 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Qatadah regarding the verse that he said: "They were reinforced with a thousand, then they became three thousand, then they became five thousand, and that was on the Day of Badr."

Ibn Jarir related from 'Ikrimah regarding His words: ﴿Yes, if you are patient and fear Allah﴾, the verse, that he said: "This is the Day of Uhud; they were not patient and did not fear Allah, so they were not reinforced on the Day of Uhud, and had they been reinforced they would not have been routed that day." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related the like from al-Dahhak.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: ﴿And they come upon you from this very moment﴾, he says: "from their journey this." 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from 'Ikrimah, "from this very moment," he said: "from their direction."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported regarding His words, ﴿that He may cut off a portion of those who disbelieve﴾, that he said: "This is the Day of Badr. Allah cut off a group of them, and a group remained."

Ibn Jarir reported from al-Suddi, who said: "Allah mentioned the dead among the polytheists at Uhud, and they were eighteen men, so He said: ﴿that He may cut off a portion of those who disbelieve﴾. Then Allah mentioned the martyrs, saying: ﴿And do not think of those who were killed in the cause of Allah as dead﴾ [Al 'Imran: 169]."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others reported from Anas: "The Prophet (ﷺ) had his front tooth broken at Uhud, and his face was wounded until the blood flowed. He said: 'How will a people prosper who have done this to their prophet, while he calls them to their Lord?' So Allah revealed: ﴿You have no say in the matter﴾, the verse." This meaning has been related in many narrations.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others reported from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said at Uhud: "O Allah, curse Abu Sufyan. O Allah, curse al-Harith ibn Hisham. O Allah, curse Suhayl ibn Amr. O Allah, curse Safwan ibn Umayya." Then this verse was revealed: ﴿You have no say in the matter﴾.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others also reported from the hadith of Abu Hurayra: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wished to invoke against someone or to invoke for someone, he would perform qunut (supplication in prayer) after the ruku' (bowing): 'O Allah, deliver al-Walid ibn al-Walid, Salama ibn Hisham, Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'a, and the weak among the believers. O Allah, tighten Your grip upon Mudar, and make it upon them as years like the years of Yusuf.' He would say this aloud. And in some of his prayers, in the Fajr prayer, he would say: 'O Allah, curse so-and-so and so-and-so,' naming some tribes of the Arabs, until Allah revealed: ﴿You have no say in the matter﴾."

In another wording: "O Allah, curse Lihyan, Ra'l, Dhakwan, and 'Usayya, who disobeyed Allah and His Messenger." Then we were informed that he abandoned this practice when the words of Allah were revealed: ﴿You have no say in the matter﴾, the verse.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported regarding His words, ﴿that He may cut off a portion of those who disbelieve﴾, that he said: "This is the Day of Badr. Allah cut off a group of them, and a group remained."

Ibn Jarir reported from al-Suddi, who said: "Allah mentioned the dead among the polytheists at Uhud, and they were eighteen men, so He said: ﴿that He may cut off a portion of those who disbelieve﴾. Then Allah mentioned the martyrs, saying: ﴿And do not think of those who were killed in the cause of Allah as dead﴾ [Al 'Imran: 169]."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Mujahid regarding His words, ﴿or He will humiliate them﴾, that he said: "He will grieve them." Ibn Jarir reported similarly from Qatada and al-Rabi'.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others reported from Anas: "The Prophet (ﷺ) had his front tooth broken at Uhud, and his face was wounded until the blood flowed. He said: 'How will a people prosper who have done this to their prophet, while he calls them to their Lord?' So Allah revealed: ﴿You have no say in the matter﴾, the verse." This meaning has been related in many narrations.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others reported from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said at Uhud: "O Allah, curse Abu Sufyan. O Allah, curse al-Harith ibn Hisham. O Allah, curse Suhayl ibn Amr. O Allah, curse Safwan ibn Umayya." Then this verse was revealed: ﴿You have no say in the matter﴾.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others also reported from the hadith of Abu Hurayra: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wished to invoke against someone or to invoke for someone, he would perform qunut (supplication in prayer) after the ruku' (bowing): 'O Allah, deliver al-Walid ibn al-Walid, Salama ibn Hisham, Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'a, and the weak among the believers. O Allah, tighten Your grip upon Mudar, and make it upon them as years like the years of Yusuf.' He would say this aloud. And in some of his prayers, in the Fajr prayer, he would say: 'O Allah, curse so-and-so and so-and-so,' naming some tribes of the Arabs, until Allah revealed: ﴿You have no say in the matter﴾."

In another wording: "O Allah, curse Lihyan, Ra'l, Dhakwan, and 'Usayya, who disobeyed Allah and His Messenger." Then we were informed that he abandoned this practice when the words of Allah were revealed: ﴿You have no say in the matter﴾, the verse.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verse 121–129 (part 1 of 2):

The governing verb of "idh" (when) is an omitted verb; that is, "and remember when you set out early in the morning from the dwelling of your family," meaning: from the dwelling in which your family was. The majority of scholars held that this verse was revealed concerning the battle of Uhud. Al-Hasan said: concerning the Day of Badr.

Mujahid, Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: concerning the battle of the Trench (al-Khandaq). His words "tubawwi'u" mean: you prepare for them seats for fighting. The origin of tabawwu' is taking a dwelling; it is said "bawwa'tuhu manzilan" (I settled him in a dwelling) when you cause him to dwell in it. The verb is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal).

The meaning of the verse: "And remember when you went out from the dwelling of your family, preparing for the believers seats for fighting," that is, places where they would sit. He expressed going out by "ghadw" (early morning departure), which is the going out in the morning, even though the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out after the Friday prayer as will come; because "ghadw" and "rawah" are sometimes used to express going out and entering without regard to their original meanings, as one says "adha" (he entered upon the time of forenoon) even when it was not the time of forenoon.

His words: ﴿When two parties among you were about to lose heart﴾ are a substitute (badal) for "when you set out early in the morning," or they are connected to His words "tubawwi'u," or to His words "All-Hearing, All-Knowing." The two parties were the Banu Salamah of the Khazraj and the Banu Harithah of the Aws, and they were the two wings of the army on the Day of Uhud. "Al-fashal" is cowardice. The concern of the two parties came after the departure, when 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy returned with those of the hypocrites who were with him, and Allah preserved the hearts of the believers so that they did not turn back. This is His words: ﴿And Allah is their protector﴾.

His words: ﴿And Allah had already helped you at Badr﴾ are a new sentence (jumlah mustanifah) brought to console them by reminding them of what follows from patience, namely victory. "Badr" is the name of a water-source that was at the site of the battle; it was also said that it is the name of the place itself. The account of the Battle of Badr will come in al-Anfal, God willing.

"Adhillah" is the plural of paucity (jam' qillah), and its meaning is that they were, because of their paucity, "adhillah" (humbled); it is the plural of "dhalil" used metaphorically for paucity, since they were not in themselves humbled, rather they were honored. "Al-nasr" is help.

The historians and biographers have explained the battles of Badr and Uhud in the most complete explanation, so there is no need for us to recount that here. His words: ﴿when you said to the believers﴾ are connected to His words "helped you," and the hamza in His words "Is it not sufficient for you" is for denial from him (ﷺ) of their not being content with that support from the angels. The meaning of "kifayah" (sufficiency) is filling the need and sustaining the matter; "imdad" in origin is giving a thing in successive states (hal ba'd hal), and the use of "lan" is to emphasize negation.

The origin of "fawr" is intending a thing and taking up with it in earnest; it is from the saying of the people: "faratil-qidr taphuru fawran wa fawaran" (the pot boiled) when it boils; "al-fawr" is boiling, and "fara ghadabuhu" (his anger surged) when it rose up; and "fa'alahu min fawrihi" means before it calmed down. "Al-fawwarah" is what boils out of the pot, and it is used metaphorically for speed. That is: if they come upon you at this very moment, your Lord will reinforce you with angels while they are coming, without delay.

His words: "(musawwamin)" with a fatha on the waw is a passive participle, and this is the reading of Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Nafi'; that is, marked with signs.

Ibn 'Amr, Ibn Kathir and 'Asim read "musawwimin" with a kasra on the waw, an active participle; that is, marking themselves with a sign. Ibn Jarir preferred this reading. Taswim is showing the distinguishing mark of a thing.

Many commentators said: "(musawwimin)" means sending their horses in the raid. It was also said that the angels wore white turbans, and it was said red, and it was said green, and it was said yellow; these are the signs by which they marked themselves. This is related from al-Zajjaj. It was also said that they were upon piebald horses, and it was said other than that.

His words: ﴿And Allah did not make it except as good tidings for you﴾ are an independent statement, not included in the content of the speech; the pronoun in "ja'alahu" refers either to the reinforcement understood from the verb, or to the marking, or to the sending down. Al-Zajjaj and the author of al-Kashshaf preferred the first.

His words "illa bushra" (except as good tidings) are an exceptive construction (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general of generals; "bushra" is a noun from "bishara" (good news); that is: only so that you be given good news that you will be helped, and so that your hearts be reassured by it, that is, by the reinforcement. The "lam" is the lam of purpose (lam kay). Allah made that reinforcement good news of victory and tranquility for the hearts. In restricting the reinforcement to these two there is an indication that the angels did not directly engage in fighting that day, and that victory is only from Allah, not from anyone else; so the multitude of fighters and the abundance of equipment avail nothing.

His words: ﴿that He might cut off a part of those who disbelieved﴾ are connected to His words "And Allah had already helped you at Badr." It was also said: they are connected to His words "And victory is only from Allah," and it was said: they are connected to His words "your Lord will reinforce you." "Tarf" is a group. The meaning: Allah helped you at Badr so that He might cut off a group of the disbelievers, namely those who were killed on the Day of Badr; or: "And victory is only from Allah" so that He might cut off that group, or "will reinforce you" so that He might cut off.

"Yakbitahum" means to grieve them, and "al-makbut" is the grieved one. Some lexicographers said its meaning is "yakidahum," that is, He afflicts them with sorrow and rage in their livers; but this is not correct, for the meaning of "kabata" is to grieve, to enrage and to humble, and the meaning of "kabida" is to strike the liver. ﴿So that they return disappointed﴾, that is, not victorious in their aim.

His words: ﴿You have no part in the affair﴾ are a parenthetical clause (jumlah i'tiradiyyah) between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined; that is, Allah is the owner of their affair, He does with them what He wills, whether by destruction, defeat, repentance if they embrace Islam, or punishment. So His words: ﴿or He will turn to them in forgiveness or punish them﴾ are conjoined to His words "or He will humble them." Al-Farra' said: "aw" here means "illa an" (except that): "You have no part in the affair except that He turns to them in forgiveness, so you rejoice in that, or He punishes them, so you are healed by them." His words: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ are a new statement to show the breadth of His dominion; ﴿He forgives whom He wills﴾, that is, to forgive him, ﴿and punishes whom He wills﴾, that is, to punish him; He does in His dominion what He wills and decides what He desires; ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾ [al-Anbiya': 23]. In His words: ﴿And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ is an indication that His mercy precedes His wrath, and good news to His servants that He is characterized by forgiveness and mercy in the highest degree. How sublime this great closing is, and how beloved to the hearts of those who know the secrets of revelation!

Allah says to His Prophet: ﴿And when you went out early from your family﴾, the verse.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim, through al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿And when you went out early from your family﴾, the verse, said: it is the Day of Uhud. Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding His words "tubawwi'u al-mu'minin" that he said: "tuwatinu" (you settle them).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan that the verse concerns the Day of the Confederates (al-Ahzab). It is recorded in the books of biography and history how the consultation with the Prophet (ﷺ) on the Day of Uhud differed: some said, "We go out to them," and some said, "We remain in Medina." So he went out. Among those who advised was 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, the chief of the hypocrites, whose opinion was to remain in Medina and fight there. Then, when his opinion was opposed, he withdrew with those of the hypocrites who were with him, and they were about a third of the people with whom the Prophet (ﷺ) had gone out.

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from Jabir who said: "Concerning us were revealed the words about Banu Harithah and Banu Salamah: ﴿When two parties among you were about to lose heart﴾, and it does not please me that it was not revealed, because of His words: ﴿And Allah is their protector﴾." 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Qatadah regarding His words ﴿When two parties were about to lose heart﴾ that he said: "That is the Day of Uhud."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "They are Banu Harithah and Banu Salamah." 'Abd ibn Humayd related from Mujahid regarding ﴿And Allah had already helped you at Badr﴾: "up to three thousand angels sent down in the account of Badr."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan regarding His words: ﴿while you were humble﴾, he says: "while you were few, and they that day were some ten and three hundred." Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Sha'bi that the Muslims were informed on the Day of Badr that Kurz ibn Jabir al-Muharibi was supplying the polytheists, which distressed them, so Allah revealed ﴿Is it not sufficient for you that your Lord reinforce you with three thousand [angels]﴾ to His words "marked." He said: "Kurz learned of this and did not supply the polytheists, and the Muslims were not supplied with the five thousand."

Ibn Jarir related from al-Sha'bi: "When the Day of Badr came, news reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)," and then he mentioned something similar, except that he said: ﴿And they come upon you from this very moment﴾, meaning Kurz and his companions, ﴿your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels marked﴾. Then Kurz and his companions were defeated, so He did not reinforce them, and the five thousand did not descend, and they were reinforced afterward (p-243) with a thousand, so they were four thousand. 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Qatadah regarding the verse that he said: "They were reinforced with a thousand, then they became three thousand, then they became five thousand, and that was on the Day of Badr."

Ibn Jarir related from 'Ikrimah regarding His words: ﴿Yes, if you are patient and fear Allah﴾, the verse, that he said: "This is the Day of Uhud; they were not patient and did not fear Allah, so they were not reinforced on the Day of Uhud, and had they been reinforced they would not have been routed that day." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related the like from al-Dahhak.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: ﴿And they come upon you from this very moment﴾, he says: "from their journey this." 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from 'Ikrimah, "from this very moment," he said: "from their direction."

Ibn Jarir related from al-Hasan, al-Rabi', Qatadah and al-Suddi the like of it; 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid, "from this very moment," he said: "from their anger." Both of them related from Abu Salih, freedman of Umm Hani', the like of it.

Ibn Jarir related from al-Sha'bi: "When the Day of Badr came, news reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)," and then he mentioned something similar, except that he said: ﴿And they come upon you from this very moment﴾, meaning Kurz and his companions, ﴿your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels marked﴾. Regarding the explanation of the taswim (marking) from the early generations there is much disagreement, none of which bears much benefit. Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verse 121–129 (part 1 of 2):

The governing verb of "idh" (when) is an omitted verb; that is, "and remember when you set out early in the morning from the dwelling of your family," meaning: from the dwelling in which your family was. The majority of scholars held that this verse was revealed concerning the battle of Uhud. Al-Hasan said: concerning the Day of Badr.

Mujahid, Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: concerning the battle of the Trench (al-Khandaq). His words "tubawwi'u" mean: you prepare for them seats for fighting. The origin of tabawwu' is taking a dwelling; it is said "bawwa'tuhu manzilan" (I settled him in a dwelling) when you cause him to dwell in it. The verb is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal).

The meaning of the verse: "And remember when you went out from the dwelling of your family, preparing for the believers seats for fighting," that is, places where they would sit. He expressed going out by "ghadw" (early morning departure), which is the going out in the morning, even though the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out after the Friday prayer as will come; because "ghadw" and "rawah" are sometimes used to express going out and entering without regard to their original meanings, as one says "adha" (he entered upon the time of forenoon) even when it was not the time of forenoon.

His words: ﴿When two parties among you were about to lose heart﴾ are a substitute (badal) for "when you set out early in the morning," or they are connected to His words "tubawwi'u," or to His words "All-Hearing, All-Knowing." The two parties were the Banu Salamah of the Khazraj and the Banu Harithah of the Aws, and they were the two wings of the army on the Day of Uhud. "Al-fashal" is cowardice. The concern of the two parties came after the departure, when 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy returned with those of the hypocrites who were with him, and Allah preserved the hearts of the believers so that they did not turn back. This is His words: ﴿And Allah is their protector﴾.

His words: ﴿And Allah had already helped you at Badr﴾ are a new sentence (jumlah mustanifah) brought to console them by reminding them of what follows from patience, namely victory. "Badr" is the name of a water-source that was at the site of the battle; it was also said that it is the name of the place itself. The account of the Battle of Badr will come in al-Anfal, God willing.

"Adhillah" is the plural of paucity (jam' qillah), and its meaning is that they were, because of their paucity, "adhillah" (humbled); it is the plural of "dhalil" used metaphorically for paucity, since they were not in themselves humbled, rather they were honored. "Al-nasr" is help.

The historians and biographers have explained the battles of Badr and Uhud in the most complete explanation, so there is no need for us to recount that here. His words: ﴿when you said to the believers﴾ are connected to His words "helped you," and the hamza in His words "Is it not sufficient for you" is for denial from him (ﷺ) of their not being content with that support from the angels. The meaning of "kifayah" (sufficiency) is filling the need and sustaining the matter; "imdad" in origin is giving a thing in successive states (hal ba'd hal), and the use of "lan" is to emphasize negation.

The origin of "fawr" is intending a thing and taking up with it in earnest; it is from the saying of the people: "faratil-qidr taphuru fawran wa fawaran" (the pot boiled) when it boils; "al-fawr" is boiling, and "fara ghadabuhu" (his anger surged) when it rose up; and "fa'alahu min fawrihi" means before it calmed down. "Al-fawwarah" is what boils out of the pot, and it is used metaphorically for speed. That is: if they come upon you at this very moment, your Lord will reinforce you with angels while they are coming, without delay.

His words: "(musawwamin)" with a fatha on the waw is a passive participle, and this is the reading of Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Nafi'; that is, marked with signs.

Ibn 'Amr, Ibn Kathir and 'Asim read "musawwimin" with a kasra on the waw, an active participle; that is, marking themselves with a sign. Ibn Jarir preferred this reading. Taswim is showing the distinguishing mark of a thing.

Many commentators said: "(musawwimin)" means sending their horses in the raid. It was also said that the angels wore white turbans, and it was said red, and it was said green, and it was said yellow; these are the signs by which they marked themselves. This is related from al-Zajjaj. It was also said that they were upon piebald horses, and it was said other than that.

His words: ﴿And Allah did not make it except as good tidings for you﴾ are an independent statement, not included in the content of the speech; the pronoun in "ja'alahu" refers either to the reinforcement understood from the verb, or to the marking, or to the sending down. Al-Zajjaj and the author of al-Kashshaf preferred the first.

His words "illa bushra" (except as good tidings) are an exceptive construction (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general of generals; "bushra" is a noun from "bishara" (good news); that is: only so that you be given good news that you will be helped, and so that your hearts be reassured by it, that is, by the reinforcement. The "lam" is the lam of purpose (lam kay). Allah made that reinforcement good news of victory and tranquility for the hearts. In restricting the reinforcement to these two there is an indication that the angels did not directly engage in fighting that day, and that victory is only from Allah, not from anyone else; so the multitude of fighters and the abundance of equipment avail nothing.

His words: ﴿that He might cut off a part of those who disbelieved﴾ are connected to His words "And Allah had already helped you at Badr." It was also said: they are connected to His words "And victory is only from Allah," and it was said: they are connected to His words "your Lord will reinforce you." "Tarf" is a group. The meaning: Allah helped you at Badr so that He might cut off a group of the disbelievers, namely those who were killed on the Day of Badr; or: "And victory is only from Allah" so that He might cut off that group, or "will reinforce you" so that He might cut off.

"Yakbitahum" means to grieve them, and "al-makbut" is the grieved one. Some lexicographers said its meaning is "yakidahum," that is, He afflicts them with sorrow and rage in their livers; but this is not correct, for the meaning of "kabata" is to grieve, to enrage and to humble, and the meaning of "kabida" is to strike the liver. ﴿So that they return disappointed﴾, that is, not victorious in their aim.

His words: ﴿You have no part in the affair﴾ are a parenthetical clause (jumlah i'tiradiyyah) between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined; that is, Allah is the owner of their affair, He does with them what He wills, whether by destruction, defeat, repentance if they embrace Islam, or punishment. So His words: ﴿or He will turn to them in forgiveness or punish them﴾ are conjoined to His words "or He will humble them." Al-Farra' said: "aw" here means "illa an" (except that): "You have no part in the affair except that He turns to them in forgiveness, so you rejoice in that, or He punishes them, so you are healed by them." His words: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ are a new statement to show the breadth of His dominion; ﴿He forgives whom He wills﴾, that is, to forgive him, ﴿and punishes whom He wills﴾, that is, to punish him; He does in His dominion what He wills and decides what He desires; ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾ [al-Anbiya': 23]. In His words: ﴿And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ is an indication that His mercy precedes His wrath, and good news to His servants that He is characterized by forgiveness and mercy in the highest degree. How sublime this great closing is, and how beloved to the hearts of those who know the secrets of revelation!

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verse 121–129 (part 1 of 2):

The governing verb of "idh" (when) is an omitted verb; that is, "and remember when you set out early in the morning from the dwelling of your family," meaning: from the dwelling in which your family was. The majority of scholars held that this verse was revealed concerning the battle of Uhud. Al-Hasan said: concerning the Day of Badr.

Mujahid, Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: concerning the battle of the Trench (al-Khandaq). His words "tubawwi'u" mean: you prepare for them seats for fighting. The origin of tabawwu' is taking a dwelling; it is said "bawwa'tuhu manzilan" (I settled him in a dwelling) when you cause him to dwell in it. The verb is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal).

The meaning of the verse: "And remember when you went out from the dwelling of your family, preparing for the believers seats for fighting," that is, places where they would sit. He expressed going out by "ghadw" (early morning departure), which is the going out in the morning, even though the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out after the Friday prayer as will come; because "ghadw" and "rawah" are sometimes used to express going out and entering without regard to their original meanings, as one says "adha" (he entered upon the time of forenoon) even when it was not the time of forenoon.

His words: ﴿When two parties among you were about to lose heart﴾ are a substitute (badal) for "when you set out early in the morning," or they are connected to His words "tubawwi'u," or to His words "All-Hearing, All-Knowing." The two parties were the Banu Salamah of the Khazraj and the Banu Harithah of the Aws, and they were the two wings of the army on the Day of Uhud. "Al-fashal" is cowardice. The concern of the two parties came after the departure, when 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy returned with those of the hypocrites who were with him, and Allah preserved the hearts of the believers so that they did not turn back. This is His words: ﴿And Allah is their protector﴾.

His words: ﴿And Allah had already helped you at Badr﴾ are a new sentence (jumlah mustanifah) brought to console them by reminding them of what follows from patience, namely victory. "Badr" is the name of a water-source that was at the site of the battle; it was also said that it is the name of the place itself. The account of the Battle of Badr will come in al-Anfal, God willing.

"Adhillah" is the plural of paucity (jam' qillah), and its meaning is that they were, because of their paucity, "adhillah" (humbled); it is the plural of "dhalil" used metaphorically for paucity, since they were not in themselves humbled, rather they were honored. "Al-nasr" is help.

The historians and biographers have explained the battles of Badr and Uhud in the most complete explanation, so there is no need for us to recount that here. His words: ﴿when you said to the believers﴾ are connected to His words "helped you," and the hamza in His words "Is it not sufficient for you" is for denial from him (ﷺ) of their not being content with that support from the angels. The meaning of "kifayah" (sufficiency) is filling the need and sustaining the matter; "imdad" in origin is giving a thing in successive states (hal ba'd hal), and the use of "lan" is to emphasize negation.

The origin of "fawr" is intending a thing and taking up with it in earnest; it is from the saying of the people: "faratil-qidr taphuru fawran wa fawaran" (the pot boiled) when it boils; "al-fawr" is boiling, and "fara ghadabuhu" (his anger surged) when it rose up; and "fa'alahu min fawrihi" means before it calmed down. "Al-fawwarah" is what boils out of the pot, and it is used metaphorically for speed. This meaning has been related in many narrations.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others reported from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said at Uhud: "O Allah, curse Abu Sufyan. O Allah, curse al-Harith ibn Hisham. O Allah, curse Suhayl ibn Amr. O Allah, curse Safwan ibn Umayya." Then this verse was revealed: ﴿You have no say in the matter﴾.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others also reported from the hadith of Abu Hurayra: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wished to invoke against someone or to invoke for someone, he would perform qunut (supplication in prayer) after the ruku' (bowing): 'O Allah, deliver al-Walid ibn al-Walid, Salama ibn Hisham, Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'a, and the weak among the believers. O Allah, tighten Your grip upon Mudar, and make it upon them as years like the years of Yusuf.' He would say this aloud. And in some of his prayers, in the Fajr prayer, he would say: 'O Allah, curse so-and-so and so-and-so,' naming some tribes of the Arabs, until Allah revealed: ﴿You have no say in the matter﴾."

In another wording: "O Allah, curse Lihyan, Ra'l, Dhakwan, and 'Usayya, who disobeyed Allah and His Messenger." Then we were informed that he abandoned this practice when the words of Allah were revealed: ﴿You have no say in the matter﴾, the verse.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verse 121–129 (part 1 of 2):

The governing verb of "idh" (when) is an omitted verb; that is, "and remember when you set out early in the morning from the dwelling of your family," meaning: from the dwelling in which your family was. The majority of scholars held that this verse was revealed concerning the battle of Uhud. Al-Hasan said: concerning the Day of Badr.

Mujahid, Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: concerning the battle of the Trench (al-Khandaq). His words "tubawwi'u" mean: you prepare for them seats for fighting. The origin of tabawwu' is taking a dwelling; it is said "bawwa'tuhu manzilan" (I settled him in a dwelling) when you cause him to dwell in it. The verb is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal).

The meaning of the verse: "And remember when you went out from the dwelling of your family, preparing for the believers seats for fighting," that is, places where they would sit. He expressed going out by "ghadw" (early morning departure), which is the going out in the morning, even though the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out after the Friday prayer as will come; because "ghadw" and "rawah" are sometimes used to express going out and entering without regard to their original meanings, as one says "adha" (he entered upon the time of forenoon) even when it was not the time of forenoon.

His words: ﴿When two parties among you were about to lose heart﴾ are a substitute (badal) for "when you set out early in the morning," or they are connected to His words "tubawwi'u," or to His words "All-Hearing, All-Knowing." The two parties were the Banu Salamah of the Khazraj and the Banu Harithah of the Aws, and they were the two wings of the army on the Day of Uhud. "Al-fashal" is cowardice. The concern of the two parties came after the departure, when 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy returned with those of the hypocrites who were with him, and Allah preserved the hearts of the believers so that they did not turn back. This is His words: ﴿And Allah is their protector﴾.

His words: ﴿And Allah had already helped you at Badr﴾ are a new sentence (jumlah mustanifah) brought to console them by reminding them of what follows from patience, namely victory. "Badr" is the name of a water-source that was at the site of the battle; it was also said that it is the name of the place itself. The account of the Battle of Badr will come in al-Anfal, God willing.

"Adhillah" is the plural of paucity (jam' qillah), and its meaning is that they were, because of their paucity, "adhillah" (humbled); it is the plural of "dhalil" used metaphorically for paucity, since they were not in themselves humbled, rather they were honored. "Al-nasr" is help.

The historians and biographers have explained the battles of Badr and Uhud in the most complete explanation, so there is no need for us to recount that here. His words: ﴿when you said to the believers﴾ are connected to His words "helped you," and the hamza in His words "Is it not sufficient for you" is for denial from him (ﷺ) of their not being content with that support from the angels. The meaning of "kifayah" (sufficiency) is filling the need and sustaining the matter; "imdad" in origin is giving a thing in successive states (hal ba'd hal), and the use of "lan" is to emphasize negation.

The origin of "fawr" is intending a thing and taking up with it in earnest; it is from the saying of the people: "faratil-qidr taphuru fawran wa fawaran" (the pot boiled) when it boils; "al-fawr" is boiling, and "fara ghadabuhu" (his anger surged) when it rose up; and "fa'alahu min fawrihi" means before it calmed down. "Al-fawwarah" is what boils out of the pot, and it is used metaphorically for speed. That is: if they come upon you at this very moment, your Lord will reinforce you with angels while they are coming, without delay.

His words: "(musawwamin)" with a fatha on the waw is a passive participle, and this is the reading of Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Nafi'; that is, marked with signs.

Ibn 'Amr, Ibn Kathir and 'Asim read "musawwimin" with a kasra on the waw, an active participle; that is, marking themselves with a sign. Ibn Jarir preferred this reading. Taswim is showing the distinguishing mark of a thing.

Many commentators said: "(musawwimin)" means sending their horses in the raid. It was also said that the angels wore white turbans, and it was said red, and it was said green, and it was said yellow; these are the signs by which they marked themselves. This is related from al-Zajjaj. It was also said that they were upon piebald horses, and it was said other than that.

His words: ﴿And Allah did not make it except as good tidings for you﴾ are an independent statement, not included in the content of the speech; the pronoun in "ja'alahu" refers either to the reinforcement understood from the verb, or to the marking, or to the sending down. Al-Zajjaj and the author of al-Kashshaf preferred the first.

His words "illa bushra" (except as good tidings) are an exceptive construction (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general of generals; "bushra" is a noun from "bishara" (good news); that is: only so that you be given good news that you will be helped, and so that your hearts be reassured by it, that is, by the reinforcement. The "lam" is the lam of purpose (lam kay). Allah made that reinforcement good news of victory and tranquility for the hearts. In restricting the reinforcement to these two there is an indication that the angels did not directly engage in fighting that day, and that victory is only from Allah, not from anyone else; so the multitude of fighters and the abundance of equipment avail nothing.

His words: ﴿that He might cut off a part of those who disbelieved﴾ are connected to His words "And Allah had already helped you at Badr." It was also said: they are connected to His words "And victory is only from Allah," and it was said: they are connected to His words "your Lord will reinforce you." "Tarf" is a group. The meaning: Allah helped you at Badr so that He might cut off a group of the disbelievers, namely those who were killed on the Day of Badr; or: "And victory is only from Allah" so that He might cut off that group, or "will reinforce you" so that He might cut off.

"Yakbitahum" means to grieve them, and "al-makbut" is the grieved one. Some lexicographers said its meaning is "yakidahum," that is, He afflicts them with sorrow and rage in their livers; but this is not correct, for the meaning of "kabata" is to grieve, to enrage and to humble, and the meaning of "kabida" is to strike the liver. ﴿So that they return disappointed﴾, that is, not victorious in their aim.

His words: ﴿You have no part in the affair﴾ are a parenthetical clause (jumlah i'tiradiyyah) between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined; that is, Allah is the owner of their affair, He does with them what He wills, whether by destruction, defeat, repentance if they embrace Islam, or punishment. So His words: ﴿or He will turn to them in forgiveness or punish them﴾ are conjoined to His words "or He will humble them." Al-Farra' said: "aw" here means "illa an" (except that): "You have no part in the affair except that He turns to them in forgiveness, so you rejoice in that, or He punishes them, so you are healed by them." His words: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ are a new statement to show the breadth of His dominion; ﴿He forgives whom He wills﴾, that is, to forgive him, ﴿and punishes whom He wills﴾, that is, to punish him; He does in His dominion what He wills and decides what He desires; ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾ [al-Anbiya': 23]. In His words: ﴿And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ is an indication that His mercy precedes His wrath, and good news to His servants that He is characterized by forgiveness and mercy in the highest degree. How sublime this great closing is, and how beloved to the hearts of those who know the secrets of revelation!

Ibn Ishaq and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il related from Ibn Shihab, 'Asim ibn 'Umar ibn Qatadah, Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Hibban and al-Husayn ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, who said: The Day of Uhud was a day of trial and purification, by which Allah tested the believers and effaced the hypocrites, those who displayed Islam with their tongues while concealing disbelief; and a day on which Allah honored, by martyrdom, whom He willed to honor from among His friends. Among what was revealed of the Qur'an concerning the Day of Uhud were sixty verses of Al 'Imran, in which is a description of what happened on that day and a rebuke of those among them who were rebuked. Allah says to His Prophet: ﴿And when you went out early from your family﴾, the verse.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim, through al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿And when you went out early from your family﴾, the verse, said: it is the Day of Uhud. Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding His words "tubawwi'u al-mu'minin" that he said: "tuwatinu" (you settle them).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan that the verse concerns the Day of the Confederates (al-Ahzab). It is recorded in the books of biography and history how the consultation with the Prophet (ﷺ) on the Day of Uhud differed: some said, "We go out to them," and some said, "We remain in Medina." So he went out. Among those who advised was 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, the chief of the hypocrites, whose opinion was to remain in Medina and fight there. Then, when his opinion was opposed, he withdrew with those of the hypocrites who were with him, and they were about a third of the people with whom the Prophet (ﷺ) had gone out.

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from Jabir who said: "Concerning us were revealed the words about Banu Harithah and Banu Salamah: ﴿When two parties among you were about to lose heart﴾, and it does not please me that it was not revealed, because of His words: ﴿And Allah is their protector﴾." 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Qatadah regarding His words ﴿When two parties were about to lose heart﴾ that he said: "That is the Day of Uhud."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "They are Banu Harithah and Banu Salamah." 'Abd ibn Humayd related from Mujahid regarding ﴿And Allah had already helped you at Badr﴾: "up to three thousand angels sent down in the account of Badr."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan regarding His words: ﴿while you were humble﴾, he says: "while you were few, and they that day were some ten and three hundred." Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Sha'bi that the Muslims were informed on the Day of Badr that Kurz ibn Jabir al-Muharibi was supplying the polytheists, which distressed them, so Allah revealed ﴿Is it not sufficient for you that your Lord reinforce you with three thousand [angels]﴾ to His words "marked." He said: "Kurz learned of this and did not supply the polytheists, and the Muslims were not supplied with the five thousand."

Ibn Jarir related from al-Sha'bi: "When the Day of Badr came, news reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)," and then he mentioned something similar, except that he said: ﴿And they come upon you from this very moment﴾, meaning Kurz and his companions, ﴿your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels marked﴾. Then Kurz and his companions were defeated, so He did not reinforce them, and the five thousand did not descend, and they were reinforced afterward (p-243) with a thousand, so they were four thousand. 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Qatadah regarding the verse that he said: "They were reinforced with a thousand, then they became three thousand, then they became five thousand, and that was on the Day of Badr."

Ibn Jarir related from 'Ikrimah regarding His words: ﴿Yes, if you are patient and fear Allah﴾, the verse, that he said: "This is the Day of Uhud; they were not patient and did not fear Allah, so they were not reinforced on the Day of Uhud, and had they been reinforced they would not have been routed that day." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related the like from al-Dahhak.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: ﴿And they come upon you from this very moment﴾, he says: "from their journey this." 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from 'Ikrimah, "from this very moment," he said: "from their direction."

Ibn Jarir related from al-Hasan, al-Rabi', Qatadah and al-Suddi the like of it; 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid, "from this very moment," he said: "from their anger." Both of them related from Abu Salih, freedman of Umm Hani', the like of it.

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh related with a weak chain from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said concerning His words 'musawwimin': 'marked.' The sign of the angels on the Day of Badr was black turbans, and on the Day of Uhud red turbans."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr that al-Zubayr had on him on the Day of Badr a yellow turban, wrapping it around himself, so the angels descended upon them with yellow turbans. Ibn Ishaq and al-Tabarani related from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "The sign of the angels on the Day of Badr was white turbans which they let hang down upon their backs, and on the Day of Hunayn red turbans; and the angels did not fight on any day other than the Day of Badr; they were only a multitude and reinforcement, not fighting."

Regarding the explanation of the taswim (marking) from the early generations there is much disagreement, none of which bears much benefit. Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah regarding His words: ﴿that He might cut off a part of those who disbelieved﴾, he said: "Allah cut off on the Day of Badr a part of the disbelievers, and killed their chieftains, their leaders and their commanders in evil."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported regarding His words, ﴿that He may cut off a portion of those who disbelieve﴾, that he said: "This is the Day of Badr. Allah cut off a group of them, and a group remained."

Ibn Jarir reported from al-Suddi, who said: "Allah mentioned the dead among the polytheists at Uhud, and they were eighteen men, so He said: ﴿that He may cut off a portion of those who disbelieve﴾. Then Allah mentioned the martyrs, saying: ﴿And do not think of those who were killed in the cause of Allah as dead﴾ [Al 'Imran: 169]."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Mujahid regarding His words, ﴿or He will humiliate them﴾, that he said: "He will grieve them." Ibn Jarir reported similarly from Qatada and al-Rabi'.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others reported from Anas: "The Prophet (ﷺ) had his front tooth broken at Uhud, and his face was wounded until the blood flowed. He said: 'How will a people prosper who have done this to their prophet, while he calls them to their Lord?' So Allah revealed: ﴿You have no say in the matter﴾, the verse." This meaning has been related in many narrations.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others reported from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said at Uhud: "O Allah, curse Abu Sufyan. O Allah, curse al-Harith ibn Hisham. O Allah, curse Suhayl ibn Amr. O Allah, curse Safwan ibn Umayya." Then this verse was revealed: ﴿You have no say in the matter﴾.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others also reported from the hadith of Abu Hurayra: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wished to invoke against someone or to invoke for someone, he would perform qunut (supplication in prayer) after the ruku' (bowing): 'O Allah, deliver al-Walid ibn al-Walid, Salama ibn Hisham, Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'a, and the weak among the believers. O Allah, tighten Your grip upon Mudar, and make it upon them as years like the years of Yusuf.' He would say this aloud. And in some of his prayers, in the Fajr prayer, he would say: 'O Allah, curse so-and-so and so-and-so,' naming some tribes of the Arabs, until Allah revealed: ﴿You have no say in the matter﴾."

In another wording: "O Allah, curse Lihyan, Ra'l, Dhakwan, and 'Usayya, who disobeyed Allah and His Messenger." Then we were informed that he abandoned this practice when the words of Allah were revealed: ﴿You have no say in the matter﴾, the verse.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verses 130–136:

His saying: ﴿O you who have believed﴾. It was said: this is a fresh statement (mubtada') for warning (tarhib) and encouragement (targhib) regarding what has been mentioned. It was also said: it is an interjection (i'tiraD) within the course of the story of Uhud.

His saying: ﴿doubled and redoubled﴾ is not a restriction of the prohibition, since the prohibition of riba is known to be absolute in every case. Rather, it was brought in consideration of the custom they were accustomed to in riba. They used to lend at interest up to a term, and when the term fell due they added an amount to the principal upon which they mutually agreed, then they extended the term of the debt. They would do this time after time until the creditor took many times the debt he had originally given. ﴿Redoubled﴾ (a'afan) is a circumstantial accusative (hal), and ﴿multiplied﴾ (mudā'afatan) is its qualifier (na't). It contains an indication of repeated multiplication year after year, and the emphasis in this expression serves to strengthen the rebuke.

His saying: ﴿And fear the Fire which has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾ contains guidance to avoid what the disbelievers do in their dealings.

Many of the exegetes said: it also means that whoever deems riba permissible disbelieves. It was also said its meaning is: fear the riba which strips faith from you, so that you deserve the Fire. The riba was singled out in this verse because it is the one for which God has threatened its practitioner with war.

His saying: ﴿And obey God and the Messenger﴾: the omission of the complement indicates generality, i.e., in every command and prohibition. ﴿So that you may receive mercy﴾, i.e., hoping for mercy from God, mighty and majestic.

His saying: ﴿And hasten﴾ is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon "obey". Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿sāri'ū﴾ without a waw, and likewise it is in the codices of the people of Medina and the people of Syria, while the rest read it with a waw.

Abu 'Ali said: both readings are valid and correct. Al-musara'a is al-mubadara (hastening), and in the verse there is an ellipsis, i.e., hasten to what necessitates forgiveness from the acts of obedience. His saying: ﴿whose width is the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Hadid: 21], i.e., its width is like the width of the heavens and the earth. A similar verse is ﴿whose width is like the width of the heaven and the earth﴾ [al-Hadid: 21]. The meaning of this has been disputed. The majority held that it means the heavens and earth are joined to one another, as garments are spread out and joined to one another, and that this is the width of Paradise. Width is mentioned to indicate length, because length is generally greater than width. It was also said that this statement came in the manner of Arabic speech through metaphor rather than literal meaning, since Paradise was at an extreme degree of vastness and expansiveness, the expression by the width of the heavens and earth was fitting as hyperbole, for they are the widest of God's creations, as far as His servants know, and it was not intended to be a precise measurement.

Al-sarrā' is ease, and al-ḍarrā' is hardship, and their explanation has already been given. It was also said: al-sarrā' is prosperity and al-ḍarrā' is adversity, which is similar to the first. It was also said: al-sarrā' is in life, and al-ḍarrā' is after death.

His saying: ﴿And those who restrain anger﴾: it is said "kaẓama ghayẓahu", i.e., he kept silent over it and did not show it. From this comes "kaẓamtu al-siqā'", i.e., I filled it. Al-kiẓāma is what blocks the course of water, and "kaẓama al-ba'īr jarratahu" means when he returned it into his inside. It is a conjunction upon the relative pronoun preceding it.

His saying: ﴿And those who pardon people﴾, i.e., those who abandon punishing one who has wronged them and deserves retribution, and this is among the most excellent kinds of good. Its apparent meaning is pardoning people, whether they are slaves or not.

Al-Zajjaj and others said: what is meant by them is slaves. The lam in ﴿the good-doers﴾ may be for the genus, so that every good-doer among these and others is included, and it may be for a specific reference, so that it is restricted to these.

The first is preferable, in consideration of the generality of the wording rather than the specificity of the context, so that every person from whom the designation of goodness proceeds is included under it, whatever goodness it may be. His saying: ﴿And those who, when they commit an immorality﴾: this is a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is ﴿those﴾. It was also said: it is conjoined to "the God-fearing".

The first is preferable. These are a category below the first category, joined with them, namely the penitent (tawwābūn). The cause of its revelation will be mentioned later. "Fāḥisha" is a descriptor of an omitted noun, i.e., a shameful deed, and it applies to every act of disobedience, though its specific use has become frequent for fornication.

His saying: ﴿or wrong themselves﴾, i.e., by committing some sin among the sins. It was also said: "aw" means "wa" (and). The intended meaning is what has been mentioned. It was said: the fāḥisha is the major sin, and wronging oneself is the minor sin. Other things have also been said.

His saying: ﴿remember God﴾, i.e., with their tongues, or they bring Him to mind in their hearts, or they remember His promise and His threat. ﴿And ask forgiveness for their sins﴾, i.e., they seek forgiveness for them from God, glorified is He. Explaining it as repentance (tawba) is contrary to its linguistic meaning. In the interrogative with His saying: ﴿And who forgives sins except God?﴾ there is a rebuke, together with what it implies of indicating that He alone, glorified is He, is specially entitled to this, to the exclusion of others; i.e., no one forgives the category of sins except God. In it there is encouragement to seek forgiveness from Him, glorified is He, and an incitement to sinners to stand in positions of humility and submission. This sentence is a parenthetical interjection between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined. His saying: ﴿and they do not persist in what they have done﴾ is a conjunction upon "they asked forgiveness"; i.e., they do not remain upon their evil deed. The explanation of persistence (iṣrār) has already been given, and what is meant by it here is the resolve to repeat the sin and not desist from it by repentance.

His saying: "while they know" is a circumstantial clause (jumla ḥāliyya); i.e., they do not persist in their deed while knowing its ugliness.

His saying: ﴿Those—their reward﴾: the demonstrative refers to those mentioned in His saying: ﴿And those who, when they commit an immorality﴾.

His saying: "their reward" is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimāl) from the demonstrative noun. His saying: "forgiveness" is the predicate, "from their Lord" is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a qualifier of "forgiveness"; i.e., coming from their Lord.

His saying: ﴿and excellent is the reward of the workers﴾: the praised element that is specified is omitted; i.e., their reward, or that mentioned. The explanation of the Gardens and how the rivers flow beneath them has already been given.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid: He said: They used to trade up to a term, and when the term came they added to them and extended the term, so ﴿O you who have believed, do not consume riba, doubled and redoubled﴾ was revealed. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from ʿAṭāʾ, who said: Thaqif used to lend to the Banu al-Mughira in the Jahiliyya, and he mentioned something similar.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Muʿawiya ibn Qurra, who said: People used to interpret this verse ﴿and fear the Fire which has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾ as: "Beware, lest I punish you for your sins in the Fire which I have prepared for the disbelievers." ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abi Rabah, who said: The Muslims said: "O Messenger of God, were the Children of Israel more honoured by God than us? When one of them committed a sin, the expiation of his sin would be written in the threshold of his door: 'Cut off your nose, cut off your ear, do such-and-such.'" The Prophet (ﷺ) was silent, and then ﴿And hasten﴾ was revealed, the verse.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Anas ibn Malik regarding "and hasten": He said: the first takbir (opening takbir of prayer). Ibn Jarir narrated through the chain of al-Suddi from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying ﴿whose width is the heavens and the earth﴾, similar to what we mentioned earlier from the majority.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated something similar from him through the chain of Kurayb. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying ﴿who spend in ease and in hardship﴾: he said: in ease and in difficulty. ﴿And those who restrain anger﴾: he said: restraining anger. Many hadiths have been related regarding the reward of one who restrains anger.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Nakha'i regarding the verse: He said: wrongdoing is from immorality and immorality is from wrongdoing. Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Tabarani, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: Indeed, in the Book of God there are two verses: no servant commits a sin, then recites them and asks God's forgiveness, except that He forgives him: ﴿And those who, when they commit an immorality﴾ the verse, and His saying: ﴿And whoever does evil or wrongs himself﴾ [al-Nisa': 110], the verse. ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Thabit al-Bunani, who said: It reached me that when this verse was revealed, ﴿And those who, when they commit an immorality﴾ the verse, Iblis wept.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi narrated from ʿAṭṭaf ibn Khalid, who said: It reached me that when His saying, exalted is He, was revealed: ﴿And who forgives sins except God, and they do not persist in what they have done﴾, Iblis cried out to his armies, threw dust upon his head, and called for woe and destruction, until his armies came to him from every land and sea, and they said: "What is wrong with you, our master?" He said: "A verse has been revealed in the Book of God after which no sin will harm any of the sons of Adam." They said: "What is it?" So he informed them. They said: "We will open for them the door of desires, so they will not repent, nor seek forgiveness, and they will see only that they are upon the truth." So he was content with that from them.

Then he recited this verse: ﴿And those who, when they commit an immorality﴾ the verse.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi regarding His saying: "and they do not persist": that they keep silent and do not seek forgiveness. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Muqatil regarding ﴿and excellent is the reward of the workers﴾: He said: the reward of those who work by obeying God is Paradise.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verses 130–136:

His saying: ﴿O you who have believed﴾. It was said: this is a fresh statement (mubtada') for warning (tarhib) and encouragement (targhib) regarding what has been mentioned. It was also said: it is an interjection (i'tiraD) within the course of the story of Uhud.

His saying: ﴿doubled and redoubled﴾ is not a restriction of the prohibition, since the prohibition of riba is known to be absolute in every case. Rather, it was brought in consideration of the custom they were accustomed to in riba. They used to lend at interest up to a term, and when the term fell due they added an amount to the principal upon which they mutually agreed, then they extended the term of the debt. They would do this time after time until the creditor took many times the debt he had originally given. ﴿Redoubled﴾ (a'afan) is a circumstantial accusative (hal), and ﴿multiplied﴾ (mudā'afatan) is its qualifier (na't). It contains an indication of repeated multiplication year after year, and the emphasis in this expression serves to strengthen the rebuke.

His saying: ﴿And fear the Fire which has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾ contains guidance to avoid what the disbelievers do in their dealings.

Many of the exegetes said: it also means that whoever deems riba permissible disbelieves. It was also said its meaning is: fear the riba which strips faith from you, so that you deserve the Fire. The riba was singled out in this verse because it is the one for which God has threatened its practitioner with war.

His saying: ﴿And obey God and the Messenger﴾: the omission of the complement indicates generality, i.e., in every command and prohibition. ﴿So that you may receive mercy﴾, i.e., hoping for mercy from God, mighty and majestic.

His saying: ﴿And hasten﴾ is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon "obey". Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿sāri'ū﴾ without a waw, and likewise it is in the codices of the people of Medina and the people of Syria, while the rest read it with a waw.

Abu 'Ali said: both readings are valid and correct. Al-musara'a is al-mubadara (hastening), and in the verse there is an ellipsis, i.e., hasten to what necessitates forgiveness from the acts of obedience. His saying: ﴿whose width is the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Hadid: 21], i.e., its width is like the width of the heavens and the earth. A similar verse is ﴿whose width is like the width of the heaven and the earth﴾ [al-Hadid: 21]. The meaning of this has been disputed. The majority held that it means the heavens and earth are joined to one another, as garments are spread out and joined to one another, and that this is the width of Paradise. Width is mentioned to indicate length, because length is generally greater than width. It was also said that this statement came in the manner of Arabic speech through metaphor rather than literal meaning, since Paradise was at an extreme degree of vastness and expansiveness, the expression by the width of the heavens and earth was fitting as hyperbole, for they are the widest of God's creations, as far as His servants know, and it was not intended to be a precise measurement.

Al-sarrā' is ease, and al-ḍarrā' is hardship, and their explanation has already been given. It was also said: al-sarrā' is prosperity and al-ḍarrā' is adversity, which is similar to the first. It was also said: al-sarrā' is in life, and al-ḍarrā' is after death.

His saying: ﴿And those who restrain anger﴾: it is said "kaẓama ghayẓahu", i.e., he kept silent over it and did not show it. From this comes "kaẓamtu al-siqā'", i.e., I filled it. Al-kiẓāma is what blocks the course of water, and "kaẓama al-ba'īr jarratahu" means when he returned it into his inside. It is a conjunction upon the relative pronoun preceding it.

His saying: ﴿And those who pardon people﴾, i.e., those who abandon punishing one who has wronged them and deserves retribution, and this is among the most excellent kinds of good. Its apparent meaning is pardoning people, whether they are slaves or not.

Al-Zajjaj and others said: what is meant by them is slaves. The lam in ﴿the good-doers﴾ may be for the genus, so that every good-doer among these and others is included, and it may be for a specific reference, so that it is restricted to these.

The first is preferable, in consideration of the generality of the wording rather than the specificity of the context, so that every person from whom the designation of goodness proceeds is included under it, whatever goodness it may be. His saying: ﴿And those who, when they commit an immorality﴾: this is a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is ﴿those﴾. It was also said: it is conjoined to "the God-fearing".

The first is preferable. These are a category below the first category, joined with them, namely the penitent (tawwābūn). The cause of its revelation will be mentioned later. "Fāḥisha" is a descriptor of an omitted noun, i.e., a shameful deed, and it applies to every act of disobedience, though its specific use has become frequent for fornication.

His saying: ﴿or wrong themselves﴾, i.e., by committing some sin among the sins. It was also said: "aw" means "wa" (and). The intended meaning is what has been mentioned. It was said: the fāḥisha is the major sin, and wronging oneself is the minor sin. Other things have also been said.

His saying: ﴿remember God﴾, i.e., with their tongues, or they bring Him to mind in their hearts, or they remember His promise and His threat. ﴿And ask forgiveness for their sins﴾, i.e., they seek forgiveness for them from God, glorified is He. Explaining it as repentance (tawba) is contrary to its linguistic meaning. In the interrogative with His saying: ﴿And who forgives sins except God?﴾ there is a rebuke, together with what it implies of indicating that He alone, glorified is He, is specially entitled to this, to the exclusion of others; i.e., no one forgives the category of sins except God. In it there is encouragement to seek forgiveness from Him, glorified is He, and an incitement to sinners to stand in positions of humility and submission. This sentence is a parenthetical interjection between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined. His saying: ﴿and they do not persist in what they have done﴾ is a conjunction upon "they asked forgiveness"; i.e., they do not remain upon their evil deed. The explanation of persistence (iṣrār) has already been given, and what is meant by it here is the resolve to repeat the sin and not desist from it by repentance.

His saying: "while they know" is a circumstantial clause (jumla ḥāliyya); i.e., they do not persist in their deed while knowing its ugliness.

His saying: ﴿Those—their reward﴾: the demonstrative refers to those mentioned in His saying: ﴿And those who, when they commit an immorality﴾.

His saying: "their reward" is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimāl) from the demonstrative noun. His saying: "forgiveness" is the predicate, "from their Lord" is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a qualifier of "forgiveness"; i.e., coming from their Lord.

His saying: ﴿and excellent is the reward of the workers﴾: the praised element that is specified is omitted; i.e., their reward, or that mentioned. The explanation of the Gardens and how the rivers flow beneath them has already been given.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid: He said: They used to trade up to a term, and when the term came they added to them and extended the term, so ﴿O you who have believed, do not consume riba, doubled and redoubled﴾ was revealed. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from ʿAṭāʾ, who said: Thaqif used to lend to the Banu al-Mughira in the Jahiliyya, and he mentioned something similar.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Muʿawiya ibn Qurra, who said: People used to interpret this verse ﴿and fear the Fire which has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾ as: "Beware, lest I punish you for your sins in the Fire which I have prepared for the disbelievers." ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abi Rabah, who said: The Muslims said: "O Messenger of God, were the Children of Israel more honoured by God than us? When one of them committed a sin, the expiation of his sin would be written in the threshold of his door: 'Cut off your nose, cut off your ear, do such-and-such.'" The Prophet (ﷺ) was silent, and then ﴿And hasten﴾ was revealed, the verse.

Ibn Jarir narrated through the chain of al-Suddi from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying ﴿whose width is the heavens and the earth﴾, similar to what we mentioned earlier from the majority.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated something similar from him through the chain of Kurayb.
