Al-Zajjaj and others said: what is meant by them is slaves. The lam in ﴿the good-doers﴾ may be for the genus, so that every good-doer among these and others is included, and it may be for a specific reference, so that it is restricted to these.

The first is preferable, in consideration of the generality of the wording rather than the specificity of the context, so that every person from whom the designation of goodness proceeds is included under it, whatever goodness it may be. His saying: ﴿And those who, when they commit an immorality﴾: this is a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is ﴿those﴾. It was also said: it is conjoined to "the God-fearing".

The first is preferable. These are a category below the first category, joined with them, namely the penitent (tawwābūn). The cause of its revelation will be mentioned later. "Fāḥisha" is a descriptor of an omitted noun, i.e., a shameful deed, and it applies to every act of disobedience, though its specific use has become frequent for fornication.

His saying: ﴿or wrong themselves﴾, i.e., by committing some sin among the sins. It was also said: "aw" means "wa" (and). The intended meaning is what has been mentioned. It was said: the fāḥisha is the major sin, and wronging oneself is the minor sin. Other things have also been said.

His saying: ﴿remember God﴾, i.e., with their tongues, or they bring Him to mind in their hearts, or they remember His promise and His threat. ﴿And ask forgiveness for their sins﴾, i.e., they seek forgiveness for them from God, glorified is He. Explaining it as repentance (tawba) is contrary to its linguistic meaning. In the interrogative with His saying: ﴿And who forgives sins except God?﴾ there is a rebuke, together with what it implies of indicating that He alone, glorified is He, is specially entitled to this, to the exclusion of others; i.e., no one forgives the category of sins except God. In it there is encouragement to seek forgiveness from Him, glorified is He, and an incitement to sinners to stand in positions of humility and submission. This sentence is a parenthetical interjection between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined. His saying: ﴿and they do not persist in what they have done﴾ is a conjunction upon "they asked forgiveness"; i.e., they do not remain upon their evil deed. The explanation of persistence (iṣrār) has already been given, and what is meant by it here is the resolve to repeat the sin and not desist from it by repentance.

His saying: "while they know" is a circumstantial clause (jumla ḥāliyya); i.e., they do not persist in their deed while knowing its ugliness.

His saying: ﴿Those—their reward﴾: the demonstrative refers to those mentioned in His saying: ﴿And those who, when they commit an immorality﴾.

His saying: "their reward" is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimāl) from the demonstrative noun. His saying: "forgiveness" is the predicate, "from their Lord" is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a qualifier of "forgiveness"; i.e., coming from their Lord.

His saying: ﴿and excellent is the reward of the workers﴾: the praised element that is specified is omitted; i.e., their reward, or that mentioned. The explanation of the Gardens and how the rivers flow beneath them has already been given.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid: He said: They used to trade up to a term, and when the term came they added to them and extended the term, so ﴿O you who have believed, do not consume riba, doubled and redoubled﴾ was revealed. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from ʿAṭāʾ, who said: Thaqif used to lend to the Banu al-Mughira in the Jahiliyya, and he mentioned something similar.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Muʿawiya ibn Qurra, who said: People used to interpret this verse ﴿and fear the Fire which has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾ as: "Beware, lest I punish you for your sins in the Fire which I have prepared for the disbelievers." ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abi Rabah, who said: The Muslims said: "O Messenger of God, were the Children of Israel more honoured by God than us? When one of them committed a sin, the expiation of his sin would be written in the threshold of his door: 'Cut off your nose, cut off your ear, do such-and-such.'" The Prophet (ﷺ) was silent, and then ﴿And hasten﴾ was revealed, the verse.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Anas ibn Malik regarding "and hasten": He said: the first takbir (opening takbir of prayer). Ibn Jarir narrated through the chain of al-Suddi from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying ﴿whose width is the heavens and the earth﴾, similar to what we mentioned earlier from the majority.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated something similar from him through the chain of Kurayb. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying ﴿who spend in ease and in hardship﴾: he said: in ease and in difficulty. ﴿And those who restrain anger﴾: he said: restraining anger. Many hadiths have been related regarding the reward of one who restrains anger.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Nakha'i regarding the verse: He said: wrongdoing is from immorality and immorality is from wrongdoing. Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Tabarani, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: Indeed, in the Book of God there are two verses: no servant commits a sin, then recites them and asks God's forgiveness, except that He forgives him: ﴿And those who, when they commit an immorality﴾ the verse, and His saying: ﴿And whoever does evil or wrongs himself﴾ [al-Nisa': 110], the verse. ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Thabit al-Bunani, who said: It reached me that when this verse was revealed, ﴿And those who, when they commit an immorality﴾ the verse, Iblis wept.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi narrated from ʿAṭṭaf ibn Khalid, who said: It reached me that when His saying, exalted is He, was revealed: ﴿And who forgives sins except God, and they do not persist in what they have done﴾, Iblis cried out to his armies, threw dust upon his head, and called for woe and destruction, until his armies came to him from every land and sea, and they said: "What is wrong with you, our master?" He said: "A verse has been revealed in the Book of God after which no sin will harm any of the sons of Adam." They said: "What is it?" So he informed them. They said: "We will open for them the door of desires, so they will not repent, nor seek forgiveness, and they will see only that they are upon the truth." So he was content with that from them.

Then he recited this verse: ﴿And those who, when they commit an immorality﴾ the verse.

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from al-Hasan as a marfu' report similar to it, but he said: "Then he went out to an open area of the land and prayed." ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "One who seeks forgiveness does not persist, even if he returns to the same sin seventy times in a day."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi regarding His saying: "and they do not persist": that they keep silent and do not seek forgiveness. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Muqatil regarding ﴿and excellent is the reward of the workers﴾: He said: the reward of those who work by obeying God is Paradise.

His saying: ﴿doubled and redoubled﴾ is not a restriction of the prohibition, since the prohibition of riba is known to be absolute in every case. Rather, it was brought in consideration of the custom they were accustomed to in riba. They used to lend at interest up to a term, and when the term fell due they added an amount to the principal upon which they mutually agreed, then they extended the term of the debt. They would do this time after time until the creditor took many times the debt he had originally given. ﴿Redoubled﴾ (a'afan) is a circumstantial accusative (hal), and ﴿multiplied﴾ (mudā'afatan) is its qualifier (na't). It contains an indication of repeated multiplication year after year, and the emphasis in this expression serves to strengthen the rebuke.

His saying: ﴿And fear the Fire which has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾ contains guidance to avoid what the disbelievers do in their dealings.

Many of the exegetes said: it also means that whoever deems riba permissible disbelieves. It was also said its meaning is: fear the riba which strips faith from you, so that you deserve the Fire. The riba was singled out in this verse because it is the one for which God has threatened its practitioner with war.

His saying: ﴿And obey God and the Messenger﴾: the omission of the complement indicates generality, i.e., in every command and prohibition. ﴿So that you may receive mercy﴾, i.e., hoping for mercy from God, mighty and majestic.

His saying: ﴿And hasten﴾ is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon "obey". Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿sāri'ū﴾ without a waw, and likewise it is in the codices of the people of Medina and the people of Syria, while the rest read it with a waw.

Al-musara'a is al-mubadara (hastening), and in the verse there is an ellipsis, i.e., hasten to what necessitates forgiveness from the acts of obedience. His saying: ﴿whose width is the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Hadid: 21], i.e., its width is like the width of the heavens and the earth. The majority held that it means the heavens and earth are joined to one another, as garments are spread out and joined to one another, and that this is the width of Paradise. Width is mentioned to indicate length, because length is generally greater than width. It was also said that this statement came in the manner of Arabic speech through metaphor rather than literal meaning, since Paradise was at an extreme degree of vastness and expansiveness, the expression by the width of the heavens and earth was fitting as hyperbole, for they are the widest of God's creations, as far as His servants know, and it was not intended to be a precise measurement.

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verses 137–148 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, ﴿Indeed, there have passed before you ways (sunan)﴾: this is a return to describing the rest of the story. By "sunan" is meant what Allah has established among the nations of His events; that is, there have passed before your time events which Allah established among the nations who denied (their messengers). The root of "sunan" is the plural of "sunnah," which is the straight path. From it is the saying of al-Hudhali:

"So do not be distressed by a path (sunnah) you have traveled; the first to be pleased with a path is the one who travels it."

And the sunnah is the leader who is followed and imitated. From it is the saying of Labid:

"From a people whose forefathers established for them (a sunnah), and for every people there is a sunnah and an imam."

And the sunnah is also the community (ummah), and the sunan are the nations (umam), as said by al-Mufaddal al-Dabbi.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning in the verse is "people of sunan," so the modifier was omitted. The fa' in His saying, ﴿so travel﴾, is causal (sababiyyah), and it was said to be conditional (shartiyyah); that is, if you doubt, then travel. "Al-'aqibah" is the final outcome. The meaning is: travel and look at how the outcome was for the deniers, for they opposed their messengers out of greed for this world, then they perished, and nothing remained of their worldly life which they had preferred. This is the saying of most of the exegetes.

What is sought from this commanded travel is the attainment of knowledge of that. If it is attained without it, the purpose has been achieved, though seeing the traces has an added benefit not attained by one who has not seen them. The indication in His saying, ﴿this﴾, refers to His saying, "there have passed." Al-Hasan said it refers to the Qur'an.

﴿A clarification for mankind﴾: that is, a making clear for them. The definiteness of "mankind" is either for the known (al-'ahd), namely the deniers, or for the genus (al-jins), that is, for the deniers and others.

In this there is an exhortation to reflect on the evil outcome of the deniers and where their affair ended.

His saying, ﴿and guidance and admonition﴾: that is, this reflection, along with being a clarification, contains guidance and admonition for the God-fearing among the believers. The conjunction of guidance and admonition to the clarification indicates difference, even if by way of their objects. Its explanation: if the lam in "mankind" is for the known, then the clarification is for the deniers, and the guidance and admonition are for the believers; if it is for the genus, then the clarification is for all mankind, believers and disbelievers, and the guidance and admonition are for the God-fearing alone.

His saying, ﴿And do not weaken and do not grieve﴾: He consoled and comforted them for what befell them on the day of Uhud of killing and wounds, urged them to fight their enemy, and forbade them from weakness and cowardice. Then He made clear to them that they would be the superior ones over their enemy with victory and triumph. This is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah); that is, while the state is that you are the superior ones over them and over others after this encounter. Allah indeed fulfilled His promise, for after the battle of Uhud the Prophet (ﷺ) gained victory over his enemy in all his battles. It was also said: the meaning is, "And you are the superior ones over them by what you inflicted upon them on the day of Badr, for it was more than what they inflicted upon you today."

His saying, ﴿if you are believers﴾ is connected to His saying, "do not weaken" and what follows it, or to His saying, "and you are the superior ones"; that is, if you are believers, then do not weaken and do not grieve, or if you are believers, then you are the superior ones. Al-qarh, with a damma or a fatha, is the wound, and these are two dialects for it, as said by al-Kisa'i and al-Akhfash. Al-Farra' said: with a fatha it is the wound, and with a damma its pain. Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa' read "qarah" with a fatha on the qaf and the ra', as a verbal noun.

The meaning of the verse: if they inflicted (wounds) upon you on the day of Uhud, then you inflicted (wounds) upon them on the day of Badr. So do not weaken over what befell you on this day, for they did not weaken over what befell them on that day, and you are more deserving of patience than them. It was also said that what is meant is what befell the believers and the disbelievers on this day, for the Muslims were victorious over them at the beginning and inflicted a group of them, then the disbelievers prevailed over them and inflicted some of them. The first is preferable, because what the Muslims inflicted upon the disbelievers on this day was not like what they inflicted upon them.

His saying, ﴿And those days﴾: that is, the days occurring among the nations in their wars and those to come after, like the days that occurred in the time of prophethood, at times this group prevails and at times the other prevails, as happened to you, O Muslims, on the day of Badr and Uhud. This is the meaning of His saying, ﴿We alternate them among mankind﴾. So "tilka" is the subject, "al-ayyam" is its attribute, and the predicate is "nudawiluha." The root of al-mudawalah is al-mu'awarah (taking turns): "dawaltuhu baynahum" means "I took turns with them." Al-dawlah means the turn. It is also permissible that "al-ayyam" is the predicate and "nudawiluha" is a circumstantial clause, but the first is preferable.

His saying, ﴿and that Allah may know﴾ is conjoined to a supposed cause, as if He said: "We alternate them among mankind so that your affair may become manifest and that it may be known," or the caused element is omitted; that is, so that Allah may know those who fear Him, our doing that. This is in the mode of figurative speech (tamthil); that is, our action is the action of one who wishes to know, because He, glorified is He, has always been knowing. Or it means: so that Allah may know those who believed through their patience, with a knowledge upon which reward falls, as He knew it with eternal knowledge. ﴿And take from among you martyrs﴾: that is, He honors them with martyrdom. "Shuhada'" is the plural of "shahid," named so because he is testified to for Paradise, or the plural of "shahid" (witness) because he is as one who witnesses Paradise. "Min" is partitive, and they are the martyrs of Uhud.

His saying, ﴿And Allah does not love the wrongdoers﴾ is a parenthetical clause between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined, to confirm the content of what precedes it. His saying, ﴿and that Allah may purify those who believed﴾ is among the causes and is conjoined to what precedes it.

Al-tamhis is testing. It was also said it is purification, with an omitted noun; that is, that He may purify the sins of those who believed, as said by al-Farra'. It was also said: yumahhis means yukhlis (sincerify), as said by al-Khalil and al-Zajjaj; that is, to purify the believers from their sins. His saying, ﴿and destroy the disbelievers﴾: that is, to uproot them by destruction. The root of al-tamhiq is the erasure of traces, and al-muhiq is its diminishment.

His saying, ﴿Or do you think you will enter Paradise﴾: a resumed statement to clarify what was mentioned of distinction. "Am" here is the disjunctive (munqati'ah), and the hamzah is for denial; that is, rather, do you suppose? The waw in His saying, "while Allah has not yet known," is the waw of circumstance, and the circumstantial clause. There is in it an illustration like the first, or a knowledge upon which reward falls.

His saying, ﴿and that He may know the patient﴾ is in the accusative by the implied "an," as said by al-Khalil and others, with the waw being for conjunction. Al-Zajjaj said: the waw is in the sense of "hatta" (until). Al-Hasan and Yahya ibn Ya'mar read "wa-ya'lama al-sabirin" in the jussive, conjoined to "wa-lamma ya'lam," and it was read in the nominative as an independent clause. It was also said that His saying, "while Allah has not yet known," is a metonymy for the negation of the known, which is jihad.

The meaning: Or do you suppose that you will enter Paradise while the reality is that jihad and patience have not been realized from you, that is, their combination. The meaning of "lamma" is the meaning of "lam" according to the majority; Sibawayh distinguished between them, making "lam" for negating the past, and "lamma" for negating the past and the expected.

His saying, ﴿And you certainly used to wish for death﴾: this is an address to those who used to wish for fighting and martyrdom in the way of Allah, from among those who had not attended the day of Badr, for they used to wish for a day in which there would be fighting. When the day of Uhud came, they fled, although they were the ones who insisted upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to go out. Only a small group among them remained steadfast, such as Anas ibn al-Nadr, the paternal uncle of Anas ibn Malik. His saying, ﴿before you met it﴾: that is, the fighting or the martyrdom which is the cause of death.

Al-A'mash read "before you encounter it" (tulaqu-hu). The prohibition on wishing for death has been reported, so it must be understood here as wishing for martyrdom. Al-Qurtubi said: the wish for death by Muslims returns to wishing for martyrdom founded upon steadfastness and patience in jihad, not to the killing of them by the disbelievers, for that is disobedience and disbelief, and the intention of disobedience is not permissible. On this is interpreted the request of Muslims from Allah that He grant them martyrdom, for they ask for patience in jihad even if it leads to killing.

His saying, ﴿Then you have seen it﴾: that is, the fighting, or what is the cause of death. The place of His saying, "while you were looking," is the accusative as a circumstantial clause. The restriction of seeing by looking, despite the unity of their meaning, is for emphasis; that is, you have seen it while witnessing it at the time when those among you were killed. Al-Akhfash said: the repetition is in the sense of emphasis, like His saying, ﴿nor a bird that flies with its wings﴾ [al-An'am: 38]. It was also said: its meaning is "seeing," without any defect in your eyes. It was also said: its meaning is: while you were looking toward Muhammad (ﷺ).

His saying, ﴿And Muhammad is not but a messenger; messengers have passed before him﴾: the reason for the revelation of this is what will come, that when the Prophet (ﷺ) was struck on the day of Uhud, Satan shouted, saying, "Muhammad has been killed," so some Muslims faltered, until one said, "Muhammad has been struck, so give up your hands, for they are only your brothers," and another said, "If he were a messenger he would not have been killed." So Allah refuted them and informed them that he is a messenger, before whom messengers have passed, and he will pass away as they passed away. Thus the clause, ﴿messengers have passed before him﴾, is an attribute of "messenger." The restriction is a restriction of singling out (qasr ifrad), as though they found his death improbable, so they attributed to him two qualities: the messengership and that he would not die. Allah refuted them by saying that he is a messenger who does not go beyond that to the quality of not dying. It was also said it is a restriction of correction (qasr qalb). Ibn 'Abbas read "qad khalat min qablu rusul."

Then Allah rebuked them by His saying, ﴿So if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?﴾: that is, how will you apostatize and abandon his religion if he dies or is killed, while you know that messengers pass away and their followers hold to their religion even if they are lost by death or killing? It was also said: the denial is for their making the passing of messengers before him a cause for turning back upon his death or killing. Killing is mentioned along with knowledge that He, glorified is He, will not be killed, because it was permissible in the view of the addressees.

His saying, ﴿And whoever turns back on his heels﴾: that is, by turning his back in retreat from the fighting, or by apostatizing from Islam, ﴿will not harm Allah at all﴾ by any harm, but he harms only himself. ﴿And Allah will reward the grateful﴾: that is, those who were patient, fought, and were martyred, for by that they gave thanks for Allah's blessing upon them with Islam. Whoever complies with what he was commanded has given thanks for the blessing with which Allah has favored him.

His saying, ﴿And it is not for a soul to die except by the permission of Allah﴾: this is a resumed statement containing an exhortation to jihad and an announcement that death is inevitable. The meaning of "by the permission of Allah" is by Allah's decree and destiny. It was also said that this clause contains a denial directed at those who faltered because of that rumor of the Prophet's (ﷺ) killing, so He made clear to them that death, whether by killing or otherwise, is subject to Allah's permission. Attributing it to "a soul," though it is not free to choose it, is to indicate that no one should approach it except by Allah's permission.

His saying, "a decree (kitaban)" is an absolute object that emphasizes what precedes it, because its meaning is "Allah prescribed death as a decree." "Mu'ajjal" is that which is fixed and does not precede or delay its term.

His saying, ﴿And whoever desires﴾: that is, by His knowledge, ﴿the reward of this world﴾, like spoils and the like. The wording covers everything called the reward of this world, even if the occasion was specific. ﴿We give him from it﴾: that is, from its reward, with an omitted noun. ﴿And whoever desires by his deed the reward of the Hereafter﴾, which is Paradise, ﴿We give him from its reward, and We will multiply for him the good deeds many times over. And We will reward the grateful﴾ by carrying out what We commanded them, such as fighting, and what We forbade them from, such as fleeing and accepting rumors.

His saying, "wa-ka'ayyin." Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: it is "ayy" which was joined by the kaf of comparison and remained with it, so after the combination it came to mean "kam" (how many). It was written in the Mushaf with a nun, because it is a word transferred from its original, and its form was changed for the change of its meaning. Then its use became frequent, and the Arabs manipulated it by metathesis and elision, so there are four dialects in it by which it was read:

The first: "ka'in," like "ka'in" (with a short vowel pattern), and Ibn Kathir read with it. A similar example is the saying of the poet:

"And how many a friend in the valleys, whom if you were struck, he would be the one struck."

And another said:

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verse 137–148 (part 2 of 2):

Wa-ka'ayyin radadna 'ankum min mudajjajin / bi-hayyin amama al-rakbi yurdi muqanna'a
And said Zuhayr:
Wa-ka'ayyin tara min mu'jibin laka shakhsuhu / ziyadatuhu aw naqsuhu fi al-takallumi

Ka'ayyin with shadda, like ka'ayyin (ka'ayyin, "how many"), and the rest (al-Baqun) recited with it, and it is the original form. The third reading: ka'ayin, like ka'ayn, without shadda. The fourth: kay'in, with a yā' followed by a hamza with a kasra; Abu 'Amr paused without the nūn and said: ka'ayy, because it is tanwin; the rest paused with the nūn. The meaning: "Many a prophet had fought alongside him, and with him were rabbiyyūn" (qutila ma'ahu ribbiyyūn). Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub recited qutila in the passive voice, and this is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, and Abu Hatim preferred it. In it there are two possibilities. The first: that qutila has a pronoun referring to the Prophet, and then his words "ma'ahu ribbiyyun" form a circumstantial clause, as one says: "qutila al-amir ma'ahu jaysh," i.e., "and with him an army." The second possibility: that the killing fell upon the rabbiyyun, so there is no pronoun in qutila, and the meaning is: some of his companions were killed, and they are the rabbiyyun.

The Kufans and Ibn 'Amir recited qatala (fought), and this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, and Abu 'Ubayd preferred it, saying: "Indeed, when Allah praises those who fought, those who were killed are included in it; and when He praises those who were killed, those who fought but were not killed are not included. So qatala is more general and more laudatory." And the other reading supports this. The second possibility for the first reading is the statement of al-Hasan: "No prophet was ever killed in battle at all," and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said likewise.

Al-Ribbiyyun with a kasra on the rā' is the reading of the majority; 'Ali recited it with a ḍamma, and Ibn 'Abbas with a fatḥa. Its singular is ribbiyy with a fatḥa, attributed to the Lord (al-Rabb). Al-Ribbiyy with a ḍamma or kasra on the rā' is attributed to al-Ribbah, with a kasra or ḍamma on the rā', which means the group. For this reason a group of the early scholars (al-salaf) explained them as "large multitudes." It was also said: they are the followers; and it was said: they are the scholars.

Al-Khalil said: al-Ribbiyy is the single one of the servants who were patient with the prophets, and they are the rabbaniyyun, attributed to devotion (al-ta'alluh), worship, and knowledge of Lordship (al-ruboobiyya). Al-Zajjaj said: al-Ribbiyyun with a ḍamma are the groups.

His words "fa-ma wahanu" are conjoined to qatala or qutila. Wahn is the breaking of resolve through fear.

Al-Hasan recited wahinu with a kasra and a ḍamma on the hā'. Abu Zayd said: they are two dialects; wahana al-shay'u yahinu wahnan: it weakened; i.e., they did not weaken on account of the killing of their prophet or the killing of those among them who were killed, and they did not weaken (wa-ma ḍa'ufu) before their enemy, and they did not submit (wa-ma istakanu) to what befell them in jihad.

Al-istikana is abjection and submission. It was recited wa-ma wahanu wa-ma ḍa'ufu with the hā' and the 'ayn sukūn. And al-Kisa'i related ḍa'afu with a fatḥa on the 'ayn. In this there is a rebuke to those who fled on the day of Uhud, were humiliated, submitted, and weakened because of that terrifying rumour that came from Satan, and did not act as the companions of the messengers who passed before them had acted.

His words: ﴿Wa-ma kana qawlahum﴾, i.e., the saying of those who were with the prophets was only this saying. "Qawlahum" is in the accusative as the predicate of kana. Ibn Kathir and 'Asim in one narration from them recited qawluhum with a ḍamma.

His words "illa an qalu" are an exceptive construction (istithna' mufarragh); i.e., their saying, when some of them were killed, the rabbaniyyun, or their prophet was killed, was only: ﴿"Our Lord, forgive us our sins"﴾. It was said: these are the minor sins. His words ﴿"and our excess in our affair"﴾ — it was said: these are the major sins. The apparent meaning is that "sins" (dhunub) covers everything that is called a sin, minor or major.

Al-israf is what involves exceeding the limit, so it is the specific following the general. They said this despite being rabbaniyyun, as a humbling of themselves. ﴿"And make firm our feet"﴾ in the places of fighting. So Allah gave them, by reason of this, the reward of this world: victory, spoils, honour and the like; ﴿"and the good reward of the Hereafter"﴾ — an idafa of the attribute to the thing described; i.e., the good reward of the Hereafter, which is the bliss of Paradise. May Allah make us among its people.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid regarding His words: ﴿"Indeed there have passed before you similar ways (sunan)"﴾, he said: it is the alternation (tadawul) between disbelievers and believers in good and evil. Ibn Abi Shayba in Kitab al-Masahif related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: the first thing revealed of Al 'Imran was ﴿"This is a clarification for mankind"﴾, then the rest of it was revealed on the day of Uhud.

Ibn Jarir related from al-Hasan regarding His words: "This is a clarification," meaning the Qur'an. Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related the like from Qatada.

Ibn Jarir related through al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Khalid ibn al-Walid came, wanting to ascend the mountain over them, so the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'O Allah, let them not overtop us,' and Allah revealed ﴿"Do not weaken and do not grieve"﴾, the verse." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Jurayj, who said: the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were routed in the glen on the day of Uhud, and they asked: "What has the Prophet (ﷺ) done? And what has so-and-so done?" Some of them informed others, and they spoke of the Prophet (ﷺ) having been killed, so they were in distress and grief. While they were thus, Khalid ibn al-Walid, with the cavalry of the polytheists, ascended above them onto the mountain. They were on one wing of the polytheists, below the glen, and when they saw the Prophet (ﷺ) they rejoiced. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, we have no strength except through You, and there is none in this land who worships You besides this band, so do not destroy them." A group of Muslim archers rallied, ascended, and shot at the polytheists' horses until Allah routed them, and the Muslims ascended the mountain. That is His words: ﴿"And you will be the superior ones if you are believers"﴾. Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Dahhak regarding ﴿"And you will be the superior ones"﴾: "and you will be the victors."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid regarding ﴿"If a wound touches you, a wound has already touched the people"﴾: he said: wounds and killing. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan regarding His words: ﴿"If a wound touches you, a wound has already touched the people like it"﴾: he said: if some of you were killed on the day of Uhud, then some of them were killed on the day of Badr.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related through al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: ﴿"And those days We alternate among the people"﴾: he said: the day of Uhud was like the day of Badr. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related through Ibn Jurayj from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words "and those days..." the verse: he said: Allah gave the polytheists power over the Prophet (ﷺ) on the day of Uhud. It has reached me that the polytheists killed about seventy of the Muslims on the day of Uhud, equal to the number of the polytheist captives taken on the day of Badr; and the number of captives on the day of Badr was seventy-three men.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: ﴿"and that He may take martyrs from among you"﴾: he said: the Muslims used to ask their Lord: "O Allah, our Lord, show us a day like the day of Badr, in which we fight the polytheists, and in which we shall show You good, and seek martyrdom in it." So they met the polytheists on the day of Uhud, and He took martyrs from among them. Both (Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir) related from him regarding His words: ﴿"and that Allah may purify those who believe"﴾: he said: He tests them; ﴿"and destroy the disbelievers"﴾: he said: He diminishes them.

Ibn Abi Hatim related through al-'Awfi from him that men among the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say: "Would that we were killed as the companions of Badr were killed, and became martyrs, or would that we had a day like the day of Badr in which we fight the polytheists and show good in it, and seek martyrdom, Paradise, life and provision." So Allah made them witness Uhud, and none of them stood firm except those whom Allah willed. Then Allah said: ﴿"And you had indeed wished for death"﴾, the verse.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Kulayb, who said: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab addressed us, reciting Al 'Imran from the pulpit, and said: "It is of Uhud." Then he said: "We scattered from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the day of Uhud, and I climbed the mountain, and I heard a Jew saying: 'Muhammad has been killed.' I said: 'I shall not hear anyone say that Muhammad has been killed without striking his neck.' Then I looked, and behold, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the people were returning to him." Then this verse was revealed: ﴿"And Muhammad is only a messenger; messengers have passed away before him"﴾.

Ibn Jarir related from al-Dahhak, who said: a caller called out on the day of Uhud: "Indeed Muhammad has been killed; return to your former religion." So Allah revealed ﴿"And Muhammad is only a messenger"﴾.

He also related the like from Mujahid. He also related from 'Ali regarding His words: ﴿"And Allah will reward the grateful"﴾, he said: "those who remained steadfast in their religion, Abu Bakr and his companions." 'Ali used to say: "Abu Bakr was the chief of the grateful."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and al-Hakim related from him that during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) he used to say: "Indeed Allah says: ﴿'If he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?'﴾ By Allah, we shall not turn back on our heels after Allah has guided us. By Allah, if he dies or is killed, I shall fight for that for which he was killed until I die." Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani related from Ibn Mas'ud regarding His words: "ribbiyyun": he said: "thousands."

Sa'id ibn Mansur related from al-Dahhak, who said: "One ribba is a thousand." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding "ribbiyyun": he said: "multitudes."

Ibn Jarir related from him: "many scholars." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding His words: "and they did not submit": he said: "they humbled themselves." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related regarding His words: ﴿"and our excess in our affair"﴾: he said: "our wrongdoings."

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verses 137–148 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, ﴿Indeed, there have passed before you ways (sunan)﴾: this is a return to describing the rest of the story. By "sunan" is meant what Allah has established among the nations of His events; that is, there have passed before your time events which Allah established among the nations who denied (their messengers). The root of "sunan" is the plural of "sunnah," which is the straight path. From it is the saying of al-Hudhali:

"So do not be distressed by a path (sunnah) you have traveled; the first to be pleased with a path is the one who travels it."

And the sunnah is the leader who is followed and imitated. From it is the saying of Labid:

"From a people whose forefathers established for them (a sunnah), and for every people there is a sunnah and an imam."

And the sunnah is also the community (ummah), and the sunan are the nations (umam), as said by al-Mufaddal al-Dabbi.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning in the verse is "people of sunan," so the modifier was omitted. The fa' in His saying, ﴿so travel﴾, is causal (sababiyyah), and it was said to be conditional (shartiyyah); that is, if you doubt, then travel. "Al-'aqibah" is the final outcome. The meaning is: travel and look at how the outcome was for the deniers, for they opposed their messengers out of greed for this world, then they perished, and nothing remained of their worldly life which they had preferred. This is the saying of most of the exegetes.

What is sought from this commanded travel is the attainment of knowledge of that. If it is attained without it, the purpose has been achieved, though seeing the traces has an added benefit not attained by one who has not seen them. The indication in His saying, ﴿this﴾, refers to His saying, "there have passed." Al-Hasan said it refers to the Qur'an.

﴿A clarification for mankind﴾: that is, a making clear for them. The definiteness of "mankind" is either for the known (al-'ahd), namely the deniers, or for the genus (al-jins), that is, for the deniers and others.

In this there is an exhortation to reflect on the evil outcome of the deniers and where their affair ended.

His saying, ﴿and guidance and admonition﴾: that is, this reflection, along with being a clarification, contains guidance and admonition for the God-fearing among the believers. The conjunction of guidance and admonition to the clarification indicates difference, even if by way of their objects. Its explanation: if the lam in "mankind" is for the known, then the clarification is for the deniers, and the guidance and admonition are for the believers; if it is for the genus, then the clarification is for all mankind, believers and disbelievers, and the guidance and admonition are for the God-fearing alone.

His saying, ﴿And do not weaken and do not grieve﴾: He consoled and comforted them for what befell them on the day of Uhud of killing and wounds, urged them to fight their enemy, and forbade them from weakness and cowardice. Then He made clear to them that they would be the superior ones over their enemy with victory and triumph. This is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah); that is, while the state is that you are the superior ones over them and over others after this encounter. Allah indeed fulfilled His promise, for after the battle of Uhud the Prophet (ﷺ) gained victory over his enemy in all his battles. It was also said: the meaning is, "And you are the superior ones over them by what you inflicted upon them on the day of Badr, for it was more than what they inflicted upon you today."

His saying, ﴿if you are believers﴾ is connected to His saying, "do not weaken" and what follows it, or to His saying, "and you are the superior ones"; that is, if you are believers, then do not weaken and do not grieve, or if you are believers, then you are the superior ones. Al-qarh, with a damma or a fatha, is the wound, and these are two dialects for it, as said by al-Kisa'i and al-Akhfash. Al-Farra' said: with a fatha it is the wound, and with a damma its pain. Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa' read "qarah" with a fatha on the qaf and the ra', as a verbal noun.

The meaning of the verse: if they inflicted (wounds) upon you on the day of Uhud, then you inflicted (wounds) upon them on the day of Badr. So do not weaken over what befell you on this day, for they did not weaken over what befell them on that day, and you are more deserving of patience than them. It was also said that what is meant is what befell the believers and the disbelievers on this day, for the Muslims were victorious over them at the beginning and inflicted a group of them, then the disbelievers prevailed over them and inflicted some of them. The first is preferable, because what the Muslims inflicted upon the disbelievers on this day was not like what they inflicted upon them.

His saying, ﴿And those days﴾: that is, the days occurring among the nations in their wars and those to come after, like the days that occurred in the time of prophethood, at times this group prevails and at times the other prevails, as happened to you, O Muslims, on the day of Badr and Uhud. This is the meaning of His saying, ﴿We alternate them among mankind﴾. So "tilka" is the subject, "al-ayyam" is its attribute, and the predicate is "nudawiluha." The root of al-mudawalah is al-mu'awarah (taking turns): "dawaltuhu baynahum" means "I took turns with them." Al-dawlah means the turn. It is also permissible that "al-ayyam" is the predicate and "nudawiluha" is a circumstantial clause, but the first is preferable.

His saying, ﴿and that Allah may know﴾ is conjoined to a supposed cause, as if He said: "We alternate them among mankind so that your affair may become manifest and that it may be known," or the caused element is omitted; that is, so that Allah may know those who fear Him, our doing that. This is in the mode of figurative speech (tamthil); that is, our action is the action of one who wishes to know, because He, glorified is He, has always been knowing. Or it means: so that Allah may know those who believed through their patience, with a knowledge upon which reward falls, as He knew it with eternal knowledge. ﴿And take from among you martyrs﴾: that is, He honors them with martyrdom. "Shuhada'" is the plural of "shahid," named so because he is testified to for Paradise, or the plural of "shahid" (witness) because he is as one who witnesses Paradise. "Min" is partitive, and they are the martyrs of Uhud.

His saying, ﴿And Allah does not love the wrongdoers﴾ is a parenthetical clause between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined, to confirm the content of what precedes it. His saying, ﴿and that Allah may purify those who believed﴾ is among the causes and is conjoined to what precedes it.

Al-tamhis is testing. It was also said it is purification, with an omitted noun; that is, that He may purify the sins of those who believed, as said by al-Farra'. It was also said: yumahhis means yukhlis (sincerify), as said by al-Khalil and al-Zajjaj; that is, to purify the believers from their sins. His saying, ﴿and destroy the disbelievers﴾: that is, to uproot them by destruction. The root of al-tamhiq is the erasure of traces, and al-muhiq is its diminishment.

His saying, ﴿Or do you think you will enter Paradise﴾: a resumed statement to clarify what was mentioned of distinction. "Am" here is the disjunctive (munqati'ah), and the hamzah is for denial; that is, rather, do you suppose? The waw in His saying, "while Allah has not yet known," is the waw of circumstance, and the circumstantial clause. There is in it an illustration like the first, or a knowledge upon which reward falls.

His saying, ﴿and that He may know the patient﴾ is in the accusative by the implied "an," as said by al-Khalil and others, with the waw being for conjunction. Al-Zajjaj said: the waw is in the sense of "hatta" (until). Al-Hasan and Yahya ibn Ya'mar read "wa-ya'lama al-sabirin" in the jussive, conjoined to "wa-lamma ya'lam," and it was read in the nominative as an independent clause. It was also said that His saying, "while Allah has not yet known," is a metonymy for the negation of the known, which is jihad.

The meaning: Or do you suppose that you will enter Paradise while the reality is that jihad and patience have not been realized from you, that is, their combination. The meaning of "lamma" is the meaning of "lam" according to the majority; Sibawayh distinguished between them, making "lam" for negating the past, and "lamma" for negating the past and the expected.

His saying, ﴿And you certainly used to wish for death﴾: this is an address to those who used to wish for fighting and martyrdom in the way of Allah, from among those who had not attended the day of Badr, for they used to wish for a day in which there would be fighting. When the day of Uhud came, they fled, although they were the ones who insisted upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to go out. Only a small group among them remained steadfast, such as Anas ibn al-Nadr, the paternal uncle of Anas ibn Malik. His saying, ﴿before you met it﴾: that is, the fighting or the martyrdom which is the cause of death.

Al-A'mash read "before you encounter it" (tulaqu-hu). The prohibition on wishing for death has been reported, so it must be understood here as wishing for martyrdom. Al-Qurtubi said: the wish for death by Muslims returns to wishing for martyrdom founded upon steadfastness and patience in jihad, not to the killing of them by the disbelievers, for that is disobedience and disbelief, and the intention of disobedience is not permissible. On this is interpreted the request of Muslims from Allah that He grant them martyrdom, for they ask for patience in jihad even if it leads to killing.

His saying, ﴿Then you have seen it﴾: that is, the fighting, or what is the cause of death. The place of His saying, "while you were looking," is the accusative as a circumstantial clause. The restriction of seeing by looking, despite the unity of their meaning, is for emphasis; that is, you have seen it while witnessing it at the time when those among you were killed. Al-Akhfash said: the repetition is in the sense of emphasis, like His saying, ﴿nor a bird that flies with its wings﴾ [al-An'am: 38]. It was also said: its meaning is "seeing," without any defect in your eyes. It was also said: its meaning is: while you were looking toward Muhammad (ﷺ).

His saying, ﴿And Muhammad is not but a messenger; messengers have passed before him﴾: the reason for the revelation of this is what will come, that when the Prophet (ﷺ) was struck on the day of Uhud, Satan shouted, saying, "Muhammad has been killed," so some Muslims faltered, until one said, "Muhammad has been struck, so give up your hands, for they are only your brothers," and another said, "If he were a messenger he would not have been killed." So Allah refuted them and informed them that he is a messenger, before whom messengers have passed, and he will pass away as they passed away. Thus the clause, ﴿messengers have passed before him﴾, is an attribute of "messenger." The restriction is a restriction of singling out (qasr ifrad), as though they found his death improbable, so they attributed to him two qualities: the messengership and that he would not die. Allah refuted them by saying that he is a messenger who does not go beyond that to the quality of not dying. It was also said it is a restriction of correction (qasr qalb). Ibn 'Abbas read "qad khalat min qablu rusul."

Then Allah rebuked them by His saying, ﴿So if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?﴾: that is, how will you apostatize and abandon his religion if he dies or is killed, while you know that messengers pass away and their followers hold to their religion even if they are lost by death or killing? It was also said: the denial is for their making the passing of messengers before him a cause for turning back upon his death or killing. Killing is mentioned along with knowledge that He, glorified is He, will not be killed, because it was permissible in the view of the addressees.

His saying, ﴿And whoever turns back on his heels﴾: that is, by turning his back in retreat from the fighting, or by apostatizing from Islam, ﴿will not harm Allah at all﴾ by any harm, but he harms only himself. ﴿And Allah will reward the grateful﴾: that is, those who were patient, fought, and were martyred, for by that they gave thanks for Allah's blessing upon them with Islam. Whoever complies with what he was commanded has given thanks for the blessing with which Allah has favored him.

His saying, ﴿And it is not for a soul to die except by the permission of Allah﴾: this is a resumed statement containing an exhortation to jihad and an announcement that death is inevitable. The meaning of "by the permission of Allah" is by Allah's decree and destiny. It was also said that this clause contains a denial directed at those who faltered because of that rumor of the Prophet's (ﷺ) killing, so He made clear to them that death, whether by killing or otherwise, is subject to Allah's permission. Attributing it to "a soul," though it is not free to choose it, is to indicate that no one should approach it except by Allah's permission.

His saying, "a decree (kitaban)" is an absolute object that emphasizes what precedes it, because its meaning is "Allah prescribed death as a decree." "Mu'ajjal" is that which is fixed and does not precede or delay its term.

His saying, ﴿And whoever desires﴾: that is, by His knowledge, ﴿the reward of this world﴾, like spoils and the like. The wording covers everything called the reward of this world, even if the occasion was specific. ﴿We give him from it﴾: that is, from its reward, with an omitted noun. ﴿And whoever desires by his deed the reward of the Hereafter﴾, which is Paradise, ﴿We give him from its reward, and We will multiply for him the good deeds many times over. And We will reward the grateful﴾ by carrying out what We commanded them, such as fighting, and what We forbade them from, such as fleeing and accepting rumors.

His saying, "wa-ka'ayyin." Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: it is "ayy" which was joined by the kaf of comparison and remained with it, so after the combination it came to mean "kam" (how many). It was written in the Mushaf with a nun, because it is a word transferred from its original, and its form was changed for the change of its meaning. Then its use became frequent, and the Arabs manipulated it by metathesis and elision, so there are four dialects in it by which it was read:

The first: "ka'in," like "ka'in" (with a short vowel pattern), and Ibn Kathir read with it. A similar example is the saying of the poet:

"And how many a friend in the valleys, whom if you were struck, he would be the one struck."

And another said:

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verse 137–148 (part 2 of 2):

Wa-ka'ayyin radadna 'ankum min mudajjajin / bi-hayyin amama al-rakbi yurdi muqanna'a
And said Zuhayr:
Wa-ka'ayyin tara min mu'jibin laka shakhsuhu / ziyadatuhu aw naqsuhu fi al-takallumi

Ka'ayyin with shadda, like ka'ayyin (ka'ayyin, "how many"), and the rest (al-Baqun) recited with it, and it is the original form. The third reading: ka'ayin, like ka'ayn, without shadda. The fourth: kay'in, with a yā' followed by a hamza with a kasra; Abu 'Amr paused without the nūn and said: ka'ayy, because it is tanwin; the rest paused with the nūn. The meaning: "Many a prophet had fought alongside him, and with him were rabbiyyūn" (qutila ma'ahu ribbiyyūn). Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub recited qutila in the passive voice, and this is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, and Abu Hatim preferred it. In it there are two possibilities. The first: that qutila has a pronoun referring to the Prophet, and then his words "ma'ahu ribbiyyun" form a circumstantial clause, as one says: "qutila al-amir ma'ahu jaysh," i.e., "and with him an army." The second possibility: that the killing fell upon the rabbiyyun, so there is no pronoun in qutila, and the meaning is: some of his companions were killed, and they are the rabbiyyun.

The Kufans and Ibn 'Amir recited qatala (fought), and this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, and Abu 'Ubayd preferred it, saying: "Indeed, when Allah praises those who fought, those who were killed are included in it; and when He praises those who were killed, those who fought but were not killed are not included. So qatala is more general and more laudatory." And the other reading supports this. The second possibility for the first reading is the statement of al-Hasan: "No prophet was ever killed in battle at all," and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said likewise.

Al-Ribbiyyun with a kasra on the rā' is the reading of the majority; 'Ali recited it with a ḍamma, and Ibn 'Abbas with a fatḥa. Its singular is ribbiyy with a fatḥa, attributed to the Lord (al-Rabb). Al-Ribbiyy with a ḍamma or kasra on the rā' is attributed to al-Ribbah, with a kasra or ḍamma on the rā', which means the group. For this reason a group of the early scholars (al-salaf) explained them as "large multitudes." It was also said: they are the followers; and it was said: they are the scholars.

Al-Khalil said: al-Ribbiyy is the single one of the servants who were patient with the prophets, and they are the rabbaniyyun, attributed to devotion (al-ta'alluh), worship, and knowledge of Lordship (al-ruboobiyya). Al-Zajjaj said: al-Ribbiyyun with a ḍamma are the groups.

His words "fa-ma wahanu" are conjoined to qatala or qutila. Wahn is the breaking of resolve through fear.

Al-Hasan recited wahinu with a kasra and a ḍamma on the hā'. Abu Zayd said: they are two dialects; wahana al-shay'u yahinu wahnan: it weakened; i.e., they did not weaken on account of the killing of their prophet or the killing of those among them who were killed, and they did not weaken (wa-ma ḍa'ufu) before their enemy, and they did not submit (wa-ma istakanu) to what befell them in jihad.

Al-istikana is abjection and submission. It was recited wa-ma wahanu wa-ma ḍa'ufu with the hā' and the 'ayn sukūn. And al-Kisa'i related ḍa'afu with a fatḥa on the 'ayn. In this there is a rebuke to those who fled on the day of Uhud, were humiliated, submitted, and weakened because of that terrifying rumour that came from Satan, and did not act as the companions of the messengers who passed before them had acted.

His words: ﴿Wa-ma kana qawlahum﴾, i.e., the saying of those who were with the prophets was only this saying. "Qawlahum" is in the accusative as the predicate of kana. Ibn Kathir and 'Asim in one narration from them recited qawluhum with a ḍamma.

His words "illa an qalu" are an exceptive construction (istithna' mufarragh); i.e., their saying, when some of them were killed, the rabbaniyyun, or their prophet was killed, was only: ﴿"Our Lord, forgive us our sins"﴾. It was said: these are the minor sins. His words ﴿"and our excess in our affair"﴾ — it was said: these are the major sins. The apparent meaning is that "sins" (dhunub) covers everything that is called a sin, minor or major.

Al-israf is what involves exceeding the limit, so it is the specific following the general. They said this despite being rabbaniyyun, as a humbling of themselves. ﴿"And make firm our feet"﴾ in the places of fighting. So Allah gave them, by reason of this, the reward of this world: victory, spoils, honour and the like; ﴿"and the good reward of the Hereafter"﴾ — an idafa of the attribute to the thing described; i.e., the good reward of the Hereafter, which is the bliss of Paradise. May Allah make us among its people.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid regarding His words: ﴿"Indeed there have passed before you similar ways (sunan)"﴾, he said: it is the alternation (tadawul) between disbelievers and believers in good and evil. Ibn Abi Shayba in Kitab al-Masahif related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: the first thing revealed of Al 'Imran was ﴿"This is a clarification for mankind"﴾, then the rest of it was revealed on the day of Uhud.

Ibn Jarir related from al-Hasan regarding His words: "This is a clarification," meaning the Qur'an. Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related the like from Qatada.

Ibn Jarir related through al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Khalid ibn al-Walid came, wanting to ascend the mountain over them, so the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'O Allah, let them not overtop us,' and Allah revealed ﴿"Do not weaken and do not grieve"﴾, the verse." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Jurayj, who said: the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were routed in the glen on the day of Uhud, and they asked: "What has the Prophet (ﷺ) done? And what has so-and-so done?" Some of them informed others, and they spoke of the Prophet (ﷺ) having been killed, so they were in distress and grief. While they were thus, Khalid ibn al-Walid, with the cavalry of the polytheists, ascended above them onto the mountain. They were on one wing of the polytheists, below the glen, and when they saw the Prophet (ﷺ) they rejoiced. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, we have no strength except through You, and there is none in this land who worships You besides this band, so do not destroy them." A group of Muslim archers rallied, ascended, and shot at the polytheists' horses until Allah routed them, and the Muslims ascended the mountain. That is His words: ﴿"And you will be the superior ones if you are believers"﴾. Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Dahhak regarding ﴿"And you will be the superior ones"﴾: "and you will be the victors."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid regarding ﴿"If a wound touches you, a wound has already touched the people"﴾: he said: wounds and killing. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan regarding His words: ﴿"If a wound touches you, a wound has already touched the people like it"﴾: he said: if some of you were killed on the day of Uhud, then some of them were killed on the day of Badr.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related through al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: ﴿"And those days We alternate among the people"﴾: he said: the day of Uhud was like the day of Badr. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related through Ibn Jurayj from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words "and those days..." the verse: he said: Allah gave the polytheists power over the Prophet (ﷺ) on the day of Uhud. It has reached me that the polytheists killed about seventy of the Muslims on the day of Uhud, equal to the number of the polytheist captives taken on the day of Badr; and the number of captives on the day of Badr was seventy-three men.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: ﴿"and that He may take martyrs from among you"﴾: he said: the Muslims used to ask their Lord: "O Allah, our Lord, show us a day like the day of Badr, in which we fight the polytheists, and in which we shall show You good, and seek martyrdom in it." So they met the polytheists on the day of Uhud, and He took martyrs from among them. Both (Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir) related from him regarding His words: ﴿"and that Allah may purify those who believe"﴾: he said: He tests them; ﴿"and destroy the disbelievers"﴾: he said: He diminishes them.

Ibn Abi Hatim related through al-'Awfi from him that men among the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say: "Would that we were killed as the companions of Badr were killed, and became martyrs, or would that we had a day like the day of Badr in which we fight the polytheists and show good in it, and seek martyrdom, Paradise, life and provision." So Allah made them witness Uhud, and none of them stood firm except those whom Allah willed. Then Allah said: ﴿"And you had indeed wished for death"﴾, the verse.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Kulayb, who said: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab addressed us, reciting Al 'Imran from the pulpit, and said: "It is of Uhud." Then he said: "We scattered from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the day of Uhud, and I climbed the mountain, and I heard a Jew saying: 'Muhammad has been killed.' I said: 'I shall not hear anyone say that Muhammad has been killed without striking his neck.' Then I looked, and behold, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the people were returning to him." Then this verse was revealed: ﴿"And Muhammad is only a messenger; messengers have passed away before him"﴾.

Ibn Jarir related from al-Dahhak, who said: a caller called out on the day of Uhud: "Indeed Muhammad has been killed; return to your former religion." So Allah revealed ﴿"And Muhammad is only a messenger"﴾.

He also related the like from Mujahid. He also related from 'Ali regarding His words: ﴿"And Allah will reward the grateful"﴾, he said: "those who remained steadfast in their religion, Abu Bakr and his companions." 'Ali used to say: "Abu Bakr was the chief of the grateful."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and al-Hakim related from him that during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) he used to say: "Indeed Allah says: ﴿'If he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?'﴾ By Allah, we shall not turn back on our heels after Allah has guided us. By Allah, if he dies or is killed, I shall fight for that for which he was killed until I die." Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani related from Ibn Mas'ud regarding His words: "ribbiyyun": he said: "thousands."

Sa'id ibn Mansur related from al-Dahhak, who said: "One ribba is a thousand." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding "ribbiyyun": he said: "multitudes."

Ibn Jarir related from him: "many scholars." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding His words: "and they did not submit": he said: "they humbled themselves." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related regarding His words: ﴿"and our excess in our affair"﴾: he said: "our wrongdoings."

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verses 137–148 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, ﴿Indeed, there have passed before you ways (sunan)﴾: this is a return to describing the rest of the story. By "sunan" is meant what Allah has established among the nations of His events; that is, there have passed before your time events which Allah established among the nations who denied (their messengers). The root of "sunan" is the plural of "sunnah," which is the straight path. From it is the saying of al-Hudhali:

"So do not be distressed by a path (sunnah) you have traveled; the first to be pleased with a path is the one who travels it."

And the sunnah is the leader who is followed and imitated. From it is the saying of Labid:

"From a people whose forefathers established for them (a sunnah), and for every people there is a sunnah and an imam."

And the sunnah is also the community (ummah), and the sunan are the nations (umam), as said by al-Mufaddal al-Dabbi.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning in the verse is "people of sunan," so the modifier was omitted. The fa' in His saying, ﴿so travel﴾, is causal (sababiyyah), and it was said to be conditional (shartiyyah); that is, if you doubt, then travel. "Al-'aqibah" is the final outcome. The meaning is: travel and look at how the outcome was for the deniers, for they opposed their messengers out of greed for this world, then they perished, and nothing remained of their worldly life which they had preferred. This is the saying of most of the exegetes.

What is sought from this commanded travel is the attainment of knowledge of that. If it is attained without it, the purpose has been achieved, though seeing the traces has an added benefit not attained by one who has not seen them. The indication in His saying, ﴿this﴾, refers to His saying, "there have passed." Al-Hasan said it refers to the Qur'an.

﴿A clarification for mankind﴾: that is, a making clear for them. The definiteness of "mankind" is either for the known (al-'ahd), namely the deniers, or for the genus (al-jins), that is, for the deniers and others.

In this there is an exhortation to reflect on the evil outcome of the deniers and where their affair ended.

His saying, ﴿and guidance and admonition﴾: that is, this reflection, along with being a clarification, contains guidance and admonition for the God-fearing among the believers. The conjunction of guidance and admonition to the clarification indicates difference, even if by way of their objects. Its explanation: if the lam in "mankind" is for the known, then the clarification is for the deniers, and the guidance and admonition are for the believers; if it is for the genus, then the clarification is for all mankind, believers and disbelievers, and the guidance and admonition are for the God-fearing alone.

His saying, ﴿And do not weaken and do not grieve﴾: He consoled and comforted them for what befell them on the day of Uhud of killing and wounds, urged them to fight their enemy, and forbade them from weakness and cowardice. Then He made clear to them that they would be the superior ones over their enemy with victory and triumph. This is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah); that is, while the state is that you are the superior ones over them and over others after this encounter. Allah indeed fulfilled His promise, for after the battle of Uhud the Prophet (ﷺ) gained victory over his enemy in all his battles. It was also said: the meaning is, "And you are the superior ones over them by what you inflicted upon them on the day of Badr, for it was more than what they inflicted upon you today."

His saying, ﴿if you are believers﴾ is connected to His saying, "do not weaken" and what follows it, or to His saying, "and you are the superior ones"; that is, if you are believers, then do not weaken and do not grieve, or if you are believers, then you are the superior ones. Al-qarh, with a damma or a fatha, is the wound, and these are two dialects for it, as said by al-Kisa'i and al-Akhfash. Al-Farra' said: with a fatha it is the wound, and with a damma its pain. Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa' read "qarah" with a fatha on the qaf and the ra', as a verbal noun.

The meaning of the verse: if they inflicted (wounds) upon you on the day of Uhud, then you inflicted (wounds) upon them on the day of Badr. So do not weaken over what befell you on this day, for they did not weaken over what befell them on that day, and you are more deserving of patience than them. It was also said that what is meant is what befell the believers and the disbelievers on this day, for the Muslims were victorious over them at the beginning and inflicted a group of them, then the disbelievers prevailed over them and inflicted some of them. The first is preferable, because what the Muslims inflicted upon the disbelievers on this day was not like what they inflicted upon them.

His saying, ﴿And those days﴾: that is, the days occurring among the nations in their wars and those to come after, like the days that occurred in the time of prophethood, at times this group prevails and at times the other prevails, as happened to you, O Muslims, on the day of Badr and Uhud. This is the meaning of His saying, ﴿We alternate them among mankind﴾. So "tilka" is the subject, "al-ayyam" is its attribute, and the predicate is "nudawiluha." The root of al-mudawalah is al-mu'awarah (taking turns): "dawaltuhu baynahum" means "I took turns with them." Al-dawlah means the turn. It is also permissible that "al-ayyam" is the predicate and "nudawiluha" is a circumstantial clause, but the first is preferable.

His saying, ﴿and that Allah may know﴾ is conjoined to a supposed cause, as if He said: "We alternate them among mankind so that your affair may become manifest and that it may be known," or the caused element is omitted; that is, so that Allah may know those who fear Him, our doing that. This is in the mode of figurative speech (tamthil); that is, our action is the action of one who wishes to know, because He, glorified is He, has always been knowing. Or it means: so that Allah may know those who believed through their patience, with a knowledge upon which reward falls, as He knew it with eternal knowledge. ﴿And take from among you martyrs﴾: that is, He honors them with martyrdom. "Shuhada'" is the plural of "shahid," named so because he is testified to for Paradise, or the plural of "shahid" (witness) because he is as one who witnesses Paradise. "Min" is partitive, and they are the martyrs of Uhud.

His saying, ﴿And Allah does not love the wrongdoers﴾ is a parenthetical clause between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined, to confirm the content of what precedes it. His saying, ﴿and that Allah may purify those who believed﴾ is among the causes and is conjoined to what precedes it.

Al-tamhis is testing. It was also said it is purification, with an omitted noun; that is, that He may purify the sins of those who believed, as said by al-Farra'. It was also said: yumahhis means yukhlis (sincerify), as said by al-Khalil and al-Zajjaj; that is, to purify the believers from their sins. His saying, ﴿and destroy the disbelievers﴾: that is, to uproot them by destruction. The root of al-tamhiq is the erasure of traces, and al-muhiq is its diminishment.

His saying, ﴿Or do you think you will enter Paradise﴾: a resumed statement to clarify what was mentioned of distinction. "Am" here is the disjunctive (munqati'ah), and the hamzah is for denial; that is, rather, do you suppose? The waw in His saying, "while Allah has not yet known," is the waw of circumstance, and the circumstantial clause. There is in it an illustration like the first, or a knowledge upon which reward falls.

His saying, ﴿and that He may know the patient﴾ is in the accusative by the implied "an," as said by al-Khalil and others, with the waw being for conjunction. Al-Zajjaj said: the waw is in the sense of "hatta" (until). Al-Hasan and Yahya ibn Ya'mar read "wa-ya'lama al-sabirin" in the jussive, conjoined to "wa-lamma ya'lam," and it was read in the nominative as an independent clause. It was also said that His saying, "while Allah has not yet known," is a metonymy for the negation of the known, which is jihad.

The meaning: Or do you suppose that you will enter Paradise while the reality is that jihad and patience have not been realized from you, that is, their combination. The meaning of "lamma" is the meaning of "lam" according to the majority; Sibawayh distinguished between them, making "lam" for negating the past, and "lamma" for negating the past and the expected.

His saying, ﴿And you certainly used to wish for death﴾: this is an address to those who used to wish for fighting and martyrdom in the way of Allah, from among those who had not attended the day of Badr, for they used to wish for a day in which there would be fighting. When the day of Uhud came, they fled, although they were the ones who insisted upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to go out. Only a small group among them remained steadfast, such as Anas ibn al-Nadr, the paternal uncle of Anas ibn Malik. His saying, ﴿before you met it﴾: that is, the fighting or the martyrdom which is the cause of death.

Al-A'mash read "before you encounter it" (tulaqu-hu). The prohibition on wishing for death has been reported, so it must be understood here as wishing for martyrdom. Al-Qurtubi said: the wish for death by Muslims returns to wishing for martyrdom founded upon steadfastness and patience in jihad, not to the killing of them by the disbelievers, for that is disobedience and disbelief, and the intention of disobedience is not permissible. On this is interpreted the request of Muslims from Allah that He grant them martyrdom, for they ask for patience in jihad even if it leads to killing.

His saying, ﴿Then you have seen it﴾: that is, the fighting, or what is the cause of death. The place of His saying, "while you were looking," is the accusative as a circumstantial clause. The restriction of seeing by looking, despite the unity of their meaning, is for emphasis; that is, you have seen it while witnessing it at the time when those among you were killed. Al-Akhfash said: the repetition is in the sense of emphasis, like His saying, ﴿nor a bird that flies with its wings﴾ [al-An'am: 38]. It was also said: its meaning is "seeing," without any defect in your eyes. It was also said: its meaning is: while you were looking toward Muhammad (ﷺ).

His saying, ﴿And Muhammad is not but a messenger; messengers have passed before him﴾: the reason for the revelation of this is what will come, that when the Prophet (ﷺ) was struck on the day of Uhud, Satan shouted, saying, "Muhammad has been killed," so some Muslims faltered, until one said, "Muhammad has been struck, so give up your hands, for they are only your brothers," and another said, "If he were a messenger he would not have been killed." So Allah refuted them and informed them that he is a messenger, before whom messengers have passed, and he will pass away as they passed away. Thus the clause, ﴿messengers have passed before him﴾, is an attribute of "messenger." The restriction is a restriction of singling out (qasr ifrad), as though they found his death improbable, so they attributed to him two qualities: the messengership and that he would not die. Allah refuted them by saying that he is a messenger who does not go beyond that to the quality of not dying. It was also said it is a restriction of correction (qasr qalb). Ibn 'Abbas read "qad khalat min qablu rusul."

Then Allah rebuked them by His saying, ﴿So if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?﴾: that is, how will you apostatize and abandon his religion if he dies or is killed, while you know that messengers pass away and their followers hold to their religion even if they are lost by death or killing? It was also said: the denial is for their making the passing of messengers before him a cause for turning back upon his death or killing. Killing is mentioned along with knowledge that He, glorified is He, will not be killed, because it was permissible in the view of the addressees.

His saying, ﴿And whoever turns back on his heels﴾: that is, by turning his back in retreat from the fighting, or by apostatizing from Islam, ﴿will not harm Allah at all﴾ by any harm, but he harms only himself. ﴿And Allah will reward the grateful﴾: that is, those who were patient, fought, and were martyred, for by that they gave thanks for Allah's blessing upon them with Islam. Whoever complies with what he was commanded has given thanks for the blessing with which Allah has favored him.

His saying, ﴿And it is not for a soul to die except by the permission of Allah﴾: this is a resumed statement containing an exhortation to jihad and an announcement that death is inevitable. The meaning of "by the permission of Allah" is by Allah's decree and destiny. It was also said that this clause contains a denial directed at those who faltered because of that rumor of the Prophet's (ﷺ) killing, so He made clear to them that death, whether by killing or otherwise, is subject to Allah's permission. Attributing it to "a soul," though it is not free to choose it, is to indicate that no one should approach it except by Allah's permission.

His saying, "a decree (kitaban)" is an absolute object that emphasizes what precedes it, because its meaning is "Allah prescribed death as a decree." "Mu'ajjal" is that which is fixed and does not precede or delay its term.

His saying, ﴿And whoever desires﴾: that is, by His knowledge, ﴿the reward of this world﴾, like spoils and the like. The wording covers everything called the reward of this world, even if the occasion was specific. ﴿We give him from it﴾: that is, from its reward, with an omitted noun. ﴿And whoever desires by his deed the reward of the Hereafter﴾, which is Paradise, ﴿We give him from its reward, and We will multiply for him the good deeds many times over. And We will reward the grateful﴾ by carrying out what We commanded them, such as fighting, and what We forbade them from, such as fleeing and accepting rumors.

His saying, "wa-ka'ayyin." Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: it is "ayy" which was joined by the kaf of comparison and remained with it, so after the combination it came to mean "kam" (how many). It was written in the Mushaf with a nun, because it is a word transferred from its original, and its form was changed for the change of its meaning. Then its use became frequent, and the Arabs manipulated it by metathesis and elision, so there are four dialects in it by which it was read:

The first: "ka'in," like "ka'in" (with a short vowel pattern), and Ibn Kathir read with it. A similar example is the saying of the poet:

"And how many a friend in the valleys, whom if you were struck, he would be the one struck."

And another said:

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verse 137–148 (part 2 of 2):

Wa-ka'ayyin radadna 'ankum min mudajjajin / bi-hayyin amama al-rakbi yurdi muqanna'a
And said Zuhayr:
Wa-ka'ayyin tara min mu'jibin laka shakhsuhu / ziyadatuhu aw naqsuhu fi al-takallumi

Ka'ayyin with shadda, like ka'ayyin (ka'ayyin, "how many"), and the rest (al-Baqun) recited with it, and it is the original form. The third reading: ka'ayin, like ka'ayn, without shadda. The fourth: kay'in, with a yā' followed by a hamza with a kasra; Abu 'Amr paused without the nūn and said: ka'ayy, because it is tanwin; the rest paused with the nūn. The meaning: "Many a prophet had fought alongside him, and with him were rabbiyyūn" (qutila ma'ahu ribbiyyūn). Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub recited qutila in the passive voice, and this is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, and Abu Hatim preferred it. In it there are two possibilities. The first: that qutila has a pronoun referring to the Prophet, and then his words "ma'ahu ribbiyyun" form a circumstantial clause, as one says: "qutila al-amir ma'ahu jaysh," i.e., "and with him an army." The second possibility: that the killing fell upon the rabbiyyun, so there is no pronoun in qutila, and the meaning is: some of his companions were killed, and they are the rabbiyyun.

The Kufans and Ibn 'Amir recited qatala (fought), and this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, and Abu 'Ubayd preferred it, saying: "Indeed, when Allah praises those who fought, those who were killed are included in it; and when He praises those who were killed, those who fought but were not killed are not included. So qatala is more general and more laudatory." And the other reading supports this. The second possibility for the first reading is the statement of al-Hasan: "No prophet was ever killed in battle at all," and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said likewise.

Al-Ribbiyyun with a kasra on the rā' is the reading of the majority; 'Ali recited it with a ḍamma, and Ibn 'Abbas with a fatḥa. Its singular is ribbiyy with a fatḥa, attributed to the Lord (al-Rabb). Al-Ribbiyy with a ḍamma or kasra on the rā' is attributed to al-Ribbah, with a kasra or ḍamma on the rā', which means the group. For this reason a group of the early scholars (al-salaf) explained them as "large multitudes." It was also said: they are the followers; and it was said: they are the scholars.

Al-Khalil said: al-Ribbiyy is the single one of the servants who were patient with the prophets, and they are the rabbaniyyun, attributed to devotion (al-ta'alluh), worship, and knowledge of Lordship (al-ruboobiyya). Al-Zajjaj said: al-Ribbiyyun with a ḍamma are the groups.

His words "fa-ma wahanu" are conjoined to qatala or qutila. Wahn is the breaking of resolve through fear.

Al-Hasan recited wahinu with a kasra and a ḍamma on the hā'.
