So Allah made them witness Uhud, and none of them stood firm except those whom Allah willed. Then Allah said: ﴿"And you had indeed wished for death"﴾, the verse.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Kulayb, who said: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab addressed us, reciting Al 'Imran from the pulpit, and said: "It is of Uhud." Then he said: "We scattered from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the day of Uhud, and I climbed the mountain, and I heard a Jew saying: 'Muhammad has been killed.' I said: 'I shall not hear anyone say that Muhammad has been killed without striking his neck.' Then I looked, and behold, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the people were returning to him." Then this verse was revealed: ﴿"And Muhammad is only a messenger; messengers have passed away before him"﴾.

Ibn Jarir related from al-Dahhak, who said: a caller called out on the day of Uhud: "Indeed Muhammad has been killed; return to your former religion." So Allah revealed ﴿"And Muhammad is only a messenger"﴾.

He also related the like from Mujahid. He also related from 'Ali regarding His words: ﴿"And Allah will reward the grateful"﴾, he said: "those who remained steadfast in their religion, Abu Bakr and his companions." 'Ali used to say: "Abu Bakr was the chief of the grateful."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and al-Hakim related from him that during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) he used to say: "Indeed Allah says: ﴿'If he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?'﴾ By Allah, we shall not turn back on our heels after Allah has guided us. By Allah, if he dies or is killed, I shall fight for that for which he was killed until I die." Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani related from Ibn Mas'ud regarding His words: "ribbiyyun": he said: "thousands."

Sa'id ibn Mansur related from al-Dahhak, who said: "One ribba is a thousand." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding "ribbiyyun": he said: "multitudes."

Ibn Jarir related from him: "many scholars." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding His words: "and they did not submit": he said: "they humbled themselves." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related regarding His words: ﴿"and our excess in our affair"﴾: he said: "our wrongdoings."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verses 149–153:

When Allah, glorified is He, commanded following those among the helpers of the prophets who came before, He warned against obeying the disbelievers, who are the polytheists of the Arabs. It was also said: the Jews and the Christians. And it was said: the hypocrites, in their saying to the believers at the time of the defeat: "Return to the religion of your fathers."

His saying: ﴿They would turn you back on your heels﴾, meaning: they would take you out of the religion of Islam into disbelief, ﴿so you would turn back as losers﴾, meaning: you would return defeated. His saying: ﴿Nay, Allah is your Master﴾ is a turning away from the implication of the first sentence; meaning: if you obey the disbelievers, they will forsake you and not help you; rather, Allah is your Helper, none other. It was also read as "Bal Allaha" in the accusative, under the assumption of the phrase "Nay, obey Allah."

His saying: "sanulqi" (We shall cast). Al-Sakhtiyani read it with the yaa (third person), and the rest read it with the nun. Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read "al-ru'ba" with a damma on the ayn, while the rest read it with a sukun. Both are dialectal variants. It is said: ra'abtuhu ru'ban and ru'uban, so he is mar'ub (terrified). It may be a verbal noun, and ar-ru'ub with a damma is the noun. *Ala ayyuha-dha al-sa'ili ayna asadat, fa-inna laha min batni Yathrib maw'ida.*

Ibn Jarir transmitted from al-Rabi' something similar.

Grief (al-ghamm) originally means covering: "ghammaytu al-shay'" means I covered the thing; "yawm ghamm" and "layla ghamma" are used when they are dark, and from it is "ghamm al-hilal" (the cloud covering the new moon). It was also said: the first grief is the defeat, and the second is the appearance of Abu Hurayra and Khalid ibn al-Walid over them on the mountain.

His saying: ﴿So that you would not grieve﴾: the lam is connected to "He rewarded you," meaning: this grief after grief, so that you would not grieve over what escaped you of the spoils nor over what befell you of defeat, as training you for calamities and preparing you to bear hardships. Al-Mufaddal said: the meaning of "li-kay la tahzanu" is "li-kay tahzanu," and "la" is superfluous, like His saying: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating?﴾ [al-A'raf: 12], meaning "an tasjuda," and His saying: ﴿So that the People of the Scripture may know﴾ [al-Hadid: 29], meaning "li-ya'lama."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Jurayj, regarding His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, if you obey those who disbelieve﴾, that he said: "Do not counsel the Jews and Christians regarding your religion, and do not trust them in anything of your religion." Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Suddi that he said: "If you obey Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, he will return you to disbelief."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him regarding His saying: ﴿We shall cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved﴾ something similar to what we have already mentioned concerning the occasion of revelation of the verse. Al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il transmitted from 'Urwa regarding His saying: ﴿And Allah had already made good to you His promise﴾, that he said: "Allah had promised them, upon patience and piety, that He would aid them with five thousand angels marked. He had done so. But when they disobeyed the command of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, and abandoned their battle lines, and the archers abandoned the Messenger's covenant with them not to leave their positions, and they desired this world, the aid of the angels was lifted from them."

The story of Uhud is fully recorded in the biographies and histories, so there is no need to lengthen the explanation here. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf regarding His saying: ﴿when you were killing them﴾, that he said: "al-hass" is killing. 'Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas something similar. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him, that he said: "al-fashal" is cowardice.

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib regarding (p-250) His saying: ﴿After He had shown you what you love﴾, that he said: "the spoils and the defeat of the people." Ibn Jarir transmitted from al-Hasan regarding His saying: ﴿And He had already pardoned you﴾, that he said: Allah says: "I have pardoned you, that I would not annihilate you." He also transmitted something similar from Ibn Jurayj. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿when you were climbing﴾, that he said: "They climbed up Uhud fleeing, while the Messenger was calling them from behind: 'To me, O servants of Allah, return! To me, O servants of Allah, return!'"

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf regarding ﴿So He rewarded you with grief upon grief﴾, that he said: "The first grief was because of the defeat, and the second was when it was said Muhammad had been killed, and that was greater for them than the defeat." 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid regarding His saying "grief upon grief," that he said: "a flight after the first flight, when they heard the cry that Muhammad had been killed." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted: "The first grief was the wounds and the killing, and the other grief was when they heard that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, had been killed." Ibn Jarir transmitted from al-Rabi' something similar.

The security (al-amanah) and security (al-amn) are the same. It has been said that al-amanah occurs only together with causes of fear, while al-amn occurs in their absence. It is in the accusative because it is governed by ﴿أنزل﴾ (anzala, "He sent down"). ﴿نُعاسًا﴾ (nu'asan, "drowsiness") is either a substitute (badal) for it, or an explicative apposition ('atf bayan), or an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu). As for what has been said, that ﴿أمنة﴾ is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of ﴿نعاسًا﴾ placed before it, or a circumstantial qualifier of the addressees, or an object of purpose, this is far-fetched.

Ibn Muhaysin read ﴿أمْنَةً﴾ with a sukun on the mim.

Regarding His words ﴿يغشى﴾ (yaghsha, "covers"): it is read with the yā' (ya) on the grounds that the pronoun refers to ﴿النعاس﴾ (drowsiness), and with the tā' (ta) on the grounds that the pronoun refers to ﴿أمنة﴾ (security). The "other group" (al-ta'ifah al-ukhra) were Mu'attib ibn Qushayr and his companions. They had gone out hoping for booty, and they began to appeal for their presence (at the battle) and to speak various falsehoods.

The meaning of ﴿أهمتهم أنفسهم﴾ (ahammathum anfusuhum, "their own selves had concerned them") is: their selves drove them to worry. One says ahammani al-amr, meaning "the matter troubled me." The waw in His words ﴿وطائفة﴾ (wa-ta'ifatun, "and a group") is for the circumstantial clause (waw al-hal), and beginning with an indefinite noun is permitted because it relies on the waw of circumstance. It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿أهمتهم أنفسهم﴾ is: they became their only concern, with no concern other than themselves.

﴿يظنون بالله غير الحق﴾ (yazunnuna billahi ghayra al-haqq, "they think about God other than the truth"): this clause is in the accusative place as a circumstantial qualifier, meaning: they think about God something other than the truth that ought to be thought about Him. ﴿ظن الجاهلية﴾ (zann al-jahiliyyah, "the thought of ignorance") is a substitute for it. It is the thought particular to the creed of the Age of Ignorance (al-jahiliyyah), or the thought of the people of the Age of Ignorance, namely their thinking that the affair of the Prophet (ﷺ) was false, that he would not be helped, and that what he called to of the religion of truth would not be completed.

His words ﴿يقولون﴾ (yaquluna, "they say") are a substitute for ﴿يظنون﴾ (yazunnuna), meaning: they say to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), ﴿هل لنا من الأمر من شيء﴾ (hal lana mina al-amri min shay', "Do we have any share in the affair?"), i.e., do we have any share in God's command? This interrogative carries the sense of denial: meaning, we have nothing of the affair. "The affair" is victory and gaining the upper hand over the enemy. It has also been said that it means going out: i.e., we only went out under compulsion. God, glorified is He, rejected that from them by His words: ﴿قل إن الأمر كله لله﴾ (qul inna al-amra kullahu lillah, "Say: indeed the whole affair belongs to God"), and nothing of it belongs to you or to your enemy. Victory is in His hand, and triumph comes from Him.

His words ﴿يخفون في أنفسهم﴾ (yukhfuna fi anfusihim, "they conceal within themselves") mean: they harbor hypocrisy within themselves and do not show that to you, but rather ask you as those seeking guidance. His words ﴿يقولون لو كان لنا من الأمر شيء ما قتلنا هاهنا﴾ (yaquluna law kana lana mina al-amri shay'un ma qutilna hahuna, "they say: If we had any share in the affair, we would not have been killed here") form a resumptive clause (isti'naf), as if it were said: what is the affair they conceal within themselves? It is said: they say among themselves, or within themselves, ﴿لو كان لنا من الأمر شيء ما قتلنا هاهنا﴾, i.e., those of us who were killed in this battle would not have been killed. God, glorified is He, rejected that from them by His words: ﴿قل لو كنتم في بيوتكم لبرز الذين كتب عليهم القتل إلى مضاجعهم﴾ (qul law kuntum fi buyutikum labaraza alladhina kutiba 'alayhimu al-qatlu ila madaji'ihim, "Say: Even if you had been in your houses, those decreed to be slain would have come forth to their resting places"), i.e., even if you had remained sitting in your houses, there would have been no escape for those destined for death from coming out to these fields where they fell, for God's decree cannot be averted.

His words ﴿وليبتلي الله ما في صدوركم﴾ (wa-liyabtaliya Allahu ma fi sudurikum, "and that God may test what is in your breasts") are a purpose clause (ʿillah) for a verb implied before it, coordinated with other purposes of His that are omitted, to indicate their abundance. It is as if it were said: perhaps what was done was for many benefits, and so that He may test, and so on. It has also been said that it is coordinated with an omitted purpose of ﴿برز﴾ (baraza, "came forth"), and the meaning is: that He may examine what is in your breasts of sincerity, and purify what is in your hearts of the whisperings of Satan.

His words ﴿إن الذين تولوا منكم يوم التقى الجمعان﴾ (inna alladhina tawallaw minkum yawma iltaqa al-jam'an, "Indeed, those of you who turned away on the day the two hosts met"): i.e., they fled on the day of Uhud. It has also been said that the meaning is: those who turned away from the polytheists on the day of Uhud. ﴿إنما استزلهم الشيطان﴾ (innama istazallahumu al-shaytan, "it was only Satan who caused them to slip") means he sought to make them slip because of some of what they had earned of sins, among which was disobedience to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). ﴿ولقد عفا الله عنهم﴾ (wa-laqad 'afa Allahu 'anhum, "And God has certainly pardoned them") because of their repentance and their apology.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the verse, he said: God made them secure that day with drowsiness that covered them, and only one who feels secure drowses. It is established in Sahih al-Bukhari and elsewhere that Abu Talhah said: "Drowsiness overtook us while we were in our ranks on the day of Uhud, and my sword kept falling from my hand, and I would take it, and it would fall, and I would take it." That is His words: ﴿ثم أنزل عليكم من بعد الغم أمنة نعاسا﴾ (thumma anzala 'alaykum min ba'di al-ghammi amanatan nu'asan, "Then He sent down upon you, after distress, security in the form of drowsiness"), the verse.

Al-Tirmidhi reported and authenticated it, and Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il reported from al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam, who said: "I raised my head on the day of Uhud and began to look, and there was not one of them but he was swaying beneath his shield from drowsiness." And he recited this verse.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Juraij, who said: The hypocrites said to 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, who was the chief of the hypocrites: "The Banu al-Khazraj were killed today." He said: "Do we have any share in the affair? By God, if we return to Medina, the more honorable will surely expel the more humble from it."

Ibn Jarir reported from Qatadah and al-Rabi' concerning His words ﴿ظن الجاهلية﴾, he said: "the thought of the people of polytheism."

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, he said: Mu'attib is the one who said on the day of Uhud: "If we had any share in the affair..."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Hasan that the one who said that was 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from (p-251) 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf concerning His words ﴿إن الذين تولوا منكم يوم التقى الجمعان﴾, he said: They were three: one of the Emigrants (muhajirun) and two of the Helpers (ansar).

Ibn Mandah and Ibn 'Asakir reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the verse, he said: It was revealed concerning Uthman, Rafi' ibn al-Mu'alla, and Kharijah ibn Zayd. Many reports have been transmitted concerning the identification of the "min" (those of you) in the verse.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verse 156–164 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Do not be like those who disbelieved﴾ refers to the hypocrites (munafiqun) who said: "If we had any say in the matter, we would not have been killed here." His saying: ﴿and who say of their brothers﴾ — in hypocrisy or in lineage; that is, they said it on account of them. ﴿when they travel through the land﴾ — when they journey in it for trade or the like. It has been said that "idha" here carries the meaning of the future in the sense of "idh" which carries the meaning of the past. It has also been said that it retains its own meaning, and what is intended here is the narration of a past state.

Al-Zajjaj said: "idha" here stands in place of what is past and what is future of time. ﴿or were raiders﴾ — the plural of ghazin (raider), like raki' and ruka' (bowers), and gha'ib and ghuyyab (absent). The poet said:

*"Say to the caravans and to the raiders, when they raid..."*

﴿So that God may make that a regret in their hearts﴾ — the lam is connected to their saying "they said," that is: they said that and believed it so that it would be a regret in their hearts. What is meant is that their opinion that had they not gone out they would not have been killed became a regret. Or it is connected to his saying "do not be," that is: do not be like them in believing that, so that God makes it a regret in their hearts alone, not in your hearts. It has also been said that the meaning is: do not turn towards them, so that God makes your not turning towards them a regret in their hearts. It has also been said that what is meant is a regret in their hearts on the Day of Resurrection, due to the disgrace and remorse in it. ﴿And God gives life and causes death﴾ — this is a refutation of their statement; that is, that is in the hand of God, glorified is He; He does what He wills and decrees what He desires, so He gives life to whom He wills and causes death to whom He wills, without travel or raiding having any effect on that.

The lam in his saying ﴿And if you are killed﴾ is a preparatory lam (muwatti'ah). His saying ﴿surely forgiveness from God and mercy are better than what they gather﴾ is the answer to the oath, standing in place of the answer to the condition. The meaning: travel and raiding are not things that bring death, and even if that occurs by the command of God, glorified is He, ﴿forgiveness from God and mercy are better than what they gather﴾ — that is, the unbelievers gather from the benefits and good things of this world for the duration of their lives, according to the reading of the one who reads with the yā' (third person), or ﴿what you gather﴾, O Muslims, of this world and its benefits, according to the reading of the one who reads with the tā' (second person).

The purpose of the verse is to explain the excellence of being killed or dying in the way of God and the greater effect of these two in attracting forgiveness and mercy. His saying ﴿And if you die or are killed﴾ — in whatever manner, according to the divine will's application ﴿surely to God you will be gathered﴾ — this is the answer to the oath indicated by the preparatory lam, standing in place of the answer to the condition, as was mentioned in the first sentence; that is: to the Lord, Vast in forgiveness, you will be gathered, not to anyone else, as is indicated by placing the adverbial phrase before the verb, together with what the specifying of God's name by mention conveys of the perfection of gentleness and dominance.

What is in His saying ﴿so by mercy from God﴾ is an extra (zā'idah) for emphasis, as Sibawayh and others said. Ibn Kaysan said: it is a noun in a position of genitive by the preposition bā', and "raḥmatin" is a substitute (badal) for it. The first view is more preferable by the rules of Arabic grammar, and similar to it is His exalted saying ﴿so for their breaking their covenant﴾ (al-Nisa' 155; al-Ma'idah 13). The prepositional phrase is connected to His saying ﴿you were gentle towards them﴾, and it was placed before it to convey restriction (qasr). The tanwin on "raḥmatin" is for magnification. The meaning: his gentleness towards them was nothing but because of a great mercy from Him. It has also been said that "ma" is interrogative, and the meaning: "by what mercy from God were you gentle towards them?" This carries the sense of wonder, but it is far-fetched; if it were so, the alif would have been dropped from "ma". It has also been said: "bi-ma raḥmatin min Allah" (by what mercy from God). Al-Fazz: the harsh, the coarse and rude. Al-Raghib said: al-Fazz is the one bad of character, and its root is fazaza like hadhira. Ghilaz al-qalb is its hardness, little compassion, and lack of responsiveness to good.

Al-infidaad is dispersal; it is said: "fadadtuhum fa-infaddu," that is: I scattered them and they scattered. The meaning: if you were harsh, hard-hearted, not gentle with them, they would have scattered from around you out of awe of you and reverence for you, because of what had occurred from their turning away. Since the matter is as mentioned, pardon them regarding what concerns your rights, and ask God's forgiveness for them regarding what is up to God, glorified is He; and consult them in the matter, that is: whatever arises for you — any matter that is consulted about in its like — or specifically in matters of war, as the context indicates, because of what that contains of consoling their hearts and attracting their affection, and to inform the community of the legitimacy of that, so that none of them shrinks from it after you. What is meant here is consultation in matters not for which the Shari'ah has come with a ruling.

The people of language said: istishara (consultation) is derived from the Arab saying: "shurtu al-dabbata" and "shawwartuha" when you know its condition; and it has been said it is from their saying "shurtu al-'asal" when you take it from its place. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿they would have scattered from around you﴾ that he said: "They would have turned away from you."

Al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding (﴿and consult them in the matter﴾) that he said: "Abu Bakr and 'Umar."

Ibn Mardawayh related from 'Ali, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about 'azm (resolve), and he said: 'Consulting the people of opinion, then following them.'"

'Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan (good), Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "This verse, ﴿It is not for a prophet to misappropriate﴾, was revealed concerning a red woolen cloak (qatifa) that was missed on the day of Badr. Some people said: 'Perhaps the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took it.' So it was revealed."

Al-Bazzar, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿It is not for a prophet to misappropriate﴾ that he said: "It is not for a prophet that his companions accuse him." Numerous hadiths have been reported on the prohibition of ghulul (misappropriation of booty).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related through the chain of al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿They are of varying ranks with Allah﴾ that he said: "According to their deeds."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verse 156–164 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Do not be like those who disbelieved﴾ refers to the hypocrites (munafiqun) who said: "If we had any say in the matter, we would not have been killed here." His saying: ﴿and who say of their brothers﴾ — in hypocrisy or in lineage; that is, they said it on account of them. ﴿when they travel through the land﴾ — when they journey in it for trade or the like. It has been said that "idha" here carries the meaning of the future in the sense of "idh" which carries the meaning of the past. It has also been said that it retains its own meaning, and what is intended here is the narration of a past state.

Al-Zajjaj said: "idha" here stands in place of what is past and what is future of time. ﴿or were raiders﴾ — the plural of ghazin (raider), like raki' and ruka' (bowers), and gha'ib and ghuyyab (absent). The poet said:

*"Say to the caravans and to the raiders, when they raid..."*

﴿So that God may make that a regret in their hearts﴾ — the lam is connected to their saying "they said," that is: they said that and believed it so that it would be a regret in their hearts. What is meant is that their opinion that had they not gone out they would not have been killed became a regret. Or it is connected to his saying "do not be," that is: do not be like them in believing that, so that God makes it a regret in their hearts alone, not in your hearts. It has also been said that the meaning is: do not turn towards them, so that God makes your not turning towards them a regret in their hearts. It has also been said that what is meant is a regret in their hearts on the Day of Resurrection, due to the disgrace and remorse in it. ﴿And God gives life and causes death﴾ — this is a refutation of their statement; that is, that is in the hand of God, glorified is He; He does what He wills and decrees what He desires, so He gives life to whom He wills and causes death to whom He wills, without travel or raiding having any effect on that.

The lam in his saying ﴿And if you are killed﴾ is a preparatory lam (muwatti'ah). His saying ﴿surely forgiveness from God and mercy are better than what they gather﴾ is the answer to the oath, standing in place of the answer to the condition. The meaning: travel and raiding are not things that bring death, and even if that occurs by the command of God, glorified is He, ﴿forgiveness from God and mercy are better than what they gather﴾ — that is, the unbelievers gather from the benefits and good things of this world for the duration of their lives, according to the reading of the one who reads with the yā' (third person), or ﴿what you gather﴾, O Muslims, of this world and its benefits, according to the reading of the one who reads with the tā' (second person).

The purpose of the verse is to explain the excellence of being killed or dying in the way of God and the greater effect of these two in attracting forgiveness and mercy. His saying ﴿And if you die or are killed﴾ — in whatever manner, according to the divine will's application ﴿surely to God you will be gathered﴾ — this is the answer to the oath indicated by the preparatory lam, standing in place of the answer to the condition, as was mentioned in the first sentence; that is: to the Lord, Vast in forgiveness, you will be gathered, not to anyone else, as is indicated by placing the adverbial phrase before the verb, together with what the specifying of God's name by mention conveys of the perfection of gentleness and dominance.

What is in His saying ﴿so by mercy from God﴾ is an extra (zā'idah) for emphasis, as Sibawayh and others said. Ibn Kaysan said: it is a noun in a position of genitive by the preposition bā', and "raḥmatin" is a substitute (badal) for it. The first view is more preferable by the rules of Arabic grammar, and similar to it is His exalted saying ﴿so for their breaking their covenant﴾ (al-Nisa' 155; al-Ma'idah 13). The prepositional phrase is connected to His saying ﴿you were gentle towards them﴾, and it was placed before it to convey restriction (qasr). The tanwin on "raḥmatin" is for magnification. The meaning: his gentleness towards them was nothing but because of a great mercy from Him. It has also been said that "ma" is interrogative, and the meaning: "by what mercy from God were you gentle towards them?" This carries the sense of wonder, but it is far-fetched; if it were so, the alif would have been dropped from "ma". It has also been said: "bi-ma raḥmatin min Allah" (by what mercy from God). Al-Fazz: the harsh, the coarse and rude. Al-Raghib said: al-Fazz is the one bad of character, and its root is fazaza like hadhira. Ghilaz al-qalb is its hardness, little compassion, and lack of responsiveness to good.

Al-infidaad is dispersal; it is said: "fadadtuhum fa-infaddu," that is: I scattered them and they scattered. The meaning: if you were harsh, hard-hearted, not gentle with them, they would have scattered from around you out of awe of you and reverence for you, because of what had occurred from their turning away. Since the matter is as mentioned, pardon them regarding what concerns your rights, and ask God's forgiveness for them regarding what is up to God, glorified is He; and consult them in the matter, that is: whatever arises for you — any matter that is consulted about in its like — or specifically in matters of war, as the context indicates, because of what that contains of consoling their hearts and attracting their affection, and to inform the community of the legitimacy of that, so that none of them shrinks from it after you. What is meant here is consultation in matters not for which the Shari'ah has come with a ruling.

The people of language said: istishara (consultation) is derived from the Arab saying: "shurtu al-dabbata" and "shawwartuha" when you know its condition; and it has been said it is from their saying "shurtu al-'asal" when you take it from its place. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: it is obligatory upon rulers to consult the scholars in what they do not know and in matters of worldly affairs that are unclear to them, and to consult the leaders of the army in matters pertaining to war, and the notables of the people in matters pertaining to the public interest, and the secretaries, officials and ministers in matters pertaining to the affairs and development of the lands.

Al-Qurtubi reported from Ibn 'Atiyyah that there is no disagreement on the obligation of removing whoever does not consult the people of knowledge and religion. (p-252) His saying ﴿So when you have resolved, then rely upon God﴾ — that is: when, after consultation, you resolve on something and your soul is at rest with it, then rely upon God in doing that; that is: depend on Him and entrust the matter to Him. It has also been said that the meaning is: when you resolve on a matter to proceed with it, then rely upon God, not upon the consultation.

Resolve (al-'azm) originally means intending to carry something out; that is: when you intend to carry out a matter, then rely upon God. Ja'far al-Sadiq and Jabir ibn Zayd read "fa-idha 'azamtu" with a ḍammah on the tā', attributing the resolve to God, the Exalted; that is: when I have resolved for you upon something and guided you to it, then rely upon God.

His saying ﴿If God helps you, none can overcome you﴾ is a resumed sentence (jumlah mustanifah) to emphasize reliance and urge it. Khidhlan is abandonment of support; that is: and if God abandons your support, ﴿who is there who can help you after Him?﴾ This interrogative is one of denial. The pronoun in "min ba'dihi" refers either to the abandonment indicated by his saying "if He abandons you," or to God. Whoever knows that there is no helper for him except God, glorified is He, and that whomever God helps cannot be overcome, and whomever He abandons has no helper, entrusts his affairs to Him, relies upon Him, and does not occupy himself with anything else. The placing of the prepositional phrase before the verb in His saying ﴿and upon God let the believers rely﴾ is to convey its restriction to Him.

His saying ﴿It is not for a prophet to deceive﴾ — that is: it is not valid for him, because deceit (ghull) and prophethood are incompatible. Abu 'Ubayd said: ghull is only from booty, and we do not see it as from treachery or from resentment; and among what clarifies that is that it is said of treachery: "aghalla, yughillu"; of resentment: "ghalla, yighillu" with kasrah; and of ghulul: "ghalla, yaghullu" with ḍammah. It is said: "the booty was embezzled (ghalla al-maghnamu ghululan)," that is: he betrayed by taking something for himself to keep from his companions. The meaning of the verse according to the reading with the active voice: it is not valid for a prophet to betray any part of the booty and take it for himself without his companions' knowledge. This contains the exoneration of the prophets from embezzlement. Its meaning according to the reading with the passive voice: it is not valid for a prophet that anyone of his companions should embezzle from him, that is, betray him regarding the spoils; and according to this other reading it is a prohibition to people against embezzlement of the spoils. The specifying of the prophets' betrayal, although betrayal by others such as imams, sultans and amirs is also forbidden, is because the betrayal of prophets is greater in sin and heavier in burden.

﴿And whoever embezzles will come with what he embezzled on the Day of Resurrection﴾ — that is: he will come bearing it upon his back, as this is authentically reported from the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, and he will be disgraced before all creation. This sentence contains emphasis on the prohibition of embezzlement and a warning against it, that it is a sin whose doer is singled out for a punishment before the heads of the witnesses, which the people of the gathering will witness: his coming on the Day of Resurrection with what he embezzled, carrying it, before he is reckoned, fully laden with good and evil. This verse covers everyone who earns good or evil, and the embezzler enters under it first because the context concerns him.

His saying ﴿Is one who follows God's pleasure like one who returns with wrath from God?﴾ The interrogative is for denial; that is: one who follows God's pleasure in His commands and prohibitions, acting on His command and avoiding His prohibition, is not like one who returns (ba'a) with a great wrath from God because of his opposition to what He commanded and forbade. Within this is included one who follows God's pleasure by abandoning and avoiding embezzlement, and one who returns with wrath from God because of his undertaking embezzlement.

Then He clarified the difference between the two groups, saying: ﴿They are of varying degrees with God﴾ — that is: they differ in degrees; the meaning: they are of degrees, or they have degrees. So the degrees of one who follows God's pleasure are not like the degrees of one who returns with wrath from God; the first are in the highest degrees and the latter in the lowest.

His saying ﴿God surely conferred a favor upon the believers﴾ — the answer to an omitted oath. He specified the believers because they are the ones who benefit from His sending. The meaning of "from among themselves": that he is an Arab like them. It has been said: a human like them. The aspect of favor according to the first: they understand him and grasp his speech and do not need an interpreter. Its meaning according to the second: they are at ease with him through the shared humanity; had he been an angel, complete intimacy would not have been achieved with him because of difference of kind. It was read "min anfusihim" with a fatḥah on the fā', that is: from their nobles, because he is of the Banu Hashim, and the Banu Hashim are the best of Quraysh, Quraysh are the best of the Arabs, and the Arabs are better than others. Perhaps the aspect of favor on this reading is that since he was among their nobles, they were more obedient to him and closer to accepting him. On the first aspect it is necessary to restrict "the believers" in this verse to the Arabs; on the second aspect there is no need for this restriction, and likewise on the reading with fatḥah on the fā' there is no need for restriction, because the Banu Hashim are the most noble of the Arabs and non-Arabs in nobility of origin, generosity of lineage, and loftiness of descent.

What indicates the first aspect is His exalted saying ﴿It is He who sent among the unlettered a messenger from among them﴾ (al-Jumu'ah 2) and His saying ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and your people﴾ (al-Zukhruf 44).

His saying ﴿reciting to them His verses﴾ — this is a second favor; that is: reciting to them the Qur'an after they were people of ignorance who knew nothing of the laws, and purifying them (yuzakkihim), that is: cleansing them from the impurity of disbelief. This sentence is conjoined to the first sentence, and both are in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), or as a description of "a messenger." Likewise His saying ﴿and teaching them the Book﴾, and "the Book" here means the Qur'an.

"Al-hikmah" means the Sunnah. This was explained earlier in al-Baqarah. ﴿And indeed they were before that﴾ — that is: before Muhammad, or before his mission ﴿in clear error﴾ — that is: manifest, with no doubt about it. The lam is for distinguishing between "in" the light form of the heavy one and "in" the negating one: it enters the predicate of the light form, not the negating one, and its subject is the pronoun of the matter, that is: indeed the matter and the event. It has also been said that it is the negating "in," and the lam means "illa" (except); that is: they were before that only in manifest error, and this is the view of the Kufans. The sentence under both interpretations is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid concerning His saying ﴿And they said of their brothers when they travel through the land﴾ — the verse — he said: this is the statement of Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul and the hypocrites. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported similarly from al-Suddi.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid concerning His saying ﴿So that God may make that a regret in their hearts﴾ that he said: their statement grieves them and benefits them not at all. They also reported from Qatadah concerning His saying ﴿so by mercy from God﴾ (p-253) that he said: "by mercy from God you were gentle with them."

It has also been said that it retains its own meaning, and what is intended here is the narration of a past state.

What is meant is that their opinion that had they not gone out they would not have been killed became a regret. It has also been said that the meaning is: do not turn towards them, so that God makes your not turning towards them a regret in their hearts. His saying ﴿surely forgiveness from God and mercy are better than what they gather﴾ is the answer to the oath, standing in place of the answer to the condition. The meaning: travel and raiding are not things that bring death, and even if that occurs by the command of God, glorified is He, ﴿forgiveness from God and mercy are better than what they gather﴾ — that is, the unbelievers gather from the benefits and good things of this world for the duration of their lives, according to the reading of the one who reads with the yā' (third person), or ﴿what you gather﴾, O Muslims, of this world and its benefits, according to the reading of the one who reads with the tā' (second person).

Ibn Kaysan said: it is a noun in a position of genitive by the preposition bā', and "raḥmatin" is a substitute (badal) for it. The first view is more preferable by the rules of Arabic grammar, and similar to it is His exalted saying ﴿so for their breaking their covenant﴾ (al-Nisa' 155; al-Ma'idah 13). The prepositional phrase is connected to His saying ﴿you were gentle towards them﴾, and it was placed before it to convey restriction (qasr). The tanwin on "raḥmatin" is for magnification. The meaning: his gentleness towards them was nothing but because of a great mercy from Him. It has also been said that "ma" is interrogative, and the meaning: "by what mercy from God were you gentle towards them?" This carries the sense of wonder, but it is far-fetched; if it were so, the alif would have been dropped from "ma". It has also been said: "bi-ma raḥmatin min Allah" (by what mercy from God). Al-Fazz: the harsh, the coarse and rude. Al-Raghib said: al-Fazz is the one bad of character, and its root is fazaza like hadhira. This verse covers everyone who earns good or evil, and the embezzler enters under it first because the context concerns him.

Whoever knows that there is no helper for him except God, glorified is He, and that whomever God helps cannot be overcome, and whomever He abandons has no helper, entrusts his affairs to Him, relies upon Him, and does not occupy himself with anything else. The placing of the prepositional phrase before the verb in His saying ﴿and upon God let the believers rely﴾ is to convey its restriction to Him.

His saying ﴿It is not for a prophet to deceive﴾ — that is: it is not valid for him, because deceit (ghull) and prophethood are incompatible. Abu 'Ubayd said: ghull is only from booty, and we do not see it as from treachery or from resentment; and among what clarifies that is that it is said of treachery: "aghalla, yughillu"; of resentment: "ghalla, yighillu" with kasrah; and of ghulul: "ghalla, yaghullu" with ḍammah. It is said: "the booty was embezzled (ghalla al-maghnamu ghululan)," that is: he betrayed by taking something for himself to keep from his companions. The meaning of the verse according to the reading with the active voice: it is not valid for a prophet to betray any part of the booty and take it for himself without his companions' knowledge. This contains the exoneration of the prophets from embezzlement. Its meaning according to the reading with the passive voice: it is not valid for a prophet that anyone of his companions should embezzle from him, that is, betray him regarding the spoils; and according to this other reading it is a prohibition to people against embezzlement of the spoils. The specifying of the prophets' betrayal, although betrayal by others such as imams, sultans and amirs is also forbidden, is because the betrayal of prophets is greater in sin and heavier in burden.

﴿And whoever embezzles will come with what he embezzled on the Day of Resurrection﴾ — that is: he will come bearing it upon his back, as this is authentically reported from the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, and he will be disgraced before all creation. This sentence contains emphasis on the prohibition of embezzlement and a warning against it, that it is a sin whose doer is singled out for a punishment before the heads of the witnesses, which the people of the gathering will witness: his coming on the Day of Resurrection with what he embezzled, carrying it, before he is reckoned, fully laden with good and evil. This verse covers everyone who earns good or evil, and the embezzler enters under it first because the context concerns him.

His saying ﴿Is one who follows God's pleasure like one who returns with wrath from God?﴾ The interrogative is for denial; that is: one who follows God's pleasure in His commands and prohibitions, acting on His command and avoiding His prohibition, is not like one who returns (ba'a) with a great wrath from God because of his opposition to what He commanded and forbade. Within this is included one who follows God's pleasure by abandoning and avoiding embezzlement, and one who returns with wrath from God because of his undertaking embezzlement.

Then He clarified the difference between the two groups, saying: ﴿They are of varying degrees with God﴾ — that is: they differ in degrees; the meaning: they are of degrees, or they have degrees. So the degrees of one who follows God's pleasure are not like the degrees of one who returns with wrath from God; the first are in the highest degrees and the latter in the lowest.

His saying ﴿God surely conferred a favor upon the believers﴾ — the answer to an omitted oath. He specified the believers because they are the ones who benefit from His sending. The meaning of "from among themselves": that he is an Arab like them. It has been said: a human like them. The aspect of favor according to the first: they understand him and grasp his speech and do not need an interpreter. Its meaning according to the second: they are at ease with him through the shared humanity; had he been an angel, complete intimacy would not have been achieved with him because of difference of kind. It was read "min anfusihim" with a fatḥah on the fā', that is: from their nobles, because he is of the Banu Hashim, and the Banu Hashim are the best of Quraysh, Quraysh are the best of the Arabs, and the Arabs are better than others. Perhaps the aspect of favor on this reading is that since he was among their nobles, they were more obedient to him and closer to accepting him. On the first aspect it is necessary to restrict "the believers" in this verse to the Arabs; on the second aspect there is no need for this restriction, and likewise on the reading with fatḥah on the fā' there is no need for restriction, because the Banu Hashim are the most noble of the Arabs and non-Arabs in nobility of origin, generosity of lineage, and loftiness of descent.

What indicates the first aspect is His exalted saying ﴿It is He who sent among the unlettered a messenger from among them﴾ (al-Jumu'ah 2) and His saying ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and your people﴾ (al-Zukhruf 44).

His saying ﴿reciting to them His verses﴾ — this is a second favor; that is: reciting to them the Qur'an after they were people of ignorance who knew nothing of the laws, and purifying them (yuzakkihim), that is: cleansing them from the impurity of disbelief. Likewise His saying ﴿and teaching them the Book﴾, and "the Book" here means the Qur'an.

"Al-hikmah" means the Sunnah. This was explained earlier in al-Baqarah. ﴿And indeed they were before that﴾ — that is: before Muhammad, or before his mission ﴿in clear error﴾ — that is: manifest, with no doubt about it. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported similarly from al-Suddi.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿they would have scattered from around you﴾ that he said: "They would have turned away from you."

Ibn 'Adi and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab (al-Suyuti said: with a good (hasan) chain) related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "When ﴿and consult them in the matter﴾ was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed, Allah and His Messenger are free of need for it, but Allah made it a mercy for my community. Al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding (﴿and consult them in the matter﴾) that he said: "Abu Bakr and 'Umar."

Ibn Mardawayh related from 'Ali, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about 'azm (resolve), and he said: 'Consulting the people of opinion, then following them.'"

'Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan (good), Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "This verse, ﴿It is not for a prophet to misappropriate﴾, was revealed concerning a red woolen cloak (qatifa) that was missed on the day of Badr. Some people said: 'Perhaps the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took it.' So it was revealed."

Al-Bazzar, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿It is not for a prophet to misappropriate﴾ that he said: "It is not for a prophet that his companions accuse him." Numerous hadiths have been reported on the prohibition of ghulul (misappropriation of booty).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related through the chain of al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿They are of varying ranks with Allah﴾ that he said: "According to their deeds."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman related from 'A'isha regarding His words ﴿Allah certainly conferred favor upon the believers﴾, the verse, that she said: "This is specific to the Arabs."

It has been said that "idha" here carries the meaning of the future in the sense of "idh" which carries the meaning of the past. It has also been said that it retains its own meaning, and what is intended here is the narration of a past state.

Al-Zajjaj said: "idha" here stands in place of what is past and what is future of time. ﴿or were raiders﴾ — the plural of ghazin (raider), like raki' and ruka' (bowers), and gha'ib and ghuyyab (absent). The poet said:

*"Say to the caravans and to the raiders, when they raid..."*

﴿So that God may make that a regret in their hearts﴾ — the lam is connected to their saying "they said," that is: they said that and believed it so that it would be a regret in their hearts. What is meant is that their opinion that had they not gone out they would not have been killed became a regret. Or it is connected to his saying "do not be," that is: do not be like them in believing that, so that God makes it a regret in their hearts alone, not in your hearts. It has also been said that the meaning is: do not turn towards them, so that God makes your not turning towards them a regret in their hearts. It has also been said that what is meant is a regret in their hearts on the Day of Resurrection, due to the disgrace and remorse in it. ﴿And God gives life and causes death﴾ — this is a refutation of their statement; that is, that is in the hand of God, glorified is He; He does what He wills and decrees what He desires, so He gives life to whom He wills and causes death to whom He wills, without travel or raiding having any effect on that.

The lam in his saying ﴿And if you are killed﴾ is a preparatory lam (muwatti'ah). His saying ﴿surely forgiveness from God and mercy are better than what they gather﴾ is the answer to the oath, standing in place of the answer to the condition. The meaning: travel and raiding are not things that bring death, and even if that occurs by the command of God, glorified is He, ﴿forgiveness from God and mercy are better than what they gather﴾ — that is, the unbelievers gather from the benefits and good things of this world for the duration of their lives, according to the reading of the one who reads with the yā' (third person), or ﴿what you gather﴾, O Muslims, of this world and its benefits, according to the reading of the one who reads with the tā' (second person).

The purpose of the verse is to explain the excellence of being killed or dying in the way of God and the greater effect of these two in attracting forgiveness and mercy. His saying ﴿And if you die or are killed﴾ — in whatever manner, according to the divine will's application ﴿surely to God you will be gathered﴾ — this is the answer to the oath indicated by the preparatory lam, standing in place of the answer to the condition, as was mentioned in the first sentence; that is: to the Lord, Vast in forgiveness, you will be gathered, not to anyone else, as is indicated by placing the adverbial phrase before the verb, together with what the specifying of God's name by mention conveys of the perfection of gentleness and dominance.

What is in His saying ﴿so by mercy from God﴾ is an extra (zā'idah) for emphasis, as Sibawayh and others said. Ibn Kaysan said: it is a noun in a position of genitive by the preposition bā', and "raḥmatin" is a substitute (badal) for it. The first view is more preferable by the rules of Arabic grammar, and similar to it is His exalted saying ﴿so for their breaking their covenant﴾ (al-Nisa' 155; al-Ma'idah 13). The prepositional phrase is connected to His saying ﴿you were gentle towards them﴾, and it was placed before it to convey restriction (qasr). The tanwin on "raḥmatin" is for magnification. The meaning: his gentleness towards them was nothing but because of a great mercy from Him. It has also been said that "ma" is interrogative, and the meaning: "by what mercy from God were you gentle towards them?" This carries the sense of wonder, but it is far-fetched; if it were so, the alif would have been dropped from "ma". It has also been said: "bi-ma raḥmatin min Allah" (by what mercy from God). Al-Fazz: the harsh, the coarse and rude. Al-Raghib said: al-Fazz is the one bad of character, and its root is fazaza like hadhira. Ghilaz al-qalb is its hardness, little compassion, and lack of responsiveness to good.

Al-infidaad is dispersal; it is said: "fadadtuhum fa-infaddu," that is: I scattered them and they scattered. The meaning: if you were harsh, hard-hearted, not gentle with them, they would have scattered from around you out of awe of you and reverence for you, because of what had occurred from their turning away. Since the matter is as mentioned, pardon them regarding what concerns your rights, and ask God's forgiveness for them regarding what is up to God, glorified is He; and consult them in the matter, that is: whatever arises for you — any matter that is consulted about in its like — or specifically in matters of war, as the context indicates, because of what that contains of consoling their hearts and attracting their affection, and to inform the community of the legitimacy of that, so that none of them shrinks from it after you. What is meant here is consultation in matters not for which the Shari'ah has come with a ruling.

The people of language said: istishara (consultation) is derived from the Arab saying: "shurtu al-dabbata" and "shawwartuha" when you know its condition; and it has been said it is from their saying "shurtu al-'asal" when you take it from its place. **Commentary on verses 165–168, from al-Shawkani's *Fath al-Qadir***

His words: ﴿Why, when a calamity struck you, though you had inflicted twice as much (on the enemy)...﴾ The *alif* is an interrogative particle used for rebuke, and the *waw* is a conjunction. *Musibah* (calamity) means the defeat and the killing they suffered on the day of Uhud. ﴿You had inflicted twice as much﴾ refers to the day of Badr. The number of Muslims killed at Uhud was seventy. On the day of Badr, they had killed seventy of the polytheists and taken seventy prisoners. So the total of those killed and captured at Badr was twice the number of Muslims killed at Uhud. The meaning is: when what befell you from the polytheists was half of what you had inflicted on them before that, you became distressed and said, "From where has this come upon us?" when we had been promised victory.

His words: "*Anna hadha*" means: from where has this defeat and killing come upon us, when we are fighting in the way of Allah, with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) among us, and Allah has promised us victory over them?

His words: ﴿Say: It is from yourselves﴾ are a command to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to answer their question with this reply. That is: this which you asked about is from yourselves, because of the archers' disobedience to what the Prophet (ﷺ) had commanded them, namely to remain at the place he had assigned to them and not to leave it under any circumstances. It has also been said that what is meant by ﴿it is from yourselves﴾ is their going out from Madinah. This is refuted by the fact that the promise of victory came only after that. It has also been said that it is their choosing ransom on the day of Badr over execution.

﴿The day the two hosts met﴾ refers to the day of Uhud. That is: what befell you on the day of Uhud of killing, wounding and defeat happened ﴿by the permission of Allah﴾, that is, by His knowledge. It has been said: by His decree and destiny. It has also been said: by His leaving you and them to one another. The *fa'* (so, then) entered the response of the relative clause because it resembles a conditional clause, as Sibawayh (the grammarian) said. His words: ﴿And that He might know the believers﴾ are coordinated with His words "by the permission of Allah," a coordination of one cause with another cause.

His words: ﴿And that He might know those who were hypocrites﴾ are coordinated with what precedes. It has been said: He repeated the verb to honour the believers, so that the verb attributed to them and to the hypocrites would not be the same. The "knowing" here means distinguishing and making manifest, because His knowledge (exalted is He) was already established before that. The hypocrites here refers to Abdullah ibn Ubayy and his companions.

His words: "*wa-qila lahum*" (and it was said to them) are coordinated with His words "those who were hypocrites," meaning: that Allah might know those who were hypocrites and those to whom it was said. It has also been said that this is a new independent statement, meaning: it was said to Abdullah ibn Ubayy and his companions: ﴿Come, fight in the way of Allah﴾, if you are among those who believe in Allah and the Last Day; or ﴿repel (the enemy) from yourselves﴾, if you do not believe in Allah and the Last Day. They refused all of that and said: "If we knew there would be a battle, we would have followed you and fought with you. But there is no fighting there." It has also been said that the meaning is: "If we were able to fight and were good at it, we would have followed you. But we are not able to do that and are not good at it." He expressed the lack of ability to fight by the lack of knowledge of it, because the former entails the latter. In this there is a remoteness for which there is no need. It has also been said that the meaning is: "If we knew what could be called fighting, we would have followed you. But what you are about to do is not fighting; it is throwing oneself into destruction, since neither we nor you have the ability to repel the army that has come against us by going out to face them and leaving Madinah." Al-Tirmidhi said after transmitting it: "Hasan gharib (a good hadith that is rare, a *gharib* meaning one reported through a single line of narration at some stage); we do not know it except from the hadith of Ibn Abi Za'idah."

Abu Usamah transmitted from Hisham something similar. It is also reported from Ibn Sirin, from Ubaydah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), as a *mursal* (a report in which the Companion is omitted from the chain). The chain of Ibn Jarir for this hadith is as follows: al-Qasim narrated to us, al-Husayn narrated to us, Isma'il ibn Ulayyah narrated to us from Ibn Awn, who said: "Sunayd, who is Husayn, said." And Hajjaj narrated to me from Jarir, from Muhammad, from Ubaydah, from Ali, and he mentioned it.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted through Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah: Qurad ibn Nuh narrated to us, Ikrimah ibn Ammar narrated to us, Simak al-Hanafi Abu Zumayl narrated to us, Ibn Abbas narrated to me, from Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: "When the year of Uhud came round the following year, they were punished for what they had done at Badr in taking ransom. Seventy of them were killed, and the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) fled from him. His front tooth was broken, the helmet on his head was smashed, and blood flowed over his face. So Allah (mighty and majestic) revealed: ﴿Why, when a calamity struck you...﴾ up to the end of the verse." Imam Ahmad also transmitted it through Abd al-Rahman ibn Ghazwan, who is Qurad ibn Nuh, with the same chain, but more fully. However, this presents a difficulty for the earlier hadith of the choice: there is the reproach that Allah (exalted is He) directed at those who took ransom, in His words: ﴿It is not for a Prophet to have captives until he has inflicted slaughter in the land﴾ [al-Anfal: 67]; and there is the report that the Prophet (ﷺ) and Abu Bakr wept out of regret for taking the ransom. Had taking it been after Allah had given them a choice, He would not have reproached them for it, nor would the Prophet (ﷺ) and those with him have experienced regret and grief; nor would the Prophet (ﷺ) have approved the opinion of Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), when he proposed killing the captives and said something to the effect of: "If a punishment had descended, none would have escaped it except Umar." All of this is in the books of hadith and biography.

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn Abbas: "You said, 'From where is this, when we are Muslims fighting out of zeal for Allah, while these are polytheists?' So He said: ﴿Say: It is from yourselves﴾ as a punishment for you, because of your disobedience to the Prophet (ﷺ) when he said: 'Do not follow them.'"

Ibn al-Mundhir also transmitted from him, regarding His words "*aw idfa'u*" (or repel), that he said: "Increase the numbers with yourselves, even if you do not fight." He also transmitted something similar from al-Dahhak. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Abu Awn al-Ansari, regarding "*aw idfa'u*," that he said: "Stand guard."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn Shihab and others, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out to Uhud with a thousand men from his companions. When they reached al-Shawt, between Uhud and Madinah, Abdullah ibn Ubayy withdrew from them with a third of the people and said: 'He obeyed them and disobeyed me. By Allah, we do not know why we should kill ourselves here!' So he returned with those who followed him from the hypocrites and the doubters. Abdullah ibn Amr ibn Haram of Banu Salamah followed them, saying: 'O people, I remind you of Allah, do not forsake your Prophet and your people when their enemy has come upon them!' They said: 'If we knew that you were going to fight, we would not have abandoned you. We do not think there will be a battle.'"

Ibn Ishaq also transmitted it, saying: "Muhammad ibn Muslim ibn Shihab al-Zuhri, Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Hibban, Asim ibn Umar ibn Qatadah, al-Husayn ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Umar ibn Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, and others of our scholars narrated to me," and he mentioned it, adding that when they disobeyed him and insisted on leaving, he said: "May Allah remove you far, enemies of Allah! Allah will suffice without you."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿If we knew there would be fighting, we would have followed you﴾ that he said: "If we knew that we would find a place for fighting with you, we would have followed you."

**Commentary on verses 165–168, from al-Shawkani's *Fath al-Qadir***

His words: ﴿Why, when a calamity struck you, though you had inflicted twice as much (on the enemy)...﴾ The *alif* is an interrogative particle used for rebuke, and the *waw* is a conjunction. *Musibah* (calamity) means the defeat and the killing they suffered on the day of Uhud. ﴿You had inflicted twice as much﴾ refers to the day of Badr. The number of Muslims killed at Uhud was seventy. On the day of Badr, they had killed seventy of the polytheists and taken seventy prisoners. So the total of those killed and captured at Badr was twice the number of Muslims killed at Uhud. The meaning is: when what befell you from the polytheists was half of what you had inflicted on them before that, you became distressed and said, "From where has this come upon us?" when we had been promised victory.

His words: "*Anna hadha*" means: from where has this defeat and killing come upon us, when we are fighting in the way of Allah, with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) among us, and Allah has promised us victory over them?

His words: ﴿Say: It is from yourselves﴾ are a command to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to answer their question with this reply. That is: this which you asked about is from yourselves, because of the archers' disobedience to what the Prophet (ﷺ) had commanded them, namely to remain at the place he had assigned to them and not to leave it under any circumstances. It has also been said that what is meant by ﴿it is from yourselves﴾ is their going out from Madinah. This is refuted by the fact that the promise of victory came only after that. It has also been said that it is their choosing ransom on the day of Badr over execution.

﴿The day the two hosts met﴾ refers to the day of Uhud. That is: what befell you on the day of Uhud of killing, wounding and defeat happened ﴿by the permission of Allah﴾, that is, by His knowledge. It has been said: by His decree and destiny. It has also been said: by His leaving you and them to one another. The *fa'* (so, then) entered the response of the relative clause because it resembles a conditional clause, as Sibawayh (the grammarian) said. His words: ﴿And that He might know the believers﴾ are coordinated with His words "by the permission of Allah," a coordination of one cause with another cause.

His words: ﴿And that He might know those who were hypocrites﴾ are coordinated with what precedes. It has been said: He repeated the verb to honour the believers, so that the verb attributed to them and to the hypocrites would not be the same. The "knowing" here means distinguishing and making manifest, because His knowledge (exalted is He) was already established before that. The hypocrites here refers to Abdullah ibn Ubayy and his companions.

His words: "*wa-qila lahum*" (and it was said to them) are coordinated with His words "those who were hypocrites," meaning: that Allah might know those who were hypocrites and those to whom it was said. It has also been said that this is a new independent statement, meaning: it was said to Abdullah ibn Ubayy and his companions: ﴿Come, fight in the way of Allah﴾, if you are among those who believe in Allah and the Last Day; or ﴿repel (the enemy) from yourselves﴾, if you do not believe in Allah and the Last Day. They refused all of that and said: "If we knew there would be a battle, we would have followed you and fought with you. But there is no fighting there." It has also been said that the meaning is: "If we were able to fight and were good at it, we would have followed you. But we are not able to do that and are not good at it." He expressed the lack of ability to fight by the lack of knowledge of it, because the former entails the latter. In this there is a remoteness for which there is no need. It has also been said that the meaning is: "If we knew what could be called fighting, we would have followed you. But what you are about to do is not fighting; it is throwing oneself into destruction, since neither we nor you have the ability to repel the army that has come against us by going out to face them and leaving Madinah." This too is remote, though less remote than what came before. It has also been said that the meaning of "repelling" here is increasing the numbers of the Muslims. It has been said that it means "stand guard" (*rabitu*). The one who said this saying of the hypocrites, which Allah (exalted is He) related, was Abdullah ibn Amr ibn Haram al-Ansari, father of Jabir ibn Abdullah.

His words: ﴿They were, that day, nearer to disbelief than to faith﴾ mean: on this day, when they withdrew from the believers, they were nearer to disbelief than to faith, according to those who thought that they were Muslims. This is because they had revealed their state, torn off their veils and exposed their hypocrisy at that time. It has also been said that the meaning is: they were, that day, nearer in support to the people of disbelief than to the people of faith.

His words: ﴿They say with their mouths what is not in their hearts﴾ is a new sentence confirming the content of what precedes it. That is: they showed faith and concealed disbelief. The mention of "mouths" is for emphasis, like His words: ﴿flies with its two wings﴾ [al-An'am: 38].

His words: ﴿Those who said to their brethren﴾ etc. That is: they are those who said to their brethren, and it is taken as the predicate of an omitted subject. It is permissible that it be a substitute for the *waw* in "they conceal," or in the accusative as a term of blame, or an attribute of "those who were hypocrites." The meaning of ﴿said to their brethren﴾ has already been explained: they said that to them, while these speakers had themselves stayed back from the fighting, saying: "If they had obeyed us by not leaving Madinah, they would not have been killed." So Allah refuted that with His words: ﴿Say: Then avert death from yourselves, if you are truthful.﴾ The *dar'* means repelling. That is: caution does not benefit against destiny, for the one who is killed is killed at his appointed time.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿Why, when a calamity struck you...﴾ up to the end of the verse, that he said: "You had inflicted on the polytheists on the day of Badr twice what they had inflicted on you on the day of Uhud." Ikrimah has explained this. Ibn Jarir transmitted from him that he said: "The Muslims killed seventy of the polytheists on the day of Badr and took seventy prisoners, and the polytheists killed seventy of the Muslims on the day of Uhud." Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Hasan concerning the verse that he said: "When they saw how many of them had been killed at Uhud, they said, 'From where is this? It was not possible for the disbelievers to kill any of us.' When Allah saw what they said, He said: 'It is because of the prisoners you took on the day of Badr.'"

Thus Allah refuted them by this and hastened for them the punishment of that in this world, so that they would be spared it in the Hereafter. This is confirmed by what Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it *hasan*), al-Nasai, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ali, who said: "Jibril came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Muhammad, Allah has disliked what your people did in taking the captives, and He has commanded you to offer them a choice between two things: either they be brought forward and their necks struck, or they take ransom on condition that you accept from them a number equal to them (who will be killed).' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called the people and mentioned this to them. They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, they are our clans and our brethren. Rather, we take their ransom, so that we may be strengthened thereby to fight our enemy, and a number equal to them among us will be martyred. There is nothing in that which we dislike.'
