It was said: what is meant is that they had not joined them in merit, although they are people of merit in general. The waw in "and they rejoice" is conjunctive, joining it to "they are provided for"; that is, "they are provided for and they rejoice." It was said: what is meant by "their brothers" here is all the Muslim martyrs and others; because when they witnessed the reward of Allah and certainty arose in them of the truth of the religion of Islam, they rejoiced for all the people of Islam who are alive and have not died. This is stronger, because its meaning is wider and its benefit greater, and the wording allows it; indeed it is the apparent meaning, and Al-Zajjaj and Ibn Fawrak said so.

His saying "that there is no fear for them, nor do they grieve" (أَلَّا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْهِمْ ولا هم يَحْزَنُونَ) is a substitute for "those"; that is, they rejoice in this state attained by their brothers, namely that there is no fear upon them nor grief. "That" (أنْ) is the light form of the heavy one, and its noun is the omitted pronoun of the matter. He repeated "they rejoice" (يَسْتَبْشِرُونَ) to emphasize the first, and to show that the rejoicing is not merely for the absence of fear and grief, but for that together with the blessing and bounty of Allah.

The blessing (النِّعْمَةُ) is what Allah bestows upon His servants. The bounty (الفَضْلُ) is what He graces them with. It was said: the blessing is the reward, and the bounty is the excess; it was said: the blessing is Paradise, and the bounty is included in the blessing, mentioned after it for its emphasis; and it was said: the first rejoicing relates to the state of their brothers, and the second rejoicing to the state of themselves.

His saying "and that Allah does not waste the reward of the believers" (وأنَّ اللَّهَ لا يُضِيعُ أجْرَ المُؤْمِنِينَ). Al-Kisa'i read with a kasra on the hamza of "inna," and the rest read with a fatha. On the first reading, it is a parenthetical fresh statement. It indicates that Allah does not waste the reward of anything of the works of the believers; and the reading of Ibn Mas'ud supports it: "And Allah does not waste the reward of the believers."

On the second reading, the clause is conjoined to "bounty," included in what they rejoice in. His saying "those who responded" (الَّذِينَ اسْتَجابُوا) is an attribute of "the believers," or a substitute of them, or of "those who had not joined them," or it is a subject whose predicate is "for those of them who did good and were mindful of Allah is a great reward" as a whole clause, or it is in the accusative by way of praise. The explanation of "the wound" has already preceded.

His saying "those to whom the people said" (الَّذِينَ قالَ لَهُمُ النّاسُ): what is meant by "the people" here is Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud, as will come in its explanation; and it is permissible to apply the word "people" to him because he is of their kind. It was said: what is meant by "the people" is the caravan of 'Abd al-Qays who passed by Abu Sufyan; it was said: they are the hypocrites. What is meant by his saying "Indeed the people have gathered against you" (إنَّ النّاسَ قَدْ جَمَعُوا لَكُمْ) is Abu Sufyan and his companions. The pronoun in "so it increased them" (فَزادَهم) refers to the implied speech, "they said," or to what was said, which is "Indeed the people have gathered against you, so fear them," or to the speaker. The meaning is that they did not falter when they heard that, nor did they turn to it; rather, they sincerely devoted themselves to Allah and their tranquillity and certainty increased.

In this is evidence that faith increases and decreases. His saying "and they said: Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Guardian" (وقالُوا حَسْبُنا اللَّهُ ونِعْمَ الوَكِيلُ): "ḥasbu" is the verbal noun of "ḥasibahu," i.e., "sufficed him," and it is in the sense of the agent; that is, "muḥsib," in the sense of "sufficient."

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: The evidence that it is in the sense of "muḥsib" is that you say: "This is a man sufficient for you," so you describe an indefinite noun with it; because its genitive construction, being in the sense of the active participle, is not a true (construct) genitive, end of quote. "Al-Wakil" is the one to whom affairs are entrusted; that is, "the best one to whom our affair is entrusted," or "the Sufficient," or "the Guardian." The one specified by the praise is omitted; that is, "the best Guardian is Allah, glorified is He."

His saying "so they returned" (فانْقَلَبُوا) is conjoined to an omitted element; that is, "so they went out to them, and so they returned" (فَخَرَجُوا إلَيْهِمْ فانْقَلَبُوا). "With a blessing" (بِنِعْمَةٍ) is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause. The tanwin is for magnification; that is, they returned clothed in a great blessing, which is safety from their enemy, and well-being, "and bounty" (وفَضْلٍ), that is, a reward which Allah bestowed upon them. It was said: it is profit in trade; it was said: the blessing is specifically worldly benefits, and the bounty is the benefits of the Hereafter. Its explanation has already been mentioned shortly before in a manner suited to that context, because the discussion there was with the martyrs who had already reached the Abode of the Hereafter, whereas the discussion here is with the living.

His saying "no harm touched them" (لَمْ يَمْسَسْهم سُوءٌ) is in the position of an accusative as a circumstantial clause; that is, safe from any harm, no killing or wounding touched them, nor anything they feared; "and they followed the pleasure of Allah" (واتَّبَعُوا رِضْوانَ اللَّهِ) in what they do and what they leave, and among that is their going out for this expedition; "and Allah is Possessor of great bounty" (واللَّهُ ذُو فَضْلٍ عَظِيمٍ), whose extent cannot be measured and whose reach cannot be attained. Among His bounty upon them is making them firm, their going out to meet their enemy, and guiding them to say this statement, which brings every good and repels every evil.

His saying "That is only" (إنَّما ذَلِكم): that is, the one who discourages you, O believers, is Satan; he is the predicate of the demonstrative. It is permissible that "Satan" be an attribute of the demonstrative, and the predicate is his saying "he frightens his allies" (يُخَوِّفُ أوْلِياءَهُ). On the first, his saying "he frightens his allies" is a fresh or circumstantial clause. The apparent meaning is that what is meant here is Satan himself, in consideration of what proceeds from him of whispering that entails discouragement. It was said: what is meant is Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud when he said that statement to them; it was said: Abu Sufyan when the threat came from him to them. The meaning is that Satan frightens the believers with his allies, who are the disbelievers. It was also said that his saying "his allies" (أوْلِياءَهُ) is in the accusative by removing the preposition, i.e., "he frightens you with his allies" or "from his allies," as said by al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and Abu 'Ali al-Farisi.

Ibn al-Anbari refuted this, saying that frightening may transitively take two objects by itself, so there is no need to suppose a preposition. On the view of al-Farra' and those with him, the object of "he frightens" is omitted; that is, "he frightens you."

On the first view, the first object is omitted and the second is mentioned. It is permissible that the meaning be that Satan frightens his allies, who are the sitting-out hypocrites, so there is no omission. His saying "so do not fear them" (فَلا تَخافُوهُمْ): that is, his allies by whom Satan frightens you; or "do not fear the people" mentioned in His saying "Indeed the people have gathered against you." He, glorified is He, forbade them from fearing them, lest they shrink from the encounter and falter about going out, and commanded them to fear Him, glorified is He, saying: "and fear Me" (وخافُونِ), so do what I command you and abandon what I forbid you; for I am the one truly deserving of fear from Me and of vigilance in obeying My command and prohibition, since good and evil are in My hand. He restricted it with His saying "if you are believers" (إنْ كُنْتُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ), because faith requires that.

Al-Hakim transmitted it and authenticated it from Ibn 'Abbas who said: this verse, "And do not think of those who were killed in the way of Allah," was revealed concerning Hamza and his companions. Sa'id ibn Mansur and 'Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from Abu al-Duha that it was revealed concerning the dead of Uhud, and Hamza was among them.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud, Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When your brothers were struck at Uhud, Allah placed their souls in the crops of green birds which go to the rivers of Paradise and eat from its fruits, and take shelter in lamps of gold hanging in the shade of the Throne. When they found the goodness of their food and drink and the beauty of their resting place, they said: 'Would that our brothers knew what Allah has done for us!'" In another wording: "They said: 'Who will convey to our brothers that we are alive in Paradise, being provided for, lest they lose interest in jihad and shrink from war?' So Allah said: 'I will convey them on your behalf.' So Allah revealed these verses, 'And do not think of those who were killed...' and what follows."

Al-Tirmidhi transmitted and graded it good, and Ibn Majah, Ibn Khuzayma, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il transmitted from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah that his father asked Allah, glorified is He, to convey to those behind him what he was in, and this verse was revealed, and he was among the dead of Uhud.

It has been narrated through many channels that the occasion of the revelation of the verse was the dead of Uhud. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Anas that the occasion of the revelation of this verse was the dead of Bi'r Ma'una. In any case, the verse by the generality of its wording includes every martyr. It has been established in many hadiths in the Sahih and other collections that the souls of the martyrs are in the crops of green birds, and there has been established concerning the virtue of the martyrs what would be lengthy to enumerate and abundant to cite, of what is well known in the books of hadith.

Al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani narrated with a sahih chain from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "When the polytheists returned from Uhud, they said: 'You have not killed Muhammad, nor have you taken the captive women. What you did was wrong. Return!' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) heard of this, so he called the Muslims to set out, and they responded until they reached Hamra' al-Asad, or Bi'r Abi 'Utba (Sufyan was unsure which), and the polytheists said: 'He will return next year.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) turned back, and that expedition was counted as a ghazwa. Then Allah, glorified is He, revealed: ﴿Those who responded to Allah and the Messenger﴾, the verse."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from 'A'isha concerning His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Those who responded to Allah and the Messenger﴾, the verse, that she said to 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr: "O nephew, your two fathers were among them: al-Zubayr and Abu Bakr. When what befell the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) at Uhud befell him, the polytheists turned away from him, and he feared that they would return. He said: 'Who will go in pursuit of them?' Seventy of them responded, among them Abu Bakr and al-Zubayr."

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr ibn Muhammad ibn 'Amr ibn Hazm, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out to Hamra' al-Asad, while Abu Sufyan had resolved to return to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions. They said: 'We will return before we annihilate them, and we will attack their remnant.' He received word that the Prophet (ﷺ) had set out in pursuit of them with his companions, so this turned Abu Sufyan and his companions back. A caravan of 'Abd al-Qays passed by, and Abu Sufyan said to them: 'Convey to Muhammad that we have resolved to return against his companions to annihilate them.' When the caravan passed by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at Hamra' al-Asad, they informed him of what Abu Sufyan had said. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Muslims with him said: 'Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.' So Allah revealed concerning that: ﴿Those who responded to Allah and the Messenger﴾, the verses."

Musa ibn 'Uqba in his Maghazi and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from Ibn Shihab, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called the Muslims to Badr for the appointment with Abu Sufyan."

Then Satan made his allies among the people fear, so they went among the people frightening them and saying: "We have been informed that they have gathered against you a host like the night, hoping to fall upon you." The reports on this topic (p-257) are numerous, and the books of hadith and biography contain them.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "al-qarh" means wounds. Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Suddi that Abu Sufyan and his companions met a Bedouin and offered him a reward on condition that he inform the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions that they had gathered against them. He informed the Prophet (ﷺ) of this, so he and the Companions said: "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs." Then they returned from Hamra' al-Asad, and Allah revealed concerning them and the Bedouin: ﴿Those to whom the people said﴾, the verse.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Rafi' that this Bedouin was from Khuza'a. Traditions have been reported on the virtue of this phrase, namely ﴿Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs﴾, among which is what Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When you fall into a grave matter, say: 'Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.'" Ibn Kathir said after citing it: "This is a gharib hadith from this route."

Abu Nu'aym narrated from Shaddad ibn Aws, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "'Sufficient for me is Allah, and He is the best Disposer of affairs' is a security for every fearful one." Ibn Abi al-Dunya in al-Dhikr narrated from 'A'isha that the Prophet (ﷺ) whenever his distress intensified would wipe his hand over his head and beard, then exhale a deep sigh and say: "Sufficient for me is Allah, and He is the best Disposer of affairs."

Al-Bukhari and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs" was said by Ibrahim when he was thrown into the fire, and it was said by Muhammad when they said: ﴿Indeed the people have gathered against you﴾.

Ahmad, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i narrated from 'Awf ibn Malik that he related to them that "the Prophet (ﷺ) judged between two men, and the one against whom judgment was given said as he turned away: 'Sufficient for me is Allah, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Bring the man back to me.' So he was brought back and asked: 'What did you say?' He said: 'I said: Sufficient for me is Allah, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Allah blames helplessness, but upon you is cleverness (al-kays). So when a matter overcomes you, say: Sufficient for me is Allah, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.'"

Ahmad narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "How can I be at ease when the one with the horn has put the horn to his mouth, bent his forehead, and is listening for when he will be commanded to blow?" Then he commanded the Companions to say: "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs; in Allah we have put our trust." It is a good hadith.

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His statement: ﴿So they returned with blessing from Allah and bounty﴾, that he said: "The blessing was that they were safe, and the bounty was that a caravan passed by during the season, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) bought it, profited in wealth, and distributed it among his companions."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning the verse, who said: "The bounty is what they gained of trade and reward." Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Suddi, who said: "As for the blessing, it is well-being; as for the bounty, it is trade; and the evil is killing."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His statement: ﴿No harm touched them﴾, he said: "No one harmed them." ﴿And they followed the pleasure of Allah﴾, he said: "They obeyed Allah and His Messenger." Ibn Jarir narrated through al-'Awfi from him concerning His statement: ﴿That is only Satan frightening his allies﴾, he said: "He means: Satan frightens with his allies."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Malik, who said: "He magnifies his allies in your eyes." Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ikrima something like the statement of Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan: "That was only the frightening of Satan, and none fears Satan except the ally of Satan."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verses 169–176 (part 1 of 2):

When Allah, glorified is He, had explained that what befell the believers on the day of Uhud was a trial, so that the believer might be distinguished from the hypocrite, and the liar from the truthful, He here explained that whoever did not flee and was killed, for him is this honour and this blessing, and that this is something in which competitors vie, not something to be feared and guarded against, as those whom Allah quoted said: ﴿If they had been with us, they would not have died or been killed﴾ [Al 'Imran: 156], and they said: ﴿If they had obeyed us, they would not have been killed﴾ [Al 'Imran: 168]. So this sentence is a fresh statement to explain this meaning. The address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone. It was also read with the yaa' (ي) at the beginning, i.e., let no reckoner reckon (لا يَحْسَبَنَّ حاسِبٌ). The people of knowledge differed concerning the martyrs mentioned in this verse: who are they? It was said: they are the martyrs of Uhud; it was said: the martyrs of Badr; and it was said: the martyrs of Bi'r Ma'una. Even supposing it was revealed concerning a specific occasion, the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion. The meaning of the verse according to the majority is that they are alive with a real, established life.

Then they differed. Some of them say that their souls are returned to them in their graves, and so they enjoy bounties. Mujahid said: they are provided from the fruit of Paradise; that is, they find its fragrance while not being in it. Those other than the majority held that it is a metaphorical life, and the meaning is that they, in the judgment of Allah, deserve to be given bounty in Paradise. The correct view is the first, and there is no reason to resort to metaphor. The purified Sunnah has indeed come that their souls are in the crops of green birds, and that they are provided for and eat and enjoy themselves in Paradise. His saying "those who were killed" (الَّذِينَ قُتِلُوا) is the first object.

The reckoner is the Prophet (ﷺ), or everyone, as preceded. It was said: it is permissible that the relative pronoun be the subject of the verb, and the first object be omitted; that is, "Let not those who killed themselves think them dead," and this is an unnecessary strain; the meaning of the Qur'anic wording is in the utmost clarity and manifestness. His saying "Rather, they are alive" (بَلْ أحْياءٌ) is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "Rather, they are alive."

It was also read in the accusative, by implying a verb; that is, "Rather, I reckon them alive" (بَلْ أحْسَبُهم أحْياءً). His saying "with their Lord" (عِنْدَ رَبِّهِمْ) is either a second predicate, or an attribute of "alive," or in the position of an accusative as a circumstantial clause (حال). It was said: there is an omission in the speech, and the estimate is: "in the honour of their Lord" (عِنْدَ كَرامَةِ رَبِّهِمْ).

Sibawayh said: this is the "withness" of honour, not the "withness" of nearness. His saying "they are provided for" (يُرْزَقُونَ) may in its grammatical analysis bear the aspects that we mentioned in his saying "with their Lord." The provision here means the provision known in custom, according to what the majority go to; and for those other than the majority, what is meant is good praise. There is no basis that requires distorting the Arabic words in the Book of Allah, the Exalted, and carrying them to remote metaphors without a reason that requires that.

His saying "rejoicing" (فَرِحِينَ) is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "they are provided for," and "with what Allah has given them of His bounty" (بِما آتاهُمُ اللَّهُ مِن فَضْلِهِ) is connected to it. Ibn al-Sumayfa' read (فارِحِينَ), and both are dialects, like (الفَرِهِ والفارِهِ) and (الحَذِرِ والحاذِرِ).

What is meant by "what Allah has given them" is the honour that Allah bestowed on them by martyrdom, the life they came to be in, and the provision from Allah, glorified is He, that reaches them. "And they rejoice in those who have not yet joined them" (وَيَسْتَبْشِرُونَ بِالَّذِينَ لَمْ يَلْحَقُوا بِهِمْ) refers to their brothers among the fighters who had not been killed at that time.

So what is meant by "joining" here is that they had not joined them in being killed and martyred, but they will join them later. It was said: what is meant is that they had not joined them in merit, although they are people of merit in general. The waw in "and they rejoice" is conjunctive, joining it to "they are provided for"; that is, "they are provided for and they rejoice." It was said: what is meant by "their brothers" here is all the Muslim martyrs and others; because when they witnessed the reward of Allah and certainty arose in them of the truth of the religion of Islam, they rejoiced for all the people of Islam who are alive and have not died. This is stronger, because its meaning is wider and its benefit greater, and the wording allows it; indeed it is the apparent meaning, and Al-Zajjaj and Ibn Fawrak said so.

His saying "that there is no fear for them, nor do they grieve" (أَلَّا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْهِمْ ولا هم يَحْزَنُونَ) is a substitute for "those"; that is, they rejoice in this state attained by their brothers, namely that there is no fear upon them nor grief. "That" (أنْ) is the light form of the heavy one, and its noun is the omitted pronoun of the matter. He repeated "they rejoice" (يَسْتَبْشِرُونَ) to emphasize the first, and to show that the rejoicing is not merely for the absence of fear and grief, but for that together with the blessing and bounty of Allah.

The blessing (النِّعْمَةُ) is what Allah bestows upon His servants. The bounty (الفَضْلُ) is what He graces them with. It was said: the blessing is the reward, and the bounty is the excess; it was said: the blessing is Paradise, and the bounty is included in the blessing, mentioned after it for its emphasis; and it was said: the first rejoicing relates to the state of their brothers, and the second rejoicing to the state of themselves.

His saying "and that Allah does not waste the reward of the believers" (وأنَّ اللَّهَ لا يُضِيعُ أجْرَ المُؤْمِنِينَ). Al-Kisa'i read with a kasra on the hamza of "inna," and the rest read with a fatha. On the first reading, it is a parenthetical fresh statement. It indicates that Allah does not waste the reward of anything of the works of the believers; and the reading of Ibn Mas'ud supports it: "And Allah does not waste the reward of the believers."

On the second reading, the clause is conjoined to "bounty," included in what they rejoice in. His saying "those who responded" (الَّذِينَ اسْتَجابُوا) is an attribute of "the believers," or a substitute of them, or of "those who had not joined them," or it is a subject whose predicate is "for those of them who did good and were mindful of Allah is a great reward" as a whole clause, or it is in the accusative by way of praise. The explanation of "the wound" has already preceded.

His saying "those to whom the people said" (الَّذِينَ قالَ لَهُمُ النّاسُ): what is meant by "the people" here is Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud, as will come in its explanation; and it is permissible to apply the word "people" to him because he is of their kind. It was said: what is meant by "the people" is the caravan of 'Abd al-Qays who passed by Abu Sufyan; it was said: they are the hypocrites. What is meant by his saying "Indeed the people have gathered against you" (إنَّ النّاسَ قَدْ جَمَعُوا لَكُمْ) is Abu Sufyan and his companions. The pronoun in "so it increased them" (فَزادَهم) refers to the implied speech, "they said," or to what was said, which is "Indeed the people have gathered against you, so fear them," or to the speaker. The meaning is that they did not falter when they heard that, nor did they turn to it; rather, they sincerely devoted themselves to Allah and their tranquillity and certainty increased.

In this is evidence that faith increases and decreases. His saying "and they said: Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Guardian" (وقالُوا حَسْبُنا اللَّهُ ونِعْمَ الوَكِيلُ): "ḥasbu" is the verbal noun of "ḥasibahu," i.e., "sufficed him," and it is in the sense of the agent; that is, "muḥsib," in the sense of "sufficient."

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: The evidence that it is in the sense of "muḥsib" is that you say: "This is a man sufficient for you," so you describe an indefinite noun with it; because its genitive construction, being in the sense of the active participle, is not a true (construct) genitive, end of quote. "Al-Wakil" is the one to whom affairs are entrusted; that is, "the best one to whom our affair is entrusted," or "the Sufficient," or "the Guardian." The one specified by the praise is omitted; that is, "the best Guardian is Allah, glorified is He."

His saying "so they returned" (فانْقَلَبُوا) is conjoined to an omitted element; that is, "so they went out to them, and so they returned" (فَخَرَجُوا إلَيْهِمْ فانْقَلَبُوا). "With a blessing" (بِنِعْمَةٍ) is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause. The tanwin is for magnification; that is, they returned clothed in a great blessing, which is safety from their enemy, and well-being, "and bounty" (وفَضْلٍ), that is, a reward which Allah bestowed upon them. It was said: it is profit in trade; it was said: the blessing is specifically worldly benefits, and the bounty is the benefits of the Hereafter. Its explanation has already been mentioned shortly before in a manner suited to that context, because the discussion there was with the martyrs who had already reached the Abode of the Hereafter, whereas the discussion here is with the living.

His saying "no harm touched them" (لَمْ يَمْسَسْهم سُوءٌ) is in the position of an accusative as a circumstantial clause; that is, safe from any harm, no killing or wounding touched them, nor anything they feared; "and they followed the pleasure of Allah" (واتَّبَعُوا رِضْوانَ اللَّهِ) in what they do and what they leave, and among that is their going out for this expedition; "and Allah is Possessor of great bounty" (واللَّهُ ذُو فَضْلٍ عَظِيمٍ), whose extent cannot be measured and whose reach cannot be attained. Among His bounty upon them is making them firm, their going out to meet their enemy, and guiding them to say this statement, which brings every good and repels every evil.

His saying "That is only" (إنَّما ذَلِكم): that is, the one who discourages you, O believers, is Satan; he is the predicate of the demonstrative. It is permissible that "Satan" be an attribute of the demonstrative, and the predicate is his saying "he frightens his allies" (يُخَوِّفُ أوْلِياءَهُ). On the first, his saying "he frightens his allies" is a fresh or circumstantial clause. The apparent meaning is that what is meant here is Satan himself, in consideration of what proceeds from him of whispering that entails discouragement. It was said: what is meant is Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud when he said that statement to them; it was said: Abu Sufyan when the threat came from him to them. The meaning is that Satan frightens the believers with his allies, who are the disbelievers. It was also said that his saying "his allies" (أوْلِياءَهُ) is in the accusative by removing the preposition, i.e., "he frightens you with his allies" or "from his allies," as said by al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and Abu 'Ali al-Farisi.

Ibn al-Anbari refuted this, saying that frightening may transitively take two objects by itself, so there is no need to suppose a preposition. On the view of al-Farra' and those with him, the object of "he frightens" is omitted; that is, "he frightens you."

On the first view, the first object is omitted and the second is mentioned. It is permissible that the meaning be that Satan frightens his allies, who are the sitting-out hypocrites, so there is no omission. His saying "so do not fear them" (فَلا تَخافُوهُمْ): that is, his allies by whom Satan frightens you; or "do not fear the people" mentioned in His saying "Indeed the people have gathered against you." He, glorified is He, forbade them from fearing them, lest they shrink from the encounter and falter about going out, and commanded them to fear Him, glorified is He, saying: "and fear Me" (وخافُونِ), so do what I command you and abandon what I forbid you; for I am the one truly deserving of fear from Me and of vigilance in obeying My command and prohibition, since good and evil are in My hand. He restricted it with His saying "if you are believers" (إنْ كُنْتُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ), because faith requires that.

Al-Hakim transmitted it and authenticated it from Ibn 'Abbas who said: this verse, "And do not think of those who were killed in the way of Allah," was revealed concerning Hamza and his companions. Sa'id ibn Mansur and 'Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from Abu al-Duha that it was revealed concerning the dead of Uhud, and Hamza was among them.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud, Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When your brothers were struck at Uhud, Allah placed their souls in the crops of green birds which go to the rivers of Paradise and eat from its fruits, and take shelter in lamps of gold hanging in the shade of the Throne. When they found the goodness of their food and drink and the beauty of their resting place, they said: 'Would that our brothers knew what Allah has done for us!'" In another wording: "They said: 'Who will convey to our brothers that we are alive in Paradise, being provided for, lest they lose interest in jihad and shrink from war?' So Allah said: 'I will convey them on your behalf.' So Allah revealed these verses, 'And do not think of those who were killed...' and what follows."

Al-Tirmidhi transmitted and graded it good, and Ibn Majah, Ibn Khuzayma, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il transmitted from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah that his father asked Allah, glorified is He, to convey to those behind him what he was in, and this verse was revealed, and he was among the dead of Uhud.

It has been narrated through many channels that the occasion of the revelation of the verse was the dead of Uhud. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Anas that the occasion of the revelation of this verse was the dead of Bi'r Ma'una. In any case, the verse by the generality of its wording includes every martyr. It has been established in many hadiths in the Sahih and other collections that the souls of the martyrs are in the crops of green birds, and there has been established concerning the virtue of the martyrs what would be lengthy to enumerate and abundant to cite, of what is well known in the books of hadith.

Al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani narrated with a sahih chain from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "When the polytheists returned from Uhud, they said: 'You have not killed Muhammad, nor have you taken the captive women. What you did was wrong. Return!' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) heard of this, so he called the Muslims to set out, and they responded until they reached Hamra' al-Asad, or Bi'r Abi 'Utba (Sufyan was unsure which), and the polytheists said: 'He will return next year.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) turned back, and that expedition was counted as a ghazwa. Then Allah, glorified is He, revealed: ﴿Those who responded to Allah and the Messenger﴾, the verse."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from 'A'isha concerning His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Those who responded to Allah and the Messenger﴾, the verse, that she said to 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr: "O nephew, your two fathers were among them: al-Zubayr and Abu Bakr. When what befell the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) at Uhud befell him, the polytheists turned away from him, and he feared that they would return. He said: 'Who will go in pursuit of them?' Seventy of them responded, among them Abu Bakr and al-Zubayr."

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr ibn Muhammad ibn 'Amr ibn Hazm, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out to Hamra' al-Asad, while Abu Sufyan had resolved to return to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions. They said: 'We will return before we annihilate them, and we will attack their remnant.' He received word that the Prophet (ﷺ) had set out in pursuit of them with his companions, so this turned Abu Sufyan and his companions back. A caravan of 'Abd al-Qays passed by, and Abu Sufyan said to them: 'Convey to Muhammad that we have resolved to return against his companions to annihilate them.' When the caravan passed by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at Hamra' al-Asad, they informed him of what Abu Sufyan had said. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Muslims with him said: 'Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.' So Allah revealed concerning that: ﴿Those who responded to Allah and the Messenger﴾, the verses."

Musa ibn 'Uqba in his Maghazi and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from Ibn Shihab, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called the Muslims to Badr for the appointment with Abu Sufyan."

Then Satan made his allies among the people fear, so they went among the people frightening them and saying: "We have been informed that they have gathered against you a host like the night, hoping to fall upon you." The reports on this topic (p-257) are numerous, and the books of hadith and biography contain them.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "al-qarh" means wounds. Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Suddi that Abu Sufyan and his companions met a Bedouin and offered him a reward on condition that he inform the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions that they had gathered against them. He informed the Prophet (ﷺ) of this, so he and the Companions said: "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs." Then they returned from Hamra' al-Asad, and Allah revealed concerning them and the Bedouin: ﴿Those to whom the people said﴾, the verse.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Rafi' that this Bedouin was from Khuza'a. Traditions have been reported on the virtue of this phrase, namely ﴿Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs﴾, among which is what Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When you fall into a grave matter, say: 'Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.'" Ibn Kathir said after citing it: "This is a gharib hadith from this route."

Abu Nu'aym narrated from Shaddad ibn Aws, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "'Sufficient for me is Allah, and He is the best Disposer of affairs' is a security for every fearful one." Ibn Abi al-Dunya in al-Dhikr narrated from 'A'isha that the Prophet (ﷺ) whenever his distress intensified would wipe his hand over his head and beard, then exhale a deep sigh and say: "Sufficient for me is Allah, and He is the best Disposer of affairs."

Al-Bukhari and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs" was said by Ibrahim when he was thrown into the fire, and it was said by Muhammad when they said: ﴿Indeed the people have gathered against you﴾.

Ahmad, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i narrated from 'Awf ibn Malik that he related to them that "the Prophet (ﷺ) judged between two men, and the one against whom judgment was given said as he turned away: 'Sufficient for me is Allah, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Bring the man back to me.' So he was brought back and asked: 'What did you say?' He said: 'I said: Sufficient for me is Allah, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Allah blames helplessness, but upon you is cleverness (al-kays). So when a matter overcomes you, say: Sufficient for me is Allah, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.'"

Ahmad narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "How can I be at ease when the one with the horn has put the horn to his mouth, bent his forehead, and is listening for when he will be commanded to blow?" Then he commanded the Companions to say: "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs; in Allah we have put our trust." It is a good hadith.

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His statement: ﴿So they returned with blessing from Allah and bounty﴾, that he said: "The blessing was that they were safe, and the bounty was that a caravan passed by during the season, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) bought it, profited in wealth, and distributed it among his companions."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning the verse, who said: "The bounty is what they gained of trade and reward." Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Suddi, who said: "As for the blessing, it is well-being; as for the bounty, it is trade; and the evil is killing."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His statement: ﴿No harm touched them﴾, he said: "No one harmed them." ﴿And they followed the pleasure of Allah﴾, he said: "They obeyed Allah and His Messenger." Ibn Jarir narrated through al-'Awfi from him concerning His statement: ﴿That is only Satan frightening his allies﴾, he said: "He means: Satan frightens with his allies."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Malik, who said: "He magnifies his allies in your eyes." Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ikrima something like the statement of Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan: "That was only the frightening of Satan, and none fears Satan except the ally of Satan."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verses 169–176 (part 1 of 2):

When Allah, glorified is He, had explained that what befell the believers on the day of Uhud was a trial, so that the believer might be distinguished from the hypocrite, and the liar from the truthful, He here explained that whoever did not flee and was killed, for him is this honour and this blessing, and that this is something in which competitors vie, not something to be feared and guarded against, as those whom Allah quoted said: ﴿If they had been with us, they would not have died or been killed﴾ [Al 'Imran: 156], and they said: ﴿If they had obeyed us, they would not have been killed﴾ [Al 'Imran: 168]. So this sentence is a fresh statement to explain this meaning. The address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone. It was also read with the yaa' (ي) at the beginning, i.e., let no reckoner reckon (لا يَحْسَبَنَّ حاسِبٌ). The people of knowledge differed concerning the martyrs mentioned in this verse: who are they? It was said: they are the martyrs of Uhud; it was said: the martyrs of Badr; and it was said: the martyrs of Bi'r Ma'una. Even supposing it was revealed concerning a specific occasion, the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion. The meaning of the verse according to the majority is that they are alive with a real, established life.

Then they differed. Some of them say that their souls are returned to them in their graves, and so they enjoy bounties. Mujahid said: they are provided from the fruit of Paradise; that is, they find its fragrance while not being in it. Those other than the majority held that it is a metaphorical life, and the meaning is that they, in the judgment of Allah, deserve to be given bounty in Paradise. The correct view is the first, and there is no reason to resort to metaphor. The purified Sunnah has indeed come that their souls are in the crops of green birds, and that they are provided for and eat and enjoy themselves in Paradise. His saying "those who were killed" (الَّذِينَ قُتِلُوا) is the first object.

The reckoner is the Prophet (ﷺ), or everyone, as preceded. It was said: it is permissible that the relative pronoun be the subject of the verb, and the first object be omitted; that is, "Let not those who killed themselves think them dead," and this is an unnecessary strain; the meaning of the Qur'anic wording is in the utmost clarity and manifestness. His saying "Rather, they are alive" (بَلْ أحْياءٌ) is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "Rather, they are alive."

It was also read in the accusative, by implying a verb; that is, "Rather, I reckon them alive" (بَلْ أحْسَبُهم أحْياءً). His saying "with their Lord" (عِنْدَ رَبِّهِمْ) is either a second predicate, or an attribute of "alive," or in the position of an accusative as a circumstantial clause (حال). It was said: there is an omission in the speech, and the estimate is: "in the honour of their Lord" (عِنْدَ كَرامَةِ رَبِّهِمْ).

Sibawayh said: this is the "withness" of honour, not the "withness" of nearness. His saying "they are provided for" (يُرْزَقُونَ) may in its grammatical analysis bear the aspects that we mentioned in his saying "with their Lord." The provision here means the provision known in custom, according to what the majority go to; and for those other than the majority, what is meant is good praise. There is no basis that requires distorting the Arabic words in the Book of Allah, the Exalted, and carrying them to remote metaphors without a reason that requires that.

His saying "rejoicing" (فَرِحِينَ) is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "they are provided for," and "with what Allah has given them of His bounty" (بِما آتاهُمُ اللَّهُ مِن فَضْلِهِ) is connected to it. Ibn al-Sumayfa' read (فارِحِينَ), and both are dialects, like (الفَرِهِ والفارِهِ) and (الحَذِرِ والحاذِرِ).

What is meant by "what Allah has given them" is the honour that Allah bestowed on them by martyrdom, the life they came to be in, and the provision from Allah, glorified is He, that reaches them. "And they rejoice in those who have not yet joined them" (وَيَسْتَبْشِرُونَ بِالَّذِينَ لَمْ يَلْحَقُوا بِهِمْ) refers to their brothers among the fighters who had not been killed at that time.

So what is meant by "joining" here is that they had not joined them in being killed and martyred, but they will join them later. It was said: what is meant is that they had not joined them in merit, although they are people of merit in general. The waw in "and they rejoice" is conjunctive, joining it to "they are provided for"; that is, "they are provided for and they rejoice." It was said: what is meant by "their brothers" here is all the Muslim martyrs and others; because when they witnessed the reward of Allah and certainty arose in them of the truth of the religion of Islam, they rejoiced for all the people of Islam who are alive and have not died. This is stronger, because its meaning is wider and its benefit greater, and the wording allows it; indeed it is the apparent meaning, and Al-Zajjaj and Ibn Fawrak said so.

His saying "that there is no fear for them, nor do they grieve" (أَلَّا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْهِمْ ولا هم يَحْزَنُونَ) is a substitute for "those"; that is, they rejoice in this state attained by their brothers, namely that there is no fear upon them nor grief. "That" (أنْ) is the light form of the heavy one, and its noun is the omitted pronoun of the matter. He repeated "they rejoice" (يَسْتَبْشِرُونَ) to emphasize the first, and to show that the rejoicing is not merely for the absence of fear and grief, but for that together with the blessing and bounty of Allah.

The blessing (النِّعْمَةُ) is what Allah bestows upon His servants. The bounty (الفَضْلُ) is what He graces them with. It was said: the blessing is the reward, and the bounty is the excess; it was said: the blessing is Paradise, and the bounty is included in the blessing, mentioned after it for its emphasis; and it was said: the first rejoicing relates to the state of their brothers, and the second rejoicing to the state of themselves.

His saying "and that Allah does not waste the reward of the believers" (وأنَّ اللَّهَ لا يُضِيعُ أجْرَ المُؤْمِنِينَ). Al-Kisa'i read with a kasra on the hamza of "inna," and the rest read with a fatha. On the first reading, it is a parenthetical fresh statement. It indicates that Allah does not waste the reward of anything of the works of the believers; and the reading of Ibn Mas'ud supports it: "And Allah does not waste the reward of the believers."

On the second reading, the clause is conjoined to "bounty," included in what they rejoice in. His saying "those who responded" (الَّذِينَ اسْتَجابُوا) is an attribute of "the believers," or a substitute of them, or of "those who had not joined them," or it is a subject whose predicate is "for those of them who did good and were mindful of Allah is a great reward" as a whole clause, or it is in the accusative by way of praise. The explanation of "the wound" has already preceded.

His saying "those to whom the people said" (الَّذِينَ قالَ لَهُمُ النّاسُ): what is meant by "the people" here is Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud, as will come in its explanation; and it is permissible to apply the word "people" to him because he is of their kind. It was said: what is meant by "the people" is the caravan of 'Abd al-Qays who passed by Abu Sufyan; it was said: they are the hypocrites. What is meant by his saying "Indeed the people have gathered against you" (إنَّ النّاسَ قَدْ جَمَعُوا لَكُمْ) is Abu Sufyan and his companions. The pronoun in "so it increased them" (فَزادَهم) refers to the implied speech, "they said," or to what was said, which is "Indeed the people have gathered against you, so fear them," or to the speaker. The meaning is that they did not falter when they heard that, nor did they turn to it; rather, they sincerely devoted themselves to Allah and their tranquillity and certainty increased.

In this is evidence that faith increases and decreases. His saying "and they said: Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Guardian" (وقالُوا حَسْبُنا اللَّهُ ونِعْمَ الوَكِيلُ): "ḥasbu" is the verbal noun of "ḥasibahu," i.e., "sufficed him," and it is in the sense of the agent; that is, "muḥsib," in the sense of "sufficient."

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: The evidence that it is in the sense of "muḥsib" is that you say: "This is a man sufficient for you," so you describe an indefinite noun with it; because its genitive construction, being in the sense of the active participle, is not a true (construct) genitive, end of quote. "Al-Wakil" is the one to whom affairs are entrusted; that is, "the best one to whom our affair is entrusted," or "the Sufficient," or "the Guardian." The one specified by the praise is omitted; that is, "the best Guardian is Allah, glorified is He."

His saying "so they returned" (فانْقَلَبُوا) is conjoined to an omitted element; that is, "so they went out to them, and so they returned" (فَخَرَجُوا إلَيْهِمْ فانْقَلَبُوا). "With a blessing" (بِنِعْمَةٍ) is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause. The tanwin is for magnification; that is, they returned clothed in a great blessing, which is safety from their enemy, and well-being, "and bounty" (وفَضْلٍ), that is, a reward which Allah bestowed upon them. It was said: it is profit in trade; it was said: the blessing is specifically worldly benefits, and the bounty is the benefits of the Hereafter. Its explanation has already been mentioned shortly before in a manner suited to that context, because the discussion there was with the martyrs who had already reached the Abode of the Hereafter, whereas the discussion here is with the living.

His saying "no harm touched them" (لَمْ يَمْسَسْهم سُوءٌ) is in the position of an accusative as a circumstantial clause; that is, safe from any harm, no killing or wounding touched them, nor anything they feared; "and they followed the pleasure of Allah" (واتَّبَعُوا رِضْوانَ اللَّهِ) in what they do and what they leave, and among that is their going out for this expedition; "and Allah is Possessor of great bounty" (واللَّهُ ذُو فَضْلٍ عَظِيمٍ), whose extent cannot be measured and whose reach cannot be attained. Among His bounty upon them is making them firm, their going out to meet their enemy, and guiding them to say this statement, which brings every good and repels every evil.

His saying "That is only" (إنَّما ذَلِكم): that is, the one who discourages you, O believers, is Satan; he is the predicate of the demonstrative. It is permissible that "Satan" be an attribute of the demonstrative, and the predicate is his saying "he frightens his allies" (يُخَوِّفُ أوْلِياءَهُ). It was said: what is meant is Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud when he said that statement to them; it was said: Abu Sufyan when the threat came from him to them. The meaning is that Satan frightens the believers with his allies, who are the disbelievers. It was also said that his saying "his allies" (أوْلِياءَهُ) is in the accusative by removing the preposition, i.e., "he frightens you with his allies" or "from his allies," as said by al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and Abu 'Ali al-Farisi.
