On the first view, the first object is omitted and the second is mentioned. It is permissible that the meaning be that Satan frightens his allies, who are the sitting-out hypocrites, so there is no omission. His saying "so do not fear them" (فَلا تَخافُوهُمْ): that is, his allies by whom Satan frightens you; or "do not fear the people" mentioned in His saying "Indeed the people have gathered against you." He, glorified is He, forbade them from fearing them, lest they shrink from the encounter and falter about going out, and commanded them to fear Him, glorified is He, saying: "and fear Me" (وخافُونِ), so do what I command you and abandon what I forbid you; for I am the one truly deserving of fear from Me and of vigilance in obeying My command and prohibition, since good and evil are in My hand. He restricted it with His saying "if you are believers" (إنْ كُنْتُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ), because faith requires that.

Al-Hakim transmitted it and authenticated it from Ibn 'Abbas who said: this verse, "And do not think of those who were killed in the way of Allah," was revealed concerning Hamza and his companions. Sa'id ibn Mansur and 'Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from Abu al-Duha that it was revealed concerning the dead of Uhud, and Hamza was among them.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud, Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When your brothers were struck at Uhud, Allah placed their souls in the crops of green birds which go to the rivers of Paradise and eat from its fruits, and take shelter in lamps of gold hanging in the shade of the Throne. When they found the goodness of their food and drink and the beauty of their resting place, they said: 'Would that our brothers knew what Allah has done for us!'" In another wording: "They said: 'Who will convey to our brothers that we are alive in Paradise, being provided for, lest they lose interest in jihad and shrink from war?' So Allah said: 'I will convey them on your behalf.' So Allah revealed these verses, 'And do not think of those who were killed...' and what follows."

Al-Tirmidhi transmitted and graded it good, and Ibn Majah, Ibn Khuzayma, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il transmitted from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah that his father asked Allah, glorified is He, to convey to those behind him what he was in, and this verse was revealed, and he was among the dead of Uhud.

It has been narrated through many channels that the occasion of the revelation of the verse was the dead of Uhud. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Anas that the occasion of the revelation of this verse was the dead of Bi'r Ma'una. In any case, the verse by the generality of its wording includes every martyr. It has been established in many hadiths in the Sahih and other collections that the souls of the martyrs are in the crops of green birds, and there has been established concerning the virtue of the martyrs what would be lengthy to enumerate and abundant to cite, of what is well known in the books of hadith.

Al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani narrated with a sahih chain from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "When the polytheists returned from Uhud, they said: 'You have not killed Muhammad, nor have you taken the captive women. What you did was wrong. Return!' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) heard of this, so he called the Muslims to set out, and they responded until they reached Hamra' al-Asad, or Bi'r Abi 'Utba (Sufyan was unsure which), and the polytheists said: 'He will return next year.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) turned back, and that expedition was counted as a ghazwa. Then Allah, glorified is He, revealed: ﴿Those who responded to Allah and the Messenger﴾, the verse."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from 'A'isha concerning His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Those who responded to Allah and the Messenger﴾, the verse, that she said to 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr: "O nephew, your two fathers were among them: al-Zubayr and Abu Bakr. When what befell the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) at Uhud befell him, the polytheists turned away from him, and he feared that they would return. He said: 'Who will go in pursuit of them?' Seventy of them responded, among them Abu Bakr and al-Zubayr."

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr ibn Muhammad ibn 'Amr ibn Hazm, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out to Hamra' al-Asad, while Abu Sufyan had resolved to return to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions. They said: 'We will return before we annihilate them, and we will attack their remnant.' He received word that the Prophet (ﷺ) had set out in pursuit of them with his companions, so this turned Abu Sufyan and his companions back. A caravan of 'Abd al-Qays passed by, and Abu Sufyan said to them: 'Convey to Muhammad that we have resolved to return against his companions to annihilate them.' When the caravan passed by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at Hamra' al-Asad, they informed him of what Abu Sufyan had said. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Muslims with him said: 'Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.' So Allah revealed concerning that: ﴿Those who responded to Allah and the Messenger﴾, the verses."

Musa ibn 'Uqba in his Maghazi and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from Ibn Shihab, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called the Muslims to Badr for the appointment with Abu Sufyan."

Then Satan made his allies among the people fear, so they went among the people frightening them and saying: "We have been informed that they have gathered against you a host like the night, hoping to fall upon you." The reports on this topic (p-257) are numerous, and the books of hadith and biography contain them.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "al-qarh" means wounds. Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Suddi that Abu Sufyan and his companions met a Bedouin and offered him a reward on condition that he inform the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions that they had gathered against them. He informed the Prophet (ﷺ) of this, so he and the Companions said: "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs." Then they returned from Hamra' al-Asad, and Allah revealed concerning them and the Bedouin: ﴿Those to whom the people said﴾, the verse.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Rafi' that this Bedouin was from Khuza'a. Traditions have been reported on the virtue of this phrase, namely ﴿Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs﴾, among which is what Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When you fall into a grave matter, say: 'Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.'" Ibn Kathir said after citing it: "This is a gharib hadith from this route."

Abu Nu'aym narrated from Shaddad ibn Aws, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "'Sufficient for me is Allah, and He is the best Disposer of affairs' is a security for every fearful one." Ibn Abi al-Dunya in al-Dhikr narrated from 'A'isha that the Prophet (ﷺ) whenever his distress intensified would wipe his hand over his head and beard, then exhale a deep sigh and say: "Sufficient for me is Allah, and He is the best Disposer of affairs."

Al-Bukhari and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs" was said by Ibrahim when he was thrown into the fire, and it was said by Muhammad when they said: ﴿Indeed the people have gathered against you﴾.

Ahmad, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i narrated from 'Awf ibn Malik that he related to them that "the Prophet (ﷺ) judged between two men, and the one against whom judgment was given said as he turned away: 'Sufficient for me is Allah, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Bring the man back to me.' So he was brought back and asked: 'What did you say?' He said: 'I said: Sufficient for me is Allah, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Allah blames helplessness, but upon you is cleverness (al-kays). So when a matter overcomes you, say: Sufficient for me is Allah, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.'"

Ahmad narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "How can I be at ease when the one with the horn has put the horn to his mouth, bent his forehead, and is listening for when he will be commanded to blow?" Then he commanded the Companions to say: "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs; in Allah we have put our trust." It is a good hadith.

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His statement: ﴿So they returned with blessing from Allah and bounty﴾, that he said: "The blessing was that they were safe, and the bounty was that a caravan passed by during the season, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) bought it, profited in wealth, and distributed it among his companions."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning the verse, who said: "The bounty is what they gained of trade and reward." Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Suddi, who said: "As for the blessing, it is well-being; as for the bounty, it is trade; and the evil is killing."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His statement: ﴿No harm touched them﴾, he said: "No one harmed them." ﴿And they followed the pleasure of Allah﴾, he said: "They obeyed Allah and His Messenger." Ibn Jarir narrated through al-'Awfi from him concerning His statement: ﴿That is only Satan frightening his allies﴾, he said: "He means: Satan frightens with his allies."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Malik, who said: "He magnifies his allies in your eyes." Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ikrima something like the statement of Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan: "That was only the frightening of Satan, and none fears Satan except the ally of Satan."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verses 169–176 (part 1 of 2):

When Allah, glorified is He, had explained that what befell the believers on the day of Uhud was a trial, so that the believer might be distinguished from the hypocrite, and the liar from the truthful, He here explained that whoever did not flee and was killed, for him is this honour and this blessing, and that this is something in which competitors vie, not something to be feared and guarded against, as those whom Allah quoted said: ﴿If they had been with us, they would not have died or been killed﴾ [Al 'Imran: 156], and they said: ﴿If they had obeyed us, they would not have been killed﴾ [Al 'Imran: 168]. So this sentence is a fresh statement to explain this meaning. The address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone. It was also read with the yaa' (ي) at the beginning, i.e., let no reckoner reckon (لا يَحْسَبَنَّ حاسِبٌ). The people of knowledge differed concerning the martyrs mentioned in this verse: who are they? It was said: they are the martyrs of Uhud; it was said: the martyrs of Badr; and it was said: the martyrs of Bi'r Ma'una. Even supposing it was revealed concerning a specific occasion, the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion. The meaning of the verse according to the majority is that they are alive with a real, established life.

Then they differed. Some of them say that their souls are returned to them in their graves, and so they enjoy bounties. Mujahid said: they are provided from the fruit of Paradise; that is, they find its fragrance while not being in it. Those other than the majority held that it is a metaphorical life, and the meaning is that they, in the judgment of Allah, deserve to be given bounty in Paradise. The correct view is the first, and there is no reason to resort to metaphor. The purified Sunnah has indeed come that their souls are in the crops of green birds, and that they are provided for and eat and enjoy themselves in Paradise. His saying "those who were killed" (الَّذِينَ قُتِلُوا) is the first object.

The reckoner is the Prophet (ﷺ), or everyone, as preceded. It was said: it is permissible that the relative pronoun be the subject of the verb, and the first object be omitted; that is, "Let not those who killed themselves think them dead," and this is an unnecessary strain; the meaning of the Qur'anic wording is in the utmost clarity and manifestness. His saying "Rather, they are alive" (بَلْ أحْياءٌ) is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "Rather, they are alive."

It was also read in the accusative, by implying a verb; that is, "Rather, I reckon them alive" (بَلْ أحْسَبُهم أحْياءً). His saying "with their Lord" (عِنْدَ رَبِّهِمْ) is either a second predicate, or an attribute of "alive," or in the position of an accusative as a circumstantial clause (حال). It was said: there is an omission in the speech, and the estimate is: "in the honour of their Lord" (عِنْدَ كَرامَةِ رَبِّهِمْ).

Sibawayh said: this is the "withness" of honour, not the "withness" of nearness. His saying "they are provided for" (يُرْزَقُونَ) may in its grammatical analysis bear the aspects that we mentioned in his saying "with their Lord." The provision here means the provision known in custom, according to what the majority go to; and for those other than the majority, what is meant is good praise. There is no basis that requires distorting the Arabic words in the Book of Allah, the Exalted, and carrying them to remote metaphors without a reason that requires that.

His saying "rejoicing" (فَرِحِينَ) is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "they are provided for," and "with what Allah has given them of His bounty" (بِما آتاهُمُ اللَّهُ مِن فَضْلِهِ) is connected to it. Ibn al-Sumayfa' read (فارِحِينَ), and both are dialects, like (الفَرِهِ والفارِهِ) and (الحَذِرِ والحاذِرِ).

What is meant by "what Allah has given them" is the honour that Allah bestowed on them by martyrdom, the life they came to be in, and the provision from Allah, glorified is He, that reaches them. "And they rejoice in those who have not yet joined them" (وَيَسْتَبْشِرُونَ بِالَّذِينَ لَمْ يَلْحَقُوا بِهِمْ) refers to their brothers among the fighters who had not been killed at that time.

So what is meant by "joining" here is that they had not joined them in being killed and martyred, but they will join them later. It was said: what is meant is that they had not joined them in merit, although they are people of merit in general. The waw in "and they rejoice" is conjunctive, joining it to "they are provided for"; that is, "they are provided for and they rejoice." It was said: what is meant by "their brothers" here is all the Muslim martyrs and others; because when they witnessed the reward of Allah and certainty arose in them of the truth of the religion of Islam, they rejoiced for all the people of Islam who are alive and have not died. This is stronger, because its meaning is wider and its benefit greater, and the wording allows it; indeed it is the apparent meaning, and Al-Zajjaj and Ibn Fawrak said so.

His saying "that there is no fear for them, nor do they grieve" (أَلَّا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْهِمْ ولا هم يَحْزَنُونَ) is a substitute for "those"; that is, they rejoice in this state attained by their brothers, namely that there is no fear upon them nor grief. "That" (أنْ) is the light form of the heavy one, and its noun is the omitted pronoun of the matter. He repeated "they rejoice" (يَسْتَبْشِرُونَ) to emphasize the first, and to show that the rejoicing is not merely for the absence of fear and grief, but for that together with the blessing and bounty of Allah.

The blessing (النِّعْمَةُ) is what Allah bestows upon His servants. The bounty (الفَضْلُ) is what He graces them with. It was said: the blessing is the reward, and the bounty is the excess; it was said: the blessing is Paradise, and the bounty is included in the blessing, mentioned after it for its emphasis; and it was said: the first rejoicing relates to the state of their brothers, and the second rejoicing to the state of themselves.

His saying "and that Allah does not waste the reward of the believers" (وأنَّ اللَّهَ لا يُضِيعُ أجْرَ المُؤْمِنِينَ). Al-Kisa'i read with a kasra on the hamza of "inna," and the rest read with a fatha. On the first reading, it is a parenthetical fresh statement. It indicates that Allah does not waste the reward of anything of the works of the believers; and the reading of Ibn Mas'ud supports it: "And Allah does not waste the reward of the believers."

On the second reading, the clause is conjoined to "bounty," included in what they rejoice in. His saying "those who responded" (الَّذِينَ اسْتَجابُوا) is an attribute of "the believers," or a substitute of them, or of "those who had not joined them," or it is a subject whose predicate is "for those of them who did good and were mindful of Allah is a great reward" as a whole clause, or it is in the accusative by way of praise. The explanation of "the wound" has already preceded.

His saying "those to whom the people said" (الَّذِينَ قالَ لَهُمُ النّاسُ): what is meant by "the people" here is Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud, as will come in its explanation; and it is permissible to apply the word "people" to him because he is of their kind. It was said: what is meant by "the people" is the caravan of 'Abd al-Qays who passed by Abu Sufyan; it was said: they are the hypocrites. What is meant by his saying "Indeed the people have gathered against you" (إنَّ النّاسَ قَدْ جَمَعُوا لَكُمْ) is Abu Sufyan and his companions. The pronoun in "so it increased them" (فَزادَهم) refers to the implied speech, "they said," or to what was said, which is "Indeed the people have gathered against you, so fear them," or to the speaker. The meaning is that they did not falter when they heard that, nor did they turn to it; rather, they sincerely devoted themselves to Allah and their tranquillity and certainty increased.

In this is evidence that faith increases and decreases. His saying "and they said: Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Guardian" (وقالُوا حَسْبُنا اللَّهُ ونِعْمَ الوَكِيلُ): "ḥasbu" is the verbal noun of "ḥasibahu," i.e., "sufficed him," and it is in the sense of the agent; that is, "muḥsib," in the sense of "sufficient."

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: The evidence that it is in the sense of "muḥsib" is that you say: "This is a man sufficient for you," so you describe an indefinite noun with it; because its genitive construction, being in the sense of the active participle, is not a true (construct) genitive, end of quote. "Al-Wakil" is the one to whom affairs are entrusted; that is, "the best one to whom our affair is entrusted," or "the Sufficient," or "the Guardian." The one specified by the praise is omitted; that is, "the best Guardian is Allah, glorified is He."

His saying "so they returned" (فانْقَلَبُوا) is conjoined to an omitted element; that is, "so they went out to them, and so they returned" (فَخَرَجُوا إلَيْهِمْ فانْقَلَبُوا). "With a blessing" (بِنِعْمَةٍ) is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause. The tanwin is for magnification; that is, they returned clothed in a great blessing, which is safety from their enemy, and well-being, "and bounty" (وفَضْلٍ), that is, a reward which Allah bestowed upon them. It was said: it is profit in trade; it was said: the blessing is specifically worldly benefits, and the bounty is the benefits of the Hereafter. Its explanation has already been mentioned shortly before in a manner suited to that context, because the discussion there was with the martyrs who had already reached the Abode of the Hereafter, whereas the discussion here is with the living.

His saying "no harm touched them" (لَمْ يَمْسَسْهم سُوءٌ) is in the position of an accusative as a circumstantial clause; that is, safe from any harm, no killing or wounding touched them, nor anything they feared; "and they followed the pleasure of Allah" (واتَّبَعُوا رِضْوانَ اللَّهِ) in what they do and what they leave, and among that is their going out for this expedition; "and Allah is Possessor of great bounty" (واللَّهُ ذُو فَضْلٍ عَظِيمٍ), whose extent cannot be measured and whose reach cannot be attained. Among His bounty upon them is making them firm, their going out to meet their enemy, and guiding them to say this statement, which brings every good and repels every evil.

His saying "That is only" (إنَّما ذَلِكم): that is, the one who discourages you, O believers, is Satan; he is the predicate of the demonstrative. It is permissible that "Satan" be an attribute of the demonstrative, and the predicate is his saying "he frightens his allies" (يُخَوِّفُ أوْلِياءَهُ). On the first, his saying "he frightens his allies" is a fresh or circumstantial clause. The apparent meaning is that what is meant here is Satan himself, in consideration of what proceeds from him of whispering that entails discouragement. It was said: what is meant is Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud when he said that statement to them; it was said: Abu Sufyan when the threat came from him to them. The meaning is that Satan frightens the believers with his allies, who are the disbelievers. It was also said that his saying "his allies" (أوْلِياءَهُ) is in the accusative by removing the preposition, i.e., "he frightens you with his allies" or "from his allies," as said by al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and Abu 'Ali al-Farisi.

Ibn al-Anbari refuted this, saying that frightening may transitively take two objects by itself, so there is no need to suppose a preposition. On the view of al-Farra' and those with him, the object of "he frightens" is omitted; that is, "he frightens you."

On the first view, the first object is omitted and the second is mentioned. It is permissible that the meaning be that Satan frightens his allies, who are the sitting-out hypocrites, so there is no omission. His saying "so do not fear them" (فَلا تَخافُوهُمْ): that is, his allies by whom Satan frightens you; or "do not fear the people" mentioned in His saying "Indeed the people have gathered against you." He, glorified is He, forbade them from fearing them, lest they shrink from the encounter and falter about going out, and commanded them to fear Him, glorified is He, saying: "and fear Me" (وخافُونِ), so do what I command you and abandon what I forbid you; for I am the one truly deserving of fear from Me and of vigilance in obeying My command and prohibition, since good and evil are in My hand. He restricted it with His saying "if you are believers" (إنْ كُنْتُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ), because faith requires that.

Al-Hakim transmitted it and authenticated it from Ibn 'Abbas who said: this verse, "And do not think of those who were killed in the way of Allah," was revealed concerning Hamza and his companions. Sa'id ibn Mansur and 'Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from Abu al-Duha that it was revealed concerning the dead of Uhud, and Hamza was among them.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud, Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When your brothers were struck at Uhud, Allah placed their souls in the crops of green birds which go to the rivers of Paradise and eat from its fruits, and take shelter in lamps of gold hanging in the shade of the Throne. When they found the goodness of their food and drink and the beauty of their resting place, they said: 'Would that our brothers knew what Allah has done for us!'" In another wording: "They said: 'Who will convey to our brothers that we are alive in Paradise, being provided for, lest they lose interest in jihad and shrink from war?' So Allah said: 'I will convey them on your behalf.' So Allah revealed these verses, 'And do not think of those who were killed...' and what follows."

Al-Tirmidhi transmitted and graded it good, and Ibn Majah, Ibn Khuzayma, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il transmitted from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah that his father asked Allah, glorified is He, to convey to those behind him what he was in, and this verse was revealed, and he was among the dead of Uhud.

It has been narrated through many channels that the occasion of the revelation of the verse was the dead of Uhud. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Anas that the occasion of the revelation of this verse was the dead of Bi'r Ma'una. In any case, the verse by the generality of its wording includes every martyr. It has been established in many hadiths in the Sahih and other collections that the souls of the martyrs are in the crops of green birds, and there has been established concerning the virtue of the martyrs what would be lengthy to enumerate and abundant to cite, of what is well known in the books of hadith.

Al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani narrated with a sahih chain from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "When the polytheists returned from Uhud, they said: 'You have not killed Muhammad, nor have you taken the captive women. What you did was wrong. Return!' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) heard of this, so he called the Muslims to set out, and they responded until they reached Hamra' al-Asad, or Bi'r Abi 'Utba (Sufyan was unsure which), and the polytheists said: 'He will return next year.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) turned back, and that expedition was counted as a ghazwa. Then Allah, glorified is He, revealed: ﴿Those who responded to Allah and the Messenger﴾, the verse."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from 'A'isha concerning His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Those who responded to Allah and the Messenger﴾, the verse, that she said to 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr: "O nephew, your two fathers were among them: al-Zubayr and Abu Bakr. When what befell the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) at Uhud befell him, the polytheists turned away from him, and he feared that they would return. He said: 'Who will go in pursuit of them?' Seventy of them responded, among them Abu Bakr and al-Zubayr."

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr ibn Muhammad ibn 'Amr ibn Hazm, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out to Hamra' al-Asad, while Abu Sufyan had resolved to return to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions. They said: 'We will return before we annihilate them, and we will attack their remnant.' He received word that the Prophet (ﷺ) had set out in pursuit of them with his companions, so this turned Abu Sufyan and his companions back. A caravan of 'Abd al-Qays passed by, and Abu Sufyan said to them: 'Convey to Muhammad that we have resolved to return against his companions to annihilate them.' When the caravan passed by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at Hamra' al-Asad, they informed him of what Abu Sufyan had said. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Muslims with him said: 'Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.' So Allah revealed concerning that: ﴿Those who responded to Allah and the Messenger﴾, the verses."

Musa ibn 'Uqba in his Maghazi and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from Ibn Shihab, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called the Muslims to Badr for the appointment with Abu Sufyan."

Then Satan made his allies among the people fear, so they went among the people frightening them and saying: "We have been informed that they have gathered against you a host like the night, hoping to fall upon you." The reports on this topic (p-257) are numerous, and the books of hadith and biography contain them.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "al-qarh" means wounds. Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Suddi that Abu Sufyan and his companions met a Bedouin and offered him a reward on condition that he inform the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions that they had gathered against them. He informed the Prophet (ﷺ) of this, so he and the Companions said: "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs." Then they returned from Hamra' al-Asad, and Allah revealed concerning them and the Bedouin: ﴿Those to whom the people said﴾, the verse.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Rafi' that this Bedouin was from Khuza'a. Traditions have been reported on the virtue of this phrase, namely ﴿Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs﴾, among which is what Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When you fall into a grave matter, say: 'Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.'" Ibn Kathir said after citing it: "This is a gharib hadith from this route."

Abu Nu'aym narrated from Shaddad ibn Aws, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "'Sufficient for me is Allah, and He is the best Disposer of affairs' is a security for every fearful one." Ibn Abi al-Dunya in al-Dhikr narrated from 'A'isha that the Prophet (ﷺ) whenever his distress intensified would wipe his hand over his head and beard, then exhale a deep sigh and say: "Sufficient for me is Allah, and He is the best Disposer of affairs."

Al-Bukhari and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs" was said by Ibrahim when he was thrown into the fire, and it was said by Muhammad when they said: ﴿Indeed the people have gathered against you﴾.

Ahmad, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i narrated from 'Awf ibn Malik that he related to them that "the Prophet (ﷺ) judged between two men, and the one against whom judgment was given said as he turned away: 'Sufficient for me is Allah, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Bring the man back to me.' So he was brought back and asked: 'What did you say?' He said: 'I said: Sufficient for me is Allah, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Allah blames helplessness, but upon you is cleverness (al-kays). So when a matter overcomes you, say: Sufficient for me is Allah, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.'"

Ahmad narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "How can I be at ease when the one with the horn has put the horn to his mouth, bent his forehead, and is listening for when he will be commanded to blow?" Then he commanded the Companions to say: "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs; in Allah we have put our trust." It is a good hadith.

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His statement: ﴿So they returned with blessing from Allah and bounty﴾, that he said: "The blessing was that they were safe, and the bounty was that a caravan passed by during the season, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) bought it, profited in wealth, and distributed it among his companions."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning the verse, who said: "The bounty is what they gained of trade and reward." Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Suddi, who said: "As for the blessing, it is well-being; as for the bounty, it is trade; and the evil is killing."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His statement: ﴿No harm touched them﴾, he said: "No one harmed them." ﴿And they followed the pleasure of Allah﴾, he said: "They obeyed Allah and His Messenger." Ibn Jarir narrated through al-'Awfi from him concerning His statement: ﴿That is only Satan frightening his allies﴾, he said: "He means: Satan frightens with his allies."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Malik, who said: "He magnifies his allies in your eyes." Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ikrima something like the statement of Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan: "That was only the frightening of Satan, and none fears Satan except the ally of Satan."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verses 177–180 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Let them not grieve you﴾ (wa-la yahzunka). Nafi' read it as yuhzinka (with a damma on the yā' and a kasra on the zāy). Ibn Muhaysin read it with a damma on both the yā' and the zāy. The rest read it as yahzunka (with a fatha on the yā' and a damma on the zāy). Both forms are acceptable: one says ḥazanani al-amr and aḥzananī al-amr. The first is more eloquent.

Talha read yusri'ūna (﴿those who hasten﴾). It was said: they are people who apostatized, and the Prophet (ﷺ) grieved over this. So God, glory be to Him, consoled him and forbade him from grieving. He gave the reason: they will never harm God in the least, but they harm only themselves, since they will have no share in the Hereafter and they will have a great punishment. It was also said that they are the disbelievers of Quraysh, and it was said that they are the hypocrites (munafiqun), and it was said that it is general to all disbelievers. Al-Qushayri said: grieving over a disbeliever's unbelief is an act of obedience, but the Prophet (ﷺ) used to exceed in grieving, so he was forbidden from it, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So let not your soul expire in regret over them﴾ [Fatir: 8], and ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over their footsteps if they do not believe in this message﴾ [al-Kahf: 6].

The verb al-sari'ūn (those who hasten) is construed with fī rather than ilā, to indicate that they are settled in it and persistent in engaging with it. Similarly: yusari'ūna fī al-khayrāt (they hasten to good deeds).

His saying: ﴿Indeed, they will never harm God at all﴾ is the reason for the prohibition. The meaning is that their disbelief does not diminish anything from the dominion of God, glory be to Him. It was said that what is meant is that they will never harm His friends. It is also possible that what is meant is that they will never harm His religion which He legislated for His servants. The word shay'an (at all) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), i.e., "any harm." It was said that it is in the accusative by removing the preposition, i.e., "by anything." The word al-ḥaẓẓ means "share." Abu Zayd said: a man is called ḥaẓīẓ if he has a share of provision. The meaning is that God wills not to give them any share in Paradise, or any share of reward. The future form is used to indicate the continuity and persistence of this will. ﴿And for them is a great punishment﴾ because of their hastening into disbelief. Thus the harm of their disbelief returns upon them, bringing about for them the absence of any share in the Hereafter and their destination in the great punishment.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who have purchased disbelief in exchange for faith﴾, meaning they substituted disbelief for faith. The explanation of this metaphor has already been given. ﴿They will never harm God at all﴾ has the same meaning as the first and is for emphasis of what preceded it. It was said that the first is specific to the hypocrites and the second includes all disbelievers, but the first is better.

His saying: (p-258) ﴿And let not those who disbelieve think that Our giving them respite is good for them﴾. Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and others read yaḥsabanna with the yā' (third person), and Hamza read it with the tā' (second person). The meaning according to the first reading: let not the disbelievers think that We give them respite with long life and abundant living, or with the victory they gained at the Battle of Uhud, ﴿is good for themselves﴾. The matter is not so; rather ﴿We only give them respite so that they may increase in sin, and for them is a humiliating punishment.﴾

According to the second reading: O Muhammad, do not think that the respite given to those who disbelieve, with what has been mentioned, is good for them. Rather, it is an evil that befalls them and descends upon them, namely that the respite We grant them is so that they increase in sin.

So in the first reading, the relative pronoun (alladhīna) is the subject of the verb, and "innamā nuṃlī" and what follows it fill the role of the two objects of the verb of thinking (ḥusbān) according to Sibawayh, or fill the role of one of them, the other being omitted, according to al-Akhfash.

As for the second reading, al-Zajjaj said that the relative pronoun is the first object, and "innamā" with what follows is an apposition (badal) to the relative pronoun, filling the role of both objects. He said that "innamā" with what follows cannot be the second object, because in this construction the second object is the first in meaning.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: if this were correct, it would be read as khayran in the accusative, because it would become an apposition to alladhīna kafarū, as if he had said: "Let not the respite of those who disbelieve be good." Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said that the verb is understood to be repeated, as if he had said: "And let not those who disbelieve think, and let not you think that 'innamā nuṃlī' is good for them," and so it fills the role of the two objects.

In al-Kashshaf it says: If you say, "How is an apposition valid when only one of the two objects is mentioned, and it is not permissible to limit the verb of thinking to one object?" I say: it is valid because the reliance is on the apposition, and the appositioned noun is in the position of what has been set aside. Do you not see that you say, "I placed your goods, some of them on top of others," even though your silence about your goods is not possible? End quote.

Yahya ibn Wathhab read innamā nuṃlī with a kasra on the inna in both places. This is a weak reading from the standpoint of Arabic grammar.

His saying: ﴿We only give them respite so that they may increase in sin﴾ is a new sentence (jumla musta'anafa) explaining the reason for the respite granted to the disbelievers. The majority of scholars (al-jumhur) have argued from this verse against what the Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school) say, because He, glory be to Him, informed that He lengthens the lives of the disbelievers and makes their living abundant so that they may increase in sin.

Abu Hatim said: I heard al-Akhfash mention a kasra on the first innamā nuṃlī and a fatha on the second, and he would argue with this on behalf of the people of qadar (the Qadariyya, those who affirm human free will) because he was one of them, and he would make this its construction: "Let not those who disbelieve think that We give them respite so that they may increase in sin; We give them respite, it is good for themselves." Al-Kashshaf says: increase in sin is a cause (ʿilla), and not every cause is an accident (ʿaraḍ). Do you not see that you say, "I sat out of the military expedition because of incapacity and poverty, and I left the town for fear of evil," and nothing befalls you; rather these are causes and reasons.

His saying: ﴿God would not leave the believers in the state you are in until He distinguishes the wicked from the good﴾. This is a new sentence. According to the majority of exegetes (mufassirun), the address is to the disbelievers and hypocrites, meaning: God would not leave the believers in the state you are in of disbelief and hypocrisy. It was said: the address is to the believers and hypocrites, meaning: God would not leave you in the mixed state you are in until He distinguishes some of you from others. It was said: the address is to the polytheists. What is meant by "the believers" is those in the loins and wombs, i.e., God would not leave your children in the state you are in until He separates them from you. It was said: the address is to the believers, meaning: God would not leave you, O company of believers, in the mixing with the hypocrites in which you are, until He distinguishes between you. On this view, and on the second view, there is iltifat (a shift of grammatical person) in the speech.

It is read yumayyiza (with doubled mīm) as the intensive form of the basic verb. From māza al-shay' yamīzuhu mayzan, when one separates between two things. If the things are multiple, it is said mayyazahu tamyīzan. ﴿Nor would God inform you of the unseen﴾ until you distinguish between the good and the wicked, for He is the one who alone possesses knowledge of the unseen. He does not disclose His unseen to anyone except whom He approves of among His messengers, whom He chooses, and then informs him of some of His unseen, so that he may distinguish among you. This is like what happened from our Prophet (ﷺ), namely his identifying many hypocrites, for that was by God's teaching him, not by his knowing the unseen. It was said the meaning is: ﴿God would not inform you of the unseen﴾ concerning who deserves prophethood, so that revelation would be by your choice. ﴿But God chooses﴾, i.e., selects, ﴿from among His messengers whom He wills.﴾

His saying: ﴿So believe in God and His messengers﴾, i.e., do the faith that is required of you, and leave off occupying yourselves with what is not your concern, such as seeking knowledge of God's unseen, glory be to Him. If you believe in what has been mentioned and are mindful of God, then in exchange for that you will have a great reward, whose worth cannot be known and whose reality cannot be reached.

His saying: ﴿And let not those who withhold what God has given them of His bounty think that it is good for them﴾. The relative pronoun is in the nominative position as the subject of the verb according to the reading of the one who reads with the yā'. The first object is omitted, i.e., "let not the stingy think their stinginess is good for them." This was said by al-Khalil, Sibawayh and al-Farra'. They said: it was omitted because of the indication of yabkhalūna (they withhold). Among this is the poet's saying:

When the foolish one is forbidden, he rushes toward it and opposes, and the foolish one is in opposition.

That is, he rushes toward foolishness, so "the foolish one" indicates "foolishness."

As for the reading of the one who reads with the tā' (second person), the verb is attributed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the first object is omitted, i.e., "O Muhammad, do not think that the stinginess of those who withhold is good for them."

Al-Zajjaj said: it is like ﴿and ask the village﴾, and the mentioned pronoun is the pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl). Al-Mubarrad said: the sīn in His saying ﴿They will be encircled with what they withheld﴾ is the sīn of threat (sīn al-waʿīd), and this sentence explains the meaning of His saying ﴿Rather, it is evil for them.﴾ It was said: the meaning of encircling here is that what they withheld of wealth will become a collar of fire around their necks. It was said: its meaning is that they will bear the punishment for what they withheld, and it is from ṭāqa (capacity) and not from taṭwīq (encircling). It was said the meaning is that they will be bound to their deeds as a collar binds the neck. One says: "So-and-so encircled his deed with the collar of a dove," i.e., he was made to bear the recompense of his deed. It was also said that wealth whose zakat has not been paid is depicted for its owner as a bald venomous serpent, and it is placed around his neck, as is reported as a hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Qurtubi said: stinginess in the language is that a person withholds a right that is obligatory. As for one who withholds what is not obligatory upon him, he is not stingy.

His saying: ﴿And to God belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth﴾, i.e., to Him alone and not to anyone else, as the placing of the word first indicates. The meaning: to Him belongs what is in them, of which their inhabitants inherit. So what is wrong with them that they withhold that and do not spend it, when it belongs to God, glory be to Him, not to them? (p-259) Rather, it was in their possession as a temporary loan that will be reclaimed. Similar to this verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We inherit the earth and whoever is upon it﴾ [Maryam: 40], and His saying: ﴿And spend of that in which He has made you successors﴾ [al-Hadid: 7]. Inheritance (mirath) in its original sense is what passes from one owner to another, and was not owned by that other before its transfer to him by inheritance. It is known that God, glory be to Him, is the true owner of all His creation.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid regarding ﴿Indeed, those who have purchased disbelief in exchange for faith﴾ that he said: they are the hypocrites.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: No soul, whether righteous or wicked, but death is better for it than life. If it is righteous, God has said: ﴿And what is with God is better for the righteous﴾ [Al 'Imran: 798]. And if it is wicked, He has said: ﴿And let not those who disbelieve think...﴾ the verse.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Abu al-Darda' something similar. Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b something similar.

'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Abu Barza also something similar. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi that he said: They said, "If Muhammad is truthful, let him inform us of who among us believes in him and who disbelieves." So God revealed ﴿God would not leave the believers...﴾ the verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: He distinguishes the people of happiness from the people of misery. 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada that he said: He distinguishes between them in jihad and emigration. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan regarding His saying: ﴿Nor would God inform you of the unseen﴾ that he said: None is informed of the unseen except a messenger. 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid regarding ﴿But God chooses﴾ that he said: He singles out.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Malik that he said: He selects. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And let not those who withhold...﴾ that he said: They are the People of the Book who withheld from making it clear to the people.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid that he said: They are the Jews. Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Suddi that he said: They withheld from spending it in the way of God and did not pay its zakat.

Al-Bukhari narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever Allah gives wealth but he does not pay its zakat, it will be depicted for him on the Day of Resurrection as a bald venomous male serpent with two black spots over its eyes. It will be hung around his neck, and it will seize him by his two cheeks, that is, his jaws, and say: 'I am your wealth, I am your treasure.'" Then he recited this verse.

This meaning has been reported in many hadiths from a group of the Companions, who trace them back to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verses 177–180 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Let them not grieve you﴾ (wa-la yahzunka). Nafi' read it as yuhzinka (with a damma on the yā' and a kasra on the zāy). Ibn Muhaysin read it with a damma on both the yā' and the zāy. The rest read it as yahzunka (with a fatha on the yā' and a damma on the zāy). Both forms are acceptable: one says ḥazanani al-amr and aḥzananī al-amr. The first is more eloquent.

Talha read yusri'ūna (﴿those who hasten﴾). It was said: they are people who apostatized, and the Prophet (ﷺ) grieved over this. So God, glory be to Him, consoled him and forbade him from grieving. He gave the reason: they will never harm God in the least, but they harm only themselves, since they will have no share in the Hereafter and they will have a great punishment. It was also said that they are the disbelievers of Quraysh, and it was said that they are the hypocrites (munafiqun), and it was said that it is general to all disbelievers. Al-Qushayri said: grieving over a disbeliever's unbelief is an act of obedience, but the Prophet (ﷺ) used to exceed in grieving, so he was forbidden from it, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So let not your soul expire in regret over them﴾ [Fatir: 8], and ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over their footsteps if they do not believe in this message﴾ [al-Kahf: 6].

The verb al-sari'ūn (those who hasten) is construed with fī rather than ilā, to indicate that they are settled in it and persistent in engaging with it. Similarly: yusari'ūna fī al-khayrāt (they hasten to good deeds).

His saying: ﴿Indeed, they will never harm God at all﴾ is the reason for the prohibition. The meaning is that their disbelief does not diminish anything from the dominion of God, glory be to Him. It was said that what is meant is that they will never harm His friends. It is also possible that what is meant is that they will never harm His religion which He legislated for His servants. The word shay'an (at all) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), i.e., "any harm." It was said that it is in the accusative by removing the preposition, i.e., "by anything." The word al-ḥaẓẓ means "share." Abu Zayd said: a man is called ḥaẓīẓ if he has a share of provision. The meaning is that God wills not to give them any share in Paradise, or any share of reward. The future form is used to indicate the continuity and persistence of this will. ﴿And for them is a great punishment﴾ because of their hastening into disbelief. Thus the harm of their disbelief returns upon them, bringing about for them the absence of any share in the Hereafter and their destination in the great punishment.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who have purchased disbelief in exchange for faith﴾, meaning they substituted disbelief for faith. The explanation of this metaphor has already been given. ﴿They will never harm God at all﴾ has the same meaning as the first and is for emphasis of what preceded it. It was said that the first is specific to the hypocrites and the second includes all disbelievers, but the first is better.

His saying: (p-258) ﴿And let not those who disbelieve think that Our giving them respite is good for them﴾. Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and others read yaḥsabanna with the yā' (third person), and Hamza read it with the tā' (second person). The meaning according to the first reading: let not the disbelievers think that We give them respite with long life and abundant living, or with the victory they gained at the Battle of Uhud, ﴿is good for themselves﴾. The matter is not so; rather ﴿We only give them respite so that they may increase in sin, and for them is a humiliating punishment.﴾

According to the second reading: O Muhammad, do not think that the respite given to those who disbelieve, with what has been mentioned, is good for them. Rather, it is an evil that befalls them and descends upon them, namely that the respite We grant them is so that they increase in sin.

So in the first reading, the relative pronoun (alladhīna) is the subject of the verb, and "innamā nuṃlī" and what follows it fill the role of the two objects of the verb of thinking (ḥusbān) according to Sibawayh, or fill the role of one of them, the other being omitted, according to al-Akhfash.

As for the second reading, al-Zajjaj said that the relative pronoun is the first object, and "innamā" with what follows is an apposition (badal) to the relative pronoun, filling the role of both objects. He said that "innamā" with what follows cannot be the second object, because in this construction the second object is the first in meaning.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: if this were correct, it would be read as khayran in the accusative, because it would become an apposition to alladhīna kafarū, as if he had said: "Let not the respite of those who disbelieve be good." Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said that the verb is understood to be repeated, as if he had said: "And let not those who disbelieve think, and let not you think that 'innamā nuṃlī' is good for them," and so it fills the role of the two objects.

In al-Kashshaf it says: If you say, "How is an apposition valid when only one of the two objects is mentioned, and it is not permissible to limit the verb of thinking to one object?" I say: it is valid because the reliance is on the apposition, and the appositioned noun is in the position of what has been set aside. Do you not see that you say, "I placed your goods, some of them on top of others," even though your silence about your goods is not possible? End quote.

Yahya ibn Wathhab read innamā nuṃlī with a kasra on the inna in both places. This is a weak reading from the standpoint of Arabic grammar.

His saying: ﴿We only give them respite so that they may increase in sin﴾ is a new sentence (jumla musta'anafa) explaining the reason for the respite granted to the disbelievers. The majority of scholars (al-jumhur) have argued from this verse against what the Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school) say, because He, glory be to Him, informed that He lengthens the lives of the disbelievers and makes their living abundant so that they may increase in sin.

Abu Hatim said: I heard al-Akhfash mention a kasra on the first innamā nuṃlī and a fatha on the second, and he would argue with this on behalf of the people of qadar (the Qadariyya, those who affirm human free will) because he was one of them, and he would make this its construction: "Let not those who disbelieve think that We give them respite so that they may increase in sin; We give them respite, it is good for themselves." Al-Kashshaf says: increase in sin is a cause (ʿilla), and not every cause is an accident (ʿaraḍ). Do you not see that you say, "I sat out of the military expedition because of incapacity and poverty, and I left the town for fear of evil," and nothing befalls you; rather these are causes and reasons.

His saying: ﴿God would not leave the believers in the state you are in until He distinguishes the wicked from the good﴾. This is a new sentence. According to the majority of exegetes (mufassirun), the address is to the disbelievers and hypocrites, meaning: God would not leave the believers in the state you are in of disbelief and hypocrisy. It was said: the address is to the believers and hypocrites, meaning: God would not leave you in the mixed state you are in until He distinguishes some of you from others. It was said: the address is to the polytheists. What is meant by "the believers" is those in the loins and wombs, i.e., God would not leave your children in the state you are in until He separates them from you. It was said: the address is to the believers, meaning: God would not leave you, O company of believers, in the mixing with the hypocrites in which you are, until He distinguishes between you. On this view, and on the second view, there is iltifat (a shift of grammatical person) in the speech.

It is read yumayyiza (with doubled mīm) as the intensive form of the basic verb. From māza al-shay' yamīzuhu mayzan, when one separates between two things. If the things are multiple, it is said mayyazahu tamyīzan. ﴿Nor would God inform you of the unseen﴾ until you distinguish between the good and the wicked, for He is the one who alone possesses knowledge of the unseen. He does not disclose His unseen to anyone except whom He approves of among His messengers, whom He chooses, and then informs him of some of His unseen, so that he may distinguish among you. This is like what happened from our Prophet (ﷺ), namely his identifying many hypocrites, for that was by God's teaching him, not by his knowing the unseen. It was said the meaning is: ﴿God would not inform you of the unseen﴾ concerning who deserves prophethood, so that revelation would be by your choice. ﴿But God chooses﴾, i.e., selects, ﴿from among His messengers whom He wills.﴾

His saying: ﴿So believe in God and His messengers﴾, i.e., do the faith that is required of you, and leave off occupying yourselves with what is not your concern, such as seeking knowledge of God's unseen, glory be to Him. If you believe in what has been mentioned and are mindful of God, then in exchange for that you will have a great reward, whose worth cannot be known and whose reality cannot be reached.

The relative pronoun is in the nominative position as the subject of the verb according to the reading of the one who reads with the yā'. The first object is omitted, i.e., "let not the stingy think their stinginess is good for them." This was said by al-Khalil, Sibawayh and al-Farra'. They said: it was omitted because of the indication of yabkhalūna (they withhold). Among this is the poet's saying:

When the foolish one is forbidden, he rushes toward it and opposes, and the foolish one is in opposition.

That is, he rushes toward foolishness, so "the foolish one" indicates "foolishness."

As for the reading of the one who reads with the tā' (second person), the verb is attributed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the first object is omitted, i.e., "O Muhammad, do not think that the stinginess of those who withhold is good for them."

Al-Zajjaj said: it is like ﴿and ask the village﴾, and the mentioned pronoun is the pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl). Al-Mubarrad said: the sīn in His saying ﴿They will be encircled with what they withheld﴾ is the sīn of threat (sīn al-waʿīd), and this sentence explains the meaning of His saying ﴿Rather, it is evil for them.﴾ It was said: the meaning of encircling here is that what they withheld of wealth will become a collar of fire around their necks. It was said: its meaning is that they will bear the punishment for what they withheld, and it is from ṭāqa (capacity) and not from taṭwīq (encircling). It was said the meaning is that they will be bound to their deeds as a collar binds the neck. One says: "So-and-so encircled his deed with the collar of a dove," i.e., he was made to bear the recompense of his deed. It was also said that wealth whose zakat has not been paid is depicted for its owner as a bald venomous serpent, and it is placed around his neck, as is reported as a hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Qurtubi said: stinginess in the language is that a person withholds a right that is obligatory. As for one who withholds what is not obligatory upon him, he is not stingy.

His saying: ﴿And to God belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth﴾, i.e., to Him alone and not to anyone else, as the placing of the word first indicates. The meaning: to Him belongs what is in them, of which their inhabitants inherit. So what is wrong with them that they withhold that and do not spend it, when it belongs to God, glory be to Him, not to them? (p-259) Rather, it was in their possession as a temporary loan that will be reclaimed. Similar to this verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We inherit the earth and whoever is upon it﴾ [Maryam: 40], and His saying: ﴿And spend of that in which He has made you successors﴾ [al-Hadid: 7]. Inheritance (mirath) in its original sense is what passes from one owner to another, and was not owned by that other before its transfer to him by inheritance. It is known that God, glory be to Him, is the true owner of all His creation.

It was also said that wealth whose zakat has not been paid is depicted for its owner as a bald venomous serpent, and it is placed around his neck, as is reported as a hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Qurtubi said: stinginess in the language is that a person withholds a right that is obligatory. As for one who withholds what is not obligatory upon him, he is not stingy.

His saying: ﴿And to God belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth﴾, i.e., to Him alone and not to anyone else, as the placing of the word first indicates. The meaning: to Him belongs what is in them, of which their inhabitants inherit. So what is wrong with them that they withhold that and do not spend it, when it belongs to God, glory be to Him, not to them? (p-259) Rather, it was in their possession as a temporary loan that will be reclaimed. Similar to this verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We inherit the earth and whoever is upon it﴾ [Maryam: 40], and His saying: ﴿And spend of that in which He has made you successors﴾ [al-Hadid: 7]. Inheritance (mirath) in its original sense is what passes from one owner to another, and was not owned by that other before its transfer to him by inheritance. It is known that God, glory be to Him, is the true owner of all His creation.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid regarding ﴿Indeed, those who have purchased disbelief in exchange for faith﴾ that he said: they are the hypocrites.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: No soul, whether righteous or wicked, but death is better for it than life. If it is righteous, God has said: ﴿And what is with God is better for the righteous﴾ [Al 'Imran: 798]. And if it is wicked, He has said: ﴿And let not those who disbelieve think...﴾ the verse.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Abu al-Darda' something similar. Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b something similar.

'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Abu Barza also something similar. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi that he said: They said, "If Muhammad is truthful, let him inform us of who among us believes in him and who disbelieves." So God revealed ﴿God would not leave the believers...﴾ the verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: He distinguishes the people of happiness from the people of misery. 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada that he said: He distinguishes between them in jihad and emigration. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan regarding His saying: ﴿Nor would God inform you of the unseen﴾ that he said: None is informed of the unseen except a messenger. 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid regarding ﴿But God chooses﴾ that he said: He singles out.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Malik that he said: He selects. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And let not those who withhold...﴾ that he said: They are the People of the Book who withheld from making it clear to the people.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid that he said: They are the Jews. Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Suddi that he said: They withheld from spending it in the way of God and did not pay its zakat.

Al-Bukhari narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever Allah gives wealth but he does not pay its zakat, it will be depicted for him on the Day of Resurrection as a bald venomous male serpent with two black spots over its eyes. It will be hung around his neck, and it will seize him by his two cheeks, that is, his jaws, and say: 'I am your wealth, I am your treasure.'" Then he recited this verse.

This meaning has been reported in many hadiths from a group of the Companions, who trace them back to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verses 181–186:

The people of tafsir said: When God revealed ﴿Who is it that will lend to God a goodly loan?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 245], a group of the Jews said this statement as a way of deceiving their weak-minded followers, not because they believed it, for they are People of the Book. Rather, they meant that if what He asked of us, the loan, came through Muhammad, then He is poor, so that they might cast doubt among their brothers in the religion of Islam.

His words ﴿We will record what they have said﴾: We will write it in the scrolls of the angels, or We will preserve it, or We will repay them for it. The meaning is a warning to them, and that this does not escape God; rather, it is prepared for them for the Day of Recompense. On this reading, the clause "We will record" (sanaktub) is a resumed sentence (mustaʾnafah), answering an implied question, as if it were said: "What did God do to those from whom He heard this monstrous statement?" So He said: "He said to them: ﴿We will record what they have said﴾." Al-Aʿmash and Hamzah read (sayuktabu), with the yaʾ and in the passive voice. And one reading (qatluhum) with a raised lam, and (wa-yaqulu) with a yaʾ below.

His words ﴿and their killing of the prophets﴾ are coordinated with (what they have said); that is: and We will record their killing of the prophets, meaning the killing by their forebears of the prophets. This is attributed to them because they were content with it. He placed that statement alongside the killing of prophets to alert that it is of such enormity and abomination that it equals the killing of prophets. His words (wa-naqulu), are coordinated with (sanaktub), meaning: We will take vengeance on them after writing down this statement which We will say to them in the Fire, or at death, or at the reckoning. Al-Harīq is the name for the blazing fire, and the use of "tasting" (dhawq) for the sensation of punishment is a eloquent hyperbole. Ibn Masʿud read (wa-yuqalu dhuqu).

The demonstrative in His words ﴿that﴾ refers to the punishment mentioned before it. He used for the near a form that is used for the distant, to indicate how far its place is in terrible severity. The mention of the hands is because they are the instruments of most sins. His words ﴿and that God is not unjust to the servants﴾ are coordinated with ﴿what your hands have sent forth﴾. It is explained that He, glory be to Him, punished them for the sins they committed and repaid them for their deeds, so that this was not injustice. Or the meaning is: He is the Owner of the dominion who disposes of His dominion as He wills, and is not unjust to whoever He punishes for his sin. It was also said that the meaning is that the negation of injustice entails justice, which requires rewarding the good-doer and punishing the wrongdoer. This was refuted: abandoning punishment when its cause exists is not injustice either by reason or by revelation. It was also said that the clause ﴿and that God is not unjust to the servants﴾ is in the nominative position, as the predicate of an omitted subject; that is: the matter is that God is not unjust to the servants. The expression of the negation of injustice in this form, although punishing them without sin is not injustice according to the People of the Sunnah, is to demonstrate His transcendence above that. The negation of (ẓallām), which implies multiplicity, establishes the basic existence of injustice.

It is answered that what He threatened to do to them, if it were injustice, would be great; so He negated it according to its greatness, were it established. His words ﴿those who said﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they are those who said. It was also said it is an adjective of (the servants). It was also said it is in the accusative as a dispraise. It was also said it is in the genitive position as an apposition to ﴿God has indeed heard the statement of those who said﴾, but this is weak, because the apposition is the intended element rather than what it replaces, and this is not the case here. These speakers are a group of the Jews, as will come. This statement, that God had covenanted with them not to believe in any messenger until he brings them an offering, is among their false claims.

It was the custom of the Children of Israel that they would present offerings. The prophet would stand and supplicate, and fire would descend from heaven and consume it. God did not make this an act of worship for all His prophets, nor did He make it a sign of the truth of prophethood. For this reason God replied to them, saying: ﴿Say: There have certainly come to you messengers before me with clear proofs and with what you have spoken of﴾ of the offering ﴿so why did you kill them, if you are truthful?﴾ such as Yahya ibn Zakariyya, Shaʿyaʾ, and the rest of the prophets who were killed.

Al-Qurban is what one draws near to God with, such as a sacrifice, charity, or righteous deed, and it is on the pattern fuʿlān, from qurbah (nearness). Then God consoled His Messenger, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, with His words: ﴿And if they deny you, messengers before you were denied, who came﴾ with the like of what you have brought of clear proofs.

Al-Zubur is the plural of zabur, which is a book, and its explanation has already passed. ﴿and the illuminating Book﴾: the clear, evident, shining one. It is said: nāra al-shayʾ, anāra, nawwarahu and istanārahu, all with the same meaning.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: Abu Bakr entered the House of Study and found the Jews gathered around a man among them called Finhas, who was one of their scholars and rabbis. Abu Bakr said: "Woe to you, Finhas! Fear God and submit. By God, you know that Muhammad is the Messenger of God; you find him written with you in the Torah." Finhas said: "By God, Abu Bakr, we have no need of God; rather He is in need of us, and we do not humble ourselves before Him as He humbles Himself before us, and we are free of Him. If He were free of us, He would not borrow from us as your companion claims, forbidding you from usury while giving it to us; if He were free of us, He would not have given us usury." Abu Bakr became angry and struck Finhas's face a severe blow, and said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, were it not for the covenant between us and you, I would strike your neck, enemy of God!" So Finhas went to the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, and said: "O Muhammad, look at what your companion has done to me!" The Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, said to Abu Bakr: "What moved you to do what you did?" He said: "O Messenger of God, he said a monstrous statement, claiming that God is poor and they are rich. When he said that, I became angry for God's sake at what he said, and I struck his face." Finhas denied it and said: "I did not say that." So God revealed concerning what Finhas said, confirming Abu Bakr: ﴿God has indeed heard the statement of those who said﴾ the verse. And there was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, and the anger that reached him over that: ﴿And you will surely hear much hurt from those who were given the Book before you and from those who associate partners﴾ the verse [Al ʿImran: 186]. This story was also reported by Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir from ʿIkrimah, and Ibn Jarir reported it from al-Suddi in a shorter form.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Diya in al-Mukhtarah reported through Saʿid ibn Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The Jews came to Muhammad, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, when God revealed ﴿Who is it that will lend to God a goodly loan?﴾ and they said: "O Muhammad, is your Lord poor, asking His servants for a loan?" So God revealed the verse. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Qatadah that the speaker of this statement was Huyayy ibn Akhtab, and that it was revealed concerning him.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-ʿAlaʾ ibn Badr that he was asked about God's words ﴿and their killing of the prophets without right﴾, though they did not witness that, and he said: "By their allegiance to those who killed the prophets." Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His words ﴿and that God is not unjust to the servants﴾ that he said: "I am not one to punish those who have not committed a crime."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Dahhak concerning His words ﴿those who said: God has covenanted with us﴾ that he said: "They are the Jews." Ibn Abi Hatim reported through al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His words ﴿until He brings us an offering which fire consumes﴾ [al-Tawbah: 30] that he said: "A man among us would give charity, and if it was accepted from him, fire would descend upon him from heaven and consume it."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Hasan concerning His words ﴿those who said: God has covenanted with us﴾ that he said: "They lied against God." Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿with the clear proofs﴾ that he said: "These are the lawful and the unlawful." ﴿and the Zubur﴾ he said: "These are the books of the prophets." ﴿and the illuminating Book﴾ he said: "It is the Qur'an."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verses 181–186:

The people of tafsir said: When God revealed ﴿Who is it that will lend to God a goodly loan?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 245], a group of the Jews said this statement as a way of deceiving their weak-minded followers, not because they believed it, for they are People of the Book. Rather, they meant that if what He asked of us, the loan, came through Muhammad, then He is poor, so that they might cast doubt among their brothers in the religion of Islam.

His words ﴿We will record what they have said﴾: We will write it in the scrolls of the angels, or We will preserve it, or We will repay them for it. The meaning is a warning to them, and that this does not escape God; rather, it is prepared for them for the Day of Recompense. On this reading, the clause "We will record" (sanaktub) is a resumed sentence (mustaʾnafah), answering an implied question, as if it were said: "What did God do to those from whom He heard this monstrous statement?" So He said: "He said to them: ﴿We will record what they have said﴾." Al-Aʿmash and Hamzah read (sayuktabu), with the yaʾ and in the passive voice. And one reading (qatluhum) with a raised lam, and (wa-yaqulu) with a yaʾ below.

His words ﴿and their killing of the prophets﴾ are coordinated with (what they have said); that is: and We will record their killing of the prophets, meaning the killing by their forebears of the prophets. This is attributed to them because they were content with it. He placed that statement alongside the killing of prophets to alert that it is of such enormity and abomination that it equals the killing of prophets. His words (wa-naqulu), are coordinated with (sanaktub), meaning: We will take vengeance on them after writing down this statement which We will say to them in the Fire, or at death, or at the reckoning. Al-Harīq is the name for the blazing fire, and the use of "tasting" (dhawq) for the sensation of punishment is a eloquent hyperbole. Ibn Masʿud read (wa-yuqalu dhuqu).

The demonstrative in His words ﴿that﴾ refers to the punishment mentioned before it. He used for the near a form that is used for the distant, to indicate how far its place is in terrible severity. The mention of the hands is because they are the instruments of most sins. His words ﴿and that God is not unjust to the servants﴾ are coordinated with ﴿what your hands have sent forth﴾. It is explained that He, glory be to Him, punished them for the sins they committed and repaid them for their deeds, so that this was not injustice. Or the meaning is: He is the Owner of the dominion who disposes of His dominion as He wills, and is not unjust to whoever He punishes for his sin. It was also said that the meaning is that the negation of injustice entails justice, which requires rewarding the good-doer and punishing the wrongdoer. This was refuted: abandoning punishment when its cause exists is not injustice either by reason or by revelation. It was also said that the clause ﴿and that God is not unjust to the servants﴾ is in the nominative position, as the predicate of an omitted subject; that is: the matter is that God is not unjust to the servants. The expression of the negation of injustice in this form, although punishing them without sin is not injustice according to the People of the Sunnah, is to demonstrate His transcendence above that. The negation of (ẓallām), which implies multiplicity, establishes the basic existence of injustice.

It is answered that what He threatened to do to them, if it were injustice, would be great; so He negated it according to its greatness, were it established. His words ﴿those who said﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they are those who said. It was also said it is an adjective of (the servants). It was also said it is in the accusative as a dispraise. It was also said it is in the genitive position as an apposition to ﴿God has indeed heard the statement of those who said﴾, but this is weak, because the apposition is the intended element rather than what it replaces, and this is not the case here.
