Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Diya in al-Mukhtarah reported through Saʿid ibn Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The Jews came to Muhammad, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, when God revealed ﴿Who is it that will lend to God a goodly loan?﴾ and they said: "O Muhammad, is your Lord poor, asking His servants for a loan?" So God revealed the verse. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Qatadah that the speaker of this statement was Huyayy ibn Akhtab, and that it was revealed concerning him.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-ʿAlaʾ ibn Badr that he was asked about God's words ﴿and their killing of the prophets without right﴾, though they did not witness that, and he said: "By their allegiance to those who killed the prophets." Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His words ﴿and that God is not unjust to the servants﴾ that he said: "I am not one to punish those who have not committed a crime."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Dahhak concerning His words ﴿those who said: God has covenanted with us﴾ that he said: "They are the Jews." Ibn Abi Hatim reported through al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His words ﴿until He brings us an offering which fire consumes﴾ [al-Tawbah: 30] that he said: "A man among us would give charity, and if it was accepted from him, fire would descend upon him from heaven and consume it."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Hasan concerning His words ﴿those who said: God has covenanted with us﴾ that he said: "They lied against God." Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿with the clear proofs﴾ that he said: "These are the lawful and the unlawful." ﴿and the Zubur﴾ he said: "These are the books of the prophets." ﴿and the illuminating Book﴾ he said: "It is the Qur'an."

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said... no, translating now.

﴿Every soul shall taste death﴾. *Dha'iqa* is from *al-dhawq* (tasting), and Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

*"Whoever does not die in his prime will die in decrepitude; death is a cup, and a man is one who tastes it."*

This verse contains a promise and a warning to the one who affirms and the one who denies, after Allah's report about the miserly who said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is poor and we are rich﴾. Al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Wathhab and Ibn Abi Ishaq read *dha'iqatu al-mawt* with tanwin and the accusative *al-mawt*.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read it in the construct form. As for His words: ﴿And you will only be paid your full reward on the Day of Resurrection﴾: the reward of the believer is reward (*al-thawab*), and the reward of the disbeliever is punishment (*al-'iqab*). That is, the full and complete payment of rewards takes place on that Day, and whatever rewards occur in this world or in the *barzakh* (the intermediate state) are only a part of the rewards.

*Al-zahzaha* means to move away, and *al-ibʿad* (distancing) is the repetition of *al-zajj*, which is pulling with haste. He said this in *al-Kashshaf* (Zamakhshari's commentary), and its discussion has already passed. That is: whoever is kept away from the Fire on that Day and is removed from it, then he has triumphed, meaning he has achieved what he desired and been saved from what he feared. This is the true triumph, beyond which there is no comparable triumph. Every triumph, even if it includes all desires apart from Paradise, is nothing in comparison to it. O Allah, there is no triumph except the triumph of the Hereafter, no life except its life, and no bliss except its bliss. So forgive our sins, cover our faults, and be pleased with us with a pleasure after which there is no displeasure, and gather for us between Your pleasure with us and Paradise.

*Al-mata'* is that which a person enjoys and benefits from, then it passes away and does not remain. So said most of the commentators.

*Al-ghurur* (delusion) is Satan, who deceives people with false hopes and lying promises. Glorified is He, who likened the world to goods that are counterfeited upon one who desires them: it has an appealing outward appearance and a hateful inward reality.

His words: ﴿You will surely be tested in your wealth and in your persons﴾. This address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) and his community, as consolation for them regarding what they will face from the disbelievers and the transgressors, so that they may prepare themselves for steadfastness and patience in the face of what is hateful (p-261).

*Al-ibtila'* is trial and examination. The meaning: you will be tested and examined in your wealth through calamities, obligatory expenditures, and the rest of the legal obligations connected to wealth. And the testing in your persons is through death, sickness, the loss of loved ones, and being killed in the way of Allah.

This clause is the answer to an implied oath, indicated by the preceding *lam al-muwatta'a* (the lam that introduces an oath): ﴿You will surely hear from those who were given the Scripture before you﴾, namely the Jews and the Christians, ﴿and from those who associated others with Allah﴾, namely the rest of the disbelieving groups other than the People of the Book, ﴿much hurt﴾, through reviling your religion and your honour. The reference in His words "Indeed, that" is to patience and piety, which are indicated by the two verbs. *'Azm al-umur* means its determined matters: that is, what you must resolve upon, since it is one of the determinations of Allah which He obligated them to uphold. It is said: *'azama al-amr*, meaning he firmed it and set it right.

His words: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture﴾. This verse is a rebuke to the People of the Book, the Jews and the Christians, or the Jews alone, according to the difference of opinion on this. The apparent meaning is that by "the People of the Book" is meant everyone to whom Allah has given knowledge of some part of the Scripture, whatever Scripture it was, as the generic definite article in "the Scripture" indicates.

Al-Hasan and Qatada said: the verse is general to every scholar. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said likewise, and the statement of Abu Hurayra supports this: "Were it not for what Allah took from the People of the Book, I would not have narrated anything to you," then he recited this verse. The pronoun in His words "you shall make it clear" refers to the Scripture. It was said that it refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), even though he was not previously mentioned, because Allah took from the Jews and Christians that they should make his prophethood clear to people and not conceal it. ﴿But they threw it behind their backs﴾.

Abu 'Amr, 'Asim in the narration of Abu Bakr, and the people of Madina read *la-yubayyinunnahu* with the yaa' (third person), and the rest read it with the taa' (second person).

Ibn 'Abbas read: "And when Allah took the covenant of the Prophets, you shall make it clear" (Q. 9:30). This reading is problematic in light of His words "they threw it," for its subject must be people. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: *la-tubayyinunnahu*. *Al-nabdh* is throwing away, and it has already been discussed in al-Baqara.

His words: ﴿behind their backs﴾ are an intensification of the throwing away and casting off, and the meaning of His words ﴿and sold it for a small price﴾ has also already passed. The pronoun refers to the Scripture, which they were commanded to make clear and forbidden to conceal. His words "a small price" mean a paltry, insignificant amount of the trash of this world and its goods. His words ﴿how wretched is what they sell﴾: "what" is an indefinite noun in the accusative, explaining the subject of *bi'sa*; *yashtaruna* is a descriptive clause; and the object of the dispraise is omitted, meaning: how wretched a thing they sell for that price.

His words: ﴿Do not think that those who rejoice﴾. The Kufans read it with the taa' (second person), and the address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) or to everyone suitable for it. His words "in what they have done" mean: in what they did.

The occasion of revelation of the verse has been disputed, as will come, and the apparent meaning is that it includes everyone who engages in what it contains, by the generality of the wording, and that is what is considered, not the specific cause. So whoever rejoices in what he has done and loves to be praised for what he did not do, do not think him safe from the punishment. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read *la yahsabanna* with the yaa' (third person), meaning: let not those who rejoice think that their rejoicing will save them from punishment. The first object is then omitted, which is their rejoicing, and the second object is "a place of safety from the punishment."

His words: ﴿so do not think them﴾ are an emphasis of the first verb in both readings. *Al-mafaza* means the place of deliverance, a noun of place from *faza* (to triumph), meaning to be saved; that is, they are not triumphant. The place of fear was called *mafaza* by way of optimism, as al-Asma'i said. It was also said that it is because it is a place of perishing and likely destruction; the Arabs say *fawz al-rajul* when he dies.

Tha'lab said: I related al-Asma'i's statement to Ibn al-A'rabi, and he said: He erred. Abu al-Makarim said to me: it is only called *mafaza* because whoever crosses it triumphs. Ibn al-A'rabi also said: rather, it is because one surrenders to what befalls him. It was also said that the meaning is: do not think them to be in a place far from the punishment, because triumph is distancing from what is hateful.

Marwan ibn al-Hakam, al-A'mash and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i read *ata'u* with the long vowel, meaning they rejoice in what they were given. The majority of reciters, the Seven and others, read *ataw* with the short vowel.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Hannad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), Ibn Hibban, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim (who graded it sound) transmitted from Abu Hurayra who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A place for a whip in Paradise is better than this world and what is in it. Recite, if you wish: ﴿Whoever is distanced from the Fire and admitted into Paradise has triumphed, and the life of this world is but the enjoyment of delusion﴾." Ibn Mardawayh transmitted a similar report from Sahl ibn Sa'd, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Zuhri regarding His words: ﴿And you will surely hear from those who were given the Scripture before you﴾, that he said: "It is Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, who used to incite the polytheists against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions in his poetry." Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted a similar report from the route of al-Zuhri, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ka'b ibn Malik.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Jurayj regarding the verse, that he said: "It means the Jews and the Christians. The Muslims used to hear from the Jews their saying: 'Uzayr is the son of Allah' (Q. 9:30), and from the Christians their saying: 'The Messiah is the son of Allah' (Q. 9:30)." ﴿And if you are patient and mindful of Allah, indeed that is of the steadfast resolve of matters﴾. He said: "Of the strength of what Allah has resolved upon and commanded you."

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture, you shall make it clear to the people﴾, that he said: "Finhas, Ashya', and their like among the rabbis."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted through al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture, you shall make it clear to the people﴾, that he said: "Allah had commanded them to follow the unlettered Prophet." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him regarding the verse, that he said: "In the Torah and the Gospel it is written that Islam is the religion of Allah which He prescribed for His servants, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah; they find him written in their possession in the Torah and the Gospel, but they threw it away."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding the verse, that he said: "They are the Jews." ﴿You shall make it clear to the people﴾: "Muhammad (ﷺ)." Ibn Jarir transmitted a similar report from al-Suddi.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatada regarding the verse, that he said: "This is a covenant which Allah took from the people of knowledge: whoever knows knowledge (p-262) should teach it to the people. Beware of concealing knowledge, for concealing knowledge is destruction." Ibn Sa'd transmitted from al-Hasan who said: "Were it not for the covenant which Allah took from the people of knowledge, I would not have narrated to you much of what you ask about."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others transmitted that Marwan said to his doorkeeper: "Go, O Rafi', to Ibn 'Abbas and say: If every one of us who rejoices in what he was given and loves to be praised for what he did not do is punished, we shall all be punished." Ibn 'Abbas said: "What is it to you with this verse? It was only revealed concerning the People of the Book." Then he recited: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture﴾ to the end of the verse. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) asked them about something, and they concealed it from him and informed him of something else. They left having shown him that they had informed him of what he asked about, and sought praise from him for that, and they rejoiced in what they had done of concealing what he asked them about."

In al-Bukhari, Muslim and others, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: that some hypocrites used to stay behind when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out to a military campaign, and they rejoiced in their sitting out, contrary to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned from the campaign, they offered excuses to him and swore oaths, and they loved to be praised for what they had not done, so the verse was revealed.

It has been related that it was revealed concerning Finhas, Ashya', and their like. It has also been related that it was revealed concerning the Jews.

Malik, Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* transmitted from Muhammad ibn Thabit that Thabit ibn Qays said: "O Messenger of Allah, I fear that I have perished." He said: "Why?" He said: "Allah has forbidden us to love to be praised for what we did not do, and I find myself loving praise; and He forbade us from pride, and I find myself loving beauty; and He forbade us to raise our voices above your voice, and I am a man of loud voice." He said: "O Thabit, are you not pleased to live praiseworthy, to be killed as a martyr, and to enter Paradise?" So he lived praiseworthy and was killed as a martyr on the day of Musaylima the Liar.

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from al-Dahhak regarding His words: ﴿a place of safety﴾ that he said: "a place of deliverance."

Ibn Jarir transmitted a similar report from Ibn Zayd.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said... no, translating now.

This verse contains a promise and a warning to the one who affirms and the one who denies, after Allah's report about the miserly who said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is poor and we are rich﴾. Al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Wathhab and Ibn Abi Ishaq read *dha'iqatu al-mawt* with tanwin and the accusative *al-mawt*.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read it in the construct form. As for His words: ﴿And you will only be paid your full reward on the Day of Resurrection﴾: the reward of the believer is reward (*al-thawab*), and the reward of the disbeliever is punishment (*al-'iqab*). That is, the full and complete payment of rewards takes place on that Day, and whatever rewards occur in this world or in the *barzakh* (the intermediate state) are only a part of the rewards.

*Al-zahzaha* means to move away, and *al-ibʿad* (distancing) is the repetition of *al-zajj*, which is pulling with haste. He said this in *al-Kashshaf* (Zamakhshari's commentary), and its discussion has already passed. That is: whoever is kept away from the Fire on that Day and is removed from it, then he has triumphed, meaning he has achieved what he desired and been saved from what he feared. This is the true triumph, beyond which there is no comparable triumph. Every triumph, even if it includes all desires apart from Paradise, is nothing in comparison to it. O Allah, there is no triumph except the triumph of the Hereafter, no life except its life, and no bliss except its bliss. So forgive our sins, cover our faults, and be pleased with us with a pleasure after which there is no displeasure, and gather for us between Your pleasure with us and Paradise.

*Al-mata'* is that which a person enjoys and benefits from, then it passes away and does not remain. So said most of the commentators.

*Al-ghurur* (delusion) is Satan, who deceives people with false hopes and lying promises. Glorified is He, who likened the world to goods that are counterfeited upon one who desires them: it has an appealing outward appearance and a hateful inward reality.

His words: ﴿You will surely be tested in your wealth and in your persons﴾. This address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) and his community, as consolation for them regarding what they will face from the disbelievers and the transgressors, so that they may prepare themselves for steadfastness and patience in the face of what is hateful (p-261).

*Al-ibtila'* is trial and examination. The meaning: you will be tested and examined in your wealth through calamities, obligatory expenditures, and the rest of the legal obligations connected to wealth. And the testing in your persons is through death, sickness, the loss of loved ones, and being killed in the way of Allah.

This clause is the answer to an implied oath, indicated by the preceding *lam al-muwatta'a* (the lam that introduces an oath): ﴿You will surely hear from those who were given the Scripture before you﴾, namely the Jews and the Christians, ﴿and from those who associated others with Allah﴾, namely the rest of the disbelieving groups other than the People of the Book, ﴿much hurt﴾, through reviling your religion and your honour. The reference in His words "Indeed, that" is to patience and piety, which are indicated by the two verbs. *'Azm al-umur* means its determined matters: that is, what you must resolve upon, since it is one of the determinations of Allah which He obligated them to uphold. It is said: *'azama al-amr*, meaning he firmed it and set it right.

His words: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture﴾. This verse is a rebuke to the People of the Book, the Jews and the Christians, or the Jews alone, according to the difference of opinion on this. The apparent meaning is that by "the People of the Book" is meant everyone to whom Allah has given knowledge of some part of the Scripture, whatever Scripture it was, as the generic definite article in "the Scripture" indicates.

Al-Hasan and Qatada said: the verse is general to every scholar. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said likewise, and the statement of Abu Hurayra supports this: "Were it not for what Allah took from the People of the Book, I would not have narrated anything to you," then he recited this verse. The pronoun in His words "you shall make it clear" refers to the Scripture. It was said that it refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), even though he was not previously mentioned, because Allah took from the Jews and Christians that they should make his prophethood clear to people and not conceal it. ﴿But they threw it behind their backs﴾.

Abu 'Amr, 'Asim in the narration of Abu Bakr, and the people of Madina read *la-yubayyinunnahu* with the yaa' (third person), and the rest read it with the taa' (second person).

Ibn 'Abbas read: "And when Allah took the covenant of the Prophets, you shall make it clear" (Q. 9:30). This reading is problematic in light of His words "they threw it," for its subject must be people. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: *la-tubayyinunnahu*. *Al-nabdh* is throwing away, and it has already been discussed in al-Baqara.

His words: ﴿behind their backs﴾ are an intensification of the throwing away and casting off, and the meaning of His words ﴿and sold it for a small price﴾ has also already passed. The pronoun refers to the Scripture, which they were commanded to make clear and forbidden to conceal. His words "a small price" mean a paltry, insignificant amount of the trash of this world and its goods. His words ﴿how wretched is what they sell﴾: "what" is an indefinite noun in the accusative, explaining the subject of *bi'sa*; *yashtaruna* is a descriptive clause; and the object of the dispraise is omitted, meaning: how wretched a thing they sell for that price.

His words: ﴿Do not think that those who rejoice﴾. The Kufans read it with the taa' (second person), and the address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) or to everyone suitable for it. His words "in what they have done" mean: in what they did.

The occasion of revelation of the verse has been disputed, as will come, and the apparent meaning is that it includes everyone who engages in what it contains, by the generality of the wording, and that is what is considered, not the specific cause. So whoever rejoices in what he has done and loves to be praised for what he did not do, do not think him safe from the punishment. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read *la yahsabanna* with the yaa' (third person), meaning: let not those who rejoice think that their rejoicing will save them from punishment. The first object is then omitted, which is their rejoicing, and the second object is "a place of safety from the punishment."

His words: ﴿so do not think them﴾ are an emphasis of the first verb in both readings. *Al-mafaza* means the place of deliverance, a noun of place from *faza* (to triumph), meaning to be saved; that is, they are not triumphant. The place of fear was called *mafaza* by way of optimism, as al-Asma'i said. It was also said that it is because it is a place of perishing and likely destruction; the Arabs say *fawz al-rajul* when he dies.

Tha'lab said: I related al-Asma'i's statement to Ibn al-A'rabi, and he said: He erred. Abu al-Makarim said to me: it is only called *mafaza* because whoever crosses it triumphs. Ibn al-A'rabi also said: rather, it is because one surrenders to what befalls him. It was also said that the meaning is: do not think them to be in a place far from the punishment, because triumph is distancing from what is hateful.

Marwan ibn al-Hakam, al-A'mash and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i read *ata'u* with the long vowel, meaning they rejoice in what they were given. The majority of reciters, the Seven and others, read *ataw* with the short vowel.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Hannad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), Ibn Hibban, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim (who graded it sound) transmitted from Abu Hurayra who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A place for a whip in Paradise is better than this world and what is in it. Recite, if you wish: ﴿Whoever is distanced from the Fire and admitted into Paradise has triumphed, and the life of this world is but the enjoyment of delusion﴾." Ibn Mardawayh transmitted a similar report from Sahl ibn Sa'd, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Zuhri regarding His words: ﴿And you will surely hear from those who were given the Scripture before you﴾, that he said: "It is Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, who used to incite the polytheists against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions in his poetry." Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted a similar report from the route of al-Zuhri, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ka'b ibn Malik.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Jurayj regarding the verse, that he said: "It means the Jews and the Christians. The Muslims used to hear from the Jews their saying: 'Uzayr is the son of Allah' (Q. 9:30), and from the Christians their saying: 'The Messiah is the son of Allah' (Q. 9:30)." ﴿And if you are patient and mindful of Allah, indeed that is of the steadfast resolve of matters﴾. He said: "Of the strength of what Allah has resolved upon and commanded you."

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture, you shall make it clear to the people﴾, that he said: "Finhas, Ashya', and their like among the rabbis."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted through al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture, you shall make it clear to the people﴾, that he said: "Allah had commanded them to follow the unlettered Prophet." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him regarding the verse, that he said: "In the Torah and the Gospel it is written that Islam is the religion of Allah which He prescribed for His servants, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah; they find him written in their possession in the Torah and the Gospel, but they threw it away."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding the verse, that he said: "They are the Jews." ﴿You shall make it clear to the people﴾: "Muhammad (ﷺ)." Ibn Jarir transmitted a similar report from al-Suddi.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatada regarding the verse, that he said: "This is a covenant which Allah took from the people of knowledge: whoever knows knowledge (p-262) should teach it to the people. Beware of concealing knowledge, for concealing knowledge is destruction." Ibn Sa'd transmitted from al-Hasan who said: "Were it not for the covenant which Allah took from the people of knowledge, I would not have narrated to you much of what you ask about."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others transmitted that Marwan said to his doorkeeper: "Go, O Rafi', to Ibn 'Abbas and say: If every one of us who rejoices in what he was given and loves to be praised for what he did not do is punished, we shall all be punished." Ibn 'Abbas said: "What is it to you with this verse? It was only revealed concerning the People of the Book." Then he recited: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture﴾ to the end of the verse. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) asked them about something, and they concealed it from him and informed him of something else. They left having shown him that they had informed him of what he asked about, and sought praise from him for that, and they rejoiced in what they had done of concealing what he asked them about."

In al-Bukhari, Muslim and others, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: that some hypocrites used to stay behind when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out to a military campaign, and they rejoiced in their sitting out, contrary to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned from the campaign, they offered excuses to him and swore oaths, and they loved to be praised for what they had not done, so the verse was revealed.

It has been related that it was revealed concerning Finhas, Ashya', and their like. It has also been related that it was revealed concerning the Jews.

Malik, Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* transmitted from Muhammad ibn Thabit that Thabit ibn Qays said: "O Messenger of Allah, I fear that I have perished." He said: "Why?" He said: "Allah has forbidden us to love to be praised for what we did not do, and I find myself loving praise; and He forbade us from pride, and I find myself loving beauty; and He forbade us to raise our voices above your voice, and I am a man of loud voice." He said: "O Thabit, are you not pleased to live praiseworthy, to be killed as a martyr, and to enter Paradise?" So he lived praiseworthy and was killed as a martyr on the day of Musaylima the Liar.

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from al-Dahhak regarding His words: ﴿a place of safety﴾ that he said: "a place of deliverance."

Ibn Jarir transmitted a similar report from Ibn Zayd.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verses 190–194:

His saying: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens﴾. This is a resumed sentence (jumlah musta'nafah) to establish His exclusive authority over what He mentioned in it. What is meant is the very existence of the heavens and the earth and their attributes, ﴿and the alternation of the night and the day﴾, i.e., their succession, each one replacing the other, the increase of one of them at the expense of the other, and their variation in length and shortness, heat and cold, and other things. ﴿Are signs﴾, i.e., clear proofs and manifest evidences that point to the Creator, glorified is He.

The interpretation of some of what is here has already been given in Surat al-Baqarah. By ﴿ulil-albab﴾ (people of understanding) is meant those with sound intellects, pure of any defect, for mere reflection upon what Allah has related in this verse suffices the intelligent person and brings him to faith that is not shaken by doubts nor repelled by skeptical objections.

His saying: ﴿Those who remember Allah standing, sitting, and on their sides﴾. The relative pronoun is an attribute (na't) of ulil-albab. It has been said that it is separate from it, being the predicate of an omitted subject, or in the accusative as an expression of praise. What is meant by remembrance here is remembering Him, glorified is He, in these states, without distinction between the state of prayer and others.

A group of exegetes went to the view that remembrance here is a metaphor for prayer; i.e., they do not neglect it in any state, so they pray standing when there is no excuse, and sitting or on their sides when there is an excuse.

His saying: ﴿And they reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ is conjoined to His saying "they remember." It has been said that it is conjoined to the state, namely ﴿standing and sitting﴾. It has been said that it is disconnected from the first, and the meaning is: they reflect upon the wondrous making of both and their perfection, together with their great bodies, for this reflection, when sincere, leads them to faith in Allah, glorified is He.

His saying: ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾. It is on the assumption of a saying; i.e., they say: You did not create this in vain and frivolously, but You created it as evidence of Your wisdom and power. "Batil" means that which is passing and perishing, and from it is the saying of Labid:

Surely everything other than Allah is perishing (batil).

It is in the accusative as an attribute of an omitted verbal noun; i.e., a vain creation. It has been said that it is in the accusative by removal of the preposition. It has been said that it is a second object, with "khalaqa" meaning "ja'ala." Or it is in the accusative as a state. The demonstrative "this" refers to the heavens and the earth, or to the creation understood as the created thing.

His saying: ﴿Glory be to You﴾, i.e., exalting You above what is unbefitting You of matters, among which is that Your creation of these created things would be in vain. His saying: ﴿So protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾: the fa' indicates the sequence of this supplication upon what precedes it.

His saying: ﴿Our Lord, indeed whoever You admit to the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him﴾. This is an emphasis on what preceded of seeking protection from the Fire from Him, glorified is He, and an explanation of the reason for which His servants called upon Him to protect them from the punishment of the Fire: that whoever He admits into the Fire, He has disgraced, i.e., humiliated and abased. Al-Mufaddal said: the meaning of "akhzaytahu" is "ahlaktahu" (You destroyed him), and he recited:

Allah disgraced the Banu al-Salib, [and] 'Unayzah, and those who wear the garments of monks.

It has been said: its meaning is "fadahtahu" (You exposed him) and "ab'adtahu" (You distanced him). It is said: "akhzahu Allah" means He distanced him and abhorred him, and the noun is "khizy." Ibn al-Sikkit said: "khazia yakhzi khizyan" means when one falls into a calamity.

His saying: ﴿Our Lord, indeed we heard a caller calling to faith﴾. The caller, according to most exegetes, is the Prophet (ﷺ). It has been said he is the Qur'an. He attached the hearing to the caller although what is heard is the call, because he described the caller with what is heard, namely His saying: ﴿calling to faith, that believe﴾.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "yunadi" is the second object, and it was mentioned although it is understood from "munadiyan," for the purpose of emphasis and magnifying the matter of that to which one calls. The lam in "li-l-iman" is in the sense of "ila" (to). It has been said that "yunadi" is transitive with lam and with ila; one says "yunadi li-kadha" and "yunadi ila kadha." It has been said that the lam is for causation, i.e., for the sake of faith. His saying: "an amanu" (that believe) is either explanatory or verbal (masdariyyah), and its origin is "bi-an amanu," so the preposition was omitted.

His saying: ﴿So we believed﴾, i.e., we complied with what this caller commands of faith, so we believed. The repetition of the call in "Our Lord" is to show humility and submission. It has been said that what is meant by sins here are the major sins, and by misdeeds the minor ones. The apparent view is that neither word is restricted to one of the two matters, and the other to the other; rather the meaning of "sins" and "misdeeds" is one, and the repetition is for emphasis and affirmation, just as the meaning of "forgiveness" and "covering" is concealment. "Al-abrar" is the plural of "barr" or "bar," and its root is from expansiveness, as if the righteous one is expansive in obedience to Allah and His mercy is expansive for him. It has been said they are the Prophets, though the meaning of the word is broader than that.

His saying: ﴿Our Lord, and give us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾. This is another supplication, and the point in repeating the call is what preceded. What is promised upon the tongues of the messengers is the reward that Allah promised to the people of His obedience. So there is an omission in the speech, namely the word "tongues," as in His saying: ﴿and ask the town﴾ (Yusuf: 82). It has been said that what is omitted is "confirmation," i.e., what You promised upon confirming Your messengers; it has been said "what You promised sent down upon Your messengers" or "carried upon Your messengers," and the first is preferable.

That this supplication came from them, while they knew that what Allah promised them through the tongues of His messengers would certainly come to pass, is either for the purpose of hastening it or for humility in supplication, since it is the marrow of worship. In their saying: ﴿Indeed You do not break the promise﴾ is evidence that they did not fear the breaking of the promise, and that what moved them to supplicate is what we have mentioned.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Quraysh came to the Jews and said: What did Musa bring you of signs? They said: His staff and his hand, white for the onlookers. They came to the Christians and said: How was 'Isa among you? They said: He healed the blind and the leper and revived the dead. Then they came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: Ask your Lord to make Safa gold for us. So he prayed to his Lord, and ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ was revealed, the verse."

It is established in the two Sahihs and others, from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "I spent the night at the house of my maternal aunt Maymunah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) slept until midnight or a little before or after, then he woke up and began wiping the sleep from his face with his hands, then he recited the last ten verses of Surat Al 'Imran until he finished."

'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in the Zawa'id of the Musnad, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim in al-Kuna, and al-Baghawi in Mu'jam al-Sahabah narrated from Safwan ibn al-Mu'attal, who said: "I was with the Prophet (ﷺ) on a journey," and he mentioned something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani narrated through the route of Juwaybir from al-Dahhak from Ibn Mas'ud concerning His saying: ﴿Those who remember Allah standing, sitting, and on their sides﴾, the verse, that he said: "This is only concerning prayer: if one cannot pray standing, then sitting, and if one cannot sit, then on his side." It is established in al-Bukhari from the hadith of 'Imran ibn Husayn, who said: "I had hemorrhoids, so I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about prayer, and he said: Pray standing; if you cannot, then sitting; if you cannot, then on a side."

It is established in it from him as well, who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about a man's prayer while sitting, and he said: Whoever prays standing, it is better; whoever prays sitting has half the reward of the one who stands; and whoever prays lying down has half the reward of the one who sits."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah concerning the verse, that he said: "These are all your states, O son of Adam: remember Allah standing; if you cannot, remember Him sitting; if you cannot sit, remember Him on your side. It is ease from Allah and lightening."

I say: this restriction he mentioned, by inability, together with generalizing the remembrance, has no basis, neither from the verse nor from anything else, for nothing has come in the Book or the Sunnah indicating that remembrance from sitting is not permitted except when one is unable to remember standing, nor that lying on one's side is not permitted except when one is unable to do so sitting. This restriction is appropriate only for one who takes remembrance here to mean prayer, as preceded from Ibn Mas'ud.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Hibban in his Sahih, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'A'ishah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Woe to whoever recites this verse and does not reflect upon it."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya in al-Tafakkur narrated from Sufyan, raising it: "Whoever recites the end of Surat Al 'Imran and does not reflect upon it, woe to him," and he counted his fingers, ten. It was said to al-Awza'i: what is the limit of reflecting upon them? He said: that one recites them while understanding them. Hadiths and reports from the early generations have come concerning the recommendation of reflection in general.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Anas concerning His saying: ﴿whoever You admit to the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him﴾, that he said: "whoever You make eternal."

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib concerning the verse, that he said: "This is specific to those who will not come out of it."

Ibn Jarir and al-Hakim narrated from 'Amr ibn Dinar, who said: "Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah came to us on 'Umrah, and I reached him, I and 'Ata', and I said: ﴿Nor will they be out of the Fire﴾. He said: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) told me they are the disbelievers.' I said to Jabir: then His saying: ﴿whoever You admit to the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him﴾? He said: 'Does He disgrace him when He burns him with the Fire? Indeed, there is a disgrace short of that.'"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Juraij concerning His saying: ﴿a caller calling to faith﴾, that he said: "It is Muhammad (ﷺ)." Ibn Jarir narrated the like from Ibn Zayd.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, who said: "It is the Qur'an, not everyone who heard the Prophet (ﷺ)."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Juraij concerning His saying: ﴿Our Lord, and give us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾, that he said: "They seek the fulfilment of Allah's promise through His messengers."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿and do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection﴾, that he said: "Do not expose us."

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani narrated through the route of Juwaybir from al-Dahhak from Ibn Mas'ud concerning His saying: ﴿Those who remember Allah standing, sitting, and on their sides﴾, the verse, that he said: "This is only concerning prayer: if one cannot pray standing, then sitting, and if one cannot sit, then on his side." It is established in al-Bukhari from the hadith of 'Imran ibn Husayn, who said: "I had hemorrhoids, so I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about prayer, and he said: Pray standing; if you cannot, then sitting; if you cannot, then on a side."

It is established in it from him as well, who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about a man's prayer while sitting, and he said: Whoever prays standing, it is better; whoever prays sitting has half the reward of the one who stands; and whoever prays lying down has half the reward of the one who sits."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah concerning the verse, that he said: "These are all your states, O son of Adam: remember Allah standing; if you cannot, remember Him sitting; if you cannot sit, remember Him on your side. It is ease from Allah and lightening."

I say: this restriction he mentioned, by inability, together with generalizing the remembrance, has no basis, neither from the verse nor from anything else, for nothing has come in the Book or the Sunnah indicating that remembrance from sitting is not permitted except when one is unable to remember standing, nor that lying on one's side is not permitted except when one is unable to do so sitting. This restriction is appropriate only for one who takes remembrance here to mean prayer, as preceded from Ibn Mas'ud.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Hibban in his Sahih, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'A'ishah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Woe to whoever recites this verse and does not reflect upon it."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya in al-Tafakkur narrated from Sufyan, raising it: "Whoever recites the end of Surat Al 'Imran and does not reflect upon it, woe to him," and he counted his fingers, ten. It was said to al-Awza'i: what is the limit of reflecting upon them? He said: that one recites them while understanding them. Hadiths and reports from the early generations have come concerning the recommendation of reflection in general.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Anas concerning His saying: ﴿whoever You admit to the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him﴾, that he said: "whoever You make eternal."

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib concerning the verse, that he said: "This is specific to those who will not come out of it."

Ibn Jarir and al-Hakim narrated from 'Amr ibn Dinar, who said: "Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah came to us on 'Umrah, and I reached him, I and 'Ata', and I said: ﴿Nor will they be out of the Fire﴾. He said: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) told me they are the disbelievers.' I said to Jabir: then His saying: ﴿whoever You admit to the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him﴾? He said: 'Does He disgrace him when He burns him with the Fire? Indeed, there is a disgrace short of that.'"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Juraij concerning His saying: ﴿a caller calling to faith﴾, that he said: "It is Muhammad (ﷺ)." Ibn Jarir narrated the like from Ibn Zayd.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, who said: "It is the Qur'an, not everyone who heard the Prophet (ﷺ)."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Juraij concerning His saying: ﴿Our Lord, and give us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾, that he said: "They seek the fulfilment of Allah's promise through His messengers."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿and do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection﴾, that he said: "Do not expose us."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verses 190–194:

His saying: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens﴾. This is a resumed sentence (jumlah musta'nafah) to establish His exclusive authority over what He mentioned in it. What is meant is the very existence of the heavens and the earth and their attributes, ﴿and the alternation of the night and the day﴾, i.e., their succession, each one replacing the other, the increase of one of them at the expense of the other, and their variation in length and shortness, heat and cold, and other things. ﴿Are signs﴾, i.e., clear proofs and manifest evidences that point to the Creator, glorified is He.

The interpretation of some of what is here has already been given in Surat al-Baqarah. By ﴿ulil-albab﴾ (people of understanding) is meant those with sound intellects, pure of any defect, for mere reflection upon what Allah has related in this verse suffices the intelligent person and brings him to faith that is not shaken by doubts nor repelled by skeptical objections.

His saying: ﴿Those who remember Allah standing, sitting, and on their sides﴾. The relative pronoun is an attribute (na't) of ulil-albab. It has been said that it is separate from it, being the predicate of an omitted subject, or in the accusative as an expression of praise. What is meant by remembrance here is remembering Him, glorified is He, in these states, without distinction between the state of prayer and others.

A group of exegetes went to the view that remembrance here is a metaphor for prayer; i.e., they do not neglect it in any state, so they pray standing when there is no excuse, and sitting or on their sides when there is an excuse.

His saying: ﴿And they reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ is conjoined to His saying "they remember." It has been said that it is conjoined to the state, namely ﴿standing and sitting﴾. It has been said that it is disconnected from the first, and the meaning is: they reflect upon the wondrous making of both and their perfection, together with their great bodies, for this reflection, when sincere, leads them to faith in Allah, glorified is He.

His saying: ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾. It is on the assumption of a saying; i.e., they say: You did not create this in vain and frivolously, but You created it as evidence of Your wisdom and power. "Batil" means that which is passing and perishing, and from it is the saying of Labid:

Surely everything other than Allah is perishing (batil).

It is in the accusative as an attribute of an omitted verbal noun; i.e., a vain creation. It has been said that it is in the accusative by removal of the preposition. It has been said that it is a second object, with "khalaqa" meaning "ja'ala." Or it is in the accusative as a state. The demonstrative "this" refers to the heavens and the earth, or to the creation understood as the created thing.

His saying: ﴿Glory be to You﴾, i.e., exalting You above what is unbefitting You of matters, among which is that Your creation of these created things would be in vain. His saying: ﴿So protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾: the fa' indicates the sequence of this supplication upon what precedes it.

His saying: ﴿Our Lord, indeed whoever You admit to the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him﴾. This is an emphasis on what preceded of seeking protection from the Fire from Him, glorified is He, and an explanation of the reason for which His servants called upon Him to protect them from the punishment of the Fire: that whoever He admits into the Fire, He has disgraced, i.e., humiliated and abased. Al-Mufaddal said: the meaning of "akhzaytahu" is "ahlaktahu" (You destroyed him), and he recited:

Allah disgraced the Banu al-Salib, [and] 'Unayzah, and those who wear the garments of monks.

It has been said: its meaning is "fadahtahu" (You exposed him) and "ab'adtahu" (You distanced him). It is said: "akhzahu Allah" means He distanced him and abhorred him, and the noun is "khizy." Ibn al-Sikkit said: "khazia yakhzi khizyan" means when one falls into a calamity.

His saying: ﴿Our Lord, indeed we heard a caller calling to faith﴾. The caller, according to most exegetes, is the Prophet (ﷺ). It has been said he is the Qur'an. He attached the hearing to the caller although what is heard is the call, because he described the caller with what is heard, namely His saying: ﴿calling to faith, that believe﴾.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "yunadi" is the second object, and it was mentioned although it is understood from "munadiyan," for the purpose of emphasis and magnifying the matter of that to which one calls. The lam in "li-l-iman" is in the sense of "ila" (to). It has been said that "yunadi" is transitive with lam and with ila; one says "yunadi li-kadha" and "yunadi ila kadha." It has been said that the lam is for causation, i.e., for the sake of faith. His saying: "an amanu" (that believe) is either explanatory or verbal (masdariyyah), and its origin is "bi-an amanu," so the preposition was omitted.

His saying: ﴿So we believed﴾, i.e., we complied with what this caller commands of faith, so we believed. The repetition of the call in "Our Lord" is to show humility and submission. It has been said that what is meant by sins here are the major sins, and by misdeeds the minor ones. The apparent view is that neither word is restricted to one of the two matters, and the other to the other; rather the meaning of "sins" and "misdeeds" is one, and the repetition is for emphasis and affirmation, just as the meaning of "forgiveness" and "covering" is concealment. "Al-abrar" is the plural of "barr" or "bar," and its root is from expansiveness, as if the righteous one is expansive in obedience to Allah and His mercy is expansive for him. It has been said they are the Prophets, though the meaning of the word is broader than that.

His saying: ﴿Our Lord, and give us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾. This is another supplication, and the point in repeating the call is what preceded. What is promised upon the tongues of the messengers is the reward that Allah promised to the people of His obedience. So there is an omission in the speech, namely the word "tongues," as in His saying: ﴿and ask the town﴾ (Yusuf: 82). It has been said that what is omitted is "confirmation," i.e., what You promised upon confirming Your messengers; it has been said "what You promised sent down upon Your messengers" or "carried upon Your messengers," and the first is preferable.

That this supplication came from them, while they knew that what Allah promised them through the tongues of His messengers would certainly come to pass, is either for the purpose of hastening it or for humility in supplication, since it is the marrow of worship. In their saying: ﴿Indeed You do not break the promise﴾ is evidence that they did not fear the breaking of the promise, and that what moved them to supplicate is what we have mentioned.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Quraysh came to the Jews and said: What did Musa bring you of signs? They said: His staff and his hand, white for the onlookers. They came to the Christians and said: How was 'Isa among you? They said: He healed the blind and the leper and revived the dead. Then they came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: Ask your Lord to make Safa gold for us. So he prayed to his Lord, and ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ was revealed, the verse."

It is established in the two Sahihs and others, from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "I spent the night at the house of my maternal aunt Maymunah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) slept until midnight or a little before or after, then he woke up and began wiping the sleep from his face with his hands, then he recited the last ten verses of Surat Al 'Imran until he finished."

'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in the Zawa'id of the Musnad, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim in al-Kuna, and al-Baghawi in Mu'jam al-Sahabah narrated from Safwan ibn al-Mu'attal, who said: "I was with the Prophet (ﷺ) on a journey," and he mentioned something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani narrated through the route of Juwaybir from al-Dahhak from Ibn Mas'ud concerning His saying: ﴿Those who remember Allah standing, sitting, and on their sides﴾, the verse, that he said: "This is only concerning prayer: if one cannot pray standing, then sitting, and if one cannot sit, then on his side." It is established in al-Bukhari from the hadith of 'Imran ibn Husayn, who said: "I had hemorrhoids, so I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about prayer, and he said: Pray standing; if you cannot, then sitting; if you cannot, then on a side."

It is established in it from him as well, who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about a man's prayer while sitting, and he said: Whoever prays standing, it is better; whoever prays sitting has half the reward of the one who stands; and whoever prays lying down has half the reward of the one who sits."

It is ease from Allah and lightening."

I say: this restriction he mentioned, by inability, together with generalizing the remembrance, has no basis, neither from the verse nor from anything else, for nothing has come in the Book or the Sunnah indicating that remembrance from sitting is not permitted except when one is unable to remember standing, nor that lying on one's side is not permitted except when one is unable to do so sitting. This restriction is appropriate only for one who takes remembrance here to mean prayer, as preceded from Ibn Mas'ud.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Hibban in his Sahih, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'A'ishah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Woe to whoever recites this verse and does not reflect upon it."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya in al-Tafakkur narrated from Sufyan, raising it: "Whoever recites the end of Surat Al 'Imran and does not reflect upon it, woe to him," and he counted his fingers, ten. It was said to al-Awza'i: what is the limit of reflecting upon them? He said: that one recites them while understanding them. Hadiths and reports from the early generations have come concerning the recommendation of reflection in general.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Anas concerning His saying: ﴿whoever You admit to the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him﴾, that he said: "whoever You make eternal."

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib concerning the verse, that he said: "This is specific to those who will not come out of it."

Ibn Jarir and al-Hakim narrated from 'Amr ibn Dinar, who said: "Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah came to us on 'Umrah, and I reached him, I and 'Ata', and I said: ﴿Nor will they be out of the Fire﴾. He said: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) told me they are the disbelievers.' I said to Jabir: then His saying: ﴿whoever You admit to the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him﴾? He said: 'Does He disgrace him when He burns him with the Fire? Indeed, there is a disgrace short of that.'"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Juraij concerning His saying: ﴿a caller calling to faith﴾, that he said: "It is Muhammad (ﷺ)." Ibn Jarir narrated the like from Ibn Zayd.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, who said: "It is the Qur'an, not everyone who heard the Prophet (ﷺ)."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Juraij concerning His saying: ﴿Our Lord, and give us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾, that he said: "They seek the fulfilment of Allah's promise through His messengers."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿and do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection﴾, that he said: "Do not expose us."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verse 195:

His saying: "fa-istajaba" (﴿So their Lord answered them﴾). Al-istijaba (response) has the same meaning as al-ijaba (answer). It has been said that ijaba is general, while istijaba is specific to granting what is asked. This verb is transitive by itself and with the preposition lam: one says istajabahu and istajaba lahu. The fa is for conjunction (ʿatf). It has also been said that it is connected to a presumed element, meaning: they supplicated with these supplications, so He answered them. It has also been said that it is connected to His saying "wa-yatafakkarun" (and they reflect). Subhanahu mentioned the response and what follows it among the good qualities that they possess, because it comes from Him, for whoever's supplication is answered, his rank has been raised.

His saying: ﴿That I do not waste the work of any worker among you﴾, i.e., that I (do not waste). Isa ibn ʿAmr read it with a kasra on the hamza, on the basis of an implied saying. Ubayy read it with the ba' present, and it is causal (sababiyya), meaning: so their Lord answered them because He does not waste the work of any worker among them. By "waste" is meant withholding reward.

His saying: ﴿whether male or female﴾. The "min" here is explanatory (bayaniyya) and emphasizes the generality implied by the indefinite noun in a negative context. His saying: ﴿you are of one another﴾, i.e., your men are like your women in obedience, and your women are like your men in it. The clause is parenthetical, explaining that each of them is from the other, given that both branch from a single origin.

His saying: ﴿Those who emigrated﴾ and the rest of the verse. This sentence contains a detailed explanation of what was summarized in His saying: ﴿that I do not waste the work of any worker﴾. Meaning: those who emigrated from their homelands to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), ﴿and were driven out from their homes﴾ for the obedience of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and fought the enemies of Allah, and were killed in the way of Allah. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Amir read (wa-qutțilū) with intensive form (for multiplication). Al-Aʿmash, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read (wa-qatalū wa-qatalū) ... and this is like the saying of the poet:

"Tasaba wa-amsa ʿalahu al-kibar"

i.e., old age has overtaken him. The original function of the waw is to indicate general conjunction without order, as the majority hold. What is meant here is that they fought and some of them were killed, as Imru' al-Qays said:

"Fa-in taqtulūna nuqattil-kum"

ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz read (wa-qatalū wa-qutilū).

The meaning of His saying: ﴿and were harmed in My way﴾ is: because of Him. Al-sabil is the true religion, and what is meant here is the harm they suffered from the polytheists because of their faith in Allah and their acting according to what Allah prescribed for His servants. His saying: ﴿I will surely expiate from them their misdeeds﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath.

His saying: ﴿a reward from Allah﴾ is, according to the Basrans, an emphatic infinitive (maṣdar muʾakkad), because the meaning of His saying: ﴿and surely I will admit them into gardens﴾ is "I will surely reward them with a reward," i.e., a rewarding or a recompense, existing ﴿from Allah﴾. Al-Kisa'i said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥal).

Al-Farra' said: by way of explanation, ﴿and with Allah is the best reward﴾, i.e., the best recompense, which is what returns to the doer from the reward of his deed, from thāba yathūbu, meaning he returned.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, ʿAbd al-Razzaq, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and al-Hakim (who authenticated it) narrated from Umm Salama, who said: "O Messenger of Allah, I do not hear that Allah mentions women in the context of emigration with anything," so Allah revealed ﴿So their Lord answered them﴾ to the end of the verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from ʿAta', who said: "No servant says 'O Lord, O Lord, O Lord' three times except that Allah looks at him." This was mentioned to al-Hasan, who said: "Do you not read the Qur'an? ﴿Our Lord, we have indeed heard a caller calling to faith﴾ [Al ʿImran: 193] to His saying: ﴿So their Lord answered them.﴾"

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Umm Salama, who said: "The last verse revealed was this verse, ﴿So their Lord answered them﴾ to its end."

Many hadiths have been reported concerning the virtue of emigration.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verses 196–200:

His saying: ﴿Let not their movement about in the land deceive you﴾ is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the intended meaning is to keep him firm in what he is upon, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, believe﴾ [al-Nisa: 136]. It is also addressed to every person. This verse includes the ugliness of the state of the disbelievers after mentioning the goodness of the state of the believers. The meaning is: let not what they are engaged in of moving about in the lands, with journeys for trade by which they expand their livelihood, deceive you. It is a small enjoyment that they enjoy in this abode, then their destination is Hell. So His saying "mata' (a provision/enjoyment)" is the predicate of an omitted subject; that is, it is a small enjoyment, of no account in comparison with the reward of Allah, glory be to Him. (﴿And their refuge﴾) i.e., what they take refuge in.

"Taqallub fi al-bilad" (the movement about in the lands) is the agitation of journeys to places. Similar to it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So let not their movement about in the lands deceive you﴾ [Ghafir: 4]. "Mata'" (provision) is that whose benefit is quickly obtained, and He called it "small" because it is perishing, and everything perishing, even if it is abundant, is small. As for His saying: ﴿and wretched is the destination﴾, it refers to what they prepared for themselves in Hell through their disbelief, or what Allah prepared for them of the Fire. The object of the dispraise is omitted: it is this implied thing.

His saying: ﴿But those who fear their Lord﴾ is a istidrak (exception/contrast) from what preceded it, because its meaning is the meaning of negation, as if he said: they have no great benefit in their movement about in the lands; ﴿but those who fear﴾ have great benefit and everlasting eternity. Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa' read "lakinna" with the nun doubled.

His saying: "nuzulan" is a verbal noun of emphasis according to the Basrans, as was mentioned in "thawaban"; and according to al-Kisa'i and al-Farra', it is like what they said regarding "thawaban". "Nuzul" is what is prepared for the guest, and its plural is "anzal". Al-Harawi said: ﴿A provision from Allah﴾, i.e., a reward from Allah, and what is with Allah of what He has prepared for those who obey Him ﴿is better for the righteous﴾ than what the disbelievers obtain of profit in journeys, for that is a small enjoyment that soon passes away.

His saying: ﴿And indeed, among the People of the Book are those who believe in Allah﴾: this sentence is brought to explain that some of the People of the Book have a share of the religion, and they are not like the rest of them in their disgraceful acts which Allah related about them previously and will relate later. For this portion combine belief in Allah and in what Allah sent down to our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) and what He sent down to their prophets, being ﴿humbly submissive to Allah, not exchanging﴾, i.e., they do not take in exchange ﴿the Signs of Allah for a small price﴾ by distortion and alteration as the rest of them do; rather they transmit the Books of Allah, glory be to Him, as they are. The indication in His saying "Those" refers to this righteous group of the People of the Book, in respect of their being characterized by these praiseworthy attributes; for them is their reward which Allah, glory be to Him, promised with His saying: ﴿Those will be given their reward twice﴾. And the fronting of the predicate indicates that this reward is specific to them.

His saying: "ʿinda rabbihim" (with their Lord) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, be patient﴾, etc.

This is the tenth verse of His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164; Al ʿImran: 190]. He concluded this surah with it because of what it contains of the admonitions which gathered the good of this world and the Hereafter, so He urged patience upon obedience and upon restraining desires. Patience (al-sabr) is restraint, and its meaning has already been verified. Mutual patience (al-muṣābara) is patience against enemies, as the majority said; i.e., outdo them in patience during hardships and in war. He singled out "muṣābara" for mention after mentioning "ṣabr" because it is stronger and more difficult than it.

It was said: the meaning is "be patient over the prayers." It was said: "be patient against the self's desires." It was said: "be patient over the promise you were given and do not despair." The first opinion is the Arabic meaning, and from it is the saying of ʿAntara:

*Then I have not seen a living people who endure as we endure, nor who confront as those we confront.*

That is: they endured the enemy in war. His saying: "wa-rabiṭū" means: stay at the frontiers, stationing your horses there as your enemies station theirs; and this is the saying of the majority of the exegetes. Abu Salama ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman said: this verse concerns waiting for prayer after prayer, and there was no campaign during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in which one would be stationed (rabāṭ), and the mention of those who departed from this will come later. The linguistic meaning of ribāṭ is the first, and it does not conflict with the Prophet (ﷺ) calling other things ribāṭ, as will come. It is possible to apply ribāṭ to the first meaning and to waiting for prayer.

Al-Khalil said: ribāṭ is the constant presence at the frontiers and persistence in prayer, thus he said, and he is among the imams of the language. Ibn Faris related from al-Shaybani that he said: it is said, "water that is mutaraabit (constant), never departing," and this requires extending ribāṭ to other than the stationing of horses at the frontiers.

His saying: ﴿And fear Allah, that you may be successful﴾, i.e., that you may be among those who attain every sought goal; and they are the successful ones. ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from ʿIkrima concerning His saying: ﴿Let not the movement of those who disbelieve deceive you﴾: the movement of their night and day and what flows upon them of blessings. ʿIkrima said: Ibn ʿAbbas said, ﴿and wretched is the resting-place﴾; i.e., wretched is the dwelling.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi concerning His saying: ﴿their movement about in the lands﴾, he said: their striking about in the lands (i.e., travel). ʿAbd ibn Humayd and al-Bukhari in al-Adab al-Mufrad and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿUmar concerning His saying: ﴿And what is with Allah is better for the righteous﴾, he said: Allah only named them "righteous" because they were dutiful to fathers and sons, just as your father has a right over you, so your son has a right over you.

Ibn Mardawayh related it from him as a marfuʿ (attributed to the Prophet) report, but the first is more authentic, as al-Suyuti said. Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Zayd: ﴿better for the righteous﴾ means for whoever obeys Allah.

al-Nasa'i, al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Anas who said: "When al-Najashi died, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: Pray over him. This is the tenth verse of His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164; Al ʿImran: 190]. He concluded this surah with it because of what it contains of the admonitions which gathered the good of this world and the Hereafter, so He urged patience upon obedience and upon restraining desires. *Then I have not seen a living people who endure as we endure, nor who confront as those we confront.*

That is: they endured the enemy in war. His saying: "wa-rabiṭū" means: stay at the frontiers, stationing your horses there as your enemies station theirs; and this is the saying of the majority of the exegetes. Abu Salama ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman said: this verse concerns waiting for prayer after prayer, and there was no campaign during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in which one would be stationed (rabāṭ), and the mention of those who departed from this will come later. It is possible to apply ribāṭ to the first meaning and to waiting for prayer.

Al-Khalil said: ribāṭ is the constant presence at the frontiers and persistence in prayer, thus he said, and he is among the imams of the language. Ibn Faris related from al-Shaybani that he said: it is said, "water that is mutaraabit (constant), never departing," and this requires extending ribāṭ to other than the stationing of horses at the frontiers.

His saying: ﴿And fear Allah, that you may be successful﴾, i.e., that you may be among those who attain every sought goal; and they are the successful ones. ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from ʿIkrima concerning His saying: ﴿Let not the movement of those who disbelieve deceive you﴾: the movement of their night and day and what flows upon them of blessings. ʿIkrima said: Ibn ʿAbbas said, ﴿and wretched is the resting-place﴾; i.e., wretched is the dwelling.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 3, verses 196–200:

His saying: ﴿Let not their movement about in the land deceive you﴾ is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the intended meaning is to keep him firm in what he is upon, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, believe﴾ [al-Nisa: 136]. It is also addressed to every person. This verse includes the ugliness of the state of the disbelievers after mentioning the goodness of the state of the believers. The meaning is: let not what they are engaged in of moving about in the lands, with journeys for trade by which they expand their livelihood, deceive you. It is a small enjoyment that they enjoy in this abode, then their destination is Hell. So His saying "mata' (a provision/enjoyment)" is the predicate of an omitted subject; that is, it is a small enjoyment, of no account in comparison with the reward of Allah, glory be to Him. (﴿And their refuge﴾) i.e., what they take refuge in.

"Taqallub fi al-bilad" (the movement about in the lands) is the agitation of journeys to places. Similar to it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So let not their movement about in the lands deceive you﴾ [Ghafir: 4]. "Mata'" (provision) is that whose benefit is quickly obtained, and He called it "small" because it is perishing, and everything perishing, even if it is abundant, is small. As for His saying: ﴿and wretched is the destination﴾, it refers to what they prepared for themselves in Hell through their disbelief, or what Allah prepared for them of the Fire. The object of the dispraise is omitted: it is this implied thing.

His saying: ﴿But those who fear their Lord﴾ is a istidrak (exception/contrast) from what preceded it, because its meaning is the meaning of negation, as if he said: they have no great benefit in their movement about in the lands; ﴿but those who fear﴾ have great benefit and everlasting eternity. Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa' read "lakinna" with the nun doubled.

His saying: "nuzulan" is a verbal noun of emphasis according to the Basrans, as was mentioned in "thawaban"; and according to al-Kisa'i and al-Farra', it is like what they said regarding "thawaban". "Nuzul" is what is prepared for the guest, and its plural is "anzal". Al-Harawi said: ﴿A provision from Allah﴾, i.e., a reward from Allah, and what is with Allah of what He has prepared for those who obey Him ﴿is better for the righteous﴾ than what the disbelievers obtain of profit in journeys, for that is a small enjoyment that soon passes away.
